content:
Euclid’s algorithm is almost two and a half millennia old. The instruction that limits it is much younger.
For nonnegative integers $a$ and $b$, the greatest common divisor satisfies
$$ \gcd(a,b)= \begin{cases} a, & b=0,\ \gcd(b,a\bmod b), & b>0. \end{cases} $$
The remainder does not change the common divisors because
$$ a\bmod b=a-\left\lfloor\frac ab\right\rfloor b. $$
This gives the familiar loop:
#include <cstdint>#include <utility> uint64_t euclid(uint64_t a, uint64_t b) { while (b != 0) { a %= b; std::swap(a, b); } return a; } Its number of iterations is logarithmic; consecutive Fibonacci numbers produce the worst remainder sequence. On a word-RAM model, the algorithm is excellent. On a real core, every iteration depends on an integer division from the preceding one. A 64-bit divide can have latency in the tens of cycles and limited throughput, leaving little independent work to overlap.
The first optimization question is therefore not “how do we unroll Euclid?” It is “can we preserve the invariant without division?”
 #Stein’s IdentitiesThe binary GCD algorithm, often called Stein’s algorithm, uses shifts and subtraction. It follows from four identities:
$$ \begin{aligned} \gcd(0,b)&=b,\ \gcd(2a,2b)&=2\gcd(a,b),\ \gcd(2a,b)&=\gcd(a,b) && \text{when $b$ is odd},\ \gcd(a,b)&=\gcd(a,b-a) && \text{when $0<a\le b$}. \end{aligned} $$
The last identity is Euclid with a deliberately small quotient. By itself that would be slow, but after removing powers of two, both values are odd. Their difference is even, so the next shift makes substantial progress.
Factor out all powers of two shared by the original inputs. Then keep one operand odd, strip every factor of two from the other, subtract the smaller odd value from the larger, and repeat.
 #Counting Zeros in One InstructionDividing an unsigned integer by its largest power-of-two factor means shifting by the number of trailing zero bits. C++20 exposes this operation as std::countr_zero; x86 commonly implements it with tzcnt when BMI1 is available or an equivalent sequence on older targets.
Unlike compiler built-ins such as __builtin_ctz, the standard function has a defined result for zero. Shifting a word by its full width is still undefined, however, so the algorithm checks for zero before using the count as a shift amount.
#include <algorithm>#include <bit>#include <concepts> template<std::unsigned_integral T> T binary_gcd(T a, T b) { if (a == 0) return b; if (b == 0) return a; // a | b is nonzero. These are exactly the factors of two  // present in both original operands.  const unsigned common = unsigned(std::countr_zero(a | b)); // Keep a odd throughout the loop.  a >>= std::countr_zero(a); while (b != 0) { b >>= std::countr_zero(b); const T lo = std::min(a, b); const T hi = std::max(a, b); a = lo; b = hi - lo; } return a << common; } The subtraction cannot underflow because hi >= lo. When the values are equal it produces zero, and the loop terminates before asking for another shift. The final left shift reconstructs the common power of two; the mathematical gcd fits in T, and unsigned shifting has defined modulo semantics in any case.
Restricting the template to unsigned types avoids three unrelated hazards:
 std::abs(INT_MIN) is not representable as a signed int; signed overflow is undefined in C++; the meaning of a right shift of a negative value is not the arithmetic operation used in the proof.  An interface accepting signed integers can convert their magnitudes carefully, as std::gcd does. That conversion is part of the interface, not part of the binary algorithm.
 #The InvariantLet $s$ be the saved common power of two. At loop entry, a is odd and
$$ 2^s\gcd(a,b) $$
equals the gcd of the original inputs.
Removing trailing zeros from b is valid because a is odd: no factor of two can be common. Afterward both values are odd. Replacing them with
$$ \min(a,b) \quad\text{and}\quad |a-b| $$
preserves every common divisor, and the difference is even unless it is zero. Assigning the minimum to a keeps a odd for the next iteration. When b reaches zero, a is the remaining odd gcd; multiplying by $2^s$ restores the answer.
This proof also explains every precondition in the code. Moving countr_zero(b) below the subtraction without checking equality would call a compiler built-in on zero in many older versions of this routine—a tiny ordering change that converts a correct algorithm into undefined behavior.
 #What the Core ExecutesThe hot loop contains:
 a trailing-zero count and variable shift; a comparison with a min/max selection; one subtraction; the loop branch.  The iterations still form a dependency chain, but no general division remains. Compilers often lower min and max to conditional moves, although instruction selection depends on the target and surrounding code. Inspect the generated assembly before reasoning from source operators.
Binary GCD is not automatically faster everywhere. Some standard libraries already use it; small operand widths may have cheaper division; and a processor can execute division differently from the machine used in an old benchmark. The input distribution also changes the iteration count. Measure the implementation you will deploy.
 #Inputs MatterA useful benchmark includes several families:
 uniformly distributed word-sized pairs; pairs with large shared powers of two; equal values and zeros; coprime consecutive Fibonacci numbers for Euclid; pairs with a deliberately large gcd; small values embedded in a wider type.  Generate inputs outside the timed region, retain a checksum so calls cannot be deleted, and compare every result with std::gcd. If one fixed pair is repeated, the branch predictor and compiler may learn a workload unlike the intended one.
For a stronger correctness test, exhaust all pairs of 12-bit values and fuzz full-width pairs. Boundary cases are disproportionately valuable: zero, equality, and the top bit are exactly where unsafe bit operations tend to fail.
 #Related ProblemsThe extended Euclidean algorithm also computes Bézout coefficients. A binary extended GCD exists, but tracking coefficients while avoiding overflow is more involved; replacing division there is not a drop-in change.
For multiprecision integers, the balance changes again. Subtracting nearly equal numbers one limb at a time can require many iterations, while Lehmer’s and half-GCD algorithms use leading limbs to batch several Euclidean quotients. Optimizing a word-sized primitive and optimizing a thousand-bit integer are different problems even when both functions are named gcd.
Binary GCD is a compact demonstration of performance engineering at its best: an expensive instruction is not replaced by a clever encoding of the same instruction, but by a different mathematical decomposition whose primitives match the hardware.
 #Further Reading Josef Stein’s 1967 description appears in Computational Problems Associated with Racah Algebra. Brent and Zimmermann’s Modern Computer Arithmetic compares Euclidean, binary, Lehmer, and half-GCD methods across operand sizes. WG21 P0553R4 specifies the C++20 bit-operation interface used above.
title: Binary GCD

content:
Binary search is short enough to memorize and subtle enough to keep producing bugs. Performance work magnifies both properties: removing one branch is useful only if the replacement still handles an empty range, duplicate keys, and the past-the-end answer.
This chapter keeps one contract throughout. Given a sorted array a and a key x, lower_bound returns the first index i such that a[i] is not less than x. The answer belongs to the half-open set $[0,n+1)$: it is n when no such element exists, including when $n=0$.
 #A Half-Open SearchThe clean reference implementation maintains a half-open candidate interval. first is its beginning and count is its length:
#include <algorithm>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <functional>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> template <class T, class U, class Less = std::less<>> std::size_t lower_bound_index(std::span<const T> values, const U& key, Less less = {}) { std::size_t first = 0; std::size_t count = values.size(); while (count != 0) { const std::size_t step = count / 2; const std::size_t middle = first + step; if (less(values[middle], key)) { first = middle + 1; count -= step + 1; } else { count = step; } } return first; } std::size_t branchless_lower_bound_index( std::span<const std::int64_t> values, std::int64_t key ) { if (values.empty()) return 0; std::size_t base = 0; std::size_t length = values.size(); while (length > 1) { const std::size_t half = length / 2; const bool move_right = values[base + half - 1] < key; base += static_cast<std::size_t>(move_right) * half; length -= half; } return base + static_cast<std::size_t>(values[base] < key); } The reference version never forms n - 1, so an empty range needs no special representation. The midpoint first + count / 2 cannot overflow because both terms describe positions inside the original span. Duplicate values go left, which is precisely what distinguishes lower_bound from upper_bound.
The second function uses a less conventional invariant. Each iteration keeps the leftmost surviving candidate at base and rounds the remaining length upward. The final comparison is essential: it turns the last element into the past-the-end index when every value is less than the key. Omitting it is a common way to make a fast search that cannot represent n.
The multiplication by a Boolean expresses predication, but C++ does not promise a conditional move. A compiler may still emit a branch, and whether that is faster depends on the target and query distribution. Inspect the generated code and measure it; source code is not a pipeline diagram. The relevant mechanisms are covered in branchless programming and branch prediction.
 #The Dependency ChainFor uniformly distributed independent queries, the left/right decision is difficult to predict. A branch miss can then dominate searches whose working set is resident in cache. Once the array is large, another dependency becomes more important: the next address is unknown until the current key arrives and the comparison finishes.
This is why binary search exposes latency rather than bandwidth. It reads only $O(\log n)$ values, but those reads are mostly serial. Speculation sometimes helps a branchy implementation by issuing a load down the predicted path. A branchless implementation removes the misprediction and may also remove that accidental prefetch.
The access probabilities are far from uniform. The first midpoint is read by every query, its two children by roughly half the queries each, and the leaves only rarely. A sorted array stores these hot and cold keys beside one another:
 Binary search repeatedly jumps between shrinking intervals  The final few probes have useful spatial locality, while the first levels have useful temporal locality. A layout optimized for one usually sacrifices some of the other.
 #Eytzinger LayoutThe Eytzinger layout stores the comparison tree in breadth-first order. With one-based indices, the root is 1 and the children of node k are 2k and 2k+1:
 A sorted sequence arranged in Eytzinger order  Breadth-first storage puts the frequently accessed upper levels together. It also places all descendants exactly $d$ levels below node k in the contiguous interval
$$ [2^d k,;2^d k+2^d). $$
That interval is the reason software prefetching becomes attractive: one cache-line request can cover several possible future paths.
 #Construction and SearchAn in-order traversal of the implicit tree consumes the sorted input from left to right. The reference implementation below stores the original rank beside every node. Remembering the best node seen during the descent is less clever than recovering it from trailing bits, but it handles every size without a sentinel or an overflowing child index.
class eytzinger_index { public: explicit eytzinger_index( std::span<const std::int64_t> sorted_values ) : size_(sorted_values.size()) { if (!std::is_sorted(sorted_values.begin(), sorted_values.end())) throw std::invalid_argument("input must be sorted"); if (size_ == std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max()) throw std::length_error("index size overflow"); tree_.resize(size_ + 1); rank_.resize(size_ + 1); std::size_t cursor = 0; build(1, sorted_values, cursor); if (cursor != size_) throw std::logic_error("Eytzinger construction failed"); } std::size_t lower_bound_index(std::int64_t key) const noexcept { std::size_t node = 1; std::size_t candidate = 0; while (node <= size_) { prefetch_descendants(node); const bool go_right = tree_[node] < key; if (!go_right) candidate = node; const std::size_t direction = static_cast<std::size_t>(go_right); if (node > (size_ - direction) / 2) break; node = node * 2 + direction; } return candidate == 0 ? size_ : rank_[candidate]; } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; } private: static constexpr std::size_t prefetch_distance = 16; void build(std::size_t node, std::span<const std::int64_t> sorted_values, std::size_t& cursor) { if (node > size_) return; if (node <= size_ / 2) build(node * 2, sorted_values, cursor); tree_[node] = sorted_values[cursor]; rank_[node] = cursor; ++cursor; if (node <= (size_ - 1) / 2) build(node * 2 + 1, sorted_values, cursor); } void prefetch_descendants(std::size_t node) const noexcept { #if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)  if (node <= size_ / prefetch_distance) { __builtin_prefetch( tree_.data() + node * prefetch_distance, 0, 1 ); } #else  static_cast<void>(node); #endif  } std::size_t size_; std::vector<std::int64_t> tree_; std::vector<std::size_t> rank_; }; The recursion depth is the tree height, $O(\log n)$, rather than $O(n)$. Both child calculations are guarded before multiplication, so even a theoretical span near SIZE_MAX cannot wrap an index. For $n=0$, construction performs no traversal and lookup returns zero.
The prefetch address is formed only when 16 * node <= n. A prefetch instruction may be non-faulting on a particular processor, but C++ still has to evaluate its address expression; forming an arbitrary pointer beyond the allocation is not a portable bounds check. The guarded version requests the first great-great-grandchild only when that element exists.
Prefetching four levels ahead is a hypothesis, not part of correctness. It spends bandwidth and cache capacity to overlap latency, and it can lose under concurrent memory traffic. Remove it, change the distance, and benchmark again for each target.
 #Padding, Sentinels, and AlignmentPadding a tree to a full final level gives every query the same number of iterations. The padding still needs a representation.
Using INT_MAX as “infinity” silently removes that value from the legal key domain. It also does not distinguish a real maximum key from a padded slot, and it says nothing useful for floating-point NaNs. Correct choices include:
 storing a validity bit or a count with every node; storing ranks and checking them against $n$; restricting the key domain explicitly and enforcing that restriction at construction.  The reference Eytzinger index needs none of these because it never reads a nonexistent node and returns an index rather than a magic key.
Alignment is similarly a contract rather than a cast. A cache-line-aligned base makes the $16$ four-byte descendants beginning at 16k occupy one aligned 64-byte line. If std::aligned_alloc is used, its byte count must be a multiple of the requested alignment and the result must be released with std::free. Round only after checking that bytes + alignment - 1 cannot overflow. C++ aligned operator new avoids the multiple-of-alignment size rule, but it must be paired with the matching aligned operator delete. A zero-length index should not depend on either allocator accepting a zero-byte request.
Alignment can reduce split-line loads; it does not make an invalid prefetch valid, guarantee a 64-byte cache line, or enable huge pages. Those are separate alignment, cache-line, and paging questions.
 #What to MeasureThere is no timeless “binary search is four times faster” result. At minimum, a useful experiment reports:
 processor, compiler, flags, integer width, and layout alignment; array sizes on both sides of each cache and TLB boundary; successful and unsuccessful queries, including duplicates and extreme keys; the query distribution, because it determines branch predictability and hot nodes; preprocessing time and extra memory for transformed layouts; independent-query throughput separately from dependency-chained latency; single-threaded results separately from bandwidth-contended runs.  Independent searches can overlap in the out-of-order core, so elapsed time divided by query count is reciprocal throughput, not single-query latency. To measure a dependency chain, derive query $i+1$ from result $i$; to measure service throughput, issue independent queries and say so.
Eytzinger order is one point in a larger design space that includes cache-line blocking, implicit B-trees, and van Emde Boas layouts. Khuong and Morin’s paper on array layouts for comparison-based searching analyzes several of them. The next chapter widens each comparison node so that one fetched block answers more than one binary decision.
title: Binary Search

content:
How long does it take to multiply two matrices?
The textbook answer begins by counting scalar operations. An $n\times n$ multiplication performs $n^3$ products and $n^2(n-1)$ additions, so its arithmetic work is $\Theta(n^3)$. This is correct, useful, and insufficient to predict elapsed time.
A compiler may fuse each multiply and add, issue several independent operations in one cycle, and apply one instruction to a vector of elements. The same program may spend most of its time waiting for noncontiguous memory rather than doing arithmetic. Reordering the loops leaves the textbook count unchanged while changing real performance by orders of magnitude.
Neither analysis is wrong. They answer questions in different cost models.
A Model Chooses What CountsA computation model defines primitive operations, their costs, and the resources an algorithm may use. The familiar word-RAM model imagines random access to machine words and charges constant cost for operations such as a word-sized addition, comparison, or memory access. An algorithm’s running time is then a function $T(n)$ of its input size.
This abstraction is powerful because it discards details that differ between machines while preserving the structure of many algorithms. Binary search performs $O(\log n)$ probes; comparison sorting needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons in the worst case; scanning an array needs $\Theta(n)$ reads. Those statements remain useful across decades of hardware.
The assumptions still have boundaries. A “word” must be large enough to address the input but not large enough to store an arbitrary answer. Arithmetic on thousand-bit integers is not constant time merely because + is one source-level operator. Random access is not constant time when one operand is in a register and another is on storage.
The right question is therefore not whether a model is realistic in every detail. It is whether the costs it hides can change the decision being made.
Asymptotic ComplexityExact operation counts are often less informative than their growth. Asymptotic notation keeps the dominant behavior and suppresses constant factors and lower-order terms:
$$ 4n^3-n^2=\Theta(n^3). $$
This lets us compare algorithms independently of one implementation. If $T_A(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$ and $T_B(n)=\Theta(n^2)$ under the same model, then $A$ eventually wins as $n$ grows, provided the hidden constants are fixed.
“Eventually” is doing real work in that sentence. The crossover may lie beyond the input range, memory capacity, or lifetime of the system. An asymptotically inferior algorithm can be the correct engineering choice for every input the application will see. Conversely, a better exponent is often the only optimization that continues to pay as the workload scales.
Asymptotic analysis is a filter, not a stopwatch. It rules out designs whose resource growth is unacceptable and gives a vocabulary for upper, lower, expected, and amortized bounds. It does not supply the constants or validate the model’s primitives.
The systematic study of time and space complexity took shape in the 1960s; Hartmanis and Stearns’ On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms is one foundational paper. Its lasting contribution is not a claim that every operation costs the same, but the idea that computational resources can be defined and reasoned about formally.
Why Source Operations Do Not Map to TimeAt the machine level, even “count every instruction and add its latency” is not a valid general timing model.
 An out-of-order superscalar core overlaps independent instructions; latency limits dependency chains, while reciprocal throughput limits streams of independent work. A branch may be nearly free when predicted and expensive when mispredicted. A load may hit a nearby cache or wait hundreds of core cycles for DRAM, and several misses may overlap. SIMD instructions perform the same operation across multiple elements but can introduce shuffle and tail costs. The compiler may remove, combine, reorder, or replace source operations when the language contract permits it. Frequency, contention, the operating system, and input-dependent control flow affect elapsed time without appearing in the abstract algorithm.  The number of cycles is not obtained by summing an instruction table. It is the schedule that emerges from dependencies, execution resources, and the memory system.
A Ladder of ModelsPerformance engineering uses several models at once, moving down the ladder only when a higher level stops predicting the outcome:
 Asymptotic work and space select a viable family of algorithms. Exact operation and byte counts expose constants relevant to the real input range. External-memory and cache models count transfers and locality rather than treating every access equally. Dependency and throughput models describe what one core can overlap. Measurement tests the complete implementation on the target workload and machine.  More detail is not automatically better. Modeling execution ports before checking that the algorithm is quadratic is wasted precision. Treating all memory accesses as equal after a profile shows cache misses dominate is too little precision.
The next sections develop this ladder. Modern hardware explains why automatic single-thread speedups slowed and parallel resources became central. Programming languages follows programs from source abstractions to executable kernels. Models of computation introduces alternatives that count the resources modern algorithms actually consume, and When to Optimize turns them into a workflow.
The guiding principle for the rest of the book is simple: choose the cheapest model that still distinguishes the alternatives. When two algorithms have the same Big-O, count bytes and dependencies. When a hardware model makes a prediction, measure it. When measurement disagrees, improve the model rather than decorating the code with more tricks.
title: Complexity Models

content:
People often pass through three mental models of floating-point arithmetic:
 Beginner programmers use it everywhere as if it was some magic unlimited-precision data type. Then they discover that 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 or some other quirk like that, freak out, start thinking that some random error term is added to every computation, and for many years avoid any real data types completely. Finally, they learn the IEEE 754 model, state an error budget, and use the representation where its contract fits.  Unfortunately, too many people are still at stage 2, breeding various misconceptions about floating-point arithmetic — thinking that it is fundamentally imprecise and unstable, and slower than integer arithmetic.
   Floating point is neither random nor universally unstable. Its basic operations and rounding modes are standardized, so computational error can be analyzed. Its performance relative to integer arithmetic depends on the operation and processor: addition and multiplication are often similarly cheap, while division, conversion, and exceptional values may behave very differently.
In fact, it is so reliable that some high-level programming languages, most notably JavaScript, use a binary64 value for their ordinary number type. Every integer from $-2^{53}$ through $2^{53}$ is exactly representable. Integer-valued operations remain exact only when their mathematical result is also representable: adding two large exact integers can leave this range, and products can require more than 53 significant bits.
One notable exception is when you need to perform bitwise operations with numbers, which floating-point units (the coprocessors responsible for operations on floating-point numbers) typically don’t support. In this case, they need to be converted to integers, which is so frequently used in JavaScript-enabled browsers that arm added a special “FJCVTZS” instruction that stands for “Floating-point Javascript Convert to Signed fixed-point, rounding toward Zero” and does what it says it does — converts real to integer the exact same way as JavaScript — which is an interesting example of the software-hardware feedback loop in action.
But unless you are a JavaScript developer who uses real types exclusively to emulate integer arithmetic, you probably need a more in-depth guide about floating-point arithmetic, so we are going to start with a broader subject.
 #Real Number RepresentationsIf you need to deal with real (non-integer) numbers, you have several options with varying applicability. Before jumping straight to floating-point numbers, which is what most of this article is about, we want to discuss the available alternatives and the motivation behind them — after all, people who avoid floating-point arithmetic do have a point.
 #Symbolic ExpressionsThe first and the most cumbersome approach is to store not the resulting values themselves but the algebraic expressions that produce them.
Here is a simple example. In some applications, such as computational geometry, apart from adding, subtracting and multiplying numbers, you also need to divide without rounding, producing a rational number, which can be exactly represented with a ratio of two integers:
struct r { int x, y; }; r operator+(r a, r b) { return {a.x * b.y + a.y * b.x, a.y * b.y}; } r operator*(r a, r b) { return {a.x * b.x, a.y * b.y}; } r operator/(r a, r b) { return {a.x * b.y, a.y * b.x}; } bool operator<(r a, r b) { return a.x * b.y < b.x * a.y; } // ...and so on, you get the idea This ratio can be made irreducible, which would even make this representation unique:
struct r { int x, y; r(int numerator, int denominator) : x(numerator), y(denominator) { assert(y != 0); if (y < 0) x = -x, y = -y; int g = std::gcd(x, y); x /= g; y /= g; } }; This is how computer algebra systems such as WolframAlpha and SageMath work: they operate solely on symbolic expressions and avoid evaluating anything as real values.
With this method, you get absolute precision, and it works well when you have a limited scope such as only supporting rational numbers. But this comes at a large computational cost because in general, you would need to somehow store the whole history of operations that led to the result and take it into account each time you perform a new operation — which quickly becomes unfeasible as the history grows.
 #Fixed-Point NumbersAnother approach is to stick to integers, but treat them as if they were multiplied by a fixed constant. This is essentially the same as changing units of measurement for more up-to-scale ones.
Because some values can’t be represented exactly, this makes computations imprecise: you need to round the results to nearest representable value.
This approach is commonly used in financial software, where you really need a straightforward way to manage rounding errors so that the final numbers add up. For example, NASDAQ uses $\frac{1}{10000}$-th of a dollar as its base unit in its stock listings, meaning that you get the precision of exactly 4 digits after comma in all transactions.
struct money { std::uint64_t v; // 1/10000th of a dollar }; std::string to_string(money x) { return std::format("${}.{:04}", x.v / 10000, x.v % 10000); } money operator*(money x, money y) { return {std::uint64_t((__uint128_t(x.v) * y.v) / 10000)}; } Apart from introducing rounding errors, a bigger problem is that they become useless when the scaling constant is misplaced. If the numbers you are working with are too large, then the internal integer value will overflow, and if the numbers are too small, they will be just rounded down to zero. Interestingly, the former case once became an issue on NASDAQ when the Berkshire Hathaway stock price approached $\frac{2^{32} - 1}{10000}$ = $429,496.7295 and could no longer fit in an unsigned 32-bit integer.
This problem makes fixed-point arithmetic fundamentally unsuitable for applications where you need to use both small and large numbers, for example, evaluating certain physics equations:
$$ E = m c^2 $$
In this particular one, $m$ may be on the order of the mass of a proton ($1.67 \cdot 10^{-27}$ kg) while $c$ is the speed of light ($3 \cdot 10^8$ m/s).
 #Floating-Point NumbersIn most numerical applications, we are mainly concerned with the relative error. We want the result of our computations to differ from the truth by no more than, say, $0.01\%$, and we don’t really care what that $0.01\%$ equates to in absolute units.
Floating-point numbers solve this by storing a certain number of the most significant digits and the order of magnitude of the number. More precisely, they are represented with an integer (called significand or mantissa) and scaled using an exponent of some fixed base — most commonly, 2 or 10. For example:
$$ 1.2345 = \underbrace{12345}\text{mantissa} \times {\underbrace{10}\text{base}!!!!} ^{\overbrace{-4}^\text{exponent}} $$
Computers operate on fixed-length binary words, so when designing a floating-point format for hardware, you’d want a fixed-length binary format where some bits are dedicated for the mantissa (for more precision) and some for the exponent (for more range).
This handmade float implementation hopefully conveys the idea:
// DIY floating-point number struct fp { int m; // mantissa  int e; // exponent }; This way we can represent numbers in the form $\pm \; m \times 2^e$ where both $m$ and $e$ are bounded and possibly negative integers — which would correspond to negative or small numbers respectively. The distribution of these numbers is very much non-uniform: there are roughly as many numbers in the $[0, 1)$ range as in the $[1, +\infty)$ range.
Note that these representations are not unique for some numbers. For example, number $1$ can be represented as
$$ 1 \times 2^0 = 2 \times 2^{-1} = 256 \times 2^{-8} $$
and in 28 other ways that don’t overflow the mantissa.
This can be problematic for some applications, such as comparisons or hashing. To fix this, we can normalize these representations using a certain convention. In decimal, the standard form is to always put the comma after the first digit (6.022e23), and for binary, we can do the same:
$$ 42 = 10101_2 = 1.0101_2 \times 2^5 $$
Notice that, following this rule, the first bit is always 1. It is redundant to store it explicitly, so we will just pretend that it’s there and only store the other bits, which correspond to some rational number in the $[0, 1)$ range. The set of representable numbers is now roughly
$$ { \pm ; (1 + m) \cdot 2^e ; | ; m = \frac{x}{2^{32}}, ; x \in [0, 2^{32}) } $$
Since $m$ is now a nonnegative value, we will now make it unsigned integer, and instead add a separate Boolean field for the sign of the number:
struct fp { bool s; // sign: "0" for "+", "1" for "-"  unsigned m; // mantissa  int e; // exponent }; Now, let’s try to implement some arithmetic operation — for example, multiplication — using our handmade floats. Using the new formula, the result should be:
$$ \begin{aligned} c &= a \cdot b \ &= (s_a \cdot (1 + m_a) \cdot 2^{e_a}) \cdot (s_b \cdot (1 + m_b) \cdot 2^{e_b}) \ &= s_a \cdot s_b \cdot (1 + m_a) \cdot (1 + m_b) \cdot 2^{e_a} \cdot 2^{e_b} \ &= \underbrace{s_a \cdot s_b}{s_c} \cdot (1 + \underbrace{m_a + m_b + m_a \cdot m_b}{m_c}) \cdot 2^{\overbrace{e_a + e_b}^{e_c}} \end{aligned} $$
The groupings now seem straightforward to calculate, but there are two nuances:
 The new mantissa is now in the $[0, 3)$ range. We need to check if it is larger than $1$ and normalize the representation, applying the following formula: $1 + m = (1 + 1) + (m - 1) = (1 + \frac{m - 1}{2}) \cdot 2$. The resulting number can be (and very likely is) not representable exactly due to the lack of precision. We need twice as many bits to account for the $m_a \cdot m_b$ term, and the best we can do here is to round it to the nearest representable number.  Since we need some extra bits to properly handle the mantissa overflow issue, we will reserve one bit from $m$ thus limiting it to $[0,2^{31})$ range.
fp operator*(fp a, fp b) { fp c; c.s = a.s ^ b.s; c.e = a.e + b.e; uint64_t x = a.m, y = b.m; // casting to wider types  uint64_t m = (x << 31) + (y << 31) + x * y; // 62- or 63-bit intermediate result  if (m & (1ULL << 62)) { // checking for overflow  m -= (1ULL << 62); // m -= 1;  m >>= 1; c.e++; } m += (1ULL << 30); // "rounding" by adding 0.5 to a value that will be floored next  c.m = m >> 31; return c; } Many applications that require higher levels of precision use software floating-point arithmetic in a similar fashion. But of course, you don’t want to execute a sequence of 10 or so instructions that this code compiles to each time you want to multiply two real numbers, so on modern CPUs, floating-point arithmetic is implemented in hardware — usually as separate coprocessors due to its complexity.
Modern x86 code normally performs scalar and vector floating-point arithmetic in SSE/AVX registers; the older x87 stack unit is still available for compatibility and extended precision. To make these operations work together predictably, some additional details of floating-point representation need to be clarified—which we will do in the next section.
title: Floating-Point Numbers

content:
As software engineers, we absolutely love building and using abstractions.
Just imagine how much stuff happens when you load a URL. You type something on a keyboard; key presses are somehow detected by the OS and get sent to the browser; browser parses the URL and asks the OS to make a network request; then comes DNS, routing, TCP, HTTP, and all the other OSI layers; browser parses HTML; JavaScript works its magic; some representation of a page gets sent over to GPU for rendering; image frames get sent to the monitor… and each of these steps probably involves doing dozens of more specific things in the process.
Abstractions help us in reducing all this complexity down to a single interface that describes what a certain module can do without fixing a concrete implementation. This provides double benefits:
 Engineers working on higher-level modules only need to know the (much smaller) interface. Engineers working on the module itself get the freedom to optimize and refactor its implementation as long as it complies with its contracts.  Hardware engineers love abstractions too. An abstraction of a CPU is called an instruction set architecture (ISA), and it defines how a computer should work from a programmer’s perspective. Similar to software interfaces, it gives computer engineers the ability to improve on existing CPU designs while also giving its users — us, programmers — the confidence that things that worked before won’t break on newer chips.
An ISA essentially defines how the hardware should interpret the machine language. Apart from instructions and their binary encodings, an ISA also defines the counts, sizes, and purposes of registers, the memory model, and the input/output model. Similar to software interfaces, ISAs can be extended too: in fact, they are often updated, mostly in a backward-compatible way, to add new and more specialized instructions that can improve performance.
 #RISC vs CISCHistorically, many incompatible ISAs competed. Today, x86-64 and AArch64 dominate general-purpose desktop, server, and mobile software, while RISC-V, Power, and several specialized instruction sets remain important. Arm Ltd. specifies and licenses the Arm architecture and also offers core designs; companies such as Apple, Ampere, and cloud providers build different processors that implement that interface. Intel and AMD are the principal vendors of contemporary x86-64 CPUs.
The labels RISC and CISC describe historical instruction-set philosophies rather than two precise classes of modern processors:
 A reduced instruction set traditionally favors regular encodings, explicit load/store operations, and a small set of broadly useful instructions. A complex instruction set traditionally permits variable-length encodings, memory operands, and instructions that perform several architectural steps.  The boundary has blurred. High-performance x86 cores decode instructions into simpler internal micro-operations, while AArch64 includes wide SIMD, cryptographic, matrix, and other specialized extensions. Either ISA can be implemented as a small in-order core or a large speculative out-of-order core. Power, area, and performance depend more on that microarchitecture, fabrication process, cache system, and workload than on the RISC/CISC label alone.
This book uses x86-64 for most assembly examples because its tools and intrinsics are widely available. The dependency, locality, and throughput arguments transfer to other ISAs; instruction encodings, registers, memory-ordering rules, and available vector operations do not.
title: Instruction Set Architectures

content:
Instrumentation means inserting timers, counters, or tracing hooks into a program. The simplest example is the Unix time utility, which measures a whole process without changing its source.
More often, we want to know which part of a program needs optimization. Profilers and tracing frameworks can instrument functions automatically, but a small experiment can use a monotonic clock directly:
#include <chrono>#include <cstdio> auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); do_something(); auto stop = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); double seconds = std::chrono::duration<double>(stop - start).count(); std::printf("do_something() took %.6f s\n", seconds); steady_clock is suitable for elapsed time because it does not run backward when the wall clock is adjusted. By contrast, the C clock() function measures processor time consumed by the process, not a current timestamp. Clock resolution and call overhead are implementation- and platform-dependent; a duration type displaying nanoseconds does not imply nanosecond measurement accuracy.
 #Measuring Short OperationsIf one operation is close to the clock’s overhead or resolution, invoke it many times, measure the whole batch, and divide:
#include <chrono>#include <cstdio> constexpr int N = 1'000'000; int main() { auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) do_something(); auto stop = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); double ns = std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(stop - start).count(); std::printf("%.2f ns per iteration\n", ns / N); } This only works if the loop still represents the operation of interest. The compiler may inline, combine, hoist, or remove work whose result is unused. Repetition can also warm caches and train predictors, changing the question from one-off latency to steady-state throughput. Benchmarking and Getting Accurate Results discuss these traps in detail.
Instrumentation itself perturbs a program. A timestamp can serialize or add calls; a counter adds memory traffic; tracing may allocate buffers. Measure the overhead with an empty or control path, and keep the instrumented boundary much larger than the timer when possible.
 #Event SamplingInstrumentation can collect algorithm-specific information that hardware counters cannot name. For example:
 for a hash function, the input-length distribution; for a binary tree, its size and observed search depth; for a sorting algorithm, the number of comparisons.  Updating a counter on every call may be too expensive. Sampling one invocation with probability $p$ reduces data volume, but calling a random-number generator for every decision can itself dominate a small function.
Repeated Bernoulli trials can instead be represented by a geometric distribution, which gives the number of failures before the next success. Draw one gap, decrement it cheaply on each call, and draw again only when a sample is taken:
#include <cstdint>#include <random> class GeometricSampler { std::mt19937_64 rng; std::geometric_distribution<int> gap; int remaining; public: GeometricSampler(double sample_rate, std::uint64_t seed) : rng(seed), gap(sample_rate), remaining(gap(rng)) {} bool sample() { if (remaining == 0) { remaining = gap(rng); return true; } --remaining; return false; } }; The sampler still needs engineering around it. Use separate state per thread or synchronize access, choose a reproducible seed when comparing runs, and account for the sampling probability when estimating totals. Sampling must also be independent of the property being measured; otherwise the estimate is biased no matter how elegant the distribution is.
Large systems frequently use techniques like this to collect low-rate telemetry from hot library paths. The goal is not zero overhead—it is controlled overhead with a known sampling process.
title: Instrumentation

content:
Assembly is the lowest-level interface to SIMD, but C and C++ programmers usually use intrinsics: compiler-provided functions and types that expose a particular instruction or a small instruction pattern. Intrinsics preserve register types and immediates while still letting the compiler allocate registers, schedule instructions, and fold memory operands.
This chapter uses x86 AVX2 for concrete examples. The algorithms often transfer to Arm NEON/SVE or another SIMD ISA, but the intrinsic names and some capabilities do not.
 #ISA and DispatchInclude <immintrin.h> for the Intel-style SSE, AVX, AVX2, and AVX-512 intrinsic declarations. Declaring an intrinsic does not make it safe to execute. The function containing it must be compiled for the required target, and the function must only run when both the CPU and operating system support the relevant state.
GCC and Clang can place one implementation behind a function-level target attribute and select it at runtime:
using AddFunction = void (*)(const double *, const double *, double *, std::size_t); void add_scalar(const double *a, const double *b, double *out, std::size_t n) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) out[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } __attribute__((target("avx2"))) void add_avx2(const double *a, const double *b, double *out, std::size_t n) { std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 4 <= n; i += 4) { const __m256d x = _mm256_loadu_pd(a + i); const __m256d y = _mm256_loadu_pd(b + i); _mm256_storeu_pd(out + i, _mm256_add_pd(x, y)); } for (; i < n; ++i) out[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } AddFunction select_add() { return __builtin_cpu_supports("avx2") ? add_avx2 : add_scalar; } The GCC x86 built-in documentation lists the accepted feature names and function-multiversioning facilities. A resolver used before normal runtime initialization has extra requirements such as __builtin_cpu_init; an ordinary call from main does not.
-march=native is convenient for a private benchmark because it targets the build machine. It is inappropriate for a redistributable binary unless that binary also has a lower baseline and dispatch. AVX-512 code must check every subset it uses—for example, AVX512F does not imply AVX512BW or AVX512VPOPCNTDQ.
 #Registers and TypesIn 64-bit mode, the architectural register view is:
 SSE exposes sixteen 128-bit registers, XMM0–XMM15; AVX exposes sixteen 256-bit registers, YMM0–YMM15, whose low halves are the XMM registers; AVX-512 exposes thirty-two 512-bit registers, ZMM0–ZMM31, and eight mask registers, k0–k7. For most masked vector instructions, k0 denotes the unmasked form, leaving k1–k7 as general write masks. The low parts of ZMM0–ZMM15 are the older YMM/XMM registers.  The 32-bit x86 ABI has fewer directly nameable vector registers, so register counts must always include the execution mode. AVX-512 is also a feature family rather than one indivisible extension.
Intrinsic vector types describe how an operation interprets the bits:
 __m128, __m128d, and __m128i hold 128 bits interpreted as floats, doubles, or integers; __m256, __m256d, and __m256i hold 256 bits; __m512, __m512d, and __m512i hold 512 bits.  An integer register has no persistent “element type”; _mm256_add_epi8 and _mm256_add_epi32 can consume the same 256 bits with different lane boundaries. Use cast intrinsics such as _mm256_castsi256_ps when only the interpretation changes. They generate no instruction. Numeric conversions such as _mm256_cvtepi32_ps do real work and are not casts.
 #Intrinsic NamesMost names resemble _mm<size>_<operation>_<element-type>. For example:
 _mm_add_epi16 adds eight packed 16-bit integers in two 128-bit operands; _mm256_sqrt_pd computes square roots of four packed doubles; _mm256_broadcast_sd broadcasts one double to four lanes; _mm256_ceil_pd rounds four doubles toward positive infinity; _mm256_cmpeq_epi32 compares eight pairs of 32-bit integers and returns all-one or all-zero lanes; _mm256_blendv_ps selects packed floats according to the sign bits of a mask.  There is no _mm256_acos_pd instruction or standard x86 intrinsic. Transcendental functions such as acos come from a vector math library or a compiler’s library-vectorization interface and generally expand to substantial algorithms.
Some operands are immediates encoded in the instruction, so their intrinsic arguments must be compile-time constants. Comparisons and shuffles expose many such modes. The authoritative searchable reference is Intel’s Intrinsics Guide, which also marks intrinsics that expand to more than one instruction.
 #What the Compiler May ChangeThe compiler preserves an intrinsic’s semantics, not a one-to-one textual assembly listing. The add loop above can become three assembly instructions because x86 arithmetic accepts one memory operand:
vmovupd ymm1, YMMWORD PTR [rdi + rax] vaddpd ymm0, ymm1, YMMWORD PTR [rsi + rax] vmovupd YMMWORD PTR [rdx + rax], ymm0 This is not a “fused vector addition.” It is one load instruction, an add with a memory source, and one store. The processor may still decode the memory-form add into separate load and arithmetic micro-operations. True arithmetic fusion is an operation such as fused multiply-add, which changes both the instruction and floating-point rounding behavior.
Likewise, a broadcast or extraction intrinsic may become a short sequence, and two neighboring intrinsics may combine. Always inspect the optimized assembly and measure on the target microarchitecture.
 #Bounds and PaddingThe vector loop uses i + 4 <= n, then handles the remainder scalarly. It never accesses outside [0,n), including for n < 4.
An alternative is to round the allocation up to four doubles and deliberately execute one final full vector. That is legal only if every load and store has four accessible elements: the input padding must be initialized if it is read, and the output allocation must also include the rounded capacity. Padding one array does not authorize an overread from another, and being on the same mapped page is irrelevant to the C++ object bound.
 #Compiler Vector ExtensionsGCC and Clang also support fixed-width vector types:
using v4si = int __attribute__((vector_size(16))); using v8si = int __attribute__((vector_size(32))); using v8sf = float __attribute__((vector_size(32))); v4si a = {1, 2, 3, 5}; v4si b = {8, 13, 21, 34}; v4si c = (a + b) * 2; They make elementwise arithmetic concise:
using v4d = double __attribute__((vector_size(32))); v4d add(v4d a, v4d b) { return a + b; } The syntax is a compiler extension, the width is fixed, and not every C++ operator has useful vector semantics. It is more readable than a long intrinsic expression but not architecture-independent by itself.
Interoperation requires a defined type on both sides. A same-size representation copy is safe and normally optimized away:
__attribute__((target("avx"))) int sign_mask(v8sf x) { __m256 raw; std::memcpy(&raw, &x, sizeof(raw)); return _mm256_movemask_ps(raw); } Portable SIMD libraries add ISA dispatch, scalable abstractions, and tested fallbacks. Notable C++ options include Highway, EVE, Vector Class Library, and xsimd. Intrinsics remain useful when an algorithm depends on a specific instruction or when profiling shows the abstraction missed an important lowering.
title: Intrinsics and Vector Types

content:
Between the CPU registers and RAM lies a hierarchy of caches. Levels nearer a core are usually smaller and quicker; levels farther away are larger and slower. Two different quantities are hidden inside the word “quick”:
 latency is the delay between issuing a request and receiving the value; bandwidth is the amount of data the system can transfer per unit of time once enough requests are in flight.  Bandwidth is often the binding resource for loops that perform little work per element. It is also relatively easy to expose: present the machine with a long stream of independent accesses and give it enough time to reach a steady state.
For a first experiment, create an array and increment every element $K$ times:
std::vector<std::uint32_t> a(N); for (std::size_t t = 0; t < K; ++t) for (std::uint32_t &x : a) ++x; The real benchmark consumes a checksum afterward; otherwise the compiler may remove or simplify the work. We vary $N$ and choose $K$ so that the number of useful element updates stays roughly constant:
 Dotted vertical lines mark the nominal cache capacities of the test machine  The transitions line up with the private and shared cache capacities on the test system. When the array is small, execution resources in the core dominate. Once the working set outgrows a cache level, moving dirty lines to and from the next level becomes increasingly important.
The vertical axis is useful updates per second, despite the historical “GFLOPS” label on some plots. An integer increment is not a floating-point operation, and an update is not a fixed amount of bus traffic. The first store miss to a line can have a very different cost from the next fifteen increments to the same resident line.
 #Frequency ScalingRe-running the experiment with boost enabled produced this graph on the Zen 2 test laptop:
 Historical measurements with and without boost on the test laptop  The cache-resident part sped up more than the DRAM-resident part. This is a useful pattern, but not a law that every cache property scales with the advertised core clock. A processor may clock its cores, last-level cache, interconnect, memory controller, and DRAM in different domains. Cache latency is often nearly constant in core cycles over part of the range, while DRAM has its own transfer clock and still incurs core-side overhead.
Control and report the frequency policy when comparing implementations. Pinning a nominal frequency also does not eliminate thermal limits, uncore frequency changes, or power-management effects; measure the effective clocks and repeat the run.
 #Directional AccessAn increment is a read-modify-write operation. To separate useful read and write throughput, we can also sum an array and fill an array:
std::uint64_t sum = 0; for (std::uint32_t x : a) sum += x; for (std::uint32_t &x : a) x = 0; Compilers readily vectorize both loops, and a zero fill may become memset. That transformation can itself select different implementations for different sizes, including streaming stores in an optimized C library, so a bandwidth experiment must inspect the final assembly rather than infer it from the source.
 Useful throughput of the three loops on the test machine  The curves are not simply “one bus direction” versus “two bus directions.” Ordinary stores to write-back memory normally use a write-allocate policy. If a line is not present with write permission, the core first obtains ownership of the whole line, commonly through a read-for-ownership request, modifies it locally, and eventually writes the dirty line back. A full-line store loop can therefore generate roughly one line fill and one line write-back even though the source never reads the old values.
An incrementing loop also obtains the line and writes it back. Once the line is resident, however, additional passes can update it without repeating both lower-level transfers. Report whether the measurement is a cold single pass, a warm repeated pass, or an average over both. Hardware counters for requested, filled, and written-back lines are more informative than multiplying the loop count by sizeof(a[0]).
Read and write traffic can still have different sustained rates. Reads occupy request-tracking resources until data returns. Writes can be buffered and combined, while DRAM buses must turn around between read and write bursts. The balance depends on the microarchitecture, memory controller, access pattern, and number of cores.
 #Streaming StoresFor a large, aligned output that will not be read soon, x86 provides non-temporal or streaming stores. They use write-combining resources and avoid the ordinary write-allocate path, reducing cache pollution and the read-for-ownership traffic of a cold full-line store.
Here are ordinary and streaming AVX2 stores, with a now denoting a separately allocated 32-byte-aligned std::uint32_t *:
const __m256i zeros = _mm256_setzero_si256(); for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 8 <= N; i += 8) _mm256_store_si256(reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(a + i), zeros); const __m256i zeros = _mm256_setzero_si256(); std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 8 <= N; i += 8) _mm256_stream_si256(reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(a + i), zeros); for (; i < N; ++i) a[i] = 0; _mm_sfence(); // include completion before stopping the timer or consuming the output For best results, streaming stores should cover complete cache lines with consecutive writes. Too-small or scattered streams may only add overhead, and evicting useful cached data is not the only possible cost: write-combining buffers are finite, and the fence needed at a synchronization boundary is observable.
 Historical cached-store and streaming-store measurements  On this machine, streaming stores substantially improved the large-array result because they avoided write allocation and combined adjacent writes efficiently. The exact ratio is not portable, and the apparent throughput can be exaggerated if the timer stops while stores are still buffered—which is why the final fence belongs inside the measured operation.
Do not assume that every memset or memcpy is a simple vector loop. Production libraries dispatch by size and ISA and may already use rep stos, rep movsb, cached vectors, or non-temporal stores. Likewise, _mm256_stream_load_si256 is not a general “uncached load”: on x86 its useful semantics depend on the memory type and processor. Treat cache-control instructions as platform-specific tools and benchmark the complete operation, including ordering and later reuse.
One core may also lack enough outstanding misses to reach the socket’s DRAM limit. We will separate this request-concurrency limit from aggregate bandwidth in Memory-Level Parallelism and Memory Sharing.
title: Memory Bandwidth

content:
No single storage technology simultaneously provides tiny latency, enormous capacity, persistence, low energy use, and low cost. Computer systems combine several technologies and keep active data near the processor while colder data remains farther away.
The words higher and lower are ambiguous here. Some authors call L1 “high” because it is at the top of a diagram; others call a storage tier “high” when it has greater capacity. This chapter avoids both terms. A level is either closer to the processor or farther from the processor. Among CPU caches, L1 is the closest, followed by L2 and then the last-level cache.
 A qualitative memory hierarchy; width suggests capacity, not a fixed scale  The triangle is conceptual. Its proportions and even its layers vary by machine. A small embedded system, a multisocket server, and a storage node do not share one universal hierarchy.
 #Comparing a BoundaryFor one adjacent pair of levels, the useful characteristics are:
 capacity: how much the closer level can retain; transfer unit: the minimum or efficient amount moved per request; latency: time until one requested value becomes usable; bandwidth: sustained transfer rate for a stream of requests; concurrency: how many requests can make progress together; volatility and durability: what survives power loss and which flush protocol is required; management: whether placement is controlled by hardware, the operating system, a runtime, or the application.  These characteristics do not collapse to one speed number. A farther level may deliver excellent aggregate bandwidth when many requests are outstanding while still responding slowly to one dependent request. A closer cache may have low hit latency but limited associativity, so an unfortunate address pattern repeatedly evicts useful lines.
Block size is also a property of the boundary, not a property of the data. CPU caches transfer cache lines. Virtual memory maps pages. Storage devices and file systems may expose sectors, pages, extents, and request-size preferences at different interfaces. An algorithm’s effective block size $B$ should describe the transfers it actually causes at the boundary being modeled.
 #Registers and CPU CachesRegisters are named by an instruction set and allocated by the compiler or assembly programmer. They are not “zero-time memory”: instructions have latency and throughput, the register file has a finite number of ports, and values that do not fit may be spilled to memory. Different register classes may hold scalar, vector, floating-point, or control state.
CPU caches retain recently fetched instructions and data in cache lines. Current general-purpose CPUs commonly have private per-core caches close to each core and a larger cache shared by some or all cores, but sizes, line widths, inclusion policies, and topology are platform properties that software should query or measure when they matter.
Cache replacement is automatic and generally only approximates textbook LRU. Hardware prefetchers may fetch lines before demand, and coherence protocols move or invalidate lines when cores share writable data. Programmers influence this system indirectly through layout, traversal order, working-set size, and occasionally platform-specific prefetch or cache-management instructions. The CPU cache chapter examines those mechanisms in detail.
 #DRAM and NUMAMain memory is normally volatile DRAM. The memory controller groups requests across channels, banks, rows, and ranks, so “random access” does not mean every address has identical timing. Sequential access makes cache-line transfer and prefetch effective; enough independent misses can exploit memory-level parallelism.
On a non-uniform memory access machine, physical memory is attached more closely to some processors than others. A virtual address remains valid from every participating processor, but local and remote accesses can have different latency and bandwidth. Placement depends on the operating system, allocation policy, and often which thread first touches a page. The Linux kernel, for example, documents explicit NUMA memory policies; other systems expose different controls.
DRAM is not a persistent file store. Power-failure protection, error correction, and persistence semantics are separate properties and vary by platform. Likewise, allocating virtual address space does not prove that an equal amount of DRAM has been committed or made resident; virtual memory mediates that relationship.
 #Persistent Local StorageSolid-state drives and hard disk drives both retain data without ordinary power, but their internal mechanics differ.
An SSD maps logical block addresses onto flash through a controller. Flash is programmed and erased at different granularities, so the controller performs address translation, garbage collection, wear management, caching, and error correction. Queueing several independent requests can expose device parallelism. Write latency and endurance depend on the drive, workload, free space, and durability mode; a single universal figure would be misleading.
An HDD moves a head across rotating media. Seeking to a distant track and waiting for rotation makes scattered requests expensive, while a long contiguous transfer amortizes that motion. File layout and request order therefore matter strongly. This mechanical distinction remains relevant even when an operating system hides it behind the same file API used for SSDs.
A completed application write may still reside in a language buffer, kernel page cache, device cache, or storage controller. Persistence requires the synchronization protocol promised by the relevant API and device. Closing or unmapping memory is not, by itself, a portable durability boundary.
 #Remote Storage Is Another HierarchyNetwork file systems, distributed databases, and object stores add protocol processing, serialization, queues, retries, and partial failure. Their natural transfer unit may be an object or range rather than a hardware block. A request can be delayed because of congestion or a remote service, and retrying a non-idempotent operation can change semantics.
Remote systems may trade latency for replication, availability, geographic durability, or elastic capacity. Those are system properties, not reasons to write infinity symbols in a capacity or bandwidth table. Limits, pricing, consistency, and performance are service-specific and change over time.
 #Choosing “Internal” and “External”The external-memory model needs only one boundary at a time. For an L1 analysis, the internal memory is L1 and the external level is everything beyond it. For an out-of-core sort, internal memory is a bounded RAM budget and external memory is a file. For a distributed shuffle, each worker’s local storage may be internal relative to the network.
This relative definition is more useful than classifying a device forever. State the boundary, measure or justify its effective $M$ and $B$, and then count the transfers that cross it. The same algorithm can be analyzed again at another boundary when a different layer becomes the bottleneck.
title: Memory Hierarchy

content:
The main disadvantage of the supercomputers of the 1960s wasn’t that they were slow — relatively speaking, they weren’t — but that they were giant, complex to use, and so expensive that only the governments of the world superpowers could afford them. Their size was the reason they were so expensive: they required a lot of custom components that had to be very carefully assembled in the macro-world, by people holding advanced degrees in electrical engineering, in a process that couldn’t be scaled up for mass production.
The turning point was the development of integrated circuits: complete circuits manufactured together on a small piece of silicon. The MOS Technology 6502, introduced in 1975 at a famously disruptive $25 price, placed a complete processor on a die of roughly 4 mm × 4 mm1. Falling cost and size helped start the home-computer revolution, with systems such as the Apple II, Atari 2600, Commodore 64, and IBM PC reaching a much wider market.
 #How Microchips are MadeMicrochips are “printed” on a slice of crystalline silicon using a process called photolithography, which involves
 growing and slicing a very pure silicon crystal, covering it with a layer of a substance that dissolves when photons hit it, hitting it with photons in a set pattern, chemically etching the now-exposed parts, removing the remaining photoresist,  …and repeating deposition, patterning, implantation, and interconnect steps across many layers. A modern fabrication flow contains far more operations than this sketch and can take months from wafer start to packaged chip.
   Consider now the exposure step. Projection optics reduce a mask pattern onto the wafer. Resolution depends on wavelength, numerical aperture, photoresist, process control, and increasingly computational techniques such as multiple patterning—not simply on making a lens “stronger.” Even early processes could place thousands of transistors in an area smaller than a fingernail, giving integrated circuits several advantages over assemblies of discrete components:
 higher clock rates (that were previously limited by the speed of light); the ability to scale the production; much lower material and power usage, translating to much lower cost per unit.  Apart from these immediate benefits, lithographic manufacturing created a repeatable path to denser circuits. Each generation still required substantial changes in devices, materials, design rules, and fabrication equipment; optical scaling was never a free source-code-compatible shrink.
 #Dennard ScalingConsider what happens when we scale a microchip down. A smaller circuit requires proportionally fewer materials, and smaller transistors take less time to switch (along with all other physical processes in the chip), allowing reducing the voltage and increasing the clock rate.
An idealized constant-field scaling argument, commonly called Dennard scaling, says that reducing transistor dimensions by 30%
 doubles the transistor density ($0.7^2 \approx 0.5$), increases the clock speed by 40% ($\frac{1}{0.7} \approx 1.4$), and leaves the overall power density the same.  Under that model, each generation offers more transistors and a higher clock without increasing power density. Real manufacturing cost, yield, leakage, interconnect, packaging, and design effort complicate the picture, but the model explains why several decades of shrinking transistors also brought large automatic speedups.
Due to the trade-offs between energy and performance you can make during the design, the fidelity of the fabrication process itself, such as “180nm” or “65nm,” directly translating to the density of transistors, became the trademark for CPU efficiency2.
For much of computing history, scaling was a main driver of performance improvements. Gordon Moore predicted that economically useful component counts would grow exponentially; the commonly quoted later cadence is a doubling about every two years. The trend remained a useful industry guide for decades, although its pace, cost, and even the appropriate density metric now vary.
   Both Dennard scaling and Moore’s law are not actual laws of physics, but just observations made by savvy engineers. They are both destined to stop at some point due to fundamental physical limitations, the ultimate one being the size of silicon atoms. In fact, Dennard scaling already did — due to power issues.
Nearly all electrical energy consumed by a processor eventually becomes heat. That heat must be removed through a package and cooling system, placing a practical limit on chip power density. Voltage, frequency, active units, leakage, and cooling are traded against one another; there is no single maximum clock chosen independently of the workload.
Around 2005–2007, this strategy stopped working because voltage could no longer be reduced in proportion to transistor dimensions. Lower threshold voltages make transistors switch quickly, but also increase subthreshold leakage; very thin gate oxides additionally allow electrons to tunnel through them. Interconnect resistance and delay were becoming important at the same time. The extra static and dynamic power still ends up as heat even when it performs no useful computation.
Chip designers responded with several techniques—new transistor geometries, power gating, multiple voltage and frequency domains, and more conservative clocks—but none restored the old constant-power scaling rule. At some point, clock rates could no longer be increased automatically with each process generation, even though transistor density continued to improve.
 #Modern ComputingDennard scaling has ended, but Moore’s law is not dead yet.
Clock rates plateaued, but the transistor count is still increasing, allowing for the creation of new, parallel hardware. Instead of chasing faster cycles, CPU designs started to focus on getting more useful things done in a single cycle. Instead of getting smaller, transistors have been changing shape.
This resulted in increasingly complex architectures capable of doing dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of different things every cycle.
 Die shot of a Zen CPU core by AMD (~1,400,000,000 transistors)  Here are some core approaches making use of more available transistors that are driving recent computer designs:
 Overlapping the execution of instructions so that different parts of the CPU are kept busy (pipelining); Executing operations without necessarily waiting for the previous ones to complete (speculative and out-of-order execution); Adding multiple execution units to process independent operations simultaneously (superscalar processors); Adding vector instructions capable of applying one operation to groups packed into 128-, 256-, or 512-bit registers (SIMD); Adding layers of on-chip cache to reduce the latency and traffic of accesses that would otherwise reach RAM; Adding multiple identical cores on a chip (parallel computing, GPUs); Using multiple chips in a motherboard and multiple cheaper computers in a data center (distributed computing); Using custom hardware to solve a specific problem with better chip utilization (ASICs, FPGAs).  For modern computers, the “let’s count all operations” approach for predicting algorithm performance isn’t just slightly wrong but is off by several orders of magnitude. This calls for new computation models and other ways of assessing algorithm performance.
  The silicon die and the packaged processor are different objects. Modern dies range from a few millimeters to more than two centimeters on a side; the package is larger because it supplies power, signaling, mechanical support, and a path for heat. ↩︎
 Modern process-node names no longer identify one literal transistor dimension. They are generational labels, so comparing “nanometers” across manufacturers requires actual density, power, and performance data. ↩︎
title: Modern Hardware

content:
A timestamp contains more information than most questions about time require. If it is Thursday and we want to know the weekday 365 days later, carrying the year, month, hour, and second through the calculation would be ceremony. We only need
$$ (3+365)\bmod 7=4, $$
where Monday is day zero. The large counter has been projected onto a seven-position clock.
This projection is not merely a space-saving trick. It gives us an arithmetic system in which values remain bounded while addition and multiplication still behave predictably.
 #ResiduesTwo integers $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo a positive integer $m$ when their difference is divisible by $m$:
$$ a\equiv b\pmod m \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\mid(a-b). $$
Congruence partitions all integers into $m$ residue classes. We usually represent each class by its unique member in $[0,m)$, although any congruent integer denotes the same class.
The useful property is that congruence respects addition and multiplication:
$$ \begin{aligned} a\equiv b\pmod m,;c\equiv d\pmod m &\Longrightarrow a+c\equiv b+d\pmod m,\ &\Longrightarrow ac\equiv bd\pmod m. \end{aligned} $$
We can therefore reduce intermediate values whenever convenient. In C++, % is a remainder operator rather than a mathematical modulo operator: for a negative dividend, its result may be negative. A normalization routine must account for that:
#include <cstdint> int64_t normalize(int64_t x, int64_t m) { int64_t r = x % m; return r < 0 ? r + m : r; } Even when the final residue is small, the expression evaluated before % can overflow. For 32-bit residues, use a 64-bit product; for 64-bit residues, use a wider product or a reduction algorithm such as Barrett reduction or Montgomery multiplication.
 #Additive CyclesConsider a calendar with $m$ weekdays and a year containing $a$ days. Starting at day zero, the weekday after $k$ years is
$$ d_k=ka\bmod m. $$
The cycle returns to zero at the smallest positive $k$ for which $m\mid ka$. Dividing both numbers by $g=\gcd(a,m)$ leaves two coprime integers, so the smallest such $k$ is
$$ \frac{m}{\gcd(a,m)}. $$
This explains, for example, why repeatedly adding 4 modulo 10 visits only $0,4,8,2,6$: the common factor 2 confines us to five residue classes.
Multiplicative cycles are subtler. If $p$ is prime and $a$ is not divisible by $p$, the powers of $a$ are nonzero, but they do not necessarily visit all $p-1$ nonzero residues. Modulo 7, powers of 2 cycle through $1,2,4$ and return after three steps. Visiting every nonzero residue requires $a$ to be a primitive root modulo $p$.
What is guaranteed is that the cycle length divides $p-1$.
 #Fermat’s TheoremFermat’s little theorem. For every prime $p$ and integer $a$,
$$ a^p\equiv a\pmod p. $$
If $p\nmid a$, division by $a$ in the residue system gives the equivalent form
$$ a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p. $$
One compact proof uses a permutation. Multiplication by a nonzero $a$ maps the nonzero residues
$$ 1,2,\ldots,p-1 $$
to
$$ a,2a,\ldots,(p-1)a\pmod p. $$
No two products can be congruent: if $ai\equiv aj\pmod p$, then the prime $p$ divides $a(i-j)$; since it does not divide $a$, it must divide $i-j$. Thus the products are merely a permutation of the original residues. Multiplying every entry yields
$$ a^{p-1}(p-1)!\equiv(p-1)!\pmod p. $$
None of the factors in $(p-1)!$ is divisible by $p$, so it can be canceled, leaving $a^{p-1}\equiv1$.
The theorem gives a cheap way to disprove primality. If for some $1<a<n$,
$$ a^{n-1}\not\equiv1\pmod n, $$
then $n$ is certainly composite. Passing the test is only evidence: Carmichael numbers pass it for every base coprime to them. Repeating a Fermat test does not turn that structural failure into a reliable error bound. Practical probabilistic primality testing normally uses Miller–Rabin; for fixed-width integers, a known finite set of bases makes Miller–Rabin deterministic.
 #Modular DivisionAddition and multiplication descend naturally to residues. Ordinary division does not. The equation
$$ bx\equiv a\pmod m $$
has a unique solution for every $a$ only when $b$ has a multiplicative inverse: a residue $b^{-1}$ satisfying
$$ bb^{-1}\equiv1\pmod m. $$
Such an inverse exists exactly when $\gcd(b,m)=1$. If the gcd is larger than one, multiplication by $b$ collapses several residues together and cannot be undone. For instance, $2x\equiv1\pmod6$ has no solution, while $5^{-1}\equiv5\pmod6$ because $5\cdot5\equiv1$.
For prime $p$ and $a\not\equiv0\pmod p$, Fermat’s theorem immediately gives
$$ a^{-1}\equiv a^{p-2}\pmod p. $$
The power can be computed in $O(\log p)$ multiplications using binary exponentiation. For a composite modulus, or when primality is not known, the extended Euclidean algorithm finds the inverse under the more general condition $\gcd(a,m)=1$.
Once the inverse is known, modular division is multiplication:
$$ \frac{a}{b}\pmod m ;:=; ab^{-1}\pmod m. $$
This notation should not hide the precondition. In modular code, “divide by $b$” is a claim that $b$ is invertible in the chosen modulus; it is worth making that contract explicit.
title: Modular Arithmetic

content:
Pipelining overlaps different stages of several instructions. This raises an immediate question: what happens when the next instruction cannot advance?
On a simple in-order pipeline, the answer may be a literal stall: hold one or more stages until the obstruction disappears, leaving an unused slot traditionally called a bubble. Modern out-of-order processors are less dramatic. They keep many decoded operations in flight, wait only where a dependency or resource requires it, and continue issuing unrelated work when possible.
The traditional taxonomy is still useful, provided we do not imagine that every hazard freezes the entire core.
 #Structural HazardsA structural hazard occurs when several operations need the same finite resource. They may compete for a decoder, an execution unit, a load port, an entry in a scheduling queue, or retirement bandwidth.
If two ready operations both need a resource that accepts only one of them, one waits. Other independent operations using different resources may still execute. When a queue is completely full, the obstruction can propagate backward and eventually stop the front-end from admitting more work.
Structural limits determine steady-state throughput. We handle them by reducing pressure on the busy resource, selecting instructions that can use other resources, or doing more useful work per operation. Instruction tables and machine-code analyzers help identify these limits.
 #Data HazardsA data hazard occurs when ordering is required to preserve values.
The unavoidable case is a read-after-write dependency: if instruction B consumes the result of instruction A, B cannot execute before that result exists. A chain of such dependencies forms a critical path, and its latency cannot be hidden by executing more copies of the dependent operation.
Two other textbook cases, write-after-read and write-after-write, often arise only because instructions reuse the same architectural register name. Modern processors map these names to a larger set of physical registers, a technique called register renaming. Different logical versions then occupy different physical locations, removing the false dependency.
Memory is harder. A younger load may or may not refer to the same address as an older store. The processor predicts or checks this relationship using its load/store machinery; a wrong guess requires replaying affected work. Compilers face a similar problem when they cannot prove that two pointers do not alias.
Data hazards are addressed by shortening dependency chains or exposing independent work. Throughput computing develops this idea using multiple accumulators.
 #Control HazardsA control hazard occurs when the processor does not yet know which instruction should come next. Conditional branches, indirect jumps, calls, and returns all affect the future instruction stream.
Rather than waiting, the front-end predicts a destination and continues fetching and executing speculatively. A correct prediction hides most of the uncertainty. A wrong prediction discards the younger wrong-path operations, redirects the front-end, and reconstructs the correct stream. Older instructions are not erased, and the penalty is not simply “the number of pipeline stages”: it depends on when the branch resolves, how much useful work was in flight, and the microarchitecture.
Control hazards are reduced by making branches easier to predict, resolving them earlier, or replacing them with data flow when computing both alternatives is cheaper. The trade-off is explored in The Cost of Branching and Branchless Programming.
The common theme is lack of usable parallel work. A resource is busy, an operand is unavailable, or the next instruction is uncertain. Out-of-order execution can search around a local obstruction, but only inside a finite window. Understanding how that search works is the purpose of instruction scheduling.
title: Pipeline Hazards

content:
