Before jumping straight to compiler optimizations, which is what most of this chapter is about, let’s briefly recap the “big picture” first. Skipping the boring parts, there are 4 stages of turning C programs into executables:
 Preprocessing expands macros, pulls included source from header files, and removes comments: gcc -E source.c (writes preprocessed source to standard output). Compilation parses the source, diagnoses errors, converts it into intermediate representations, performs optimizations, and emits assembly: gcc -S source.c (writes source.s). Assembly encodes assembly as machine code plus relocation and symbol information: gcc -c source.s (writes the object file source.o). Linking combines object files and libraries, resolves symbols, applies relocations that can be fixed at link time, and produces an executable: gcc -o binary source.o.  The compiler driver can perform several stages in one invocation. For example, gcc -c source.c preprocesses, compiles, and assembles without linking, while gcc source.c -o binary runs all four stages.
There are possibilities to improve program performance in each of these stages.
 #Interprocedural OptimizationWe have the last stage, linking, because it is both easier and faster to compile programs on a file-by-file basis and then combine the results. Independent files can be compiled in parallel, and unchanged object files can be reused.
It also gives the ability to distribute code as libraries, which can be either static or shared:
 Static libraries are archives of object files. The linker copies the required members into the final link. Dynamic or shared libraries are loadable objects whose symbols can be resolved by the dynamic linker. Their code and read-only data can be mapped into several processes.  Static linking and interprocedural optimization are separate choices. Passing -static selects static libraries where possible; it does not expose function bodies to the optimizer by itself.
With link-time optimization (LTO), compilation preserves an intermediate representation in specially produced object files and optimization is resumed during the final link. In GCC and Clang this is normally requested with -flto during both compilation and linking. LTO can optimize across translation units, including object files selected from a static archive, but only when they contain compatible LTO information.
Header-only libraries provide another way to expose definitions to each compiling translation unit, which often enables inlining and constant propagation without LTO. This is not a guarantee of optimal code: visibility is still incomplete, compile times and code size may grow, and an optimizer can make an unprofitable decision even with full source available.
 #Inspecting the OutputExamining output from each of these stages can yield useful insights into what’s happening in your program.
You can get assembly from the source by passing the -S flag to the compiler, which will then generate a human-readable *.s file. If you pass -fverbose-asm, this file will also contain compiler comments about source code line numbers and some info about variables being used. If it is just a little snippet and you are feeling lazy, you can use Compiler Explorer, which is a very handy online tool that converts source code to assembly, highlights logical asm blocks by color, includes a small x86 instruction set reference, and also has a large selection of other compilers, targets, and languages.
Apart from the assembly, the other most helpful level of abstraction is the intermediate representation on which compilers perform optimizations. The IR defines the flow of computation itself and is much less dependent on architecture features like the number of registers or a particular instruction set. It is often useful to inspect these to get insight into how the compiler sees your program, but this is a bit out of the scope of this book.
We will mainly use GCC in this chapter, but also try to duplicate examples for Clang when necessary. The two compilers are largely compatible with each other, for the most part only differing in some optimization flags and minor syntax details.
title: Stages of Compilation

content:
CPUs are controlled with machine language, which is just a stream of binary-encoded instructions that specify
 the instruction number (called opcode), what its operands are (if there are any), and where to store the result (if one is produced).  A much more human-friendly rendition of machine language, called assembly language, uses mnemonic codes to refer to machine code instructions and symbolic names to refer to registers and other storage locations.
Jumping right into it, here is how you add two numbers (*c = *a + *b) in Arm assembly:
; *a = x0, *b = x1, *c = x2 ldr w0, [x0] ; load 4 bytes from wherever x0 points into w0 ldr w1, [x1] ; load 4 bytes from wherever x1 points into w1 add w0, w0, w1 ; add w0 with w1 and save the result to w0 str w0, [x2] ; write contents of w0 to wherever x2 points Here is the same operation in x86 assembly:
; *a = rsi, *b = rdi, *c = rdx  mov eax, DWORD PTR [rsi] ; load 4 bytes from wherever rsi points into eax add eax, DWORD PTR [rdi] ; add whatever is stored at rdi to eax mov DWORD PTR [rdx], eax ; write contents of eax to wherever rdx points Assembly is very simple in the sense that it doesn’t have many syntactical constructions compared to high-level programming languages. From what you can observe from the examples above:
 A program is a sequence of instructions, each written as its name followed by a variable number of operands. The [reg] syntax is used for “dereferencing” a pointer stored in a register, and on x86 you need to prefix it with size information (DWORD here means 32 bit). The ; sign is used for line comments, similar to # and // in other languages.  Assembly is a very minimal language because it needs to be. It reflects the machine language as closely as possible, up to the point where there is almost 1:1 correspondence between machine code and assembly. In fact, you can turn any compiled program back into its assembly form using a process called disassembly1 — although everything non-essential like comments will not be preserved.
Note that the two snippets above are not just syntactically different. Both are optimized codes produced by a compiler, but the Arm version uses 4 instructions, while the x86 version uses 3. The add eax, [rdi] instruction is what’s called fused instruction that does a load and an add in one go — this is one of the perks that the CISC approach can provide.
Since there are far more differences between the architectures than just this one, from here on and for the rest of the book we will only provide examples for x86, which is probably what most of our readers will optimize for, although many of the introduced concepts will be architecture-agnostic.
 #Instructions and RegistersFor historical reasons, instruction mnemonics in most assembly languages are very terse. Back when people used to write assembly by hand and repeatedly wrote the same set of common instructions, one less character to type was one step away from insanity.
For example, mov is for “store/load a word,” inc is for “increment by 1,” mul is for “multiply,” and idiv is for “integer division.” You can look up the description of an instruction by its name in one of x86 references, but most instructions do what you’d think they do.
Most instructions write their result into the first operand, which can also be involved in the computation like in the add eax, [rdi] example we saw before. Operands can be either registers, constant values, or memory locations.
Registers are named rax, rbx, rcx, rdx, rdi, rsi, rbp, rsp, and r8-r15 for a total of 16 of them. The “letter” ones are named like that for historical reasons: rax is “accumulator,” rcx is “counter,” rdx is “data” and so on — but, of course, they don’t have to be used only for that.
There are also 32-, 16-bit and 8-bit register names (rax → eax → ax → al). They are not fully separate but aliased: ax and al name the low parts of rax, while writing eax also clears the upper 32 bits of rax. These names primarily exist for compatibility with earlier x86 generations. Some integer casts therefore need no instruction, although widening a signed value or converting between integer and floating-point types still does.
These are just the general-purpose registers that you can, with some exceptions, use however you like in most instructions. There is also a separate set of registers for floating-point arithmetic, a bunch of very wide registers used in vector extensions, and a few special ones that are needed for control flow, but we’ll get there in time.
Constants are just integer or floating-point values: 42, 0x2a, 3.14, 6.02e23. They are more commonly called immediate values because they are embedded right into the machine code. Because it may considerably increase the complexity of the instruction encoding, some instructions don’t support immediate values or allow just a fixed subset of them. In some cases, you have to load a constant value into a register and then use it instead of an immediate value.
 #Moving DataSome instructions may have the same mnemonic, but have different operand types, in which case they are considered distinct instructions as they may perform slightly different operations and take different times to execute. The mov instruction is a vivid example of that, as it comes in around 20 different forms, all related to moving data: either between the memory and registers or just between two registers. Despite the name, it doesn’t move a value into a register, but copies it, preserving the original.
On many out-of-order x86 cores, some register-to-register mov instructions can be handled by move elimination: the renamer makes the destination refer to the same physical register as the source. This is microarchitecture-dependent and still consumes front-end resources. A register xchg is a real data operation and is not generally free.
As we’ve seen above with the fused add, you don’t have to use mov for every memory operation: some arithmetic instructions conveniently support memory locations as operands.
 #Addressing ModesMemory addressing is done with the [] operator, but it can do more than just reinterpret a value stored in a register as a memory location. The address operand takes up to 4 parameters presented in the syntax:
SIZE PTR [base + index * scale + displacement] where displacement needs to be an integer constant and scale can be 1, 2, 4, or 8. What it does is calculate the pointer base + index * scale + displacement and dereferences it.
Complex addressing is often handled by dedicated address-generation units, although the available forms and their throughput depend on the microarchitecture. It is useful when you have, for example, an array of structures and want to load a specific field of its $i$-th element.
Addressing operator needs to be prefixed with a size specifier for how many bits of data are needed:
 BYTE for 8 bits WORD for 16 bits DWORD for 32 bits QWORD for 64 bits  There is also a more rare TBYTE for 80 bits, and XMMWORD, YMMWORD, and ZMMWORD for 128, 256, and 512 bits respectively. All these types don’t have to be written in uppercase, but this is how most compilers emit them.
The address computation is often useful by itself: the lea (“load effective address”) instruction calculates the memory address of the operand and stores it in a register in one cycle, without doing any actual memory operations. While its intended use is for actually computing memory addresses, it is also often used as an arithmetic trick that would otherwise involve 1 multiplication and 2 additions — for example, you can multiply by 3, 5, and 9 with it.
It also frequently serves as a replacement for add because it doesn’t need a separate mov instruction if you need to move the result somewhere else: add only works in the two-register a += b mode, while lea lets you do a = b + c (or even a = b + c + d if one of them is a constant).
 #Alternative SyntaxThere are actually multiple assemblers (the programs that produce machine code from assembly) with different assembly languages, but only two x86 syntaxes are widely used now. They are commonly called after the two companies that used them and had a dominant influence on programming during that era:
 The AT&T syntax, used by default by all Linux tools. The Intel syntax, used by default, well, by Intel.  These syntaxes are also sometimes called GAS and NASM respectively, by the names of the two primary assemblers that use them (GNU Assembler and Netwide Assembler).
We used Intel syntax in this chapter and will continue to preferably use it for the rest of the book. For comparison, here is how the same *c = *a + *b example looks like in AT&T asm:
movl (%rsi), %eax addl (%rdi), %eax movl %eax, (%rdx) The key differences can be summarized as follows:
 The last operand is used to specify the destination. Registers and constants need to be prefixed by % and $ respectively (e.g., addl $1, %rdx increments rdx). Memory addressing looks like this: displacement(%base, %index, scale). GNU assembler uses # for line comments in its normal AT&T mode. A semicolon separates statements rather than reliably introducing a comment.  And, most importantly, in AT&T syntax, the instruction names need to be “suffixed” (addq, movl, cmpq, etc.) to specify what size operands are being manipulated:
 b = byte (8 bit) w = word (16 bit) l = long (32 bit integer or 64-bit floating-point) q = quad (64 bit) s = single (32-bit floating-point) t = ten bytes (80-bit floating-point)  In Intel syntax, this information is inferred from operands (which is why you also need to specify sizes of pointers).
Most tools that produce or consume x86 assembly can do so in both syntaxes, so you can just pick the one you like more and don’t worry.
  On Linux, to disassemble a compiled program, you can call objdump -d {path-to-binary}. ↩︎
title: Assembly Language

content:
Computing $a^n$ by multiplying by $a$ exactly $n-1$ times is reasonable when $n$ is five. It is less attractive when $n$ is a 64-bit integer or a cryptographic exponent.
The exponent contains enough structure to do better. Every time it is even, we can halve it by squaring the base:
$$ \begin{aligned} a^{2k} &= (a^k)^2,\ a^{2k+1} &= (a^k)^2a. \end{aligned} $$
This is binary exponentiation, also called exponentiation by squaring. Each step removes one binary digit of $n$, so it uses $O(\log n)$ multiplications.
 #A Recursive DerivationThe most direct recurrence computes the half-power only once:
$$ f(a,n)= \begin{cases} 1, & n=0,\ f(a,\lfloor n/2\rfloor)^2, & n>0\text{ and }n\text{ is even},\ f(a,\lfloor n/2\rfloor)^2a, & n\text{ is odd}. \end{cases} $$
For multiplication modulo $m$, reduction after every product keeps the values bounded. A 128-bit intermediate is enough for two 64-bit residues:
#include <cstdint> uint64_t mul_mod(uint64_t a, uint64_t b, uint64_t m) { return uint64_t((__uint128_t(a) * b) % m); } uint64_t pow_mod_recursive(uint64_t a, uint64_t n, uint64_t m) { if (n == 0) return 1 % m; uint64_t half = pow_mod_recursive(a, n / 2, m); uint64_t square = mul_mod(half, half, m); return n % 2 == 0 ? square : mul_mod(square, a % m, m); } The function requires $m>0$. Writing 1 % m handles the unusual but valid modulus $m=1$, where every residue is zero.
The recursion is only $O(\log n)$ levels deep, but it is unnecessary. More importantly, the iterative form exposes two useful dependency chains to the processor.
 #Reading the Exponent as BitsThe binary expansion of 42 is $101010_2$, or $32+8+2$. Therefore,
$$ a^{42}=a^{32}a^8a^2. $$
While scanning the exponent from its least significant bit, maintain two invariants:
 base is $a^{2^k}$ after $k$ bits have been consumed; result is the product selected by the consumed bits.  uint64_t pow_mod(uint64_t a, uint64_t n, uint64_t m) { uint64_t result = 1 % m; uint64_t base = a % m; while (n != 0) { if (n & 1) result = mul_mod(result, base, m); n >>= 1; if (n != 0) base = mul_mod(base, base, m); } return result; } The final guard avoids a square whose value will not be used. It is not necessary for correctness.
If the exponent has $L=\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor+1$ bits, the algorithm performs $L-1$ squarings and popcount(n) multiplications into the result. Thus its exact multiplication count is
$$ L-1+\operatorname{popcount}(n), $$
apart from small special cases. The asymptotic bound hides this dependence on the bit pattern.
 #Modular InversesFor prime $p$ and $a\not\equiv0\pmod p$, Fermat’s theorem gives
$$ a^{-1}\equiv a^{p-2}\pmod p. $$
The implementation is consequently one line once binary exponentiation is available:
uint64_t inverse_prime(uint64_t a, uint64_t p) { // Preconditions: p is prime and a % p != 0.  return pow_mod(a, p - 2, p); } This is convenient, but not always the fastest route. The extended Euclidean algorithm also takes $O(\log p)$ arithmetic steps, works for composite moduli whenever the inverse exists, and avoids a long sequence of modular multiplications.
For a compile-time exponent, the branch pattern is fixed. A compiler may unroll or partially evaluate the loop, but source-level unrolling should be justified by measurement: it increases code size, and modular multiplication—not the loop counter—is usually the expensive part. When the modulus is also fixed, constant-division optimizations apply; when many products share an odd run-time modulus, Montgomery multiplication may be more suitable.
 #The Algorithm Is Not About IntegersNothing in the derivation requires ordinary multiplication. It requires an associative operation and an identity element—a monoid. The same loop can raise matrices to a power, compose permutations, or repeatedly apply a state transition.
For example, powers of the Fibonacci transition matrix
$$ \begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&0\end{pmatrix} $$
compute Fibonacci numbers in $O(\log n)$ matrix multiplications. Binary exponentiation is best understood as a way to repeat any associative transformation, not as a number-theory party trick.
The performance lesson is similarly general: a better representation of the work—in this case, the bits of the exponent—can remove an exponential amount of repetition before instruction-level optimization even begins.
title: Binary Exponentiation

content:
When I began learning how to optimize programs myself, one big mistake I made was to rely primarily on the empirical approach. Not understanding how computers really worked, I would semi-randomly swap nested loops, rearrange arithmetic, combine branch conditions, inline functions by hand, and follow all sorts of other performance tips I’ve heard from other people, blindly hoping for improvement.
Unfortunately, this is how most programmers approach optimization. Most texts about performance do not teach you to reason about software performance qualitatively. Instead they give you general advice about certain implementation approaches — and general performance intuition is clearly not enough.
It would have probably saved me dozens, if not hundreds of hours if I learned computer architecture before doing algorithmic programming. So, even if most people aren’t excited about it, we are going to spend the first few chapters studying how CPUs work and start with learning assembly.
title: Computer Architecture

content:
The first step of getting high performance from the compiler is to ask for it, which is done with over a hundred different compiler options, attributes, and pragmas.
 #Optimization LevelsThere are 4 and a half main levels of optimization for speed in GCC:
 -O0 is the default one that does no optimizations (although, in a sense, it does optimize: for compilation time). -O1 (also aliased as -O) does a few “low-hanging fruit” optimizations, almost not affecting the compilation time. -O2 enables a broad set of generally profitable transformations with moderate compile-time and code-size costs (this is what many projects use for production builds). -O3 adds more aggressive loop and vector transformations that may increase compile time or code size and are not guaranteed to speed up every workload. -Ofast includes -O3 and enables options that disregard parts of strict language semantics. In particular, its floating-point assumptions affect NaNs, infinities, signed zero, rounding, and reassociation, which may be unacceptable for numerically sensitive code.  There are also many other optimization flags that are not included even in -Ofast, because they are very situational, and enabling them by default is more likely to hurt performance rather than improve it — we will talk about some of them in the next section.
 #Specifying TargetsThe next thing you may want to do is tell the compiler more about the computers this code will run on: the smaller the required platform set, the more features it may use. The default x86 baseline is chosen when the toolchain is configured and is intentionally conservative. The simplest way to narrow it is -march, for example -march=haswell. If the binary will run on the build machine, -march=native asks the compiler to detect its features.
The instruction sets are generally backward-compatible, so it is often enough to just use the name of the oldest microarchitecture you need to support. A more robust approach is to list specific features that the CPU is guaranteed to have: -mavx2, -mpopcnt. When you just want to tune the program for a particular machine without using any instructions that may crash it on incompatible CPUs, you can use the -mtune flag (by default -march=x also implies -mtune=x).
GCC can also apply these options to functions defined in a region of a source file. Push and pop the current options so the setting does not accidentally leak into the rest of the file:
#pragma GCC push_options #pragma GCC optimize("O3") #pragma GCC target("avx2")  unsigned hot_function(unsigned x) { return x * x; } #pragma GCC pop_options Function attributes are usually clearer when only one definition needs a different target. Pragmas and attributes are compiler extensions; keep a portable fallback when the code is intended for other toolchains.
 #Multiversioned FunctionsSometimes you may want to provide several architecture-specific implementations in one binary. On supported x86 ELF targets, GCC can emit the versions plus a resolver that detects CPU features and selects an implementation at runtime, as described in the official function multiversioning documentation:
__attribute__(( target("default") )) // fallback implementation int popcnt(unsigned x) { int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) s += (x >> i) & 1u; return s; } __attribute__(( target("popcnt") )) // selected when the running CPU supports POPCNT int popcnt(unsigned x) { return __builtin_popcount(x); } The exact multiversioning syntax and dispatch mechanism are target- and toolchain-specific. Clang supports per-function target attributes, but source-level optimization pragmas are not interchangeable with GCC’s.
title: Flags and Targets

content:
When we designed our DIY floating-point type, we omitted quite a lot of important little details:
 How many bits do we dedicate for the mantissa and the exponent? Does a 0 sign bit mean +, or is it the other way around? How are these bits stored in memory? How do we represent 0? How exactly does rounding happen? What happens if we divide by zero? What happens if we take the square root of a negative number? What happens if we increment the largest representable number? Can we somehow detect if one of the above three happened?  Most of the early computers didn’t support floating-point arithmetic, and when vendors started adding floating-point coprocessors, they had slightly different visions for what the answers to these questions should be. Diverse implementations made it difficult to use floating-point arithmetic reliably and portably — especially for the people who develop compilers.
In 1985, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers published a standard (called IEEE 754) that provided a formal specification of how floating-point numbers should work, which was quickly adopted by the vendors and is now used in virtually all general-purpose computers.
 #Float FormatsSimilar to our handmade float implementation, hardware floats use one bit for sign and a variable number of bits for the exponent and the mantissa parts. For example, the standard 32-bit float encoding uses the first (highest) bit for sign, the next 8 bits for the exponent, and the 23 remaining bits for the mantissa.
   One of the reasons why they are stored in this exact order is that it is easier to compare and sort them: you can use mostly the same comparator circuit as for unsigned integers, except for maybe flipping some bits in case one of the numbers is negative.
For the same reason, the exponent is biased: the actual value is 127 less than the stored unsigned integer, which lets us also cover the values less than one (with negative exponents). In the example above:
$$ (-1)^0 \times 2^{01111100_2 - 127} \times (1 + 2^{-2}) = 2^{124 - 127} \times 1.25 = \frac{1.25}{8} = 0.15625 $$
IEEE 754 and a few consequent standards define not one but several representations that differ in sizes, most notably:
   Type Sign Exponent Mantissa Total bits Approx. decimal digits     single 1 8 23 32 ~7.2   double 1 11 52 64 ~15.9   half 1 5 10 16 ~3.3   extended 1 15 64 80 ~19.2   quadruple 1 15 112 128 ~34.0   bfloat16 1 8 7 16 ~2.3    Their availability ranges from chip to chip:
 Most CPUs support single- and double-precision — which is what float and double types refer to in C. C and C++ leave the representation of long double to the implementation. x86 ABIs commonly use the 80-bit extended format, while other targets may use binary64, binary128, or another ABI-defined format. The 64-bit significand of x87 extended precision can represent every 64-bit integer exactly. Binary128 is mainly implemented in software on general-purpose CPUs and used for specialized scientific computations. Half-precision arithmetic only supports a small subset of operations and is generally used for applications such as machine learning, especially neural networks, because they tend to perform large amounts of calculations but don’t require high levels of precision. Binary16 and bfloat16 coexist because they make different trade-offs. Bfloat16 keeps the exponent range of binary32 while using only 7 stored fraction bits; it is widely supported by machine-learning accelerators, CPUs, FPGAs, and GPUs.  Lower-precision types need less memory bandwidth to move them around and usually take fewer cycles to operate on (e.g., the division instruction may take $x$, $y$, or $z$ cycles depending on the type), which is why they are preferred when error tolerance allows it.
Deep learning, emerging as a very popular and computationally-intensive field, created a huge demand for low-precision matrix multiplication, which led to manufacturers developing separate hardware or at least adding specialized instructions that support these types of computations — most notably, Google developing a custom chip called TPU (tensor processing unit) that specializes on multiplying 128-by-128 bfloat matrices, and NVIDIA adding “tensor cores,” capable of performing 4-by-4 matrix multiplication in one go, to all their newer GPUs.
Apart from their sizes, most of the behavior is the same between all floating-point types, which we will now clarify.
 #Handling Corner CasesThe default way integer arithmetic deals with corner cases such as division by zero is to crash.
Sometimes a software crash, in turn, causes a real, physical one. In 1996, the maiden flight of the Ariane 5 (the space launch vehicle that ESA uses to lift stuff into low Earth orbit) ended in a catastrophic explosion due to the policy of aborting computation on arithmetic error, which in this case was a floating-point to integer conversion overflow, that led to the navigation system thinking that it was off course and making a large correction, eventually causing the disintegration of a $200M rocket.
There is a way to gracefully handle corner cases like these: hardware interrupts. When an exception occurs, the CPU
 interrupts the execution of a program; packs all relevant information into a data structure called “interrupt vector”; passes it to the operating system, which in turn either calls the handling code if it exists (the “try-except” block) or terminates the program otherwise.  This is a complex mechanism that deserves an article of its own, but since this is a book about performance, the only thing you need to know is that they are quite slow and not desirable in real-time systems such as navigating rockets.
 #NaNs, Zeros and InfinitiesFloating-point arithmetic often deals with noisy, real-world data. Exceptions there are much more common than in the integer case, and for this reason, the default behavior when handling them is different. Instead of crashing, the result is substituted with a special value without interrupting the program execution (unless the programmer explicitly wants it to).
The first type of such value is the two infinities: a positive and a negative one. They are generated if the result of an operation can’t fit within the representable range, and they are treated as such in arithmetic.
$$ \begin{aligned} -∞ < x &< ∞ \ ∞ + x &= ∞ \ x ÷ ∞ &= 0 \end{aligned} $$
What happens if we, say, divide a value by zero? Should it be a negative or a positive infinity? This case is actually unambiguous because, somewhat less intuitively, there are also two zeros: a positive and a negative one.
$$ \frac{1}{+0} = +∞ ;;;; \frac{1}{-0} = -∞ $$
Fun fact: x + 0.0 can’t be folded to x, but x + (-0.0) can, so the negative zero is a better initializer value than the positive zero as it is more likely to be optimized away by the compiler. The reason why +0.0 doesn’t work is that IEEE says that +0.0 + -0.0 == +0.0, so it will give a wrong answer for x = -0.0. The presence of two zeros frequently causes headaches like this — good news that you can pass -fno-signed-zeros to the compiler if you want to disable this behavior.
Zeros are encoded by setting all bits to zero, except for the sign bit in the negative case. Infinities are encoded by setting all their exponent bits to one and all mantissa bits to zero, with the sign bit distinguishing between positive and negative infinity.
The other type is the “not-a-number” (NaN), which is generated as the result of mathematically incorrect operations:
$$ \log(-1),; \arccos(1.01),; ∞ − ∞,; −∞ + ∞,; 0 × ∞,; 0 ÷ 0,; ∞ ÷ ∞ $$
There are two types of NaNs: a signaling NaN and a quiet NaN. A signaling NaN raises an exception flag, which may or may not cause immediate hardware interrupt depending on the FPU configuration, while a quiet NaN just propagates through almost every arithmetic operation, resulting in more NaNs.
In binary, both NaNs have their exponent bits all set and the mantissa part being anything other than all zeros (to distinguish them from infinities). Note that there are very many valid encodings for a NaN.
 #Further ReadingThe classic paper What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic develops the representation and error model in detail. For shortest correctly rounded conversion to decimal, modern algorithms include Ryu and Dragonbox; Grisu3 is an important earlier design but no longer the final word.
title: IEEE 754 Floats

content:
Bandwidth is easiest to expose with many independent requests: the out-of-order core, prefetchers, and memory subsystem can overlap them. Measuring latency requires the opposite experiment—each address must depend on the value returned by the previous load.
A standard construction is one randomly ordered cycle. Every node is visited exactly once per lap, but the next address cannot be known until the current node arrives:
std::vector<std::uint32_t> order(N), next(N); std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0); std::mt19937 rng(42); std::shuffle(order.begin(), order.end(), rng); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) next[order[i]] = order[(i + 1) % N]; std::uint32_t k = order[0]; for (std::size_t t = 0; t < K; ++t) for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) k = next[k]; return k; // make the final state observable This is pointer chasing. The chain prevents vectorization and exposes a load-to-use dependency: a cache miss stalls this chain even though unrelated work elsewhere in a real program could still proceed.
 Throughput of a dependent random cycle on the test machine  For a serial chain, the reciprocal of visits per second is approximately the average time per dependent load, including loop and address-generation overhead:
 Average time per step of the dependent cycle  The transitions are smoother than in a streaming bandwidth plot. A working set does not suddenly move wholesale from one level to another: even when it exceeds a cache’s nominal capacity, some requested lines still hit there. Cache associativity, replacement, packed indices, TLB misses, and prefetching also blur the boundary.
 #A Capacity ModelWe can build a rough model by pretending that the cycle samples its $N$ nodes uniformly and that each cache behaves like a fully associative store of an effective cumulative capacity $C_i$. Let $C_0=0$, and let $l_i$ be the hit latency at level $i$. Then the approximate probability of being served by that level is
$$ p_i = \frac{\min(N,C_i)-\min(N,C_{i-1})}{N}, $$
and the remaining probability reaches memory:
$$ p_{RAM}=1-\frac{\min(N,C_k)}{N}. $$
The resulting estimate is
$$ E[L] \approx \sum_{i=1}^{k} p_i l_i + p_{RAM}l_{RAM}. $$
For $N>C_k$, this has the form $l_{RAM}-C/N$ for a machine-dependent constant $C$, so it approaches the memory latency gradually rather than as a step function.
This derivation is an intuition pump, not a way to recover authoritative cache latencies from one curve. Real cache levels may be inclusive, exclusive, or neither; set conflicts make the effective capacity access-pattern dependent; sixteen 32-bit indices share a 64-byte line; and the measured time includes address translation and loop overhead. Dedicated latency tools similarly use dependent loads but subtract overhead, control page placement, and test several patterns.
 #Frequency ScalingThe historical boost experiment on the test laptop produced these curves:
 Dependent-load latency with two frequency policies   Relative speedup from the higher-frequency run  Cache-resident accesses benefited more from the higher core frequency than DRAM accesses. Even a DRAM miss was not frequency-independent, because the measured path also includes address generation, TLB lookup, cache tags, interconnect crossings, retirement, and the loop itself. Conversely, last-level cache and fabric clocks do not have to track the core clock exactly.
Report both cycles and nanoseconds when diagnosing this distinction. A nearly fixed latency in cycles points toward a core-clocked component; a nearly fixed latency in nanoseconds points toward another clock domain, but neither inference is exact without counters and platform documentation.
The following sections isolate three effects hidden in this curve: cache-line packing, memory-level parallelism, and address translation.
title: Memory Latency

content:
Elementwise arithmetic is usually the easy part of SIMD. The difficult part is arranging data so that a useful amount arrives in the right lanes without spending more work on loads, conversions, shuffles, and tails than the arithmetic saves.
 #Aligned and Unaligned AccessAVX offers aligned load/store intrinsics and unaligned loadu/storeu intrinsics. Their contract is precise:
 _mm256_load_si256 and _mm256_store_si256 require the memory address itself to be divisible by 32; _mm256_loadu_si256 and _mm256_storeu_si256 accept any address for which all 32 accessed bytes belong to valid objects.  Fitting inside one cache line is not sufficient for an aligned load. An address at offset 4 inside a line is still not 32-byte aligned, and an aligned instruction may fault or the compiler may assume the impossible case never occurs.
Use unaligned operations in a general API:
void add(const std::int32_t *a, const std::int32_t *b, std::int32_t *out, std::size_t n) { std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 8 <= n; i += 8) { const __m256i x = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(a + i)); const __m256i y = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(b + i)); _mm256_storeu_si256( reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(out + i), _mm256_add_epi32(x, y)); } for (; i < n; ++i) out[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } The scalar expression can overflow for arbitrary signed inputs; this example assumes the mathematical sums fit in int32_t. Use unsigned lanes for defined modulo arithmetic or widen the result when that is not true.
When an API guarantees alignment, aligned operations document and exploit it:
alignas(32) std::int32_t a[N]; std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 8 <= N; i += 8) { const __m256i x = _mm256_load_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(a + i)); // ... } Because i advances by eight integers, every vector begins 32 bytes after the previous one. Dynamic allocations need the same base guarantee, as described in Alignment and Packing.
On many modern x86 cores, an unaligned instruction whose data lies within one cache line has the same throughput as its aligned counterpart. Crossing a line can require two cache accesses, and crossing a page can be more expensive still; unaligned stores have additional microarchitectural constraints. The exact penalty varies by instruction and processor. The historical Zen 2 benchmark in this book found an offset-three add loop about 30% slower because roughly half its 32-byte accesses crossed 64-byte lines, not because the mnemonic ended in u.
Alignment is therefore a property to measure, not a reason to manufacture undefined behavior. Aligned intrinsics are not “free runtime assertions”: the compiler is entitled to assume their precondition without checking it.
Non-temporal operations have a separate contract. Streaming stores can avoid ordinary write allocation for large, write-only output, but they need suitable alignment, complete streams, and an ordering fence at the relevant boundary. They are covered in Memory Bandwidth; a non-temporal load is not a portable “do not cache” switch.
 #Register History and AliasingMMX did not introduce a clean independent register file. Its eight 64-bit registers alias the physical x87 floating-point stack registers, and code had to execute EMMS before returning to x87 arithmetic. They were not simply aliases for an 80-bit value’s mantissa.
SSE introduced separate XMM registers. AVX extended them: XMM0 is the low 128 bits of YMM0, and YMM0 is the low 256 bits of ZMM0 when AVX-512 is present. This is architectural naming, not evidence that the registers “live in the FPU”; modern cores rename vector registers internally.
Legacy SSE and VEX/EVEX encodings also differ in what happens to upper bits. A 128-bit VEX instruction normally zeros the upper part of the corresponding YMM register, while many legacy SSE instructions preserve it. Mixing legacy SSE with AVX could trigger transition penalties on some older processors, so compilers insert vzeroupper at suitable call boundaries. Do not add it blindly inside a hot loop; inspect the ABI boundary and target CPU.
 #Extract, Insert, and BroadcastExtracting lane zero is usually cheap:
vmovd eax, xmm0 Extracting a high lane of a 256-bit integer vector may first select the upper 128-bit half:
vextracti128 xmm1, ymm0, 1 vpextrd eax, xmm1, 3 The index argument to _mm256_extract_epi32 and _mm256_insert_epi32 is an immediate and must be a compile-time constant. Exact sequences vary because the compiler can reuse an already available half or choose a shuffle. Occasional extraction is fine; repeatedly moving every lane to scalar registers usually defeats the point of SIMD.
Constants and broadcasts have direct intrinsics:
const __m256i indices = _mm256_setr_epi32(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7); const __m256i answer = _mm256_set1_epi32(42); const __m256i zero = _mm256_setzero_si256(); setr lists lanes in increasing memory order; _mm256_set_epi32 lists them in the opposite argument order. A compiler may load a constant pool or synthesize the value. _mm256_broadcast_ss(p) broadcasts one float from memory to eight lanes.
For debugging, store a vector into a real array rather than aliasing the vector object through an unrelated pointer:
void print(__m256i value) { alignas(32) std::array<std::uint32_t, 8> lane{}; _mm256_store_si256(reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(lane.data()), value); for (std::uint32_t x : lane) std::cout << std::bitset<32>(x) << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; }  #Gather and ScatterA gather loads elements from addresses formed by a base, vector indices, and a scale. AVX2 provides integer and floating-point gathers; AVX-512 adds scatter forms and masked variants. They require the AVX2 or relevant AVX-512 feature at runtime, and every active index must be in bounds.
This complete AVX2 checksum handles a query tail and uses modulo-$2^{32}$ arithmetic:
std::uint32_t gather_sum(const std::int32_t *data, const std::int32_t *query, std::size_t count) { __m256i sum = _mm256_setzero_si256(); std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 8 <= count; i += 8) { const __m256i index = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(query + i)); const __m256i value = _mm256_i32gather_epi32(data, index, 4); sum = _mm256_add_epi32(sum, value); } alignas(32) std::array<std::uint32_t, 8> lane{}; _mm256_store_si256(reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(lane.data()), sum); std::uint32_t result = std::accumulate(lane.begin(), lane.end(), 0u); for (; i < count; ++i) result += static_cast<std::uint32_t>(data[query[i]]); return result; } The precondition is 0 <= query[i] < data_size for every query; the function would need data_size to check it itself. On the original Zen 2 experiment, gather plus one add was not faster than scalar indexed loads except for small working sets. Other cores differ. Gather is most valuable when keeping the values in vector registers enables enough subsequent arithmetic to repay its latency and throughput cost.
Irregular SIMD memory access is still not the same as eight independent scalar threads. Gather/scatter instructions share execution and memory resources and can touch many lines or pages. Data layout that turns a gather into one or two contiguous loads is often the larger optimization.
title: Moving Data

content:
There are two superficially similar prime-number problems. To decide whether one 64-bit integer is prime, we use algorithms such as Miller–Rabin. To enumerate every prime up to a limit $N$, testing the numbers independently repeats almost all of the work. A sieve wins by turning divisibility into a streaming memory problem.
This makes prime generation an unusually clear performance case study. The arithmetic is elementary; the important decisions are which candidates we store, where each crossing-off pass starts, whether the working set fits in cache, and whether an expression such as p * p is even defined for the requested limit.
We will build two implementations:
 an odd-only in-memory sieve, useful when the whole range fits comfortably in memory; a segmented sieve that keeps only a small interval hot and can stream its output.  Both enumerate primes in the inclusive interval $[2,N]$ and use unsigned 64-bit limits.
 #From Trial Division to SievingTrial division tests a candidate $x$ against possible divisors up to $\sqrt{x}$. Repeating it for every $x\le N$ performs many divisions and revisits the same factors.
The sieve of Eratosthenes reverses the loops. For each prime $p$, it marks all multiples of $p$ as composite. Marking may begin at $p^2$, because every smaller composite multiple $kp$, with $k<p$, was already handled when processing $k$’s prime factor.
std::vector<std::uint8_t> composite(limit + 1, 0); for (std::uint64_t p = 2; p <= limit / p; ++p) if (!composite[p]) for (std::uint64_t x = p * p; x <= limit; x += p) composite[x] = 1; The condition p <= limit / p is the overflow-safe form of p * p <= limit. The inner loop still needs care: after marking a value near UINT64_MAX, x += p can wrap to a small number and continue forever. We will use a subtraction-based termination check in the complete implementations.
The classical running time is $O(N\log\log N)$. For performance engineering, the more immediate fact is that it performs a large number of tiny stores spread over an array of size $N$.
 #Do Not Store Even CandidatesAfter reporting 2, every prime is odd. Represent candidate
$$ x_i = 2i+3 $$
by slot $i$. Multiples of an odd prime that are themselves odd are separated by $2p$ in value and therefore by $p$ slots:
$$ p^2,\ p^2+2p,\ p^2+4p,\ldots $$
This halves both the main array and the crossing work associated with the prime 2. Here is a complete byte-per-odd-candidate implementation:
#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> std::vector<std::uint32_t> odd_primes(std::uint64_t limit) { if (limit > std::numeric_limits<std::uint32_t>::max()) throw std::invalid_argument("dense sieve limit exceeds uint32 output"); std::vector<std::uint32_t> primes; if (limit >= 2) primes.push_back(2); if (limit < 3) return primes; // Slots represent 3, 5, ..., the largest odd number <= limit.  std::uint64_t count64 = (limit - 1) / 2; if (count64 > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max()) throw std::length_error("sieve does not fit address space"); std::size_t count = static_cast<std::size_t>(count64); std::vector<std::uint8_t> composite(count, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != count; ++i) { std::uint64_t p = 2 * std::uint64_t(i) + 3; if (p > limit / p) break; if (composite[i]) continue; std::size_t first = static_cast<std::size_t>((p * p - 3) / 2); std::size_t step = static_cast<std::size_t>(p); std::size_t last = count - 1; for (std::size_t j = first;;) { composite[j] = 1; if (step > last - j) break; j += step; } } for (std::size_t i = 0; i != count; ++i) if (!composite[i]) primes.push_back(static_cast<std::uint32_t>(2 * i + 3)); return primes; } There are several contracts hidden in this small function:
 limit is inclusive, so odd_primes(3) returns {2, 3}; $p^2$ is evaluated only after p <= limit / p proves that it fits; the final increment is guarded as step > last - j, so an unsigned wrap cannot restart the loop; limits above UINT32_MAX are rejected because the output element type cannot represent them.  The last condition is naturally satisfied when the helper generates base primes up to the square root of a 64-bit segmented limit. For a standalone dense sieve with a larger limit, change the output type to uint64_t; memory will become the practical limit much earlier.
 #Bytes or bits?A byte array spends eight bits to store one answer, but every update is a simple byte store. A packed bitmap reduces the footprint eightfold and can keep a larger range in cache, at the cost of read-modify-write operations and more address arithmetic. There is no context-free winner.
The comparison must include the transition between cache levels. A byte sieve can win while both representations fit in a nearby cache and lose abruptly when only the packed version still fits. A wheel that omits multiples of 3 and 5 reduces traffic further but complicates the mapping from numbers to slots and changes the regular stride pattern.
 #SegmentationFor a large $N$, the full candidate array is not only large; it is revisited once for every base prime. A segmented sieve first computes the primes up to $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$, then crosses off a small interval at a time:
base primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... <= sqrt(N) [low ........ high] mark multiples of every base prime emit the survivors advance to the next segment The segment should be small enough to remain in a chosen cache and large enough that initialization, loop setup, and output do not dominate. It also lets us stream primes through a callback instead of storing $\pi(N)$ output values.
First we need an integer square root. Converting through floating point is useful for an initial estimate, but the result is corrected with division so rounding cannot omit a necessary base prime:
#include <cmath> std::uint64_t floor_sqrt(std::uint64_t n) { std::uint64_t r = static_cast<std::uint64_t>(std::sqrt((long double)n)); while (r != 0 && r > n / r) --r; while (r + 1 <= n / (r + 1)) ++r; return r; } For a 64-bit input, the true result is at most $2^{32}-1$, so r + 1 cannot overflow during the correction. The segmented core can now reuse the odd-number mapping:
#include <algorithm>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> template <class Emit> void segmented_primes(std::uint64_t limit, std::size_t block_odds, Emit emit) { if (block_odds == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("empty sieve segment"); if (limit < 2) return; emit(std::uint64_t(2)); if (limit < 3) return; auto base = odd_primes(floor_sqrt(limit)); std::vector<std::uint8_t> composite; for (std::uint64_t low = 3;;) { // `low` is odd. Count the odd values from low through limit.  std::uint64_t remaining = (limit - low) / 2 + 1; std::uint64_t count64 = std::min<std::uint64_t>(remaining, block_odds); std::uint64_t high = low + 2 * (count64 - 1); composite.assign(static_cast<std::size_t>(count64), 0); for (std::uint32_t p32 : base) { if (p32 == 2) continue; std::uint64_t p = p32; std::uint64_t square = p * p; // p <= floor_sqrt(limit)  if (square > high) break; std::uint64_t first = square; if (first < low) { std::uint64_t remainder = low % p; std::uint64_t delta = remainder == 0 ? 0 : p - remainder; if (delta > high - low) continue; first = low + delta; } if ((first & 1) == 0) { if (p > high - first) continue; first += p; } std::uint64_t step = 2 * p; for (std::uint64_t x = first;;) { composite[static_cast<std::size_t>((x - low) / 2)] = 1; if (step > high - x) break; x += step; } } for (std::size_t i = 0; i != composite.size(); ++i) if (!composite[i]) emit(low + 2 * std::uint64_t(i)); if (count64 == remaining) break; low = high + 2; // another odd value exists, so this cannot overflow  } } The first multiple of $p$ in a segment is
$$ \max\left(p^2,\left\lceil\frac{low}{p}\right\rceil p\right), $$
rounded up once more when it is even. Starting at $p^2$ is still necessary: otherwise a segment containing the prime $p$ would mark the prime itself as composite.
The implementation allocates one byte per odd value in the segment and $O(\sqrt N)$ bytes for its dense base sieve. More advanced large-interval sieves retain the next hit for each prime or bucket hits by destination segment, avoiding repeated quotient/remainder work and out-of-cache state. The locality problem and bucketed approach are studied in the primary work on a cache-optimized sieve; a detailed production example appears in the cache-efficient segmented sieve used for the Goldbach verification.
 #Mapping the Work to HardwareSmall primes generate dense, regular stores and are friendly to hardware prefetching. Large base primes produce only a few stores per segment, with little spatial locality. This suggests several independent tuning dimensions:
 candidate encoding: byte, bit, or a small wheel; segment size and alignment; crossing primes one at a time versus bucketing future hits; clearing a segment versus using generation counters; collecting primes versus counting or streaming them.  SIMD is not automatically useful for composite[x] = 1 because successive addresses for one prime are strided. It is more natural for clearing blocks, scanning bytes for survivors, expanding packed masks, or processing several small-prime patterns. As usual, vectorizing the visible line of arithmetic is less important than arranging the data stream.
Parallelization is comparatively simple after the base primes are known: different segments can be crossed independently. Static scheduling works when segments are similar; ordered output needs either per-segment buffers or a later merge. Sharing one output vector with a lock can erase much of the benefit.
 #Reproducible EvaluationA useful sieve benchmark states:
 inclusive limit and whether primes are counted, stored, or printed; byte, bit, and wheel encoding; segment size and cache level it is intended to fit; cost of generating base primes; cold versus warm allocation and page state; compiler, flags, ISA target, CPU, and frequency policy.  Test boundary limits 0, 1, 2, 3, every square around a prime, the last partial segment, and limits near the chosen integer type’s endpoints. Differential tests can compare both sieves against trial division for small ranges; larger tests can compare their complete outputs and known prime-count values.
Do not time printing unless formatted output is the subject of the benchmark. A sieve that writes decimal text is usually an integer-formatting benchmark with some prime generation attached.
The central optimization is segmentation, not because it changes $O(N\log\log N)$, but because it changes repeated main-memory traffic into repeated cache traffic. The asymptotic algorithm stays ancient; the useful machine model does not.
title: Prime Number Sieves

content:
If you are reading this book, then somewhere on your computer science journey you had a moment when you first started to care about the efficiency of your code.
Mine was in high school, when I realized that making websites and doing useful programming won’t get you into a university, and entered the exciting world of algorithmic programming olympiads. I was an okay programmer, especially for a highschooler, but I had never really wondered how much time it took for my code to execute before. But suddenly it started to matter: each problem now has a strict time limit. I started counting my operations. How many can you do in one second?
I didn’t know much about computer architecture to answer this question. But I also didn’t need the right answer — I needed a rule of thumb. My thought process was: “2-3GHz means 2 to 3 billion instructions executed every second, and in a simple loop that does something with array elements, I also need to increment loop counter, check end-of-loop condition, do array indexing and stuff like that, so let’s add room for 3-5 more instructions for every useful one” and ended up with using $5 \cdot 10^8$ as an estimate. None of these statements are true, but counting how many operations my algorithm needed and dividing it by this number was a good rule of thumb for my use case.
The real answer, of course, is much more complicated and highly dependent on what kind of “operation” you have in mind. It can be as low as $10^7$ for things like pointer chasing and as high as $10^{11}$ for SIMD-accelerated linear algebra. To demonstrate these striking differences, we will use the case study of matrix multiplication implemented in different languages — and dig deeper into how computers execute them.
 #Execution StrategiesOn the lowest level, computers execute machine code consisting of binary-encoded instructions which are used to control the CPU. They are specific, quirky, and require a great deal of intellectual effort to work with, so one of the first things people did after creating computers was create programming languages, which abstract away some details of how computers operate to simplify the process of programming.
A programming language is an interface between source code and its permitted behavior. An implementation still has to realize that behavior on hardware, and several strategies can be combined:
 an ahead-of-time compiler emits native machine code before the program runs; an interpreter dispatches source-level or bytecode operations at run time; a just-in-time compiler translates observed hot code to machine code while the program is running; a runtime may provide garbage collection, dynamic loading, profiling, or other services regardless of how instructions were produced.  These are properties of an implementation, not a clean partition of languages. CPython interprets bytecode; PyPy JIT-compiles much of the same Python program. Java virtual machines commonly interpret code first and compile hot methods later. C and Rust are usually compiled ahead of time, while emulators and dynamic binary translators can even interpret or recompile machine code from another ISA.
There is no universally right strategy. Dynamic types, late-bound operations, memory safety, startup latency, peak throughput, compilation time, and portability pull an implementation in different directions. The examples below are measurements of particular implementations and programs, not fixed multipliers attached to language names.
 #Interpreted languagesHere is an example of a by-definition $1024 \times 1024$ matrix multiplication in pure Python:
import time import random n = 1024 a = [[random.random() for row in range(n)] for col in range(n)] b = [[random.random() for row in range(n)] for col in range(n)] c = [[0 for row in range(n)] for col in range(n)] start = time.time() for i in range(n): for j in range(n): for k in range(n): c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j] duration = time.time() - start print(duration) In the original experiment, this CPython program ran in 630 seconds. That historical number is useful for accounting, but it should not be treated as current Python performance on an unspecified machine.
Let’s try to put this number in perspective. The CPU that ran it has a clock frequency of 1.4GHz, meaning that it does $1.4 \cdot 10^9$ cycles per second, totaling to about $8.8 \cdot 10^{11}$ cycles for the entire computation, or roughly 821 cycles per innermost-loop iteration.
CPython parses the source once and compiles it to bytecode; it does not parse the expression on every iteration. The repeated cost instead comes from interpreting and dispatching bytecodes over dynamic objects:
 bytecode dispatch and loop bookkeeping happen around each scalar operation; global or local names and nested Python lists lead to several dependent pointer loads; list elements point to Python objects rather than storing unboxed doubles inline; arithmetic dispatch checks dynamic types and creates or updates Python-level values; reference-count and error-handling machinery surrounds the useful multiply and add.  Interpreters specialize and cache some of this work, and newer CPython versions contain adaptive bytecodes. The nested boxed-list representation still leaves far more instructions and memory dependencies than a loop over contiguous native doubles. Moving the work into an array kernel can remove that overhead without changing the language used for the rest of the application.
 #Managed LanguagesThe same matrix multiplication procedure, but implemented in Java:
import java.util.Random; public class Matmul { static int n = 1024; static double[][] a = new double[n][n]; static double[][] b = new double[n][n]; static double[][] c = new double[n][n]; public static void main(String[] args) { Random rand = new Random(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) { a[i][j] = rand.nextDouble(); b[i][j] = rand.nextDouble(); c[i][j] = 0; } } long start = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]; double diff = (System.nanoTime() - start) * 1e-9; System.out.println(diff); } } In the same historical setup it ran in about 10 seconds, roughly 13 CPU cycles per scalar multiply-accumulate and 63 times faster than the CPython version. The comparison includes implementation, representation, warm-up, and benchmark choices; it is not a general Java-to-Python ratio.
Java source normally compiles to JVM bytecode. A production virtual machine may interpret that bytecode initially, profile it, and just-in-time compile frequently executed methods to native code. The resulting loop can approach ahead-of-time native performance, while array layout, bounds checks, garbage collection, and warm-up still affect a particular run.
JIT compilation is not a feature of the language itself, but of its implementation. There is also a JIT-compiled version of Python called PyPy, which needs about 12 seconds to execute the code above without any changes to it.
 #Compiled LanguagesNow it’s turn for C:
#include <stdlib.h>#include <stdio.h>#include <time.h> #define n 1024 double a[n][n], b[n][n], c[n][n]; int main() { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) { a[i][j] = (double) rand() / RAND_MAX; b[i][j] = (double) rand() / RAND_MAX; } } clock_t start = clock(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]; float seconds = (float) (clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC; printf("%.4f\n", seconds); return 0; } It took about 9 seconds in the original setup when compiled with gcc -O3.
That is not a huge improvement over the warmed JIT implementations, but ahead-of-time compilation makes the target and arithmetic contract easy to control. In the original experiment, adding -march=native and -ffast-math reduced the time to about 0.6 seconds.
-march=native exposes the current CPU’s instruction-set extensions. -ffast-math permits transformations such as reassociation that strict floating-point semantics forbid, enabling vectorization of the reduction. The second flag changes the numerical contract and is only valid when the application accepts those changes.
It’s not like it is impossible to tune the JIT-compilers of PyPy and Java to achieve the same performance without significant changes to the source code, but it is certainly easier for languages that compile directly to native code.
 #BLASFinally, let’s take a look at what an expert-optimized implementation is capable of. We will test a widely-used optimized linear algebra library called OpenBLAS. The easiest way to use it is to go back to Python and just call it from numpy:
import time import numpy as np n = 1024 a = np.random.rand(n, n) b = np.random.rand(n, n) start = time.time() c = np.dot(a, b) duration = time.time() - start print(duration) The original run took about 0.12 seconds: roughly five times faster than the auto-vectorized C loop and thousands of times faster than scalar Python. Repeating the comparison today requires recording the BLAS implementation, thread count, CPU, matrix layout, and whether initialization and packing are included.
The gain comes from more than replacing scalar instructions with vectors. BLAS implementations dispatch to architecture-specific microkernels, pack panels into cache-friendly layouts, block several cache levels, and parallelize large matrices. OpenBLAS contains substantial handwritten assembly kernels, but the surrounding data movement is equally important. The matrix-multiplication case study develops these layers one at a time.
 #TakeawayThe key lesson is that a native, low-level language does not automatically give performance, but it often exposes more direct control over representation, compilation, and hardware-specific kernels.
There is no single multiplier called “the speed of a language.” The executed algorithm, data representation, library boundary, compiler or runtime, warm-up state, and target machine all contribute. Convenient abstractions can either hide expensive work or route a one-line call to a kernel better than most applications could reproduce. Performance belongs to the complete implementation and workload.
title: Programming Languages

The way rounding works in hardware floats is remarkably simple: it occurs if and only if the result of the operation is not representable exactly, and by default gets rounded to the nearest representable number (in case of a tie preferring the number that ends with a zero).
Consider the following code snippet:
float x = 0; for (int i = 0; i < (1 << 25); i++) x++; printf("%f\n", x); Instead of printing $2^{25} = 33554432$ (what the result mathematically should be), it outputs $16777216 = 2^{24}$. Why?
When we repeatedly increment a floating-point number $x$, we eventually hit a point where it becomes so big that $(x + 1)$ gets rounded back to $x$. The first such number is $2^{24}$ (the number of mantissa bits plus one) because
$$2^{24} + 1 = 2^{24} \cdot 1.\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{\times 23} 1$$
has the exact same distance from $2^{24}$ and $(2^{24} + 1)$ but gets rounded down to $2^{24}$ by the above-stated tie-breaker rule. At the same time, the increment of everything lower than that can be represented exactly, so no rounding happens in the first place.
 #Rounding Errors and Operation OrderThe result of a floating-point computation may depend on the order of operations despite being algebraically correct.
For example, addition and multiplication are associative over real numbers but not over floating-point values: with three variables $x$, $y$, and $z$, (x + y) + z may differ from x + (y + z). Their ordinary finite forms remain commutative; it is regrouping a longer expression that changes where rounding occurs.
Compilers are not allowed to produce non-spec-compliant results, so this annoying nuance disables some potential optimizations that involve rearranging operands in arithmetic. You can disable this strict compliance with the -ffast-math flag in GCC and Clang. If we add it and re-compile the code snippet above, it runs considerably faster and also happens to output the correct result, 33554432 (although you need to be aware that the compiler also could have chosen a less precise computation path).
 #Rounding ModesApart from the default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even mode, the standard environment exposes three directed modes:
 round up (toward $+∞$; negative results thus round toward zero); round down (toward $-∞$; negative results thus round away from zero); round toward zero (a truncation of the binary result).  For example, if you call fesetround(FE_UPWARD) before running the loop above, it outputs not $2^{24}$, and not even $2^{25}$, but $67108864 = 2^{26}$. This happens because when we get to $2^{24}$, $(x + 1)$ starts rounding to the next nearest representable number $(x + 2)$, and we reach $2^{25}$ in half the time, and after that, $(x + 1)$ rounds up to $(x+4)$, and we start going four times as fast.
One use for alternative rounding modes is diagnosing numerical sensitivity. If an algorithm changes substantially between upward and downward rounding, round-off deserves investigation. The program must also be compiled in a mode that honors dynamic rounding—for example, with the implementation’s strict floating-point environment options; calling fesetround alone does not force an optimizing compiler to abandon assumptions it was permitted to make.
This test complements, rather than replaces, higher-precision references and conditioning analysis. Round-to-nearest errors are not guaranteed to be independent or unbiased in a particular algorithm, so repeated operations can accumulate systematic error instead of canceling.
 #Measuring ErrorsIEEE 754 requires correctly rounded results for its basic operations and square root. Transcendental library functions such as logarithm are a different matter: their accuracy guarantees depend on the implementation. Even for the basic model, explicit assumptions about normal values, rounding mode, and exceptional cases make error analysis much safer.
There are two natural ways to measure computational errors:
 The engineers who create hardware or spec-compliant exact software are concerned with units in the last place (ulps), which is the distance between two numbers in terms of how many representable numbers can fit between the precise real value and the actual result of the computation. People that are working on numerical algorithms care about relative precision, which is the absolute value of the approximation error divided by the real answer: $|\frac{v-v’}{v}|$.  In either case, the usual tactic to analyze errors is to assume the worst case and simply bound them.
If a basic arithmetic operation has a finite result in the normal range, round-to-nearest introduces at most 0.5 ulp. Machine epsilon $\epsilon$ is the distance from 1 to the next larger representable value; for a binary format with $p$ significand bits it is $2^{1-p}$. The corresponding unit roundoff is $u=\epsilon/2$.
Under the usual assumptions—round-to-nearest and no overflow or underflow—the standard model for an exact real result $z$ is
$$ \operatorname{fl}(z)=z(1+\delta), \qquad |\delta|\le u. $$
Subnormal results need an absolute-error bound instead, and exceptional values such as infinity and NaN require separate reasoning.
The omnipresence of errors is especially important to remember when making discrete “yes or no” decisions based on floating-point calculations. There is no universal epsilon comparison: a tolerance must come from the scale and error budget of the application. A common combined test is:
#include <algorithm>#include <cmath> bool approx_equal(float a, float b, float abs_tol, float rel_tol) { float scale = std::max(std::abs(a), std::abs(b)); return std::abs(a - b) <= std::max(abs_tol, rel_tol * scale); } abs_tol handles values near zero, while rel_tol scales with magnitude. Neither should be guessed from the data type alone: iterations, conditioning, measurement noise, and the consequence of a false comparison all matter.
 #Interval ArithmeticAn algorithm is called numerically stable if its error, whatever its cause, does not grow much larger during the calculation. This can only happen if the problem itself is well-conditioned, meaning that the solution changes only by a small amount if the input data are changed by a small amount.
When analyzing numerical algorithms, it is often useful to adopt the same method that is used in experimental physics: instead of working with unknown real values, we will work with the intervals where they may be in.
For example, consider a chain of operations where we consecutively multiply a variable by arbitrary real numbers:
float x = 1; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) x *= a[i]; After the first multiplication, the value of $x$ relative to the value of the real product is bounded by $(1 + \epsilon)$, and after each additional multiplication, this upper bound is multiplied by another $(1 + \epsilon)$. By induction, after $n$ multiplications, the computed value is bound by $(1 + \epsilon)^n = 1 + n \epsilon + O(\epsilon^2)$ and a similar lower bound.
This implies that the relative error is $O(n \epsilon)$, which is sort of okay, because usually $n \ll \frac{1}{\epsilon}$.
For example of a numerically unstable computation, consider the function
$$ f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 $$
Assuming $x > y$, the maximum value this function can return is roughly
$$ x^2 \cdot (1 + \epsilon) - y^2 \cdot (1 - \epsilon) $$
corresponding to the absolute error of
$$ x^2 \cdot (1 + \epsilon) - y^2 \cdot (1 - \epsilon) - (x^2 - y^2) = (x^2 + y^2) \cdot \epsilon $$
and hence the relative error of
$$ \frac{x^2 + y^2}{x^2 - y^2} \cdot \epsilon $$
If $x$ and $y$ are close in magnitude, the absolute error remains on the order of $\epsilon (x^2+y^2)$ while the true difference approaches zero, so the relative error can become arbitrarily large.
Under direct computation, the subtraction “magnifies” the errors of squaring. But this can be fixed by instead using the following formula:
$$ f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 = (x + y) \cdot (x - y) $$
The factored form avoids rounding two separate squares before subtracting them. Under the usual normal-number model its absolute error is on the order of $\epsilon |x+y||x-y|$, so it often retains useful relative accuracy when $x$ and $y$ are close. It is also faster because it needs two additions and one multiplication: one fast addition more and one slow multiplication less than the original.
 #Kahan SummationFrom the previous example, we can see that long chains of operations are not a problem, but adding and subtracting numbers of different magnitude is. The general approach to dealing with such problems is to try to keep big numbers with big numbers and small numbers with small numbers.
Consider the standard summation algorithm:
float s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i]; Since we are performing summations and not multiplications, its relative error is no longer just bounded by $O(\epsilon \cdot n)$, but heavily depends on the input.
In the most ridiculous case, if the first value is $2^{24}$ and the other values are equal to $1$, the sum is going to be $2^{24}$ regardless of $n$, which can be verified by executing the following code and observing that it simply prints $16777216 = 2^{24}$ twice:
const int n = (1<<24); printf("%d\n", n); float s = n; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += 1.0; printf("%f\n", s); This happens because float has 24 bits of significand precision (including the implicit leading bit), and so $2^{24} + 1$ is the first positive integer that cannot be represented exactly and rounds back down. The mathematical result is $2^{25}$ while the loop returns $2^{24}$, so the absolute error in this example is $2^{24}$, not a small constant. If severe cancellation makes the true sum close to zero, the relative error can be unbounded.
The obvious solution is to switch to a larger type such as double, but this isn’t really a scalable method. An elegant solution is to store the parts that weren’t added in a separate variable, which is then added to the next variable:
float s = 0, c = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { float y = a[i] - c; // c is zero on the first iteration  float t = s + y; // s may be big and y may be small, losing low-order bits of y  c = (t - s) - y; // (t - s) cancels high-order part of y  s = t; } This trick is known as Kahan summation. A typical forward-error bound is proportional to $\epsilon \sum_i |a_i|$ plus higher-order terms, largely removing the naive factor of $n$ from first-order error growth. Turning that into a small relative bound still requires a well-conditioned sum: if large positive and negative terms nearly cancel, any method can have large relative error with respect to the tiny result.
Of course, a more general approach that works not just for array summation would be to switch to a more precise data type, like double, also effectively squaring the machine epsilon. Furthermore, it can (sort of) be scaled by bundling two double variables together: one for storing the value and another for its non-representable errors so that they represent the value $a+b$. This approach is known as double-double arithmetic, and it can be similarly generalized to define quad-double and higher precision arithmetic.
title: Rounding Error and Interval Arithmetic

content:
The Eytzinger layout turns binary search into a walk through an implicit tree. A static B-tree applies the same idea with wider nodes: fetch a block of sorted keys, determine one child number, and discard several binary decisions at once.
The word static matters. Without insertions or deletions, child positions can be derived from indices and nodes can be packed densely. A dynamic B-tree needs spare capacity, ownership, and explicit child references; that is the subject of the next chapter.
 #From Binary to Wide NodesLet a node contain at most $B$ keys and therefore have $F=B+1$ child positions. Child $i$ contains values between parent keys $i-1$ and $i$, with either boundary omitted at an edge.
Number the root zero. In a complete $F$-ary Eytzinger layout, child $i$ of node $k$ is
$$ \operatorname{child}(k,i)=Fk+i+1, \qquad 0\le i\le B. $$
If there are
$$ q=\left\lceil\frac{n}{B}\right\rceil $$
physical nodes, keep exactly the breadth-first prefix $[0,q)$. Its exact height is zero for $q=0$; otherwise it is one plus the number of times the last index $q-1$ can be replaced by its parent $\lfloor(k-1)/F\rfloor$ before reaching zero. Equivalently, it is the least $h$ such that
$$ q\le 1+F+\cdots+F^{h-1}. $$
This definition handles a partial final layer without evaluating an overflowing power. The key capacity is $qB$, so fewer than $B$ slots are unused, but those slots are not necessarily all in the physically last node: in-order position and breadth-first position are different.
 A B-tree node separates several child ranges   #An Implicit Static B-TreeConstruction performs an in-order traversal of the implicit tree and consumes the sorted input sequentially. Each node stores a count, so every 64-bit integer remains a legal key; no INT_MAX padding value is needed.
#include <algorithm>#include <array>#include <bit>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <optional>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <utility>#include <vector> template <std::size_t Block = 16> class static_b_tree_i64 { static_assert(Block >= 2); static_assert( Block < std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() ); struct node { std::array<std::int64_t, Block> keys{}; std::size_t count = 0; }; public: explicit static_b_tree_i64( std::span<const std::int64_t> sorted_values ) : size_(sorted_values.size()) { if (!std::is_sorted(sorted_values.begin(), sorted_values.end())) throw std::invalid_argument("input must be sorted"); const std::size_t count = size_ / Block + static_cast<std::size_t>(size_ % Block != 0); if (count > nodes_.max_size() || count > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / Block) throw std::length_error("B-tree capacity overflow"); nodes_.resize(count); std::size_t cursor = 0; if (!nodes_.empty()) build(0, sorted_values, cursor); if (cursor != size_) throw std::logic_error("B-tree construction failed"); } std::optional<std::int64_t> lower_bound(std::int64_t key) const { std::optional<std::int64_t> candidate; std::size_t index = 0; while (index < nodes_.size()) { const node& current = nodes_[index]; const auto first = current.keys.begin(); const auto last = first + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(current.count); const auto found = std::lower_bound(first, last, key); const std::size_t slot = static_cast<std::size_t>( std::distance(first, found) ); if (slot < current.count) candidate = current.keys[slot]; const auto next = child_index(index, slot); if (!next) break; index = *next; } return candidate; } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; } std::size_t height() const noexcept { if (nodes_.empty()) return 0; constexpr std::size_t fanout = Block + 1; std::size_t index = nodes_.size() - 1; std::size_t result = 1; while (index != 0) { index = (index - 1) / fanout; ++result; } return result; } private: std::optional<std::size_t> child_index(std::size_t parent, std::size_t slot) const noexcept { constexpr std::size_t fanout = Block + 1; if (slot > Block) return std::nullopt; const std::size_t offset = slot + 1; if (parent > ( std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() - offset ) / fanout) return std::nullopt; const std::size_t child = parent * fanout + offset; if (child >= nodes_.size()) return std::nullopt; return child; } void build(std::size_t index, std::span<const std::int64_t> sorted_values, std::size_t& cursor) { node& current = nodes_[index]; for (std::size_t slot = 0; slot < Block; ++slot) { if (const auto child = child_index(index, slot)) build(*child, sorted_values, cursor); if (cursor < sorted_values.size()) { current.keys[current.count] = sorted_values[cursor]; ++current.count; ++cursor; } } if (const auto child = child_index(index, Block)) build(*child, sorted_values, cursor); } std::size_t size_; std::vector<node> nodes_; }; At each node, the local lower bound selects a child. A local candidate is remembered before descending because the answer may be a separator in an ancestor rather than a key in the final node. An absent child ends the walk.
The child calculation checks multiplication and addition before forming the index. Real allocations will fail long before size_t is exhausted, but an arena bound is not a proof that intermediate arithmetic cannot wrap.
