Spread bandwidth-heavy workers across the topology when that improves the measured application, while keeping communicating workers close enough to share data efficiently. “Always split symmetrically” is too strong: the right placement depends on whether the bottleneck is private cache, shared cache, coherence, NUMA distance, or DRAM channels.
 #False SharingEven threads that update different variables can interfere if those variables occupy one cache line. Coherence tracks ownership at line granularity, so writes from different cores make the line bounce between their private caches. This false sharing can serialize an otherwise independent counter loop.
Padding per-thread writable state to the machine’s destructive-interference size is one remedy:
struct alignas(64) Counter { std::atomic<std::uint64_t> value{0}; }; The 64 is appropriate for the test machine, not a portable constant. C++17 exposes std::hardware_destructive_interference_size when the implementation supplies a useful value; otherwise obtain the line size from the target and validate the layout. Padding read-mostly data can waste cache capacity, so apply it only where counters demonstrate ownership traffic.
title: Memory Sharing

content:
Reducing one product modulo $n$ is a division problem. Reducing a thousand products by the same $n$ is a representation problem.
Montgomery multiplication changes the representation of every residue so that reduction uses the inexpensive operations modulo a power of two. Entering and leaving the representation has a cost, so the method is useful for chains of products—modular exponentiation is the standard example—not for one isolated %.
 #Montgomery SpaceChoose a radix $R=2^w$ larger than an odd modulus $n$. The oddness condition is essential: it makes $\gcd(n,R)=1$, so $R$ has an inverse modulo $n$.
Represent a residue $x$ by
$$ \bar x=xR\bmod n. $$
Addition works as usual because
$$ \bar x+\bar y\equiv(x+y)R\pmod n. $$
Ordinary multiplication introduces one factor of $R$ too many:
$$ \bar x\bar y\equiv xyR^2\pmod n. $$
To obtain the representation of $xy$, we need a reduction operation
$$ \operatorname{REDC}(T)=TR^{-1}\bmod n. $$
Then
$$ \operatorname{REDC}(\bar x\bar y) \equiv xyR\pmod n, $$
which is exactly $\overline{xy}$.
 #Making the Low Word VanishPrecompute
$$ n^\prime=-n^{-1}\bmod R. $$
For an input $0\le T<nR$, calculate
$$ q=(T\bmod R)n^\prime\bmod R. $$
The low $w$ bits of $T+qn$ are zero:
$$ T+qn \equiv T+T(-n^{-1})n \equiv0\pmod R. $$
Division by $R$ is therefore exact, and because $R$ is a power of two, it is just a shift:
$$ t=\frac{T+qn}{R}. $$
Modulo $n$, the added term disappears, so
$$ t\equiv TR^{-1}\pmod n. $$
The range is small as well. Since $T<nR$ and $q<R$,
$$ 0\le t<2n. $$
At most one subtraction is needed to obtain the canonical residue in $[0,n)$.
The trick is worth pausing over. We do not approximate the quotient. We deliberately add a multiple of $n$ whose low word cancels the low word of the input, making an exact division by the machine radix possible.
 #A 32-Bit ImplementationThe following implementation uses $R=2^{32}$. Restricting $n<2^{31}$ keeps T + q*n from overflowing 64 bits for products of reduced residues. A wider temporary can remove this restriction.
#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept> class Montgomery32 { uint32_t n; uint32_t n_prime; // -n^{-1} modulo 2^32  uint32_t r2; // R^2 modulo n  public: explicit Montgomery32(uint32_t modulus) : n(modulus) { if (n <= 1 || n >= (uint32_t(1) << 31) || (n & 1) == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("modulus must be odd and in (1, 2^31)"); // Start with the inverse modulo 2. Each Newton step doubles  // the number of correct low bits: x <- x(2 - n*x).  uint32_t inverse = 1; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) inverse *= 2 - n * inverse; n_prime = 0 - inverse; uint64_t r = (uint64_t(1) << 32) % n; r2 = uint32_t(r * r % n); } uint32_t reduce(uint64_t T) const { // Precondition for this implementation: T < n^2.  uint32_t q = uint32_t(T) * n_prime; uint64_t t = (T + uint64_t(q) * n) >> 32; return uint32_t(t >= n ? t - n : t); } uint32_t transform(uint32_t x) const { // REDC(x * R^2) = x * R.  return reduce(uint64_t(x % n) * r2); } uint32_t canonical(uint32_t x) const { // Precondition: x is a Montgomery representative in [0, n).  // If x = a * R modulo n, REDC(x) = a modulo n.  return reduce(x); } uint32_t multiply(uint32_t x, uint32_t y) const { // x and y are canonical Montgomery representatives in [0, n).  return reduce(uint64_t(x) * y); } uint32_t one() const { return transform(1); } }; The type deliberately distinguishes transform from canonical: the former enters Montgomery space, while the latter leaves it. Applying ordinary % n to a Montgomery representative does not leave the representation—it is already a residue modulo $n$, just one encoding a different value.
 #Computing the Inverse of the ModulusThe constructor uses a Newton-style lift. If $x$ is an inverse of odd $n$ modulo $2^k$, write $nx=1+c2^k$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} n x(2-nx) &=(1+c2^k)(1-c2^k)\ &=1-c^2 2^{2k}\ &\equiv1\pmod{2^{2k}}. \end{aligned} $$
Thus x *= 2 - n*x doubles the number of correct low bits. Every odd number is congruent to one modulo 2, so x=1 is a valid starting point. Five doublings take us from 1 correct bit to all 32 bits—not 32 iterations.
Unsigned overflow in this loop is intentional: C++ defines it modulo $2^{32}$, exactly the arithmetic we need. The final negation produces $n^\prime=-n^{-1}$ rather than $n^{-1}$; this sign matches the T + q*n form of REDC. An implementation using T - q*n would use the opposite convention. Mixing the two is a common and remarkably quiet bug.
 #Exponentiation in Montgomery SpaceValues should cross the representation boundary only once:
uint32_t pow_mod(uint32_t a, uint64_t exponent, const Montgomery32& space) { uint32_t base = space.transform(a); uint32_t result = space.one(); while (exponent != 0) { if (exponent & 1) result = space.multiply(result, base); exponent >>= 1; if (exponent != 0) base = space.multiply(base, base); } return space.canonical(result); } The loop contains multiplication, shifts, and a conditional subtraction, but no division by $n$. The divisions used to construct r2 are paid once per modulus. As written, transform also evaluates x % n so that it accepts an arbitrary 32-bit input; that conversion cost is paid once per value before a multiplication chain. An interface requiring x < n could omit the normalization. When the modulus is a compile-time constant, compiler-generated reciprocal reduction may already be excellent; when the modulus changes frequently, Montgomery setup may never pay for itself. Benchmark the whole workload.
 #Bounds, Limbs, and Constant TimeProduction implementations vary in three important ways.
First, some keep a lazy result in $[0,2n)$ and postpone the final subtraction. This can shorten a dependency chain, but every following operation must honor the wider range. A bound proved for normalized operands cannot simply be reused.
Second, 64-bit and multiprecision variants use instructions that return the high and low halves of a product. Multiword REDC cancels one limb at a time and is the basis of many large-integer modular exponentiation routines.
Third, cryptographic code must consider timing and other side channels. A source-level ternary operator is not a guarantee of constant-time machine code, and a fast educational implementation is not a replacement for a reviewed cryptographic library. Use vetted primitives when secrets are involved.
Montgomery multiplication is a particularly clean performance transformation: the mathematical operation stays the same, but choosing a representation aligned with the hardware turns a hard division into low-word cancellation and a shift.
 #Further Reading Peter Montgomery’s original paper, Modular Multiplication Without Trial Division, gives the general construction. The Handbook of Applied Cryptography develops single- and multiple-precision variants. BearSSL’s constant-time notes explain why arithmetic correctness and side-channel safety are separate requirements.
title: Montgomery Multiplication

content:
Logistic regression is a small model with an honest performance lesson. Its mathematics fits on a page, but the program contains several distinct kernels: a dot product or matrix multiplication, a nonlinear probability conversion, a loss reduction, and—during training—an optimizer that decides how many times those kernels run.
Combining them into one benchmark makes it easy to optimize the wrong thing. For class prediction, the exponential may be unnecessary. For probability output, it is required and must be evaluated stably. For training, a faster gradient kernel can still lose end to end if a different optimizer needs many more iterations.
We will first make the numerical contract correct, then map the linear algebra to the machine, and finally discuss quantization without assuming that “machine learning tolerates error” is an overflow proof.
 #Binary Logistic RegressionFor a feature vector $x\in\mathbb R^d$, weights $w$, and bias $b$, the model computes a logit
$$ z = b + \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} w_jx_j $$
and maps it to a probability with the sigmoid
$$ \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}. $$
The predicted class at threshold $1/2$ is simply z >= 0: the sigmoid is monotone and $\sigma(0)=1/2$. If the caller needs only a class label, evaluating an exponential and dividing does not improve the answer.
When a probability is required, the direct formula overflows for a large negative z because it evaluates $e^{-z}$. Use two algebraically equivalent branches:
#include <cmath> double sigmoid(double z) { if (z >= 0) { double e = std::exp(-z); return 1 / (1 + e); } else { double e = std::exp(z); return e / (1 + e); } } In each branch the exponential’s argument is nonpositive, so it cannot overflow. Underflow for an extreme logit produces the correct limiting probability, zero or one.
 #Loss from logitsFor a binary label $y\in{0,1}$, cross entropy is often written
$$ -y\log\sigma(z)-(1-y)\log(1-\sigma(z)). $$
Computing the probability first is a numerical mistake: it may round to exactly zero or one, after which a logarithm produces infinity even when the loss has a finite representable expression. Define
$$ \operatorname{softplus}(t)=\log(1+e^t) $$
and evaluate the loss directly from the logit:
double softplus(double x) { if (x > 0) return x + std::log1p(std::exp(-x)); return std::log1p(std::exp(x)); } double binary_log_loss(double logit, bool label) { return label ? softplus(-logit) : softplus(logit); } This also handles infinite logits in the expected limiting way; NaN propagates. The derivative with respect to the logit is still the compact
$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial z}=\sigma(z)-y. $$
 #Multiclass Logistic RegressionFor $C$ classes, each class has a weight vector and bias. The model produces logits
$$ z_c=b_c+\sum_j W_{cj}x_j $$
and the softmax distribution
$$ p_c=\frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}}. $$
Exponentiating raw logits can overflow. Subtract their maximum $m=\max_c z_c$:
$$ p_c=\frac{e^{z_c-m}}{\sum_k e^{z_k-m}}. $$
Every exponent is now at most zero, and at least one term equals one. This shifted evaluation is analyzed in the primary numerical study Accurate Computation of the Log-Sum-Exp and Softmax Functions.
#include <algorithm>#include <cmath>#include <cstddef>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> void require_finite(std::span<const double> values) { if (values.empty()) throw std::invalid_argument("empty logit vector"); for (double x : values) if (!std::isfinite(x)) throw std::domain_error("softmax requires finite logits"); } std::vector<double> softmax(std::span<const double> logits) { require_finite(logits); double shift = *std::max_element(logits.begin(), logits.end()); std::vector<double> probabilities(logits.size()); double sum = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i != logits.size(); ++i) { probabilities[i] = std::exp(logits[i] - shift); sum += probabilities[i]; } for (double &p : probabilities) p /= sum; return probabilities; } double multiclass_log_loss(std::span<const double> logits, std::size_t label) { require_finite(logits); if (label >= logits.size()) throw std::out_of_range("class label"); double shift = *std::max_element(logits.begin(), logits.end()); double sum = 0; for (double z : logits) sum += std::exp(z - shift); return std::log(sum) - (logits[label] - shift); } The loss uses log-sum-exp directly instead of taking the logarithm of a rounded softmax probability. Its gradient with respect to logit $z_c is $p_c-[c=y].
Again, class prediction does not require softmax:
std::size_t predicted_class(std::span<const double> logits) { require_finite(logits); return std::size_t(std::max_element(logits.begin(), logits.end()) - logits.begin()); } max_element resolves an exact tie in favor of the first class. If class ordering should not decide ties, specify and implement another policy explicitly.
Subtracting the maximum and exponentiating preserves the order. Skipping softmax is an algorithmic optimization with an exact proof, not an approximation.
 #The Linear KernelFor one sample, inference is a matrix-vector product. The following scalar reference uses class-major weights: every class row is contiguous, arbitrary feature counts are valid, and there is no hidden SIMD-width requirement.
#include <cmath>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> std::vector<double> logits(std::span<const double> features, std::span<const double> weights, std::span<const double> bias) { std::size_t classes = bias.size(); std::size_t dimensions = features.size(); if (classes == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("model has no classes"); if (dimensions != 0 && classes > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / dimensions) throw std::length_error("model shape overflow"); if (weights.size() != classes * dimensions) throw std::invalid_argument("weight shape mismatch"); std::vector<double> result(bias.begin(), bias.end()); for (std::size_t c = 0; c != classes; ++c) { double sum = result[c]; for (std::size_t j = 0; j != dimensions; ++j) sum = std::fma(weights[c * dimensions + j], features[j], sum); result[c] = sum; } return result; } This loop exposes one dependency chain per class. Several independent class accumulators can execute in parallel, while SIMD can process adjacent features inside a row. A vectorized implementation must still reduce each vector accumulator horizontally and handle the final dimensions % lanes features with a scalar or masked tail.
Class-major storage is natural when processing one sample. With many samples, inference becomes matrix multiplication:
$$ Z=XW^T+b. $$
A tuned GEMM reuses blocks of both samples and weights in cache and amortizes packing. Calling a matrix-vector kernel separately for each row of a large batch leaves much of that reuse on the table. The relevant case study is therefore matrix multiplication, not a more ornate sigmoid.
When the number of classes is small, feature-major weights can instead update several class accumulators from one loaded feature. This may reuse features[j] better and vectorize across padded classes. It also changes the best layout for training and batches. Layout belongs in the benchmark contract.
 #Training Is More Than the KernelFor one labeled sample, multiclass gradient accumulation is
$$ G_{cj} \mathrel{+}= (p_c-[c=y])x_j. $$
Computing logits and this outer product is the training kernel. Stochastic gradient descent, momentum, Adam, L-BFGS, regularization, line search, stopping criteria, and data ordering are optimization algorithms. They determine which parameter updates are made and how many full or partial passes are required.
This distinction prevents a common benchmarking error. Comparing two training programs after the same number of iterations says little if their optimizers reach different objective values. Compare kernel throughput with fixed tensors, and separately compare end-to-end time to a fixed validation metric or loss under a documented optimizer configuration.
Training also has more data movement than inference. It writes gradients, optimizer state, and perhaps per-sample probabilities. Fusing loss and gradient production can avoid materializing a full probability matrix, but the fused code must retain the same reduction order and numerical contract.
 #QuantizationReducing weights and activations from floating point to 8-bit integers can reduce model traffic and let one instruction process more products. It is not valid merely because the input data is noisy. Quantization changes the model and needs calibration or quantization-aware training; the primary integer-only inference work describes scales, zero points, and the co-design with training in detail.
Even the simplest symmetric int8_t dot product needs a proved accumulator range. A product can be as large as $(-128)^2=16384$. Therefore a signed 32-bit sum is safe for at most
$$ \left\lfloor\frac{2^{31}-1}{16384}\right\rfloor=131071 $$
unbiased terms:
#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> std::int32_t dot_i8(std::span<const std::int8_t> a, std::span<const std::int8_t> b) { if (a.size() != b.size()) throw std::invalid_argument("dot-product shape mismatch"); constexpr std::size_t safe_terms = std::size_t(std::numeric_limits<std::int32_t>::max()) / (128 * 128); if (a.size() > safe_terms) throw std::overflow_error("int32 accumulator can overflow"); std::int32_t sum = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i != a.size(); ++i) sum += std::int32_t(a[i]) * std::int32_t(b[i]); return sum; } Nonzero quantization zero points introduce correction terms; bias accumulation and batching may require wider intermediates. Production kernels commonly widen partial products, accumulate into 32 or 64 bits, and requantize with a documented rounding rule. Saturating a too-small accumulator does not make the result safe—it merely turns undefined or wrapped behavior into a silent model error.
Integer SIMD instructions often compute several widened dot products at once. The scalar function above remains the reference for arbitrary lengths; an optimized version processes full vectors and sends the tail through the same scalar arithmetic. Accuracy must then be evaluated on the complete calibrated model, not inferred from one dot product.
 #Benchmarking the Right ThingA reproducible evaluation separates at least three levels:
 kernel: fixed-shape logits, softmax/loss, or gradient accumulation with data already resident; model inference: input preparation, batching, all kernels, and required probability or label output; training: time and resources required to reach a fixed objective or validation target.  Record batch size, classes, features, sparsity, data layout, precision, accumulator width, tail policy, compiler and math flags, ISA target, CPU, and thread count. Fast-math flags may reassociate reductions and change NaN, infinity, and signed-zero behavior; they are part of the numerical method, not merely a speed switch.
Test stable functions on logits around zero, large positive and negative values, and class vectors with wide dynamic range. Check that probabilities are nonnegative and sum close to one, compare losses against a higher-precision reference, and finite-difference-check gradients. For quantized kernels, test the all--128 overflow boundary and compare every vector/tail path with the scalar reference.
The optimization hierarchy is now clear. Remove probability conversion when order alone is required. Make required nonlinear functions stable. Arrange the dot products as matrix-vector or matrix-matrix work with explicit tails. Quantize only with an accumulator proof and an accuracy-validation process. And never report a faster optimizer merely because one iteration became cheaper.
title: Optimizing Logistic Regression

content:
Segment trees are a useful test of data-structure engineering because the asymptotic answer is known before optimization begins. Point updates and range reductions both take $O(\log n)$ time; the interesting questions are how many nodes are touched, how they are laid out, and which operation receives the simpler inner loop.
We start with one precise interface over a zero-initialized array:
 add(i, delta) changes $a_i$ by delta; prefix_sum(k) returns the sum on the half-open range $[0,k)$; range_sum(l,r) returns the sum on $[l,r)$.  Thus prefix_sum(0) and range_sum(k,k) are zero, while prefix_sum(n) includes the entire array. An update requires $i<n$; a query permits an endpoint equal to $n$.
 #Range CoverageA binary segment tree associates every node with a half-open interval. Its two children partition that interval at the midpoint. Any query $[l,r)$ can be represented by $O(\log n)$ disjoint nodes: while moving both endpoints toward their least common ancestor, take a right child exposed on the left boundary and a left child exposed on the right boundary.
 Nodes covering a prefix and a point-update path  The full-coverage test for a node interval $[l_b,r_b)$ is
$$ l\le l_b \quad\text{and}\quad r_b\le r, $$
not a comparison between the node’s right boundary and both query boundaries. Disjointness is $r\le l_b$ or $r_b\le l$. Mixing these predicates was the source of an especially plausible recursive implementation that returned an entire node lying before the query.
For $n>0$, a recursively split tree with exactly the original leaves has $2n-1$ logical nodes. A flat power-of-two layout instead pads to
$$ p=2^{\lceil\log_2 n\rceil} $$
leaves and stores $2p-1$ useful nodes. These are different layouts and should not borrow each other’s size claims.
 #A Bottom-Up Sum TreePadding with zero-valued leaves makes every real leaf occupy p + i and every parent occupy half its child’s index. The standard two-endpoint query then works for every $n$, including non-powers of two, without a special leaf permutation.
The implementation below checks all public bounds. Signed overflow is not allowed to become undefined behavior: construction and queries throw on an unrepresentable result, and an update validates its complete root path before changing any cell.
#include <array>#include <bit>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> std::int64_t checked_add_i64(std::int64_t left, std::int64_t right) { if (right > 0 && left > std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max() - right) throw std::overflow_error("signed sum overflow"); if (right < 0 && left < std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min() - right) throw std::overflow_error("signed sum overflow"); return left + right; } std::int64_t checked_sub_i64(std::int64_t left, std::int64_t right) { if (right > 0 && left < std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min() + right) throw std::overflow_error("signed difference overflow"); if (right < 0 && left > std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max() + right) throw std::overflow_error("signed difference overflow"); return left - right; } class segment_sum_tree { public: explicit segment_sum_tree( std::span<const std::int64_t> values ) : size_(values.size()), base_(choose_base(size_)) { if (base_ > tree_.max_size() / 2) throw std::length_error("segment-tree allocation overflow"); tree_.assign(base_ * 2, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) tree_[base_ + i] = values[i]; for (std::size_t node = base_; node-- > 1;) tree_[node] = checked_add_i64( tree_[node * 2], tree_[node * 2 + 1] ); } void add(std::size_t index, std::int64_t delta) { if (index >= size_) throw std::out_of_range("update index is outside the array"); constexpr std::size_t path_capacity = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::digits + 1; std::array<std::size_t, path_capacity> path{}; std::size_t count = 0; for (std::size_t node = base_ + index; node != 0; node /= 2) path[count++] = node; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) static_cast<void>( checked_add_i64(tree_[path[i]], delta) ); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) tree_[path[i]] = checked_add_i64(tree_[path[i]], delta); } std::int64_t range_sum(std::size_t left, std::size_t right) const { if (left > right || right > size_) throw std::out_of_range("invalid half-open range"); std::size_t first = base_ + left; std::size_t last = base_ + right; std::int64_t left_sum = 0; std::int64_t right_sum = 0; while (first < last) { if ((first & 1U) != 0) left_sum = checked_add_i64(left_sum, tree_[first++]); if ((last & 1U) != 0) right_sum = checked_add_i64(tree_[--last], right_sum); first /= 2; last /= 2; } return checked_add_i64(left_sum, right_sum); } std::int64_t prefix_sum(std::size_t count) const { return range_sum(0, count); } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; } private: static std::size_t choose_base(std::size_t size) { if (size <= 1) return 1; constexpr std::size_t digits = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::digits; constexpr std::size_t largest_safe_base = std::size_t{1} << (digits - 2); if (size > largest_safe_base) throw std::length_error("segment-tree index overflow"); return std::bit_ceil(size); } std::size_t size_; std::size_t base_; std::vector<std::int64_t> tree_; }; The two accumulators preserve left-to-right order. Addition does not need that distinction, but the same loop can support any associative operation with an identity element, including non-commutative ones, if the right accumulator prepends rather than appends its nodes.
The empty tree still owns a two-cell implementation buffer with base = 1. It accepts the empty range and rejects every point update. Treating this small allocation as an implementation detail is simpler than giving zero a fictitious tree height and then subtracting one from it.
 #Fenwick TreesFor prefix sums, many segment-tree values are redundant. A Fenwick tree stores one value for every original element, using one-based index $i$ for the interval
$$ [i-\operatorname{lowbit}(i),,i). $$
Here lowbit(i) is the least significant set bit. With an unsigned index,
class fenwick_sum_tree { public: explicit fenwick_sum_tree(std::size_t size) : size_(size) { if (size_ == std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() || size_ + 1 > tree_.max_size()) throw std::length_error("Fenwick-tree allocation overflow"); tree_.assign(size_ + 1, 0); } void add(std::size_t index, std::int64_t delta) { if (index >= size_) throw std::out_of_range("update index is outside the array"); constexpr std::size_t path_capacity = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::digits + 1; std::array<std::size_t, path_capacity> path{}; std::size_t count = 0; std::size_t node = index + 1; while (node <= size_) { path[count++] = node; const std::size_t step = lowbit(node); if (step > size_ - node) break; node += step; } for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) static_cast<void>( checked_add_i64(tree_[path[i]], delta) ); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) tree_[path[i]] = checked_add_i64(tree_[path[i]], delta); } std::int64_t prefix_sum(std::size_t count) const { if (count > size_) throw std::out_of_range("prefix endpoint is outside the array"); std::int64_t result = 0; for (std::size_t node = count; node != 0; node &= node - 1) result = checked_add_i64(result, tree_[node]); return result; } std::int64_t range_sum(std::size_t left, std::size_t right) const { if (left > right || right > size_) throw std::out_of_range("invalid half-open range"); return checked_sub_i64( prefix_sum(right), prefix_sum(left) ); } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; } private: static std::size_t lowbit(std::size_t value) noexcept { return value & (~value + 1); } std::size_t size_; std::vector<std::int64_t> tree_; }; Unsigned arithmetic makes ~i + 1 well-defined modulo $2^w$. The equivalent signed expression i & -i is safe only after proving that negation cannot overflow. The update also checks step > n - i before adding, so its loop cannot wrap beyond SIZE_MAX.
No power-of-two assumption is needed. The update stops at $n$, and the prefix walk only clears bits of an endpoint already in $[0,n]$:
 Fenwick prefix decomposition   Fenwick update path  A Fenwick range sum subtracts two prefixes. This requires an inverse operation. Integer addition forms a group while representable, and XOR is its own inverse; minimum, maximum, and string concatenation do not have the required inverse. A binary segment tree needs only associativity and an identity—a monoid—so it supports those operations without pretending that one prefix can “cancel” another.
 #Wide Segment TreesA binary tree uses one scalar from each fetched cache line. A wide tree instead groups $B$ children in one node. For dynamic prefix sums, store the $B$ in-node prefixes. A query reads one prefix per level; an update adds its delta to a suffix of every node on the path:
 A wide segment tree groups several children per node  For arbitrary $n$, define $m_0=n$ and
$$ m_{h+1}=\left\lceil\frac{m_h}{B}\right\rceil. $$
One level is allocated for each $m_h>1$, plus the level that directly stores the final group. Replacing the ceiling with m / B undercounts the height whenever a partial group propagates upward—for example, $B^2+1$ elements need three levels, not two.
The following portable implementation stores each level separately. Every physical node has $B$ initialized lanes; lanes beyond the logical tail are zero padding, not nonexistent objects.
template <std::size_t Branch = 16> class wide_prefix_sum_tree { static_assert(Branch >= 2); struct level_data { std::size_t child_count = 0; std::vector<std::int64_t> prefix; }; public: explicit wide_prefix_sum_tree(std::size_t size) : size_(size) { std::size_t children = size_; while (children != 0) { const std::size_t nodes = ceil_div(children, Branch); level_data level; level.child_count = children; if (nodes > level.prefix.max_size() / Branch) throw std::length_error( "wide-tree allocation overflow" ); level.prefix.assign(nodes * Branch, 0); levels_.push_back(std::move(level)); if (nodes == 1) break; children = nodes; } } void add(std::size_t index, std::int64_t delta) { if (index >= size_) throw std::out_of_range("update index is outside the array"); std::size_t child = index; for (const level_data& level : levels_) { const std::size_t node = child / Branch; const std::size_t slot = child % Branch; const std::size_t base = node * Branch; for (std::size_t lane = slot; lane < Branch; ++lane) static_cast<void>(checked_add_i64( level.prefix[base + lane], delta )); child = node; } child = index; for (level_data& level : levels_) { const std::size_t node = child / Branch; const std::size_t slot = child % Branch; const std::size_t base = node * Branch; for (std::size_t lane = slot; lane < Branch; ++lane) level.prefix[base + lane] = checked_add_i64( level.prefix[base + lane], delta ); child = node; } } std::int64_t prefix_sum(std::size_t count) const { if (count > size_) throw std::out_of_range("prefix endpoint is outside the array"); std::int64_t result = 0; std::size_t remaining = count; for (const level_data& level : levels_) { const std::size_t width = remaining % Branch; if (width != 0) { const std::size_t node = remaining / Branch; const std::size_t position = node * Branch + width - 1; result = checked_add_i64( result, level.prefix.at(position) ); } remaining /= Branch; } if (remaining != 0) { if (remaining != 1 || levels_.empty()) throw std::logic_error("invalid wide-tree height"); result = checked_add_i64( result, levels_.back().prefix.back() ); } return result; } std::int64_t range_sum(std::size_t left, std::size_t right) const { if (left > right || right > size_) throw std::out_of_range("invalid half-open range"); return checked_sub_i64( prefix_sum(right), prefix_sum(left) ); } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; } std::size_t height() const noexcept { return levels_.size(); } private: static std::size_t ceil_div(std::size_t value, std::size_t divisor) noexcept { return value / divisor + static_cast<std::size_t>(value % divisor != 0); } std::size_t size_; std::vector<level_data> levels_; }; The query decomposes count into base-$B$ digits. A nonzero digit selects one stored prefix at that level; the final leading digit selects the root total. This handles count == n even when $n$ is an exact power of $B$, a boundary case that disappears if the implementation assumes there is always a partial tail.
For an update at in-node position $k$, the affected prefix lanes are
$$ j\ge k. $$
A mask using $j>k$ misses the prefix ending at the updated element. A SIMD implementation broadcasts the delta, masks with this greater-or-equal suffix, and adds full vectors. The scalar reference uses the same inequality and is suitable as a differential oracle. See SIMD masking, moving data, and horizontal reductions for target-specific implementations.
Padding lanes are deliberately updated when they lie in the suffix. The last physical lane then remains the total of the logical partial node, which is exactly the value its parent needs. No query exposes a padded lane as an array element.
 #Choosing a StructureThe three layouts optimize different things:
 A binary segment tree stores more values but handles any monoid and general ranges directly. A Fenwick tree uses $n+1$ scalars and gives very small loops for an invertible prefix operation. A wide prefix tree shortens the dependency chain, at the cost of updating $B$ lanes per level and storing padded nodes.  The total wide-tree storage is
$$ B\left\lceil\frac{n}{B}\right\rceil +B\left\lceil\frac{\lceil n/B\rceil}{B}\right\rceil+\cdots, $$
which is $O(n)$ but not exactly $nB/(B-1)$ because every partial level rounds up. Its optimal branch factor depends on scalar width, vector ISA, update/query ratio, cache-line size, and contention.
Benchmark half-open boundary cases before timing: $n=0$, $n=1$, $B-1$, $B$, $B+1$, $B^2-1$, $B^2$, and $B^2+1$. Then use randomized differential tests against a plain array. Performance results should report query mix, arithmetic width, overflow policy, compiler target, hardware, and whether timings measure independent throughput or a dependency chain.
The wide-prefix idea is closely related to the layouts evaluated by Pibiri and Venturini in “Practical Trade-Offs for the Prefix-Sum Problem”. Their results motivate the design; they do not replace validation on the machine and workload where the structure will run.

Suppose a request spends most of its time waiting for a database. Replacing an integer division in the response formatter with a shift may produce magnificent assembly and an entirely invisible product improvement.
Performance engineering begins one step before optimization: deciding what is worth making faster.
 #Choose the Objective“Fast” is not a complete requirement. Depending on the application, the quantity we care about may be:
 latency: how long one operation takes; throughput: how many operations finish per unit of time; tail latency: how long an unusually slow operation takes; resource efficiency: CPU time, memory, energy, or money per operation; scalability: how performance changes with input size or load.  These objectives can conflict. Batching requests often improves throughput while delaying the first request in the batch. A lookup table spends memory to save computation. Parallel execution may reduce latency while consuming more total CPU time. Before touching the implementation, write down the workload, the metric, and the constraint that is currently being violated.
Correctness is part of that definition. An optimization measured on convenient inputs but wrong on an edge case is not a faster implementation of the same program; it is a benchmark for a different program.
 #Estimate the CeilingAssume a fraction $f$ of the current running time belongs to a component we can speed up by a factor of $s$. After optimization, the normalized running time is
$$ T’ = (1-f) + \frac{f}{s}, $$
so the total speedup is
$$ S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/s}. $$
This is commonly known as Amdahl’s law. Its most useful feature is not the formula but the disappointment it calculates in advance. If the target occupies 10% of execution time, making it infinitely fast can improve the whole program by at most $1/0.9 \approx 1.11$ times. If the target occupies 90%, even a modest local improvement may matter.
The fraction must be measured on a representative workload. Optimizing the startup path using a profile of a week-long server process is as misguided as optimizing steady-state throughput using only startup measurements.
 #Move Up Before Moving DownOptimization opportunities form a rough hierarchy. Changes near the top tend to be more powerful and more invasive:
 Avoid the work. Cache a result, remove an unnecessary conversion, or stop requesting data that will be discarded. Change the contract or representation. A binary format can be cheaper to parse than JSON; a flat array can be cheaper to traverse than a graph of tiny allocations. Choose a better algorithm. Improve asymptotic work, expected work, or the model that matches the bottleneck, such as I/O complexity. Expose information to the compiler. Use suitable types, remove accidental aliasing, select the target architecture, and enable optimization. Improve the data path. Arrange accesses for locality, remove unpredictable branches, shorten dependency chains, and use SIMD. Tune individual instructions. Only now do instruction selection and hand-written assembly become likely candidates.  This is not a law that forbids working from the bottom. Sometimes the interface is fixed, the algorithm is already optimal, and one instruction really is the bottleneck. The hierarchy is a search order: check high-leverage explanations before spending an afternoon polishing a loop that should not exist.
 #Measure, Explain, ChangeA productive optimization cycle is short:
 Establish a correct baseline and a reproducible benchmark. Use profiling to locate where the relevant resource is spent. Form a mechanism-level hypothesis: cache misses, dependency latency, branch misprediction, excessive work, or something else. Change one important variable. Measure again, including correctness and secondary metrics.  The explanation matters. A faster result without a causal account may be a change in CPU frequency, input distribution, code alignment, or compiler behavior that will disappear in production. Conversely, a good explanation predicts when the optimization should stop helping. A cache-blocking transformation should lose importance when the working set already fits in cache; branch removal should lose to a cheap, predictable branch.
For small kernels, it is useful to compare the measurement with a physical bound. If the loop already consumes nearly all available memory bandwidth, replacing additions with cheaper additions cannot help much. If a dependency chain determines latency, adding execution units does not shorten it. The performance-limits chapter develops this style of accounting.
 #Include the Engineering CostRuntime is not the only scarce resource. An optimization may also cost:
 development and review time; portability across compilers and architectures; readability and future modification speed; test surface and risk of rare failures; binary size or memory; additional operational complexity.  These costs do not imply that low-level code is bad. They imply that it should earn its keep. Isolate architecture-specific kernels behind small interfaces, retain a simple reference implementation for testing, and document the assumptions that make the fast path correct.
The expected value of an optimization is roughly its benefit over the lifetime and scale of the program, discounted by implementation risk. Saving a fraction of a microsecond in a function called trillions of times can justify heroic work. Saving a second in a tool run once during installation may not justify making the installer mysterious.
 #Know When to StopStop when one of the following becomes true:
 the original performance requirement is met with adequate margin; the optimized region is no longer a meaningful part of the profile; another resource has become the bottleneck; expected benefit is smaller than measurement noise or engineering cost; further changes would violate a more important objective.  For important performance properties, turn the stopping point into a regression test. Record the workload and metric, track distributions rather than only the best run, and allow enough tolerance for real machine noise. Performance then becomes a maintained property of the system instead of folklore about a benchmark somebody ran on a laptop three years ago.
Premature optimization is not the act of caring about efficiency early. Choosing compact data structures and avoiding needless work during design is usually cheap. Premature optimization is committing to a complicated solution before establishing that its resource is important. The cure is not indifference; it is measurement and a model.
title: When to Optimize

Algorithms for Modern Hardware is an open-source book by Sergey Slotin about performance engineering and practical algorithm design.
It is intended for readers ranging from undergraduate computer-science students to performance engineers and algorithm researchers: anyone who wants to understand not only how many abstract operations an algorithm performs, but how those operations travel through a modern machine.
The book source is hosted in the Algorithmica repository, with companion experiments in a separate code repository.
FAQBug and typo fixes. The preferred way to report a problem is to fix the source directly through the edit link on each page or open a pull request on GitHub. You can also create an issue or contact the author. A useful technical report includes a minimal counterexample, the affected machine or compiler when relevant, and a primary source.
What does a release mean for an open-source book? The web edition can improve continuously. A release-quality part has all essential sections present, a stable table of contents, completed technical and copyediting passes, reproducible code, cleared illustration rights, and a print-oriented build. Later corrections and changes reflecting new hardware or algorithms can still be incorporated.
Can the web version disappear behind a paywall? The project has committed to keeping the web version freely available. Sharing it and contributing corrections are the most direct ways to support it.
Translations. Independent translations of individual articles are welcome. Because technical chapters evolve, a translation should record the source revision it follows so later corrections can be merged deliberately. The articles at ru.algorithmica.org/cs/ cover mostly classical computer-science algorithms and are not simply a Russian edition of this performance-engineering part.
Why teach performance engineering after algorithms? The standard asymptotic model remains indispensable, but computers have changed substantially since the canonical algorithm textbooks were written. Modern algorithm design also has to account for parallel execution inside a core, memory hierarchy, vector instructions, compilation, and the real input range. Courses such as MIT’s Performance Engineering of Software Systems, Aalto University’s Programming Parallel Computers, and the independent Performance Ninja curriculum demonstrate how these topics can be taught systematically.
Part I: Performance EngineeringPart I covers the architecture and optimization of single-threaded CPU algorithms. Short examples introduce caching, instruction-level parallelism, arithmetic transformations, profiling, compilation, and SIMD. Larger case studies then combine these mechanisms in complete algorithms and data structures.
Measured speedups in the case studies are evidence from the named processor, compiler, and workload—not promises for every machine. The durable result is the causal explanation and the method used to reproduce it.

Conditionals Functions and Recursion Indirect Branching Machine Code Layout Interrupts and System Calls Virtualization   Instruction-Level Parallelism  Pipeline Hazards The Cost of Branching Code Analyzers Benchmarking Getting Accurate Results   Arithmetic  Floating-Point Numbers and IEEE 754 Rounding and Interval Arithmetic Newton’s Method Fast Inverse Square Root Integers Integer Division Bit Manipulation Data Compression   Number Theory  Modular Arithmetic, Binary Exponentiation, and the Extended Euclidean Algorithm Montgomery Multiplication Finite Fields Error Correction Blending In-Register Shuffles Auto-Vectorization and SPMD   Algorithm Case Studies  Binary GCD Prime Number Sieves Integer Factorization Logistic Regression Big Integers and Karatsuba Multiplication concludes with a performance engineering checklist and a probability and measurement appendix.
Later PartsThe broader roadmap includes parallel algorithms; distributed systems and communication-constrained algorithms; and the software–hardware boundary, including compiler back ends, JIT compilation, GPUs, FPGAs, and specialized accelerators. These subjects remain separate from Part I’s single-threaded completion boundary.
AcknowledgementsThe book builds on research papers, manuals, talks, articles, and implementations by many people. Particularly influential sources include the work of Agner Fog, Daniel Lemire, Andrei Alexandrescu, Chandler Carruth, Wojciech Muła, Malte Skarupke, Travis Downs, Brendan Gregg, Andreas Abel, Pat Morin, Victor Eijkhout, Robert van de Geijn, Peter Cordes, Geoff Langdale, Matt Kulukundis, Denis Bakhvalov, Paul Khuong, Matt Pharr, Jan Wassenberg, Marshall Lochbaum, Pavel Zemtsov, Gustavo Duarte, and the many other authors cited in individual chapters.
Technology ChoicesExamples primarily use C++, GCC or Clang, and x86-64 because they expose the mechanisms under discussion and are widely available. The principles are broader than this stack; the exact instructions, ABI, compiler behavior, and performance figures are not.

content:
Most good software engineering practices in one way or another address the issue of making development cycles faster: you want to compile your software faster (build systems), catch bugs as soon as possible (static analysis, continuous integration), release as soon as the new version is ready (continuous deployment), and react to user feedback without much delay (agile development).
Performance engineering is not different. If you do it correctly, it should also resemble a cycle:
 Run the program and collect metrics. Figure out where the bottleneck is. Remove the bottleneck and go to step 1.  In this section, we will discuss practical benchmarking techniques that make this cycle shorter. Many examples of these setups live in the book’s code repository.
 #Benchmarking Inside C++There are several approaches to writing benchmarking code. Perhaps the most popular one is to include several same-language implementations you want to compare in one file, separately invoke them from the main function, and calculate all the metrics you want in the same source file.
The disadvantage of this method is that you need to write a lot of boilerplate code and duplicate it for each implementation, but it can be partially neutralized with metaprogramming. For example, when you are benchmarking multiple gcd implementations, you can reduce benchmarking code considerably with this higher-order function:
const int N = 1e6, T = 1e9 / N; int a[N], b[N]; void timeit(int (*f)(int, int)) { clock_t start = clock(); int checksum = 0; for (int t = 0; t < T; t++) for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= f(a[i], b[i]); double seconds = double(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC; printf("checksum: %d\n", checksum); printf("%.2f ns per call\n", 1e9 * seconds / N / T); } int main() { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = rand(), b[i] = rand(); timeit([](int a, int b) { return std::gcd(a, b); }); timeit(my_gcd); timeit(my_another_gcd); // ...  return 0; } This compact method lets you run many experiments and get more accurate results. A call through a function pointer may itself matter for a very small function, although whole-program optimization can sometimes specialize it. Benchmarking frameworks handle this and other details more systematically; Google Benchmark is a popular C++ choice. Some languages also provide dedicated tools, such as Python’s timeit and Julia’s @benchmark.
Although efficient in terms of execution speed, C and C++ are not the most productive languages, especially when it comes to analytics. When your algorithm depends on some parameters such as the input size, and you need to collect more than just one data point from each implementation, you really want to integrate your benchmarking code with the outside environment and analyze the results using something else.
 #Splitting Up ImplementationsOne way to improve modularity and reusability is to separate all testing and analytics code from the actual implementation of the algorithm, and also make it so that different versions are implemented in separate files, but have the same interface.
In C/C++, you can do this by creating a single header file (e.g., gcd.hh) with a function interface and all its benchmarking code in main:
int gcd(int a, int b); // to be implemented  // for data structures, you also need to create a setup function // (unless the same preprocessing step for all versions would suffice)  int main() { const int N = 1e6, T = 1e9 / N; int a[N], b[N]; // careful: local arrays are allocated on the stack and may cause stack overflow  // for large arrays, allocate with "new" or create a global array  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = rand(), b[i] = rand(); int checksum = 0; clock_t start = clock(); for (int t = 0; t < T; t++) for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= gcd(a[i], b[i]); double seconds = double(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC; printf("%d\n", checksum); printf("%.2f ns per call\n", 1e9 * seconds / N / T); return 0; } Then you create many implementation files for each algorithm version (e.g., v1.cc, v2.cc, and so on, or some meaningful names if applicable) that all include that single header file:
#include "gcd.hh" int gcd(int a, int b) { if (b == 0) return a; else return gcd(b, a % b); } The whole purpose of doing this is to be able to benchmark a specific algorithm version from the command line without touching any source code files. For this purpose, you may also want to expose any parameters that it may have — for example, by parsing them from the command line arguments:
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { int N = (argc > 1 ? atoi(argv[1]) : 1e6); if (N <= 0 || N > 1'000'000'000) return 1; const int T = 1'000'000'000 / N; // ... } Another way is to use a preprocessor definition and pass it with -DN=... during compilation:
#ifndef N #define N 1000000 #endif  const int T = 1e9 / N; This way you can make use of compile-time constants, which may be very beneficial for the performance of some algorithms, at the expense of having to re-build the program each time you want to change the parameter, which considerably increases the time you need to collect metrics across a range of parameter values.
 #MakefilesSplitting source files also lets an incremental build system such as Make rebuild only targets whose prerequisites changed.
I usually carry a version of this Makefile across my projects:
compile := g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native -Wall %: %.cc gcd.hh $(compile) $< -o $@ %.s: %.cc gcd.hh $(compile) -S -fverbose-asm $< -o $@ %.run: % FORCE @./$< .PHONY: FORCE FORCE: You can now compile example.cc with make example, and automatically run it with make example.run.
You can also add scripts for calculating statistics in the Makefile, or incorporate it with perf stat calls to make profiling automatic.
 #Jupyter NotebooksTo speed up high-level analytics, you can create a Jupyter notebook where you put all your scripts and do all the plots.
It is convenient to add a wrapper for benchmarking an implementation, which just returns a scalar result:
def bench(source, n=2**20): !make -s {source} if _exit_code != 0: raise Exception("Compilation failed") res = !./{source} {n} if _exit_code != 0 or not res: raise Exception("Benchmark failed") duration = float(res[-1].split()[0]) return duration Then you can use it to write clean analytics code:
ns = list(int(1.17**k) for k in range(30, 60)) baseline = [bench('std_lower_bound', n=n) for n in ns] results = [bench('my_binary_search', n=n) for n in ns] # plotting relative speedup for different array sizes import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.plot(ns, [x / y for x, y in zip(baseline, results)]) plt.show() Once established, this workflow makes you iterate much faster and focus on optimizing the algorithm itself.
title: Benchmarking

content:
Machine integers have a useful property: their cost does not depend on their value. Arbitrary-precision integers give up that abstraction. Adding a thousand-limb number touches a thousand limbs; multiplying two of them creates a small algorithm-selection problem.
This chapter builds a nonnegative big integer from first principles. We begin with a normalized limb representation and schoolbook multiplication, derive Karatsuba’s three-product identity, and add a crossover that preserves the fast base case for small and strongly unbalanced operands.
The implementation is educational rather than a replacement for GMP. It nevertheless has a precise domain, checked size arithmetic, defined carry bounds, canonical zero, and a differential-testable C++20 core.
 #Limbs and InvariantsChoose a base $B$ that fits one limb and store
$$ x = x_0 + x_1B + x_2B^2 + \cdots + x_{n-1}B^{n-1} $$
in little-endian order. We use uint32_t limbs and $B=10^9$. Decimal conversion is convenient, and a limb product plus two carry-sized terms fits in uint64_t:
$$ (B-1)^2+(B-1)+(B-1)<10^{18}+2\cdot10^9<2^{64}. $$
Every object maintains three invariants:
 each limb is smaller than $B$; the most significant stored limb is nonzero; zero is represented by an empty limb vector.  The last two make equality, comparisons, and recursion boundaries unambiguous. Every arithmetic helper normalizes before returning; “we will remove leading zeros later” is how noncanonical zeros escape into the rest of a library.
#include <algorithm>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <iomanip>#include <limits>#include <sstream>#include <span>#include <stdexcept>#include <string>#include <utility>#include <vector> class big_uint { static constexpr std::uint64_t base = 1'000'000'000ULL; std::vector<std::uint32_t> limb_; // least significant first  void normalize() { while (!limb_.empty() && limb_.back() == 0) limb_.pop_back(); } static int compare(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b) { if (a.limb_.size() != b.limb_.size()) return a.limb_.size() < b.limb_.size() ? -1 : 1; for (std::size_t i = a.limb_.size(); i != 0; --i) if (a.limb_[i - 1] != b.limb_[i - 1]) return a.limb_[i - 1] < b.limb_[i - 1] ? -1 : 1; return 0; } static big_uint add(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b) { big_uint result; std::size_t n = std::max(a.limb_.size(), b.limb_.size()); if (n == result.limb_.max_size()) throw std::length_error("big integer is too large"); result.limb_.reserve(n + 1); std::uint64_t carry = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i != n; ++i) { std::uint64_t current = carry; if (i < a.limb_.size()) current += a.limb_[i]; if (i < b.limb_.size()) current += b.limb_[i]; result.limb_.push_back(std::uint32_t(current % base)); carry = current / base; } if (carry != 0) result.limb_.push_back(std::uint32_t(carry)); return result; } // Precondition: a >= b.  static big_uint subtract(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b) { if (compare(a, b) < 0) throw std::logic_error("negative big_uint subtraction"); big_uint result; result.limb_.resize(a.limb_.size()); std::int64_t borrow = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i != a.limb_.size(); ++i) { std::int64_t current = std::int64_t(a.limb_[i]) - borrow; if (i < b.limb_.size()) current -= b.limb_[i]; if (current < 0) { current += std::int64_t(base); borrow = 1; } else { borrow = 0; } result.limb_[i] = std::uint32_t(current); } result.normalize(); return result; } static big_uint slice(const big_uint &x, std::size_t first, std::size_t last) { big_uint result; if (first >= x.limb_.size()) return result; last = std::min(last, x.limb_.size()); result.limb_.assign(x.limb_.begin() + first, x.limb_.begin() + last); result.normalize(); return result; } static big_uint shifted(const big_uint &x, std::size_t limbs) { if (x.limb_.empty()) return {}; big_uint result; if (limbs > result.limb_.max_size() - x.limb_.size()) throw std::length_error("big integer shift is too large"); result.limb_.assign(limbs, 0); result.limb_.insert(result.limb_.end(), x.limb_.begin(), x.limb_.end()); return result; } static big_uint schoolbook(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b) { if (a.limb_.empty() || b.limb_.empty()) return {}; big_uint result; if (b.limb_.size() >= result.limb_.max_size() || a.limb_.size() > result.limb_.max_size() - b.limb_.size() - 1) throw std::length_error("big integer product is too large"); result.limb_.assign(a.limb_.size() + b.limb_.size() + 1, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != a.limb_.size(); ++i) { std::uint64_t carry = 0; for (std::size_t j = 0; j != b.limb_.size(); ++j) { std::uint64_t current = result.limb_[i + j] + std::uint64_t(a.limb_[i]) * b.limb_[j] + carry; result.limb_[i + j] = std::uint32_t(current % base); carry = current / base; } std::size_t k = i + b.limb_.size(); while (carry != 0) { std::uint64_t current = result.limb_[k] + carry; result.limb_[k] = std::uint32_t(current % base); carry = current / base; ++k; } } result.normalize(); return result; } static big_uint karatsuba(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b, std::size_t crossover) { if (a.limb_.empty() || b.limb_.empty()) return {}; std::size_t small = std::min(a.limb_.size(), b.limb_.size()); std::size_t large = std::max(a.limb_.size(), b.limb_.size()); // Karatsuba's additions and allocations lose on small operands.  // A balanced split also matters: use the base case when one side is  // more than twice as long as the other.  if (small < crossover || large - small > small) return schoolbook(a, b); std::size_t split = large / 2; big_uint a0 = slice(a, 0, split); big_uint a1 = slice(a, split, a.limb_.size()); big_uint b0 = slice(b, 0, split); big_uint b1 = slice(b, split, b.limb_.size()); big_uint z0 = karatsuba(a0, b0, crossover); big_uint z2 = karatsuba(a1, b1, crossover); big_uint z1 = karatsuba(add(a0, a1), add(b0, b1), crossover); z1 = subtract(subtract(z1, z0), z2); big_uint low_and_middle = add(z0, shifted(z1, split)); return add(low_and_middle, shifted(z2, 2 * split)); } public: big_uint() = default; explicit big_uint(std::uint64_t value) { while (value != 0) { limb_.push_back(std::uint32_t(value % base)); value /= base; } } static big_uint from_limbs(std::span<const std::uint32_t> limbs) { big_uint result; for (std::uint32_t limb : limbs) if (limb >= base) throw std::invalid_argument("limb exceeds representation base"); result.limb_.assign(limbs.begin(), limbs.end()); result.normalize(); return result; } std::string to_string() const { if (limb_.empty()) return "0"; std::ostringstream out; out << limb_.back(); for (std::size_t i = limb_.size() - 1; i != 0; --i) out << std::setw(9) << std::setfill('0') << limb_[i - 1]; return out.str(); } static big_uint multiply(const big_uint &a, const big_uint &b, std::size_t crossover = 32) { if (crossover < 2) throw std::invalid_argument("Karatsuba crossover is too small"); return karatsuba(a, b, crossover); } friend bool operator==(const big_uint &, const big_uint &) = default; }; The code supports nonnegative integers only. from_limbs validates every limb and canonicalizes any high zero limbs, which is useful for binary deserialization and tests. A signed big integer should store sign separately, keep zero signless, and multiply magnitudes before combining signs. Mixing sign into the top limb makes normalization and comparison considerably harder.
 #Schoolbook MultiplicationFor limb arrays $a$ and $b$, schoolbook multiplication evaluates
$$ c_{i+j}\mathrel{+}=a_i b_j $$
for every pair of limbs, propagating the base-$B$ carry after each inner iteration. Its $nm$ limb products give $O(nm)$ running time and a wonderfully compact hot loop.
The accumulator bound is part of the representation choice. With $B=10^9$, current is safely below $2^{64}$. If we changed to base $2^{32}$ and kept the same expression, the limb product alone could require all 64 bits, leaving no room for an existing result and carry. Such a representation normally uses a 128-bit intermediate or a multiply instruction that exposes high and low halves.
Schoolbook multiplication has strong locality and little control overhead. For small inputs it beats asymptotically faster methods because the compiler can keep the carry chain and several limbs in registers. It is not a temporary “slow implementation”; it remains the leaf kernel of a fast big-integer library.
 #Karatsuba’s IdentitySplit balanced operands after $k$ limbs:
$$ x=x_0+B^k x_1,\qquad y=y_0+B^k y_1. $$
Expanding directly requires four half-size products. Karatsuba observes that the middle coefficient can be recovered with one product:
$$ \begin{aligned} z_0 &= x_0y_0,\ z_2 &= x_1y_1,\ z_1 &= (x_0+x_1)(y_0+y_1)-z_0-z_2,\ xy &= z_0+B^kz_1+B^{2k}z_2. \end{aligned} $$
The recurrence
$$ T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n) $$
solves to $O(n^{\log_2 3})\approx O(n^{1.585})$. The original result was published by Karatsuba and Ofman in Multiplication of Many-Digital Numbers by Automatic Computers.
Our implementation uses nonnegative sums. Mathematically, z1 is the sum of the two cross products, so both checked subtractions are valid. Normalizing each recursive result is essential: split positions count limbs, and a stray high zero would change balance decisions and termination.
 #The crossover is empiricalKaratsuba replaces one recursive multiplication with several additions, slices, shifts, and temporary allocations. It wins only above a machine- and implementation-specific size. The default of 32 limbs in the example is a policy value, not a published constant.
Benchmark a range of balanced operand sizes, locate a stable crossover, and retune after changing the base-case kernel, allocator, limb width, or CPU. The official GNU MP multiplication documentation uses tuned thresholds between schoolbook, Karatsuba, Toom variants, and FFT multiplication; its Karatsuba notes explain why optimizing the base case can move the threshold upward.
Unbalanced operands need separate treatment. Splitting a 32-limb value against a 10,000-limb value creates many zero high halves and temporary work. The code deliberately returns to schoolbook multiplication when one operand is more than twice as long as the other. Production libraries use blocked base cases or specialized unbalanced Toom algorithms.
 #Mapping Multiplication to HardwareThe base-case inner loop has two dependency chains: the carry and repeated updates to the destination. Useful optimizations include:
 accumulating several output diagonals independently; unrolling to overlap multiply latency; using the target’s full-width multiply-high/low operations; separating allocation from arithmetic and reusing scratch buffers; specializing squaring, where cross products occur in symmetric pairs.  Naively vectorizing limb products does not solve carry propagation. SIMD can generate several partial products, but those products still need exact column accumulation. Wider vector lanes are most useful when paired with a redundant representation, delayed normalization, or an instruction set designed for multi-precision arithmetic.
Karatsuba is more sensitive to memory management than its recurrence suggests. The self-contained code allocates at every slice and addition so the invariants are obvious. A performance implementation passes preallocated scratch space through the recursion and writes shifted results directly into the destination. That changes constants, not the algebra.
 #Conversion and Other OperationsBase $10^9$ makes decimal output simple: print the high limb normally and every lower limb as exactly nine digits. Parsing can consume groups of nine decimal digits with
$$ x\leftarrow 10^9x+g, $$
using a multiply-by-one-limb and add-one-limb primitive. Binary bases make shifts, bit operations, and division normalization easier. The right base follows the surrounding workload.
Addition, subtraction, comparison, and multiplication are not a complete integer type. Division, modular reduction, parsing errors, allocation limits, signed semantics, and exception guarantees need equally explicit contracts. Cryptographic code additionally needs constant-time control flow and memory access; this teaching implementation does not provide it.
 #Validation and BenchmarkingDifferential-test the complete decimal result against a mature arbitrary-precision implementation. Include zero, one, values exactly at limb boundaries, long runs of base - 1, unequal sizes, leading-zero-producing subtractions inside Karatsuba, and sizes immediately around the crossover. Random testing should vary both values and limb counts.
Useful algebraic properties include
$$ x(y+z)=xy+xz,\qquad xy=yx,\qquad x\cdot0=0, $$
although a shared bug in addition can make the first property less independent than it looks. Sanitizers are valuable for size and indexing errors; a big-integer oracle is still needed for arithmetic truth.
For performance, report operand limb counts and balance, representation base, crossover, allocation policy, whether operands are equal, and whether conversion is timed. Benchmark cold one-shot products separately from repeated products with reusable scratch storage. Plot schoolbook and Karatsuba across the crossover instead of timing one conveniently large input.
The important transition is not “quadratic bad, Karatsuba good.” It is a hierarchy: canonical limbs make the arithmetic trustworthy, a tight schoolbook kernel wins the small regime, and Karatsuba earns its extra machinery only where three recursive products finally cost less than four.
title: Big Integers and Karatsuba Multiplication

content:
The integers modulo $m$ look almost like ordinary numbers. We can add, subtract, and multiply them, but division is troublesome: modulo $10$, there is no value $x$ for which $2x \equiv 1$. The element $2$ has no multiplicative inverse because it shares a factor with the modulus.
When the modulus is prime, this obstruction disappears. Every nonzero residue has an inverse, algebra works the way we expect, and a finite set of integers becomes a field. More surprisingly, prime moduli are only the beginning: fields can also contain $p^k$ elements for any prime $p$ and positive integer $k$. The power-of-two cases fit computer words especially well and power everything from error-correcting codes to cryptographic instructions.
 #From Rings to FieldsA group is a set with one associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for every element. A ring has addition and multiplication: addition forms a commutative group, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition. A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element also has a multiplicative inverse.
The residues modulo $m$, written $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$, always form a ring. They form a field exactly when $m$ is prime. If $p$ is prime and $a \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, then $\gcd(a,p)=1$, so the extended Euclidean algorithm finds $x$ and $y$ such that
$$ ax + py = 1. $$
Reducing the equation modulo $p$ gives $ax \equiv 1$, making $x$ the inverse of $a$. We denote this field by $\mathbb F_p$ or $GF(p)$.
This distinction matters in code. Overflowing an 8-bit integer performs arithmetic modulo $2^8$, but $\mathbb Z/256\mathbb Z$ is not a field: every even element lacks an inverse. A field with 256 elements exists, but it needs a different multiplication.
 #Polynomials as NumbersStart with the smallest field, $\mathbb F_2={0,1}$, where addition and subtraction are both XOR. Now consider polynomials whose coefficients come from $\mathbb F_2$:
$$ a(x)=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots. $$
Because each coefficient is one bit, a polynomial of degree below $k$ fits naturally in a $k$-bit integer. Bit $i$ stores the coefficient of $x^i$. Polynomial addition is therefore exactly bitwise XOR—there are no carries.
Polynomial multiplication is ordinary convolution with coefficients reduced modulo two. If we multiplied without another rule, degrees would keep growing and the set would not be finite. We make it finite by choosing a degree-$k$ polynomial $P(x)$ and reducing products modulo $P(x)$, just as integer arithmetic reduces modulo an integer.
There is one essential condition: $P$ must be irreducible over $\mathbb F_2$, meaning that it cannot be factored into lower-degree nonconstant polynomials. Then
$$ \mathbb F_2[x] / (P(x)) $$
is a field with $2^k$ elements. If $P$ were reducible, its factors would become nonzero elements whose product is zero, and neither could have an inverse.
The same construction works over any prime field. For every prime power $q=p^k$, a field with $q$ elements exists, and any two fields of that size are isomorphic. The selected irreducible polynomial changes the bit-level representation, however, so implementations must agree on it.
 #A Field in One ByteAES specifies arithmetic in $GF(2^8)$ using
$$ P(x)=x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1, $$
represented as 0x11b. The current AES standard, FIPS 197, defines this representation explicitly.
Multiplying a field element by $x$ shifts its polynomial left by one. If the old coefficient of $x^7$ was set, the shift creates an $x^8$ term. From $P(x)=0$ inside the quotient field,
$$ x^8 = x^4+x^3+x+1, $$
so we remove the high term and XOR the low byte 0x1b. This operation is often called xtime.
#include <cstdint>#include <optional> std::uint8_t gf256_xtime(std::uint8_t x) { const bool high_bit = (x & 0x80u) != 0; x = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(x << 1); return static_cast<std::uint8_t>(x ^ (high_bit ? 0x1bu : 0u)); } std::uint8_t gf256_multiply(std::uint8_t a, std::uint8_t b) { std::uint8_t result = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) { if ((b & 1u) != 0) result = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(result ^ a); b = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(b >> 1); a = gf256_xtime(a); } return result; } std::uint8_t gf256_power(std::uint8_t a, unsigned exponent) { std::uint8_t result = 1; while (exponent != 0) { if ((exponent & 1u) != 0) result = gf256_multiply(result, a); a = gf256_multiply(a, a); exponent >>= 1; } return result; } std::optional<std::uint8_t> gf256_inverse(std::uint8_t a) { if (a == 0) return std::nullopt; return gf256_power(a, 254); } The inverse uses the fact that the 255 nonzero elements form a multiplicative group. For nonzero $a$,
$$ a^{255}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a^{-1}=a^{254}. $$
This reference implementation is deliberately direct: eight iterations per multiplication, with the reduction visible. It is useful for tests and for understanding the representation. It is not automatically the fastest way to process a large buffer.
 #Multiplication as Carryless ArithmeticNormal binary multiplication combines partial products with integer addition, propagating carries. Polynomial multiplication over $\mathbb F_2$ combines them with XOR instead. It is therefore often called carryless multiplication.
There are several implementation strategies:
 shift and XOR, as above, has constant storage and predictable work; logarithm and exponent tables turn multiplication into two lookups and an addition modulo $255$, but require special handling for zero and create data-dependent memory accesses; a full multiplication table needs $256^2$ bytes for a byte field, not 256 bytes; bitslicing stores the same bit position from many independent values together and evaluates field operations with Boolean instructions; carryless-multiply instructions produce a wider polynomial product that is then reduced modulo $P$; x86 GFNI instructions directly perform selected byte-field multiplications and affine transformations.  The Intel Intrinsics Guide documents PCLMULQDQ and the GF2P8... instruction families. Their presence changes the best representation, but not the field being computed. A table can win for a few scalar operations and lose for parallel workloads because of cache traffic; a bitsliced or instruction-based version does more Boolean work while processing many values at once. As usual, benchmark the complete algorithm on the intended target.
For security-sensitive code, table lookups indexed by secret data can also leak through the cache. Use a vetted constant-time implementation or dedicated instructions rather than turning this educational code into a cipher implementation.
 #Roots, Evaluation, and ApplicationsThe nonzero elements of a finite field form a cyclic multiplicative group. If the field has $q$ elements, that group has order $q-1$. Consequently, the equation
$$ x^n=1 $$
has exactly $\gcd(n,q-1)$ solutions in the field. When $n$ divides $q-1$, these roots of unity support Fourier-like transforms over finite fields without floating-point rounding.
Finite fields also make polynomial evaluation unusually powerful. A polynomial of degree below $k$ is uniquely determined by its values at any $k$ distinct field points. If we evaluate it at more than $k$ points, the extra values are redundant and can recover missing or corrupted ones—the central idea behind Reed–Solomon codes.
The same algebra appears in several performance-critical systems:
 AES uses $GF(2^8)$ in its byte transformations; authenticated encryption uses large binary fields, while CRCs use closely related polynomial arithmetic; storage systems use field-valued erasure codes to reconstruct lost fragments; number-theoretic transforms use suitable prime fields for exact convolution; cryptographic protocols use arithmetic in prime fields and extension fields.  The representation changes from one application to another, but the design questions stay the same: which field is required, how are its elements encoded, which operations dominate, and which kind of parallelism the hardware exposes. Once those are explicit, finite-field arithmetic stops being mysterious—it becomes another carefully chosen machine representation.
 #Further ReadingThe algebra used by AES is specified in FIPS 197. For the coding-theory application, the original paper by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon, “Polynomial Codes over Certain Finite Fields”, is remarkably short and remains a useful next step.
title: Finite Fields

content:
Masks select lanes without changing their order. Shuffles go further: they copy or rearrange elements inside a vector. No single x86 instruction implements every possible permutation at every element width. Some shuffles use an immediate pattern, some take vector indices, and many AVX2 byte shuffles operate independently in two 128-bit lanes.
Two examples show why these details matter: table-driven population count and stable filtering.
 #Scalar Population CountPopulation count, or Hamming weight, is the number of one bits. C++20 exposes it as std::popcount; GCC and Clang also provide built-ins:
std::uint64_t popcount_words(const std::uint64_t *data, std::size_t n) { std::uint64_t total = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) total += std::popcount(data[i]); return total; } When compiled with the x86 POPCNT feature, this usually becomes one scalar popcnt per word plus accumulation. POPCNT has its own CPUID bit; it is not “an SSE4 instruction,” even though it appeared in processors of a similar era. A dispatched implementation should test popcnt separately.
Without POPCNT, a byte lookup table is a useful intermediate design:
constexpr std::array<std::uint8_t, 256> make_popcount_table() { std::array<std::uint8_t, 256> table{}; for (std::size_t value = 0; value < table.size(); ++value) table[value] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>( std::popcount(static_cast<unsigned>(value))); return table; } inline constexpr auto byte_popcount = make_popcount_table(); std::uint64_t popcount_bytes_table(const std::uint8_t *data, std::size_t bytes) { std::uint64_t total = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < bytes; ++i) total += byte_popcount[data[i]]; return total; } This avoids signed right shifts and pointer punning. It also exposes the next optimization: put a smaller table in a vector register.
 #Nibble Lookup with pshufbSSSE3 introduced the 128-bit pshufb byte shuffle. AVX2 _mm256_shuffle_epi8 applies the same 16-entry lookup independently to the low and high 128-bit lanes, so a 16-byte table must be repeated:
const __m256i lookup = _mm256_setr_epi8( 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4, 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4); Split every byte into low and high nibbles, look up both counts, and add them. A byte lane can then increase by at most 8 per vector, so at most
$$ \left\lfloor\frac{255}{8}\right\rfloor=31 $$
vectors may accumulate before widening. The old 15-iteration bound was both arithmetically wrong and tied to an invalid loop shape.
std::uint64_t popcount_avx2(const std::uint8_t *data, std::size_t bytes) { const __m256i lookup = _mm256_setr_epi8( 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4, 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4); const __m256i low_nibble = _mm256_set1_epi8(0x0f); const __m256i zero = _mm256_setzero_si256(); __m256i wide_total = zero; std::size_t i = 0; while (i + 32 <= bytes) { const std::size_t blocks = std::min<std::size_t>(31, (bytes - i) / 32); __m256i byte_count = zero; for (std::size_t block = 0; block < blocks; ++block) { const __m256i x = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(data + i + 32 * block)); const __m256i low = _mm256_and_si256(x, low_nibble); const __m256i high = _mm256_and_si256( _mm256_srli_epi16(x, 4), low_nibble); byte_count = _mm256_add_epi8( byte_count, _mm256_shuffle_epi8(lookup, low)); byte_count = _mm256_add_epi8( byte_count, _mm256_shuffle_epi8(lookup, high)); } wide_total = _mm256_add_epi64( wide_total, _mm256_sad_epu8(byte_count, zero)); i += 32 * blocks; } alignas(32) std::array<std::uint64_t, 4> partial{}; _mm256_store_si256( reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(partial.data()), wide_total); std::uint64_t total = std::accumulate( partial.begin(), partial.end(), std::uint64_t{0}); for (; i < bytes; ++i) total += std::popcount(static_cast<unsigned>(data[i])); return total; } The loop advances in bytes, loads exactly 32 bytes per vector, and handles every remaining byte scalarly. It requires AVX2 at compile time and runtime; the equivalent 128-bit lookup only requires SSSE3. The historical Zen 2 implementation processed about 30 input bytes per cycle, but modern AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ or BITALG implementations and other processors have different best kernels.
Wojciech Muła’s SIMD popcount repository and the associated Harley–Seal paper cover several stronger algorithms.
 #Stable Filtering with a Permutation TableA stable filter writes values satisfying a predicate in their original order:
std::size_t filter_scalar(const std::int32_t *input, std::size_t n, std::int32_t threshold, std::int32_t *output) { std::size_t written = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (input[i] < threshold) output[written++] = input[i]; return written; } For eight AVX2 lanes there are only 256 possible comparison masks. Precompute, for each mask, the indices of selected lanes followed by harmless zeros:
struct alignas(32) PermutationTable { std::array<std::array<std::int32_t, 8>, 256> row{}; constexpr PermutationTable() { for (std::size_t mask = 0; mask < row.size(); ++mask) { std::size_t out = 0; for (std::int32_t lane = 0; lane < 8; ++lane) if (mask & (std::size_t{1} << lane)) row[mask][out++] = lane; } } }; inline constexpr PermutationTable permutation{}; _mm256_permutevar8x32_epi32 copies lanes according to eight vector indices. Duplicates are allowed, so “permute” is broader here than a mathematical permutation:
