std::size_t filter_avx2(const std::int32_t *input, std::size_t n, std::int32_t threshold, std::int32_t *output) { const __m256i limit = _mm256_set1_epi32(threshold); std::size_t written = 0; std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 8 <= n; i += 8) { __m256i value = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(input + i)); const __m256i selected = _mm256_cmpgt_epi32(limit, value); const unsigned mask = static_cast<unsigned>( _mm256_movemask_ps(_mm256_castsi256_ps(selected))); const __m256i order = _mm256_load_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(permutation.row[mask].data())); value = _mm256_permutevar8x32_epi32(value, order); _mm256_storeu_si256( reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(output + written), value); written += std::popcount(mask); } for (; i < n; ++i) if (input[i] < threshold) output[written++] = input[i]; return written; } The output allocation must contain at least n elements. That is enough for every full store: before the block at i, written <= i, hence the eight-lane store ends no later than i + 7 < n. The scalar tail avoids an input overread and needs no extra padding. The unused lanes written after the valid prefix are overwritten by a later block or remain outside the returned prefix.
 Historical scalar and AVX2 filtering measurements  The original Zen 2 result was roughly 6–7 times faster for its random predicate, while predictable scalar branches narrowed the gap. Port pressure and shuffle throughput are processor-specific, so retain the result as historical evidence rather than predicting another x86 core from it.
AVX-512F provides compress instructions and mask registers that remove the 256-row table. A compress-store writes only selected lanes contiguously, and an AVX-512 masked tail can avoid scalar cleanup. It still requires runtime dispatch, sufficient output capacity, and the precise AVX-512 features used by that implementation.
title: In-Register Shuffles

content:
A normal branch says where it is going in its own machine code. An indirect branch takes the destination from a register or memory location:
jmp rax call QWORD PTR [rdi] This small difference lets us implement switch tables, function pointers, interpreters, and runtime polymorphism. It also creates a harder prediction problem: the processor must guess not only whether a branch is taken, but which of many possible addresses comes next.
 #Jump TablesConsider a dense switch:
int classify(unsigned x) { switch (x) { case 0: return 11; case 1: return 19; case 2: return 23; case 3: return 31; default: return -1; } } For a tiny example the compiler may discover a formula or use a table of results. When each case contains real code, a common implementation is a jump table: check that x is in range, load the x-th destination from an array, and jump there.
cmp edi, 3 ja default lea rax, [rip + table] jmp QWORD PTR [rax + rdi * 8] This dispatch takes constant time regardless of the number of cases. A chain of comparisons can be better when cases are sparse or one value is overwhelmingly common, so compilers choose between trees, tables, and arithmetic using density and profile information.
An indirect jump is not automatically mispredicted. Modern processors maintain target-prediction structures, and a stable sequence—an interpreter repeatedly executing the same opcode pattern, for example—can be learned. Unpredictable target changes are the expensive case because a wrong target sends the front-end down the wrong instruction stream and later forces it to discard that work.
 #Function PointersA function pointer separates an operation from the code that invokes it:
using operation = float (*)(float); float map_sum(const float* a, int n, operation op) { float sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) sum += op(a[i]); return sum; } The indirect call happens once per element, so it can easily cost more than the operation itself. More importantly, the compiler usually cannot inline op, which blocks simplification and SIMD vectorization across the call.
If the operation is fixed for the whole array, moving dispatch outward helps. A caller can select one specialized loop once, or make the operation a template parameter so the target is known during compilation. If each element genuinely needs a different operation, the indirection is part of the problem rather than syntactic overhead.
 #Virtual FunctionsC++ virtual dispatch is normally implemented with the same mechanism. Here is a valid class hierarchy:
#include <cstdio> struct Animal { virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual void speak() const = 0; }; struct Dog final : Animal { void speak() const override { std::puts("Bark"); } }; struct Cat final : Animal { void speak() const override { std::puts("Meow"); } }; In common ABIs, each polymorphic object contains a hidden pointer called a vptr. It points to a virtual table containing function pointers in fixed slots. A call such as
void announce(const Animal& animal) { animal.speak(); } is conceptually implemented as:
; rdi = &animal mov rax, QWORD PTR [rdi] ; load vptr call QWORD PTR [rax + SLOT] ; call the speak entry Derived methods are not padded to equal machine-code lengths and are not stored consecutively inside every object. The fixed-size part is the table entry: one pointer per virtual slot. The object usually pays one vptr, while each class contributes a table and its actual method bodies elsewhere in the binary.
Virtual dispatch therefore has several possible costs:
 one or more dependent loads to find the target; an indirect call that may be mispredicted when object types vary; loss of inlining and the optimizations it would expose; extra object and table storage.  The last two are often more important than the call instruction itself. If speak performs milliseconds of I/O, dispatch is irrelevant. If a virtual method adds two floats inside a loop, it is probably the entire bottleneck.
Compilers can devirtualize a call when they prove the dynamic type—for example, when a class is final, construction is visible, or whole-program analysis finds only one target. Profile-guided optimization can also specialize a common type and retain a fallback for the rest.
 #Data Layout Still WinsA heterogeneous array of pointers creates two independent problems: indirect control flow and pointer chasing. Even perfect branch prediction cannot make scattered objects contiguous in cache.
For data-oriented workloads, it is often better to group objects by type and process each group with a direct loop. This converts many per-object decisions into one outer decision and usually improves both instruction and data locality. The representation is less flexible for frequent type changes, which is the trade-off the virtual interface was designed to avoid.
Indirect branching is a powerful tool, not a performance defect. Use it at coarse boundaries where flexibility matters, and try not to hide two arithmetic instructions behind it a billion times per second.
title: Indirect Branching

content:
Consider the following function:
#include <cstdint> std::uint64_t f(std::uint64_t a, std::uint64_t b, std::uint64_t c, std::uint64_t d) { return (a + 1) * (b + 1) + (c + 1) * (d + 1); } Written as a sentence, it appears to request four additions, then one multiplication, then another multiplication, then a final addition. The data dependencies tell a different story. The two products are independent: either can be computed first, and on a suitable processor they can progress at the same time. Only the final addition needs both.
Modern CPUs schedule the dependency graph, not the punctuation of the source code.
 #From Instructions to OperationsThe front-end fetches and decodes machine instructions. On x86, many instructions translate into one or more simpler internal operations, commonly called micro-operations or uops. A register addition may become one uop; a read-modify-write instruction may require address generation, a load, arithmetic, and a store; sufficiently complex instructions may be supplied by a microcode sequencer.
This does not mean that the x86 instruction set is secretly replaced with one universal internal language. Uop formats and fusion rules are properties of a particular microarchitecture. The useful abstraction is merely that execution resources usually schedule finer-grained operations than the assembly listing suggests.
Decoded uops enter a bounded out-of-order part of the core. Names vary between vendors and generations, but the mechanism has a few recurring pieces:
 register renaming creates a new physical destination for each register-writing operation; a reorder buffer tracks operations in program order; scheduling queues hold operations until their inputs and an appropriate execution resource are available; load and store queues track memory operations; completed operations retire in program order.  The Intel optimization manual documents concrete instances of these structures. Their exact sizes and grouping are implementation details; code should not assume that every x86 CPU has one scheduler with the same shape.
 #Register RenamingAn architectural register such as rax is a name in the instruction-set interface, not necessarily one fixed storage cell throughout execution. Suppose three instructions successively assign rax. The renamer can map their results to three physical registers and remember which version each later input needs.
This removes two kinds of false dependency:
 write after read: a later write need not wait merely because an older operation still needs the previous value; write after write: two outputs can be computed independently and made visible in the required order later.  A true read-after-write dependency remains. Renaming can give (a + 1) and (c + 1) different homes, but it cannot multiply a + 1 by b + 1 before either value exists.
Renaming is also finite. Every in-flight destination consumes a physical register until the old mapping can be reclaimed. Excessive unrolling can exhaust this and other bookkeeping capacity even when the source language offers an unlimited supply of variable names.
 #Wake Up, Select, ExecuteAfter dispatch, an operation waits until its input operands are ready. It then becomes a candidate for an execution resource capable of handling it. Each cycle, scheduling logic selects from the ready candidates, subject to issue width and resource availability.
This is dynamic scheduling: the decision reflects events only known at runtime, such as cache hits, cache misses, and the actual progress of older operations. If one product in our example waits for an operand while the other is ready, the ready product may issue first even if it appeared later in machine code.
Execution resources are commonly connected through ports or similar routing structures. Different uops can use different subsets of them. Two instructions with equal latency may therefore have very different effects on throughput: one may have several eligible units, while another monopolizes a single specialized unit. This is why an instruction table needs both latency and reciprocal throughput, and why port pressure matters for loops.
The scheduler is not omniscient. It sees only operations already admitted to its finite window. A long dependency chain, full reorder buffer, exhausted load queue, or unresolved branch can prevent useful future work from entering the window.
 #Memory SchedulingRegisters carry explicit dependencies; memory addresses must be compared or predicted.
Stores are kept until the processor can make them architecturally visible in the required order. Loads may execute before older stores when the processor determines, or predicts, that their addresses do not overlap. If an address later proves the prediction wrong, dependent operations are replayed.
There is another useful kind of speculation here. A cache miss does not normally stop all execution. Independent loads and arithmetic can continue while the missing line is requested. This memory-level parallelism is limited by dependencies and by finite tracking structures. Pointer chasing performs poorly because each missing load reveals the address of the next one too late to overlap them.
Memory-ordering rules, fences, device memory, and atomic operations impose additional constraints. Static analyzers often model only a subset of them, so a beautifully scheduled report is not evidence that the cache will cooperate.
 #Retirement and Precise StateIf operations execute out of order, why do exceptions not expose a half-finished future?
The processor separates execution from retirement. Results can be computed and forwarded speculatively, but operations retire in program order. If a branch was mispredicted or an older instruction faults, younger operations can be discarded before their speculative state becomes architecturally visible. The machine then appears to have executed up to one precise point in the original instruction stream.
Stores require special care because writing cache-visible memory is difficult to undo. Their addresses and data may be prepared early, but ordinary stores are committed only when they are safe to retire.
In-order retirement is itself a finite resource. A slow old instruction can occupy the head of the reorder buffer while many younger instructions have finished behind it. Once the window fills, the front-end must wait even if execution units would otherwise be available.
 #The Compiler’s PartHardware scheduling is automatic, but software determines which opportunities it can see.
The compiler can reorder independent instructions, unroll loops, use several accumulators, and choose instructions with suitable resource usage. It can do this only when language rules and alias information prove the transformation correct. A possible pointer overlap or strict floating-point order may create dependencies at compile time even when a particular dataset would have allowed more freedom.
The processor then adapts the resulting instruction stream to runtime events. These roles complement each other:
 the compiler has broad program context but limited runtime information; the CPU has exact runtime timing but only a small future window.  Hand scheduling every instruction is rarely useful on out-of-order CPUs, and a sequence tuned for one core may be poor on another. The durable goal is to expose independent work without creating excessive code size, register pressure, or memory traffic.
For a small loop, llvm-mca can estimate dependencies, reciprocal throughput, and resource pressure using LLVM’s processor scheduling models. Its own documentation is explicit about the limitations: the default analysis does not model instruction fetch, branch prediction, or real cache behavior. Use it to test a scheduling hypothesis, then verify that hypothesis with measurements on the target machine.
Once independent operations are available, the next question is how many parallel chains are required to keep a pipelined execution unit busy. That is the subject of throughput computing.
title: Instruction Scheduling

content:
If you are reading this chapter sequentially from the beginning, you might be wondering: why would I introduce integer arithmetic after floating-point one? Isn’t it supposed to be easier?
True: plain integer representations are simpler. But, counterintuitively, their simplicity allows for more possibilities for operations to be expressed in terms of others. And if floating-point representations are so unwieldy that most of their operations are implemented in hardware, efficiently manipulating integers requires much more creative use of the instruction set.
 #Binary FormatsUnsigned integers are just natural numbers written in binary:
$$ \begin{aligned} 5_{10} &= 101_2 = 4 + 1 \ 42_{10} &= 101010_2 = 32 + 8 + 2 \ 256_{10} &= 100000000_2 = 2^8 \end{aligned} $$
When the result of an operation can’t fit into the word size (e.g., is more or equal to $2^{32}$ for 32-bit unsigned integers), it overflows by leaving only the lowest 32 bits of the result. Similarly, if the result is a negative value, it underflows by adding it to $2^{32}$, so that it always stays in the $[0, 2^{32})$ range.
This is equivalent to performing all operations modulo a power of two:
$$ \begin{aligned} 256 &\equiv 0 \pmod {2^8} \ 2021 &\equiv 229 \pmod {2^8} \ -42 \equiv 256 - 42 &\equiv 214 \pmod {2^8} \end{aligned} $$
In either case, it raises a special flag which you can check, but usually when people explicitly use unsigned integers, they are expecting this behavior.
 #Signed IntegersSigned integers support storing negative values by dedicating the highest bit to represent the sign of the number, in a similar fashion as floating-point numbers do. This halves the range of representable non-negative numbers: the maximum possible 32-bit integer is now $(2^{31}-1)$ and not $(2^{32}-1)$. But the encoding of negative values is not quite the same as for floating-point numbers.
Computer engineers are even lazier than programmers — and this is not only motivated by the instinctive desire for simplification, but also by saving transistor space. This can be achieved by reusing circuitry that you already have for other operations, which is what they aimed for when designing the signed integer format:
 For an $n$-bit signed integer type, the encodings of all numbers in the $[0, 2^{n-1})$ range remain the same as their unsigned binary representations. All numbers in the $[-2^{n-1}, 0)$ range are encoded sequentially right after the “positive” range — that is, starting with $(-2^{n - 1})$ that has code $(2^{n-1})$ and ending with $(-1)$ that has code $(2^n - 1)$.  One way to look at this is that all negative numbers are just encoded as if they were subtracted from $2^n$ — an operation known as two’s complement:
$$ \begin{aligned} -x &= 2^{32} - x \ &= \bar{x} + 1 \end{aligned} $$
Here $\bar{x}$ represents bitwise negation, which can be also thought of as subtracting $x$ from $(2^n - 1)$.
As an exercise, here are some facts about signed integers:
 All positive numbers and zero remain the same as their binary notation. All negative numbers have the highest bit set to one. There are more negative numbers than positive numbers (exactly by one — because of zero). At the hardware bit-pattern level, adding one to the largest two’s-complement pattern wraps to the most negative pattern. In C and C++, however, overflowing a signed int is undefined behavior; use an unsigned type when modular wraparound is intended. Knowing a binary notation of a positive number x, you can get the binary notation of -x as ~x + 1. -1 is represented as ~1 + 1 = 11111110 + 00000001 = 11111111. -42 is represented as ~42 + 1 = 11010101 + 00000001 = 11010110. The number -1 = 11111111 is followed by 0 = -1 + 1 = 11111111 + 00000001 = 00000000.  The main advantage of this encoding is that you don’t have to do anything to convert unsigned integers to signed ones (except maybe check for overflow), and you can reuse the same circuitry for most operations, possibly only flipping the sign bit for comparisons and such.
That said, you need to be careful with signed integer overflows. Even though they almost always overflow the same way as unsigned integers, programming languages usually consider the possibility of overflow as undefined behavior. If you need to overflow integer variables, convert them to unsigned integers: it’s free anyway.
Exercise. Why can std::abs(INT_MIN) not produce a representable int result? In C++, evaluating that case has undefined behavior rather than a specified wrapped answer.
 #Integer TypesIntegers come in different sizes, but all function roughly the same.
   Bits Bytes Signed C type Unsigned C type Assembly     8 1 signed char1 unsigned char byte   16 2 short unsigned short word   32 4 int unsigned int dword   64 8 long long unsigned long long qword    Endianness is the order of bytes within a multi-byte value, not the order of bits inside each byte. The 32-bit value 42 has bytes 2a 00 00 00 in little-endian memory and 00 00 00 2a in big-endian memory. A one-byte value has no endianness.
Ordinary arithmetic and numeric casts operate on values and normally hide this distinction. Endianness becomes visible when bytes are reinterpreted directly: binary file formats, network protocols, hashing, serialization, and low-level SIMD shuffles all need a specified byte order. Truncating a register value is also not the same operation as loading the first bytes of its in-memory representation; compilers select the correct instructions for the target architecture.
Most desktop and server systems are little-endian, network byte order is conventionally big-endian, and some architectures can operate in either mode. Portable code should convert explicitly at the boundary rather than infer a machine’s order from pointer casts.
 #128-bit IntegersSometimes we need to multiply two 64-bit integers to get a 128-bit integer — usually to serve as a temporary value and be reduced modulo a 64-bit integer right away.
General-purpose x86-64 registers are 64 bits wide, but the one-operand forms of mul (unsigned) and imul (signed) produce a full 128-bit result. They multiply rax by their operand and write the low and high halves to rax and rdx:
; input: 64-bit integers a and b, stored in rsi and rdi ; output: 128-bit product a * b, stored in rax (lower 64-bit) and rdx (higher 64-bit) mov rax, rdi imul rsi Some compilers have a separate type supporting this operation. In GCC and Clang it is available as __int128:
void prod(int64_t a, int64_t b, __int128 *c) { *c = a * (__int128) b; } Its typical use case is to immediately extract either the lower or the higher part of the multiplication and forget about it:
__int128_t x = 1; int64_t hi = x >> 64; int64_t lo = (int64_t) x; // will be just truncated For all purposes other than multiplication, 128-bit integers are just bundled as two registers. This makes it too weird to have a full-fledged 128-bit type, so the support for it is limited, other than for basic arithmetic operations. For example:
__int128_t add(__int128_t a, __int128_t b) { return a + b; } is compiled into:
add: mov rax, rdi add rax, rdx ; this sets the carry flag in case of an overflow adc rsi, rcx ; +1 if the carry flag is set mov rdx, rsi ret Other platforms provide similar mechanisms for dealing with longer-than-word multiplication. AArch64 uses mul for the low half and umulh or smulh for the unsigned or signed high half; x86 SIMD extensions have related narrower-lane operations.
  Note that char, unsigned char, and signed char are technically three distinct types. The C standard leaves it up to the implementation whether the plain char is signed or unsigned (on most compilers, it is signed). ↩︎
title: Integers

content:
A linked list is easy to traverse and difficult to lay out. If successor nodes occupy unrelated blocks, following $N$ pointers can cause $\Theta(N)$ I/Os even though the records themselves occupy only $\Theta(N/B)$ blocks.
List ranking converts that pointer structure into numeric positions without assuming that list order matches storage order.
 #Define the Rank FirstLet every record contain a unique identifier, a successor identifier or null, and a nonnegative edge weight $w(v)$. The records must form one acyclic chain with exactly one head and one tail.
This chapter defines the rank as weighted distance from a node to the tail:
$$ \operatorname{rank}(\text{tail})=0, $$
and for every other node
$$ \operatorname{rank}(v) =w(v)+\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{next}(v)). $$
Use the harmless convention $w(\text{tail})=0$.
For an unweighted list, set every non-tail edge weight to one. The rank is then the number of links after the node: the tail has rank zero, its predecessor has rank one, and the head has rank $N-1$. This convention is different from a prefix position measured from the head, so an implementation must not alternate between the two.
Before ranking untrusted records, validate the structural contract. Duplicate identifiers, multiple predecessors, missing successors, multiple components, or a cycle make the recurrence undefined or describe a different problem.
 #Pointer Jumping as a BaselinePointer jumping stores for each node a current successor $s_i(v)$ and accumulated distance $d_i(v)$. Initially,
$$ s_0(v)=\operatorname{next}(v), \qquad d_0(v)=w(v). $$
One round joins every record with its current successor and doubles the covered distance:
$$ \begin{aligned} d_{i+1}(v) &= d_i(v)+d_i(s_i(v)),\ s_{i+1}(v) &= s_i(s_i(v)). \end{aligned} $$
The tail contributes zero, and a null successor remains null. After $\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$ rounds, every node has jumped to the tail and $d_i(v)$ is its rank.
With records sorted by identifier, each round can be implemented as a sort–merge join. It is parallel and conceptually clean, but it costs
$$ O(\operatorname{Sort}(N)\log N) $$
I/Os because all $N$ records participate in every round. Randomized contraction removes this extra logarithm.
 #Contract an Independent SetAssign an independent random bit $b(v)$ to every node. Keep the head and tail, and select an internal node $v$ for removal when
$$ b(v)=1 \quad\text{and}\quad b(\operatorname{next}(v))=0. $$
Two consecutive nodes cannot both satisfy the rule: the shared bit would need to be both zero and one. Each eligible internal node is selected with probability $1/4$, so the expected remaining list has at most $3N/4+O(1)$ nodes.
Suppose selected node $v$ lies between retained nodes $u$ and $x$:
$$ u\xrightarrow{,w(u),}v \xrightarrow{,w(v),}x. $$
Contract it by replacing the two edges with
$$ \operatorname{next}’(u)=x, \qquad w’(u)=w(u)+w(v). $$
The weighted distance from $u$ to the tail is unchanged. Store the restoration record $(v,x,w(v))$, recurse on the contracted list, and reconstruct the removed rank with
$$ \operatorname{rank}(v) =w(v)+\operatorname{rank}(x). $$
The independent-set property guarantees that $u$ and $x$ survived this level, so both contraction and restoration use one retained neighbor on each required side.
 #Performing a Level with SortsThe list is stored as tables keyed by node identifier, not as in-memory pointers. A contraction level consists of a constant number of bulk operations:
 sort records by successor identifier to attach each successor’s random bit; mark the independent set and emit restoration records; join selected nodes with their predecessors; rewrite the retained predecessor’s successor and weight; after recursion, join restoration records with successor ranks.  Each operation is a scan, external sort, or merge join, so a level on $n$ records costs $O(\operatorname{Sort}(n))$ I/Os. The expected recurrences are
$$ W(N)\le W(3N/4+O(1))+O(N)=O(N) $$
for ordinary work and
$$ Q(N)\le Q(3N/4+O(1)) +O(\operatorname{Sort}(N)) =O(\operatorname{Sort}(N)) $$
for I/O. The sorting costs decrease geometrically with the contracted input sizes; they are not paid on the original $N$ records for every recursion level.
This result is expected because the contraction size is random. The random bits must come from a generator suitable for randomized algorithms, and a production pipeline should make the seed reproducible for debugging.
 #Why It Is a PrimitiveMany external-memory graph algorithms first express an irregular structure as linked records and then rank or prefix-sum that list. For a tree Euler tour, represent each traversal of a directed edge as one list item, link each item to the next traversal, break the resulting cycle at a chosen root position, and rank the list. The ranks give the tour order without chasing tree pointers in that order.
Weighted ranking also supplies suffix sums. Prefix positions follow from the total weight and a node’s suffix rank once the edge convention is fixed. Similar contraction ideas underlie tree contraction and parallel expression evaluation.
The randomized list-ranking primitive is used in the original work on external-memory graph algorithms. Its broader lesson is useful on its own: when pointer order is hostile to storage order, replace pointer chasing with sorting and joining on stable identifiers.
title: List Ranking

content:
A core can have several cache misses in flight at once. This overlap is called memory-level parallelism (MLP). It is why a linear scan can approach bandwidth, while one dependent pointer-chasing chain pays almost the full latency of every miss.
MLP counts outstanding misses, not arbitrary loads and stores. A hundred loads that all hit L1 are not a hundred concurrent memory misses, and two requests can be in flight without the DRAM chips literally servicing them at the same instant. The core, cache hierarchy, and memory controller queue and overlap different stages.
The amount of concurrency required to sustain a bandwidth follows Little’s law. If a level supplies $B$ bytes per second, a miss returns $L$ seconds after issue, and each miss transfers a line of $S$ bytes, then the average number of line fills in flight at saturation is approximately
$$ Q = \frac{B \cdot L}{S}. $$
 Bandwidth-delay product inferred from the historical latency and bandwidth curves  This bandwidth-delay product is the concurrency needed for the measured rate, not a specification of the maximum MLP available to one core. The maximum can instead be limited by load buffers, line-fill or miss-status entries, the reorder window, translation resources, cache queues, DRAM banks, and requests generated by prefetchers. Many of these limits are undocumented or count different kinds of request.
 #Independent ChainsWe can expose MLP by chasing $D$ independent random cycles. Each lane is internally serial, but different lanes can miss concurrently. A flat allocation avoids non-standard variable-length arrays:
template <std::size_t D> std::uint64_t chase(const std::vector<std::uint32_t> &next, std::size_t length, std::size_t rounds) { std::array<std::uint32_t, D> state{}; for (std::size_t r = 0; r < rounds; ++r) for (std::size_t i = 0; i < length; ++i) for (std::size_t d = 0; d < D; ++d) state[d] = next[d * length + state[d]]; return std::accumulate(state.begin(), state.end(), std::uint64_t{0}); } Each row next[d * length ... (d + 1) * length) must first be initialized as one permutation cycle. Instantiate the template separately for each $D$ so the compiler can unroll the lane loop, and inspect the assembly. If state spills to the stack, the benchmark is measuring those extra cache accesses as well as the intended chains.
Keeping the total number of nodes $D \cdot \text{length}$ fixed produced the following historical graph:
 Several independent dependent-load streams  Throughput initially rises because another chain hides part of the previous chain’s latency. It eventually plateaus. In the original runtime-loop implementation, register pressure caused spills near that plateau, so the graph cannot identify a clean hardware limit of “13–17 memory lanes.” It measures the complete generated loop on that compiler and Zen 2 system.
A stronger experiment uses compile-time lane counts, verifies that each state remains in a register, reports cache-miss counters, and repeats with hardware prefetchers controlled where the platform permits it. The plateau can still represent several limits at once: issue bandwidth for the loads, tracking entries in one cache level, TLB misses, or the memory controller.
MLP is an algorithmic resource. Batch independent queries, use several traversal lanes, or rearrange data so that future addresses become known early. But concurrency is not free: more lanes consume registers and queues, and beyond saturation they add no throughput while increasing cache and bandwidth pressure.
title: Memory-Level Parallelism

content:
Consider two perfectly reasonable ways of storing a matrix:
std::vector<std::vector<float>> a(n, std::vector<float>(m)); std::vector<float> b(n * m); Both let us address an element using two indices. Both take $O(nm)$ space. Both can be hidden behind an interface called Matrix. But only one is actually a matrix in memory.
The first representation contains $n$ separately allocated vectors. Reading a[i][j] first loads the pointer to row $i$ and only then loads the element. Rows are not guaranteed to be adjacent, and constructing or destroying the matrix performs $n+1$ allocations. The second representation is one contiguous allocation, and b[i * m + j] needs no pointer chase.
This is the uncomfortable part of the phrase zero-cost abstraction: the compiler can remove the syntax of an abstraction, but it cannot remove the semantics we asked for. Separate growable rows really do require separate objects. Reference counting really does require updating counters. Runtime polymorphism really does require choosing an implementation at runtime.
Abstractions are not the enemy. Unexamined contracts are.
 #What “Zero Cost” MeansThe useful interpretation of a zero-cost abstraction has two parts:
 You do not pay for a feature you do not use. When you use it, the generated code should be no worse than a careful direct implementation with the same semantics.  Templates are a good example. A generic min does not need to be slower than a handwritten comparison:
template <class T> constexpr const T& min(const T& a, const T& b) { return b < a ? b : a; } After instantiation and inlining, the type machinery disappears. This is also approximately how the ordinary two-argument std::min works. Its initializer-list overload is a different operation: it searches an arbitrary-length list and therefore has different semantics and a different cost.
The compiler is very good at erasing names, wrappers, iterators, and small functions. It is much less successful at erasing allocations, pointer topology, aliasing possibilities, and decisions that are deliberately postponed until runtime.
 #Views Instead of ContainersWe can keep the contiguous representation and recover the convenient two-dimensional interface with a view:
#include <cassert>#include <cstddef> template <class T> struct matrix_view { T* data; std::size_t rows, cols, stride; constexpr T& operator()(std::size_t i, std::size_t j) const noexcept { return data[i * stride + j]; } constexpr matrix_view submatrix(std::size_t i, std::size_t j, std::size_t h, std::size_t w) const { assert(i + h <= rows && j + w <= cols); return {data + i * stride + j, h, w, stride}; } }; The view owns nothing. It is just a pointer and three integers describing how to interpret somebody else’s memory. In an optimized build, operator() is normally inlined into the same multiply-add address calculation we would have written by hand. A submatrix is created without copying any elements or allocating memory.
This distinction between storage and view is broadly useful. std::span, std::string_view, iterators, and tensor views all exist to let algorithms operate on data without inheriting the allocation policy of its owner.
There is still a cost: passing the dimensions consumes registers, and a dynamic stride requires a multiplication. If dimensions are known at compile time, making them template parameters may remove even that. If they are not, no abstraction can honestly pretend that they are.
 #Runtime PolymorphismAn indirect call through a virtual function, function pointer, or type-erased wrapper has two main costs:
 the target may not be known early enough to inline the call; changing targets may make indirect branch prediction difficult.  This does not mean that every virtual call causes a branch misprediction. A call site that repeatedly sees one type is usually easy to predict, and compilers can sometimes devirtualize a call when whole-program information proves its target. The expensive case is a small operation invoked in a hot heterogeneous loop, where both inlining and prediction matter.
When the set of implementations is known at compile time, static polymorphism moves the choice out of runtime:
template <class Operation> float transform_sum(const float* a, std::size_t n, Operation op) { float sum = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) sum += op(a[i]); return sum; } The compiler sees Operation while instantiating the function and can inline it into the loop. This often enables further simplification and vectorization.
The trade-off is code size: instantiating the same large function for many operations duplicates machine code, increasing compilation time and putting more pressure on the instruction cache. Runtime dispatch can therefore be faster when it keeps a large program compact. Performance engineering is rude to slogans in both directions.
 #Hidden WorkSome abstractions carry work that is easy to overlook because it is not visible at the call site.
Allocation. Growing a std::vector, constructing a node-based container, or storing a large callable in std::function may allocate. An allocation is not merely a function call: it modifies allocator metadata, may synchronize with other threads, and can eventually ask the operating system for more pages. Reuse buffers or use an arena when object lifetimes permit it.
Shared ownership. Copying a std::shared_ptr updates a reference count, commonly with atomic operations. This is required by its cross-thread ownership contract. If ownership is unique or borrowed, express that instead.
Type erasure. std::function, trait objects, and interface objects are useful because they can hold unrelated implementations behind one type. That generally requires indirect dispatch and may prevent inlining. A plain template parameter makes a different promise and gives the optimizer more information.
Safety checks. Bounds and validity checks consume instructions only when the compiler cannot prove them redundant. In a canonical loop, a check may be hoisted or eliminated completely; in irregular control flow, it may remain. Removing a check manually is only an optimization if its precondition is enforced somewhere else.
Conversions and temporaries. A clean-looking expression may construct intermediate strings, vectors, or arbitrary-precision values. Move semantics remove many copies, but they do not remove the work required to create the intermediate result in the first place.
 #Moving the BoundaryWhen an abstraction is expensive, the first instinct is often to delete it from the entire program. Usually only the hot loop needs attention.
A more maintainable approach is to move the abstraction boundary outward:
 Keep parsing, ownership, validation, and dynamic dispatch at the edge. Convert the data once into a compact representation. Pass a simple view to a small computational kernel. Convert the result back only if the caller needs it.  This design is common in databases, numerical libraries, interpreters, and graphics engines. Their outer layers may be highly generic while their inner loops look suspiciously like C. The two styles are not in conflict: the outer abstraction exists partly to protect the invariants that make the inner code fast.
Before replacing a high-level component, inspect optimized assembly or compiler IR and measure the whole application. If the wrapper inlines away, there is nothing to fix. If it does not, identify which promise blocks the optimization: layout, aliasing, ownership, dispatch, error handling, or code size. Then change that promise deliberately.
The best abstraction is not the one with the fewest characters in its implementation. It is the one whose cost model is visible from its interface.
title: Non-Zero-Cost Abstractions

content:
Staring at the source code or its assembly is a popular, but not the most effective way of finding performance issues. When the performance doesn’t meet your expectations, you can identify the root cause much faster using one of the special program analysis tools collectively called profilers.
There are many different types of profilers. I like to think about them by analogy of how physicists and other natural scientists approach studying small things, picking the right tool depending on the required level of precision:
 When objects are on a micrometer scale, they use optical microscopes. When objects are on a nanometer scale, and light no longer interacts with them, they use electron microscopes. When objects are smaller than that (e.g., the insides of an atom), they resort to theories and assumptions about how things work (and test these assumptions using intricate and indirect experiments).  Similarly, there are several complementary profiling techniques, each operating by different principles and answering different questions:
 Instrumentation lets you time the program as a whole or by parts and count specific events you are interested in. Statistical profiling lets you go down to the assembly level and track various hardware events such as branch mispredictions or cache misses, which are critical for performance. Program simulation runs code under a software model, which can count modeled cache accesses and branch predictions deterministically. Machine-code analysis estimates dependency and execution-resource limits for a small assembly block without modeling the surrounding program.  Practical algorithm design is an empirical field too. Modern computers are too complicated for one model to capture every interaction, and some microarchitectural details are intentionally undocumented. Measurements and reverse-engineered resources therefore complement, rather than replace, vendor documentation.
In this chapter, we will study these methods and some time-tested practices for managing performance experiments.
title: Profiling

content:
A comparison tree learns one bit of order at each branch. A trie consumes one symbol of the query.
For a set of strings, this changes the natural complexity from “number of keys times comparison cost” to the length of the queried prefix. It also creates a hardware problem: the textbook implementation allocates one node per prefix and follows a dependent pointer for every byte. The asymptotic improvement can disappear into memory latency.
This case study keeps the trie semantics and changes the representation.
 #The Dense BaselineFor an alphabet of 26 lowercase letters, the direct implementation stores one child index for every possible next character:
#include <array>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <stdexcept>#include <string_view>#include <vector> struct DenseNode { std::array<int32_t, 26> child; bool terminal = false; DenseNode() { child.fill(-1); } }; class DenseTrie { std::vector<DenseNode> nodes{1}; public: void insert(std::string_view key) { uint32_t node = 0; for (char raw : key) { uint8_t c = static_cast<uint8_t>(static_cast<unsigned char>(raw)); if (c < 'a' || c > 'z') throw std::invalid_argument("DenseTrie expects lowercase ASCII"); uint32_t label = c - 'a'; int32_t next = nodes[node].child[label]; if (next == -1) { if (nodes.size() > std::size_t(std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max())) throw std::length_error("DenseTrie index does not fit"); next = int32_t(nodes.size()); nodes[node].child[label] = next; nodes.emplace_back(); } node = uint32_t(next); } nodes[node].terminal = true; } }; Lookup is excellent: one range check, one indexed load, and one dependent transition per character. Storage is not. DenseNode uses at least 105 bytes even if it has one child, and most nodes in a string trie have only one or two. Expanding the alphabet to all 256 byte values makes the waste absurd.
Replacing the array with a hash table saves empty slots but adds a separate allocation, hash computation, and more pointer chasing per node. A sorted vector of (label, child) pairs is compact, but every node needs an offset and a search over its outgoing labels.
The right choice depends on the degree distribution. We will build a static representation that keeps one small fixed-size bitmap per node and packs all child nodes into one array.
 #A Bitmap Is an IndexFor a byte alphabet, store a 256-bit bitmap saying which outgoing labels exist. If the children of one node are placed contiguously in label order, the child for byte $c$ has index
$$ \mathtt{first_child} +\operatorname{rank}(c), $$
where rank(c) is the number of set bits with labels smaller than $c$. Four 64-bit words and a few popcount operations replace 256 child pointers.
The representation is immutable: insertion happens in a convenient temporary tree, followed by a packing pass. Static dictionaries are common in routers, parsers, language models, and search indexes, so trading update support for compact lookup is often reasonable.
#include <array>#include <bit>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <map>#include <stdexcept>#include <string_view>#include <vector> class PackedByteTrie { struct Node { std::array<uint64_t, 4> labels{}; uint32_t first_child = 0; bool terminal = false; }; std::vector<Node> nodes; static bool has_label(const Node& node, uint8_t c) { return (node.labels[c / 64] >> (c % 64)) & 1; } static uint32_t rank_before(const Node& node, uint8_t c) { const unsigned word = c / 64; const unsigned bit = c % 64; uint32_t rank = 0; for (unsigned i = 0; i < word; ++i) rank += uint32_t(std::popcount(node.labels[i])); uint64_t lower = node.labels[word] & ((uint64_t(1) << bit) - 1); return rank + uint32_t(std::popcount(lower)); } public: PackedByteTrie() : nodes(1) {} static PackedByteTrie build(const std::vector<std::string_view>& keys) { struct Temporary { std::map<uint8_t, uint32_t> child; bool terminal = false; }; std::vector<Temporary> temporary(1); for (std::string_view key : keys) { uint32_t node = 0; for (char raw : key) { uint8_t c = static_cast<uint8_t>(static_cast<unsigned char>(raw)); auto it = temporary[node].child.find(c); if (it == temporary[node].child.end()) { if (temporary.size() >= std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max()) throw std::length_error("PackedByteTrie index does not fit"); uint32_t next = uint32_t(temporary.size()); temporary[node].child.emplace(c, next); temporary.emplace_back(); node = next; } else { node = it->second; } } temporary[node].terminal = true; } PackedByteTrie result; result.nodes.reserve(temporary.size()); std::vector<uint32_t> source{0}; // `source[p]` identifies the temporary node represented by nodes[p].  for (std::size_t p = 0; p < source.size(); ++p) { const Temporary& old = temporary[source[p]]; Node& packed = result.nodes[p]; packed.terminal = old.terminal; packed.first_child = uint32_t(result.nodes.size()); for (auto [label, child] : old.child) { packed.labels[label / 64] |= uint64_t(1) << (label % 64); result.nodes.emplace_back(); source.push_back(child); } } return result; } bool contains(std::string_view key) const { uint32_t node = 0; for (char raw : key) { uint8_t c = static_cast<uint8_t>(static_cast<unsigned char>(raw)); const Node& current = nodes[node]; if (!has_label(current, c)) return false; node = current.first_child + rank_before(current, c); } return nodes[node].terminal; } }; The shift in rank_before is safe when bit==0: shifting by zero produces one, and subtracting one produces an empty mask. It never shifts by 64.
The packing loop is breadth-first. When node p is processed, all of its children are appended consecutively and in the order supplied by std::map, so first_child + rank is valid. Reserving the known final node count also keeps the packed reference valid while those children are appended.
 #Following the Dependency ChainPacking reduces bytes, but lookup still has one true dependency per input character: the current node determines where the next node lives. Out-of-order execution cannot overlap a single query very far.
There are three ways to find more parallelism:
 look up several independent strings together; compress chains of one-child nodes so one transition compares several bytes; store frequently used shallow levels in a dense or direct-indexed form.  Batching is the least invasive. Four simultaneous queries create four independent node streams, letting the core overlap cache misses. This improves throughput, not the latency of one query.
Path compression produces a radix tree: an edge is labeled by a string rather than one byte. It saves unary nodes and turns several dependent loads into a contiguous comparison. The new branch must store an edge offset and length, and insertion becomes more complicated because an edge may need to split.
PATRICIA applies the same compression to bitwise tries. Adaptive Radix Trees go further by choosing different node layouts for 4, 16, 48, or 256 children. Sparse nodes stay compact; dense nodes retain constant-time indexing. This is a recurring data-structure pattern: represent different degree regimes differently instead of forcing one layout to serve all of them.
 #Prefix QueriesExact membership is only the simplest trie operation. To find every key with prefix pre, follow the prefix to one node and enumerate its descendants. The breadth-first layout above keeps siblings together, not entire subtrees, so descendant enumeration jumps around.
If prefix scans dominate, pack nodes in depth-first order and store each node’s subtree interval, or keep terminal key identifiers in lexicographic order. The prefix then maps to one contiguous range of identifiers. Layout should follow the query that moves the most data, not the method that makes the builder prettiest.
For longest-prefix matching—used in routing and tokenization—remember the most recent terminal node while consuming the query. A failed transition returns that remembered match rather than simply returning false.
 #Measuring the RepresentationReport more than queries per second:
 bytes per key and bytes per input character; node degree and path-length distributions; successful, unsuccessful, and prefix-query ratios; cold versus repeated queries; single-query latency versus batched throughput; build time if the dictionary changes.  Test membership against a reference set, including the empty string, embedded zero bytes, duplicate keys, prefixes that are also keys, and absent strings sharing long prefixes. A useful structural test also verifies for every node that the bitmap population count equals the number of appended children.
The trie removes repeated key comparisons at the algorithmic level. Packing then removes empty child slots at the memory level. Both are necessary: a theoretically direct lookup built from a million tiny heap allocations is still a long sequence of serialized cache misses.
 #Further Reading Edward Fredkin’s original trie paper introduced the retrieval structure and its name. Donald Morrison, PATRICIA—Practical Algorithm To Retrieve Information Coded in Alphanumeric, develops path compression for binary tries. Leis et al., The Adaptive Radix Tree, matches node layout to degree and modern cache behavior. The DARTS double-array trie is another compact static representation with array-based transitions.
title: Tries

content:
Arithmetic operations have unequal costs and unequal semantics. Integer addition wraps only when the type says it may; signed overflow is undefined in C++. Floating-point addition rounds, preserves exceptional values, and may or may not be reassociated under the compilation contract. Division can take far longer than multiplication, while a count-trailing-zeros instruction can expose an entire power-of-two factor at once.
This chapter develops number representations before optimizing operations on them. It covers IEEE 754 and rounding error, Newton iterations and reciprocal square roots, word-sized integer arithmetic, constant and modular division, bit manipulation, and compression.
Every strength reduction carries a proof obligation. State the input range, intermediate width, rounding rule, and exceptional cases before replacing an operation. A sequence that is faster for ordinary values but invokes undefined behavior at zero is not a specialized implementation; it is a different and usually accidental contract.
title: Arithmetic

content:
The best SIMD code is often an ordinary loop. A compiler can choose the vector width, unroll it, version it for aliasing or alignment, and generate a scalar or masked tail. This keeps the source readable and lets the same algorithm target several ISAs.
Auto-vectorization is not guaranteed, and there is no universal “5–10x” speedup. A loop may already be limited by memory, may contain a dependency, or may spend most of its time in setup and tails. Treat vectorization as a compiler transformation to inspect and benchmark.
Consider elementwise addition:
void add(const float *a, const float *b, float *out, std::size_t n) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) out[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } Several facts determine whether and how this loop is vectorized.
 #Trip Count and TailsThe compiler can vectorize an unknown trip count. It usually emits a profitability check, a vector loop, and cleanup for the remaining elements. One extra branch outside a long loop is rarely the deciding cost.
Compile-time sizes can simplify the result, but padding is not automatically better. A manual vector loop may round n up only when all input and output allocations contain that rounded number of accessible elements and any read padding is initialized. Otherwise the scalar or masked tail is required. For a small or frequently varying n, code-size and dispatch overhead can outweigh SIMD.
 #Aliasing and DependenciesThe three pointers may overlap. For example, out == a + 1 creates a forward loop-carried dependency: writing one element changes an input used by the next scalar iteration. A vector loop would change the result.
Compilers often solve the common case with loop versioning: a runtime overlap check selects a vector loop when the ranges are independent and a scalar loop otherwise. If non-overlap is an actual API contract, GCC and Clang accept the C-style __restrict__ extension in C++:
void add_restricted(const float * __restrict__ a, const float * __restrict__ b, float * __restrict__ out, std::size_t n) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) out[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } Calling this function with accesses that violate the restrict contract makes the optimizer’s assumptions invalid. Do not add it merely to silence a vectorization report.
#pragma GCC ivdep and equivalent compiler pragmas assert that apparent loop-carried dependencies do not affect the result:
#pragma GCC ivdep for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = b[index[i]]; This is stronger than a performance suggestion. It is appropriate only when the programmer has proved the relevant independence; the compiler cannot repair a false assertion.
 #Alignment AssumptionsModern x86 often vectorizes with unaligned loads, but a proven alignment can remove versioning or help targets with stricter or more expensive unaligned access. C++20 std::assume_aligned returns the pointer carrying the assumption. The implementation is permitted to exploit the assumption only through that returned value:
void add_aligned(const float * __restrict__ a, const float * __restrict__ b, float * __restrict__ out, std::size_t n) { const float *aa = std::assume_aligned<32>(a); const float *bb = std::assume_aligned<32>(b); float *cc = std::assume_aligned<32>(out); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) cc[i] = aa[i] + bb[i]; } Ignoring the return value and continuing to use a, b, and out can discard the useful optimizer fact. Passing an address that is not actually 32-byte aligned violates the function’s precondition; assume_aligned does not adjust or check it. The current C++ wording makes this explicit in [ptr.align].
 #Confirming the TransformationCompiler reports are the quickest first check:
 GCC: -fopt-info-vec-optimized and -fopt-info-vec-missed; Clang: -Rpass=loop-vectorize -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize.  Then inspect optimized assembly and benchmark. Merely finding an instruction whose name starts with v is not proof: scalar AVX instructions also use VEX-encoded v... mnemonics. Look for packed operations, a vector induction step, runtime version checks, and the tail. Reports can also reveal that a loop was vectorized at a narrower width than expected because that was cheaper.
The available width follows the compilation target. -mavx2 or -march=native can make the whole object require that ISA. A distributable program needs baseline code plus compiler multiversioning, separate translation units, or a SIMD library that performs runtime dispatch.
 #SPMDSingle program, multiple data (SPMD) lets the programmer describe one logical program instance while a compiler executes a gang of instances across SIMD lanes. Per-instance conditions become masks, so SPMD can express divergent control flow more naturally than hand-written intrinsics.
ISPC is the main CPU example. It compiles for explicit target ISAs or a selected set of targets; it does not guarantee the same vectorization or performance on every architecture. Its launch mechanism can create tasks for multiple cores, but ordinary SPMD gangs alone describe SIMD execution on one hardware thread. See the official ISPC language and performance guide.
OpenMP separates the concepts too: simd requests vector execution of loop iterations, parallel for distributes iterations across threads, and combined constructs can request both. Neither implicitly proves that memory accesses are race-free. Julia’s @simd is likewise an optimization annotation rather than a general multicore SPMD runtime.
GPUs expose a related SIMT/SPMD programming model at much larger scale, with hardware-specific rules for divergence, memory coalescing, and synchronization. The common idea is writing lane-level work; mapping it to SIMD lanes, threads, tasks, or devices remains an explicit compiler and runtime choice.
title: Auto-Vectorization and SPMD

content:
Copying a bit gives us no protection: if we later read 1, we cannot know whether the original value was 1 or whether a stored 0 was flipped. Copying it three times does. The valid representations are 000 and 111; after one bit flip, the received word is still closer to the correct one.
This is the central trade-off of error-correcting codes. We spend extra space or bandwidth to move valid messages farther apart, then use that distance to detect or repair corruption. The redundancy is mathematical, but choosing it is a systems problem: memory sees different faults from a radio link, a lost storage shard is easier to locate than a silently corrupted one, and an active attacker is not noise at all.
 #Distance Buys RecoveryA binary code maps $k$ data bits to an $n$-bit codeword. Only $2^k$ of the $2^n$ possible words are valid. The Hamming distance $d(x,y)$ is the number of bit positions in which two words differ, and the minimum distance of a code is
$$ d_{min}=\min_{x\ne y}d(x,y) $$
over valid codewords.
If fewer than $d_{min}$ bits change, the corrupted word cannot equal a different valid codeword, so the error is detectable. If at most
$$ t=\left\lfloor\frac{d_{min}-1}{2}\right\rfloor $$
bits change, the original codeword is the unique nearest one, so those errors are correctable.
The repetition code above has $d_{min}=3$: it corrects one flipped bit, but spends three physical bits per data bit. Useful codes arrange many data bits together and get substantially more protection from the same amount of redundancy.
This distance model makes assumptions. It counts independent symbol changes and treats all positions equally. Real failures may arrive in bursts, erase an entire device, or correlate across adjacent cells. Before choosing a code, define the fault unit and what the decoder is told.
 #Detection Is Cheaper Than CorrectionThe smallest error-detecting code is a parity bit. Append the XOR of all data bits; any odd number of flips changes the total parity. Two flips pass undetected, and parity gives no clue where an error occurred.
A checksum retains more information, but its quality depends on the error model. Simple sums are useful for catching accidental implementation mistakes and some random corruption, yet structured changes can cancel. A cyclic redundancy check instead treats the message as a polynomial over $\mathbb F_2$, multiplies it by $x^r$, and stores the remainder after division by a selected generator polynomial $G(x)$ of degree $r$.
The receiver repeats the polynomial division. A valid codeword is divisible by $G$, so a nonzero remainder is a syndrome proving that corruption occurred. Which errors are guaranteed to be detected depends on $G$, the message length, and the fault pattern; CRC strength cannot be summarized as merely “32 random check bits.” RFC 3385 analyzes CRC32C specifically under independent and burst-error models.
CRCs are fast because polynomial division maps well to shifts, XOR, table lookup, and carryless-multiply instructions. They are not cryptographic authentication. Anyone who can modify the message can also compute a matching CRC; adversarial integrity needs a keyed message-authentication code.
 #Locating One Bad BitRichard Hamming’s original 1950 paper asks a productive question: if parity checks fail, can their pattern identify the broken position?
In a Hamming $(7,4)$ code, positions are numbered from 1 to 7. Positions 1, 2, and 4 hold parity; the remaining four hold data. Each position participates in a unique combination of three checks, given by the three bits of its position number:
 check 1 covers positions 1, 3, 5, 7; check 2 covers positions 2, 3, 6, 7; check 4 covers positions 4, 5, 6, 7.  If position 6 flips, checks 2 and 4 fail, producing binary syndrome 110, which is 6. The error reports its own address.
#include <cstdint> std::uint8_t hamming74_encode(std::uint8_t data) { data &= 0x0fu; std::uint8_t code = 0; // Data bits go to positions 3, 5, 6, and 7.  code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((data & 0x01u) << 2); code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((data & 0x02u) << 3); code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((data & 0x04u) << 3); code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((data & 0x08u) << 3); const unsigned d0 = (data >> 0) & 1u; const unsigned d1 = (data >> 1) & 1u; const unsigned d2 = (data >> 2) & 1u; const unsigned d3 = (data >> 3) & 1u; code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((d0 ^ d1 ^ d3) << 0); // position 1  code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((d0 ^ d2 ^ d3) << 1); // position 2  code |= static_cast<std::uint8_t>((d1 ^ d2 ^ d3) << 3); // position 4  return code; } std::uint8_t hamming74_correct(std::uint8_t received) { received &= 0x7fu; const auto bit = [received](unsigned position) { return (received >> (position - 1)) & 1u; }; const unsigned s1 = bit(1) ^ bit(3) ^ bit(5) ^ bit(7); const unsigned s2 = bit(2) ^ bit(3) ^ bit(6) ^ bit(7); const unsigned s4 = bit(4) ^ bit(5) ^ bit(6) ^ bit(7); const unsigned syndrome = s1 | (s2 << 1) | (s4 << 2); if (syndrome != 0) received ^= static_cast<std::uint8_t>(1u << (syndrome - 1)); return received; } std::uint8_t hamming74_decode(std::uint8_t received) { const std::uint8_t code = hamming74_correct(received); return static_cast<std::uint8_t>( ((code >> 2) & 1u) | ((code >> 3) & 2u) | ((code >> 3) & 4u) | ((code >> 3) & 8u) ); } This decoder has an explicit contract: at most one of the seven bits was changed. The code has minimum distance 3, so two flips can produce the syndrome of a third position and cause a miscorrection. Adding one overall parity bit raises the minimum distance to 4, producing the common SECDED arrangement—single-error correction, double-error detection—provided the decoder reports the uncorrectable case instead of blindly flipping a bit.
 #Correcting Symbols with PolynomialsHamming codes operate naturally on bits. Storage and network systems often lose or corrupt larger symbols: a byte, packet, or whole disk fragment. Reed–Solomon codes work over a finite field and make the same distance idea algebraic.
Interpret $k$ message symbols as the coefficients of a polynomial
$$ P(x)=m_0+m_1x+\cdots+m_{k-1}x^{k-1}. $$
Choose $n$ distinct field elements $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$ and store the evaluations $P(\alpha_i)$. Any two degree-below-$k$ polynomials agree at fewer than $k$ points, so two codewords differ in at least
$$ d_{min}=n-k+1 $$
symbols. The decoder can recover from $s$ known erasures and $e$ unknown corruptions whenever
$$ 2e+s \le n-k. $$
An erasure costs half as much because its location is already known. This is why distributed storage carefully distinguishes “server did not reply” from “server returned plausible but wrong bytes.” With only erasures, any $k$ surviving evaluations determine the polynomial by interpolation.
Production erasure codes are often put into systematic form: the original $k$ data shards remain unchanged and the encoder computes $n-k$ parity shards. Reads need no decoding while all data shards are present. Recovery becomes matrix multiplication over a finite field, typically $GF(2^8)$ or a larger binary field.
 #Performance Engineering a CodeThe mathematical code specifies which symbols to combine; representation determines how fast that happens.
 Small-field multiplication can use tables, shift-and-XOR code, bitslicing, or GFNI/carryless-multiply instructions. Encoding independent shards exposes SIMD and thread-level parallelism. Interleaving spreads a physical burst across several logical codewords, turning one hard multi-symbol error into several easy single-symbol errors. Large blocks amortize setup and improve throughput, while small blocks reduce recovery latency and excess I/O. A decoder should have a fast path for the overwhelmingly common no-error case.  Do not quote a code’s correction strength without its symbol size, block length, and fault model. “Two parity shards” can recover any two missing shards, but it does not automatically correct two arbitrary corrupted shards; unknown errors consume twice the redundancy, and correlated failures may violate the assumptions completely.
Finally, error correction and compression pull in opposite directions but compose well. Compression removes predictable redundancy; an error-correcting code then adds carefully structured redundancy for the channel or storage medium. The order matters: corrupting compressed data can affect a long suffix, so systems usually compress blocks, protect the resulting blocks, and frame them so damage remains bounded.
Error correction is not about making failure impossible. It is about choosing a precise set of failures and making recovery from that set cheaper than repeating or losing the computation.
title: Error Correction

content:
A cache with room for $k$ blocks eventually sees a request for block $k+1$. If all resident blocks are still eligible for reuse, one must leave. An eviction policy chooses which one.
The classic paging model assumes equal-size pages, equal miss cost, and a known sequence of page references. Real caches may store variable-size objects, charge extra to write dirty data, prefetch, or serve requests concurrently. The simple model is still useful, but its conclusions should not be silently transferred to a different cost model.
 #Online PoliciesAn online policy sees the past and current request, not the future.
 FIFO evicts the block admitted earliest. It is cheap to maintain but ignores later reuse. LRU evicts the block whose most recent access is oldest. It adapts to temporal locality and has a useful worst-case guarantee. MRU evicts the most recently used block. It can suit scans or cycles whose newest block will not be revisited soon. LFU favors blocks with high historical frequency. Without aging, an obsolete formerly-hot block can remain forever. Clock/second chance approximates recency with a reference bit and a circular scan. Random replacement keeps little ordering metadata and avoids deterministic pathological choices for some traces.  No policy dominates every request sequence. A scan larger than the cache can evict a hot working set under LRU; frequency can lag after a phase change; FIFO can exhibit Bélády’s anomaly, where adding capacity increases misses. Production policies often combine recency, frequency, admission filtering, and workload-specific costs.
Hardware CPU caches add another constraint: decisions are made within an associativity set and must fit a short pipeline. They commonly use pseudo-LRU, random, or other approximations rather than a global software-style LRU list. File caches, database buffer pools, and content caches can afford different metadata and policies.
 #Bélády’s Offline MinimumIf the complete future reference string is known, the optimal rule is to evict the resident block whose next use is farthest in the future, treating “never again” as infinitely far. This is Bélády’s MIN rule, developed in the original replacement-algorithm study.
The exchange proof is short. Suppose an optimal schedule evicts $x$ while MIN evicts $y$, and $y$ is used no earlier than $x$. Modify the optimal cache to retain $x$ in place of $y$ until the next access to either one. Every intervening request behaves identically, and the first relevant request is to $x$ or neither is used again, so the modified schedule incurs no more misses. Repeating the exchange makes an optimal schedule agree with MIN.
MIN is not implementable for an unknown online workload. It is useful as an offline lower bound for traces and as the comparator in competitive analysis.
 #What LRU Actually GuaranteesLRU is not within a fixed constant factor of MIN when both have the same arbitrary cache size. With $k$ slots, an adversarial sequence can make any deterministic online policy incur about $k$ times the misses of the offline optimum.
The precise resource-augmentation result is more informative. For a request sequence $\sigma$, let $\operatorname{LRU}_k(\sigma)$ use $k$ slots and $\operatorname{MIN}_h(\sigma)$ use $h\le k$ slots. Sleator and Tarjan proved
$$ \operatorname{LRU}_k(\sigma) \le \frac{k}{k-h+1}\operatorname{MIN}_h(\sigma)+h. $$
Their paging analysis also shows the factor is essentially optimal for online algorithms. If LRU has $k=2h$ slots, its multiplicative factor is below two, plus the additive warm-up term. If both caches have $k=h$, the factor is $k$, not two.
This is why ideal-cache proofs sometimes compare LRU with a smaller optimal cache. The result does not say that every vaguely reasonable policy has the same asymptotic behavior: LIFO and unaged LFU have request sequences with far worse guarantees.
 #A Collision-Safe LRU CacheSoftware LRU uses two structures:
 a hash table maps each full key to its cache entry; a doubly linked list orders entries from most to least recent.  A hit moves one existing list node to the front. An insertion evicts the back node when capacity is exceeded. std::list::splice performs the move without invalidating the iterator stored in the table.
#include <cstddef>#include <list>#include <optional>#include <string>#include <unordered_map>#include <utility> class string_lru_cache { using entry = std::pair<std::string, std::string>; using iterator = std::list<entry>::iterator; public: explicit string_lru_cache(std::size_t capacity) : capacity_(capacity) { index_.reserve(capacity); } std::optional<std::string> get(const std::string& key) { const auto found = index_.find(key); if (found == index_.end()) return std::nullopt; entries_.splice(entries_.begin(), entries_, found->second); return found->second->second; } void put(std::string key, std::string value) { if (capacity_ == 0) return; if (const auto found = index_.find(key); found != index_.end()) { found->second->second = std::move(value); entries_.splice(entries_.begin(), entries_, found->second); return; } entries_.emplace_front(std::move(key), std::move(value)); try { index_.emplace(entries_.front().first, entries_.begin()); } catch (...) { entries_.pop_front(); throw; } if (entries_.size() > capacity_) { index_.erase(entries_.back().first); entries_.pop_back(); } } std::size_t size() const noexcept { return entries_.size(); } private: std::size_t capacity_; std::list<entry> entries_; std::unordered_map<std::string, iterator> index_; }; The hash table stores full strings and resolves collisions with equality; it never treats a hash digest as the key. This makes collisions a performance issue rather than a correctness error. Standard unordered lookup is expected $O(1)$, not worst-case $O(1)$; adversarial keys may require a keyed hash, collision-resistant table design, or an ordered map.
This reference cache counts entries. A database cache usually budgets bytes and may charge dirty writeback or pin pages that cannot currently be evicted. It also needs synchronization if accessed concurrently. Those additions change the policy’s cost model and should be part of its tests.
 #Choosing and MeasuringMeasure misses, admitted bytes, evicted bytes, dirty writes, and metadata/lock overhead on representative traces. Report warm and cold starts separately. A lower miss ratio can still lose if the policy performs expensive bookkeeping on every hit or admits objects that cost more to retain than to recompute.
An eviction policy is a prediction about future value. Theoretical analysis states what happens on every sequence; workload measurements state whether that prediction matches the sequences the system actually receives. Both are needed.
title: Eviction Policies

content:
The discrete Fourier transform is a dense matrix-vector multiplication with an extraordinary matrix. Its entries are powers of one complex root, and that algebraic repetition lets us reduce $n^2$ work to $n\log n$. The fast Fourier transform is therefore not one algorithm but a family of factorizations of the DFT.
We will derive the radix-2 Cooley–Tukey transform, implement an in-place iterative C++20 core, use it for linear convolution, and then examine the parts hidden by big-O notation: permutation, twiddle generation, vectorization, inverse scaling, and floating-point error.
Our code accepts a nonempty power-of-two length and uses std::complex<double>. Other lengths need mixed-radix, Bluestein, Rader, or library support; silently padding a transform changes the mathematical object unless the operation is specifically convolution.
 #The Transform PairFor $n$ complex samples $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$, define
$$ \omega_n=e^{-2\pi i/n} $$
and the forward DFT
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j\omega_n^{jk}. $$
Our inverse convention reverses the sign and divides by $n$:
$$ a_j=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A_k\omega_n^{-jk}. $$
Libraries use several scaling conventions. Some leave both directions unscaled, some split the factor symmetrically, and some match the convention above. Composing code with different conventions can produce an answer that is exactly wrong by a factor of $n$.
A literal implementation evaluates every pair $(j,k)$ and costs $O(n^2)$. It is valuable as a small oracle, but it ignores the identities among roots.
 #Splitting Even and Odd IndicesSeparate the input into its even and odd subsequences. For $0\le k<n/2$, let $E_k$ and $O_k$ be their length-$n/2$ transforms. Since $\omega_n^2=\omega_{n/2}$,
$$ \begin{aligned} A_k &=E_k+\omega_n^kO_k,\ A_{k+n/2}&=E_k-\omega_n^kO_k. \end{aligned} $$
One multiplication by the twiddle factor $\omega_n^k$ and two additions form a butterfly:
u --------(+ )-------- u + w v \ / \/ /\ / \ v --(times w)--(- )--- u - w v Applying the split recursively gives
$$ T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)=O(n\log n). $$
Cooley and Tukey’s primary 1965 paper, An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series, develops the general factorization for composite lengths. Radix 2 is the simplest special case, not a fundamental restriction of the FFT idea.
 #An Iterative Radix-2 FFTA recursive decimation-in-time implementation naturally gathers even and odd elements. To perform the same butterflies in place and iteratively, first permute indices by reversing their $\log_2 n$ bits. Then execute stages of length 2, 4, 8, and so on.
#include <algorithm>#include <bit>#include <cmath>#include <complex>#include <cstddef>#include <numbers>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> using complex64 = std::complex<double>; void fft(std::span<complex64> values, bool inverse = false) { std::size_t n = values.size(); if (!std::has_single_bit(n)) throw std::invalid_argument("FFT length must be a nonzero power of two"); // In-place bit-reversal permutation.  for (std::size_t i = 1, reversed = 0; i < n; ++i) { std::size_t bit = n >> 1; while ((reversed & bit) != 0) { reversed ^= bit; bit >>= 1; } reversed ^= bit; if (i < reversed) std::swap(values[i], values[reversed]); } if (n > 1) { for (std::size_t length = 2;; length *= 2) { double angle = (inverse ? 2.0 : -2.0) * std::numbers::pi_v<double> / double(length); complex64 root(std::cos(angle), std::sin(angle)); std::size_t half = length / 2; for (std::size_t first = 0; first != n; first += length) { complex64 w(1, 0); for (std::size_t j = 0; j != half; ++j) { complex64 even = values[first + j]; complex64 odd = w * values[first + j + half]; values[first + j] = even + odd; values[first + j + half] = even - odd; w *= root; } } if (length == n) break; // prevents the next doubling from overflowing  } } if (inverse) for (complex64 &x : values) x /= double(n); } The implementation has explicit behavior at every awkward boundary:
 length zero is rejected rather than passed to log2 or division; length one is a valid identity transform; non-power-of-two lengths are rejected; the stage loop exits before doubling the final length; inverse scaling happens exactly once.  The forward sign is negative, matching the definition above. Changing just the sign or just the scaling creates a different convention; tests should treat the forward/inverse pair as one interface.
 #Linear ConvolutionFor sequences $a$ and $b$, linear convolution is
$$ c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_i b_j. $$
The convolution theorem turns this into pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain. To avoid circular wraparound, pad to at least a.size() + b.size() - 1:
#include <limits>#include <vector> std::vector<double> convolve(std::span<const double> a, std::span<const double> b) { if (a.empty() || b.empty()) return {}; constexpr std::size_t maximum = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max(); if (a.size() > maximum - b.size() + 1) throw std::length_error("convolution length overflow"); std::size_t needed = a.size() + b.size() - 1; std::size_t n = 1; while (n < needed) { if (n > maximum / 2) throw std::length_error("FFT length overflow"); n *= 2; } std::vector<complex64> fa, fb; if (n > fa.max_size() || n > fb.max_size()) throw std::length_error("FFT allocation is too large"); fa.assign(n, complex64(0, 0)); fb.assign(n, complex64(0, 0)); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != a.size(); ++i) fa[i] = a[i]; for (std::size_t i = 0; i != b.size(); ++i) fb[i] = b[i]; fft(fa); fft(fb); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != n; ++i) fa[i] *= fb[i]; fft(fa, true); std::vector<double> result(needed); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != needed; ++i) result[i] = fa[i].real(); return result; } Padding is exact with respect to linear versus cyclic convolution, but the arithmetic is still floating point. A small imaginary residual after the inverse is normal. A large residual indicates an implementation, conditioning, overflow, or input-scale problem and should not be discarded silently.
Rounding the real parts to integers is justified only when an application-specific error bound proves that every result lies within less than one half of the correct integer. Large coefficients, long transforms, or adversarial cancellation can break that assumption. The number-theoretic transform provides exact modular convolution when an appropriate finite field exists.
 #What the Machine ExecutesEach stage performs $n/2$ independent butterflies. Within one block, reads and writes are contiguous, and the same twiddle sequence is reused by every block of that stage. These properties create several optimization paths.
 #Twiddle factorsThe reference code computes one sine/cosine pair per stage and obtains later twiddles by repeated complex multiplication. This is cheap, but recurrence error accumulates as w drifts away from the unit circle.
