Alternatives include precomputed tables, computing twiddles in short independently restarted groups, or periodically recalculating them from an angle.
Computing sin and cos inside every butterfly is usually too expensive. A table costs memory traffic. The best compromise depends on transform length, precision, reuse, and cache capacity.
 #Complex layout and SIMDstd::complex<double> normally stores interleaved real and imaginary parts, which is convenient for scalar complex multiplication. SIMD kernels may prefer separate real and imaginary vectors or carefully shuffled interleaved data. The butterfly itself has ample parallelism; moving values into the desired lane arrangement can cost as much as its arithmetic.
Vectorize across several butterflies that use compatible twiddles, unroll to keep independent operations in flight, and handle the final partial vector explicitly. Radix 4 or higher combines stages, reducing some loads and twiddle multiplications at the price of a larger kernel.
 #PermutationBit reversal is $O(n)$ and therefore invisible in the asymptotic bound, but it performs an irregular permutation before useful arithmetic begins. Table-based bit reversal, blocked permutation, and Stockham autosort variants trade extra storage or passes for more regular access. Whether the separate permutation matters depends on how often the same plan and layout are reused.
This is why production FFT libraries plan rather than expose one fixed loop. The primary FFTW3 design paper describes codelets, planner-selected decompositions, cache considerations, and machine adaptation across transform shapes.
 #Floating-Point ErrorThe FFT replaces one sum of $n$ terms with $\log_2 n$ stages of additions and multiplications. Every operation rounds, computed roots are approximate, and twiddle recurrences add their own drift. Primary work on the accumulation of FFT roundoff gives error bounds under explicit models; there is no universal decimal-digit promise independent of data and scale.
Useful checks include:
 forward followed by inverse, compared with the original input; Parseval’s identity under the chosen normalization; comparison with the $O(n^2)$ DFT at small sizes; convolution versus a direct long-double accumulation; maximum imaginary residual for nominally real output.  Absolute tolerance alone is misleading across scales. Report an error such as
$$ \frac{\lVert\widehat x-x\rVert_2} {\max(1,\lVert x\rVert_2)} $$
and also inspect componentwise error when small coefficients matter. Inputs near DBL_MAX, NaN, and infinities need a stated policy; the core routine permits IEEE propagation rather than pretending they are ordinary finite signals.
Compiler flags are part of this policy. Fast-math may reassociate complex expressions, contract operations, ignore signed zero, and assume finite inputs. It can improve a benchmark while changing both reproducibility and exceptional-value behavior.
 #Reproducible EvaluationRecord transform direction, length distribution, in-place versus out-of-place layout, precision, complex representation, twiddle strategy, inclusion of planning/allocation, compiler flags, ISA target, CPU, and thread count. Warm repeated transforms and one-shot cold transforms answer different questions.
Verify output before timing. The historical companion directory for this chapter contains several recursive and iterative sketches, but some variants transform only a prefix, repeatedly transform already transformed data, or remain incomplete experiments. They are useful for reconstructing the intended recursion and permutation work, not as evidence for a performance record.
Benchmark the full application as well as the FFT kernel. For convolution, padding and two forward transforms may dominate small inputs. For repeated transforms of the same shape, planning and twiddle tables amortize. For real-valued data, a real-to-complex transform can avoid nearly half the redundant spectrum, but it has a different interface and packing contract.
The FFT’s artistry lies in matching algebraic factorization to a memory hierarchy. The butterfly proves the asymptotic improvement; a reliable implementation must also choose a convention, permute safely, scale the inverse, manage twiddles, and quantify the error it introduces.
title: Fast Fourier Transform

content:
It is not uncommon for two library implementations to maintain separate benchmarks and each claim to be faster. This confuses everyone involved, especially users who have to choose between them.
Situations like these are usually not caused by fraudulent actions by their authors; they just have different definitions of what “faster” means, and indeed, defining and using just one performance metric is often very problematic.
 #Measuring the Right ThingThere are many things that can introduce bias into benchmarks.
Differing datasets. There are many algorithms whose performance somehow depends on the dataset distribution. In order to define, for example, what the fastest sorting, shortest path, or binary search algorithms are, you have to fix the dataset on which the algorithm is run.
This sometimes applies even to algorithms that process a single piece of input. For example, it is not a good idea to feed GCD implementations sequential numbers because it makes branches very predictable:
// don't do this int checksum = 0; for (int a = 0; a < 1000; a++) for (int b = 0; b < 1000; b++) checksum ^= gcd(a, b); To isolate ordering from the input distribution, build the same million pairs and shuffle them before measuring:
#include <algorithm>#include <random>#include <utility>#include <vector> std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> inputs; inputs.reserve(1'000'000); for (int a = 0; a < 1000; ++a) for (int b = 0; b < 1000; ++b) inputs.emplace_back(a, b); std::mt19937 rng(42); std::shuffle(inputs.begin(), inputs.end(), rng); int checksum = 0; for (auto [a, b] : inputs) checksum ^= gcd(a, b); The shuffled version processes the same multiset, but a learned predictor may still exploit patterns other than simple order. Uniform random data is convenient, yet many real applications are far from uniform. A good benchmark uses distributions representative of the intended workload and reports enough detail to reproduce them.
Multiple objectives. Some algorithm-design problems have more than one objective. Hash tables, in addition to depending on the key distribution, must balance:
 memory usage, insertion latency, latency of positive membership query, latency of negative membership query.  The only way to choose between hash table implementations is to try and put multiple variants into the application.
Latency vs Throughput. Another aspect that people often overlook is that the execution time can be defined in more than one way, even for a single query.
When you write code like this:
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) q[i] = rand(); int checksum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= lower_bound(q[i]); and then time the whole thing and divide it by the number of iterations, you are actually measuring the throughput of the query — how many operations it can process per unit of time. This is usually less than the time it actually takes to process one operation separately because of interleaving.
To measure actual latency, you need to introduce a dependency between the invocations:
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= lower_bound(checksum ^ q[i]); It usually makes the most difference in algorithms with possible pipeline stall issues, e.g., when comparing branchy and branch-free algorithms.
Cold cache. Another source of bias is the cold cache effect, when memory reads initially take longer time because the required data is not in cache yet.
If you are interested in steady-state performance, make a warm-up run before starting measurements:
// warm-up run  volatile int checksum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= lower_bound(q[i]); // actual run  clock_t start = clock(); checksum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) checksum ^= lower_bound(q[i]); It is also sometimes convenient to combine the warm-up run with answer validation, if it is more complicated than just computing some sort of checksum. If cold-start latency is the quantity you care about, warming the cache would instead remove part of the behavior you are trying to measure.
Over-optimization. Sometimes the compiler removes benchmarked work because its result is unobservable. Consume and validate a checksum, return a result to an opaque caller, or use the “do not optimize” facilities of a benchmarking framework. volatile can make particular accesses observable, but it changes the generated code and does not stop the CPU from executing independent instructions out of order.
For algorithms that only write data, make the resulting memory observable to the harness. A hardware memory fence such as __sync_synchronize() is not a general antidote to dead-code elimination; frameworks provide compiler barriers such as Google Benchmark’s ClobberMemory() for this purpose.
 #Reducing NoiseThe issues we’ve described produce bias in measurements: they consistently give advantage to one algorithm over the other. There are other types of possible problems with benchmarking that result in either unpredictable skews or just completely random noise, thus increasing variance.
These types of issues are caused by side effects and some sort of external noise, mostly due to noisy neighbors and CPU frequency scaling:
 For a compute-bound kernel, perf stat cycle counts are often more stable than wall time, but frequency changes can still alter memory latency in core cycles and can change the microarchitecture’s power behavior. Report both when it matters. Control frequency policy when reproducibility requires it. On Linux, cpupower frequency-info and cpupower frequency-set can inspect or configure the available governors and limits, but selecting a governor alone does not guarantee one fixed frequency on every driver. If applicable, turn hyper-threading off and attach jobs to specific cores. Make sure no other jobs are running on the system, turn off networking and try not to fiddle with the mouse.  You cannot remove noise and bias completely. Even a program’s name can affect a result: arguments and environment strings occupy the initial process stack, changing address layout and potentially moving later objects across cache-line or page boundaries.
It is important to account for the noise when guiding optimizations and especially when reporting results to someone else. Unless you are expecting a 2x kind of improvement, treat all microbenchmarks the same way as A/B testing.
Short laptop benchmarks can fluctuate by several percent, but there is no universal noise allowance. Measure the distribution on the machine you are using, repeat the comparison in independent runs, and report an effect size with an uncertainty estimate. A p-value alone neither tells you how large the improvement is nor rules out systematic bias.
 #Further ReadingFor a broader catalogue of benchmarking failure modes, see Mytkowicz et al., Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong. The paper demonstrates why code placement and uncontrolled environment state can reverse an apparent result.
You can also watch this great talk by Emery Berger on how to do statistically sound performance evaluation.
title: Getting Accurate Results

content:
Integer addition is a short trip through a carry chain. Integer division is a search for a quotient, and the hardware has much more work to do.
On contemporary CPUs, an integer divide commonly has a latency measured in tens of cycles. The exact number depends on the microarchitecture, operand width, and sometimes the values being divided. It is also usually only partly pipelined. This makes division unusual: replacing one div can matter more than deleting a small loop around it.
Before trying to replace it, we need to be precise about which division we are performing. This chapter deals with nonzero integer divisors. C++ integer division truncates toward zero; the corresponding remainder has the sign of the dividend. Most reciprocal techniques are easiest to derive for unsigned integers and require an extra adjustment for signed ones.
 #Division and Remainder on x86x86 uses the same instruction to produce a quotient and a remainder. The instruction has an implicit double-width dividend:
 div r/m32 divides edx:eax by its operand and writes the quotient to eax and the remainder to edx; div r/m64 divides rdx:rax by its operand and writes the quotient to rax and the remainder to rdx.  For an ordinary unsigned 32-by-32 division, the upper half is zero:
; uint32_t quotient(uint32_t x, uint32_t y) mov eax, edi xor edx, edx div esi ret Signed division uses idiv. The cdq instruction sign-extends eax into edx:eax (cqo does the 64-bit version):
; int32_t quotient(int32_t x, int32_t y) mov eax, edi cdq idiv esi ret The remainder is already in edx, so % differs only in which result is returned:
; uint32_t remainder(uint32_t x, uint32_t y) mov eax, edi xor edx, edx div esi mov eax, edx ret The double-width form is useful in multiple-precision arithmetic. For example, this divides a 128-bit unsigned integer hi:lo by a 64-bit divisor:
; uint64_t quotient(uint64_t lo, uint64_t hi, uint64_t d) ; precondition: d != 0 and hi < d mov rcx, rdx ; save d before overwriting rdx mov rax, rdi mov rdx, rsi div rcx ; rdx:rax / rcx ret The precondition hi < d is not cosmetic. If the quotient does not fit in 64 bits—or if the divisor is zero—div raises a divide exception. A compiler implementing an unconstrained __uint128_t / uint64_t must therefore handle the other cases too, often by calling a software routine.
 #Powers of TwoUnsigned division by $2^k$ is a right shift, and the remainder is a mask:
uint32_t q = x >> k; uint32_t r = x & ((uint32_t(1) << k) - 1); The mask expression requires $k<32$; a shift by the width of a type is undefined in C++. Signed division is less direct because an arithmetic shift rounds negative values down, while C++ division rounds toward zero. Compilers insert a bias before shifting when it is needed.
This distinction is a recurring theme: a strength reduction is valid only when it preserves the language operation, not merely when it resembles the corresponding arithmetic identity.
 #Reciprocal MultiplicationSuppose an unsigned divisor $d$ is known before the program runs. We would like to replace
$$ q=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\right\rfloor $$
with multiplication by a fixed-point approximation to $1/d$. A product naturally gives us twice as many bits. Keeping its high half is equivalent to dividing by the scale factor:
$$ \operatorname{high}_w(xm)=\left\lfloor\frac{xm}{2^w}\right\rfloor. $$
With a carefully chosen multiplier $m$, a shift, and—in some cases—one add or correction, this is exactly equal to $\lfloor x/d\rfloor$ for every $w$-bit input. These constants are usually called magic numbers. Their construction must account for the rounding error and the full input range; simply choosing $\lceil 2^w/d\rceil$ is not sufficient for every divisor.
For example, division of a 64-bit unsigned integer by 10 can be implemented as
 #$$ \left\lfloor\frac{x}{10}\right\rfloor\operatorname{high}_{64}(x\cdot\mathtt{0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD})\mathbin{\gg}3. $$
On x86-64, the multiplication that produces both halves is cheaper than a general div. The remainder then follows from
$$ r=x-qd. $$
You normally should not write the magic constant yourself. GCC and Clang already perform this transformation for compile-time divisors, including the awkward signed cases. Libraries such as libdivide extend the same idea to divisors that are fixed only at run time: they precompute a small descriptor once and reuse it for many divisions.
The break-even point depends on how often the divisor is reused. One division plus precomputation is rarely a win; a million divisions by the same value often is.
 #Barrett ReductionReciprocal multiplication for a quotient and Barrett reduction are related, but they are not the same algorithm.
Barrett reduction targets repeated modular reductions. Let $0<n<2^w$, choose a scale $2^k$, and precompute
$$ \mu=\left\lfloor\frac{2^k}{n}\right\rfloor. $$
For an input in a stated range—commonly a product $0\le x<n^2$—we estimate the quotient from the high part of $x\mu$:
$$ \hat q=\left\lfloor\frac{x\mu}{2^k}\right\rfloor, \qquad \hat r=x-\hat qn. $$
Because $\mu$ rounds $2^k/n$ down, $\hat q$ may be slightly too small. Choosing $k$ for the promised input range bounds that error; one or a small fixed number of conditional subtractions then puts $\hat r$ in $[0,n)$. The range and scale are part of the algorithm. Without them, the claim that the approximation is exact is false.
This is particularly useful in large-integer and cryptographic code, where products are already represented as several machine words. The implementation can select limb-sized shifts and avoid a general multiword division.

 #Direct Remainders for 32-Bit InputsIf the input and divisor are 32-bit but a 128-bit product is available, Daniel Lemire’s method computes the remainder without first materializing the quotient. For $2\le d<2^{32}$, precompute
$$ m=\left\lceil\frac{2^{64}}{d}\right\rceil =\left\lfloor\frac{2^{64}-1}{d}\right\rfloor+1. $$
Then the low half of $mx$ acts like the fractional part of $x/d$. Multiplying that fraction by $d$ and taking the high half recovers the exact remainder:
#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept> struct fast_remainder_u32 { uint32_t d; uint64_t m; explicit fast_remainder_u32(uint32_t divisor) : d(divisor), m(0) { if (d < 2) throw std::invalid_argument("divisor must be at least 2; handle 1 separately"); m = UINT64_MAX / d + 1; } uint32_t operator()(uint32_t x) const { uint64_t low = m * x; return uint32_t((static_cast<__uint128_t>(low) * d) >> 64); } }; The special case $d=1$ should return zero directly: $\lceil2^{64}/1\rceil$ does not fit in 64 bits. The use of __uint128_t also makes this implementation specific to compilers that provide that extension. On other targets, the same calculation can use a high-half multiplication intrinsic.
The same intermediate gives a fast divisibility test:
bool is_divisible(uint32_t x) const { return m * x < m; } This comparison is exact under the same preconditions. It is a useful example of a broader optimization pattern: once an expensive transformation has produced both a high and a low half, ask whether the half you were about to discard already encodes the answer to a nearby problem.
 #Choosing a MethodThere is no universally fastest replacement for division:
 for a compile-time constant, let the compiler generate reciprocal multiplication; for one run-time divisor reused many times, use a tested divider object such as libdivide; for bounded modular products, Barrett reduction is often a natural fit; for long chains modulo an odd integer, Montgomery multiplication avoids division in a different representation; for a single unpredictable divisor, the hardware instruction may be the simplest and fastest correct choice.  Measure the complete computation rather than an isolated instruction. A replacement can use more multiplications and registers, increase pressure on execution ports, or lengthen a dependency chain. Removing div is an opportunity, not a proof of speedup.
 #Further Reading Division by Invariant Integers Using Multiplication derives the compiler transformations and their bounds. Faster Remainder by Direct Computation develops the direct-remainder method. Hacker’s Delight treats constant division, remainders, and the signed edge cases in detail. libdivide provides production implementations for reused run-time divisors.
title: Integer Division

content:
Computer engineers like to mentally split the pipeline of a CPU into two parts: the front-end, where instructions are fetched from memory and decoded, and the back-end, where they are scheduled and finally executed. Typically, the performance is bottlenecked by the execution stage, and for this reason, most of our efforts in this book are going to be spent towards optimizing around the back-end.
But sometimes the reverse can happen when the front-end doesn’t feed instructions to the back-end fast enough to saturate it. This can happen for many reasons, all ultimately having something to do with how the machine code is laid out in memory, and affect performance in anecdotal ways, such as removing unused code, swapping “if” branches, or even changing the order of function declarations causing performance to either improve or deteriorate.
 #CPU Front-EndBefore the machine code gets transformed into instructions, and the CPU understands what the programmer wants, it first needs to go through two important stages that we are interested in: fetch and decode.
During the fetch stage, the CPU obtains aligned regions of instruction bytes, normally from the L1 instruction cache or a decoded-instruction cache rather than directly from main memory. The exact fetch width and boundaries vary between microarchitectures; 32 bytes per cycle is a useful model for the Zen 2 system used here. An instruction that straddles a fetch or decode boundary needs bytes from both regions and may reduce front-end throughput, although buffers can hide some of that cost.
Next comes the decode stage: the CPU splits the byte stream into instructions. x86 instructions have variable length: even simple 64-bit instructions commonly need two or three bytes (inc rax is three), while an instruction with prefixes, addressing, and an immediate may use up to 15. So a fetched region contains a variable number of instructions, but no more than a machine-dependent decode width. On my CPU (a Zen 2), the decode width is 4, which means that on each cycle, up to 4 instructions can be decoded and passed to the next stage.
The stages work in a pipelined fashion: if the CPU can tell (or predict) which instruction block it needs next, then the fetch stage doesn’t wait for the last instruction in the current block to be decoded and loads the next one right away.
 #Code AlignmentOther things being equal, compilers typically prefer instructions with shorter machine code, because this way more instructions can fit in a single 32B fetch block, and also because it reduces the size of the binary. But sometimes the reverse is preferable, due to the fact that the fetched instruction blocks must be aligned.
Imagine that you need to execute an instruction sequence that starts on the last byte of a 32B-aligned block. You may be able to execute the first instruction without additional delay, but for the subsequent ones, you have to wait for one additional cycle to do another instruction fetch. If the code block was aligned on a 32B boundary, then up to 4 instructions could be decoded and then executed concurrently (unless they are extra long or interdependent).
Having this in mind, compilers often do a seemingly harmful optimization: they sometimes prefer instructions with longer machine codes, and even insert dummy instructions that do nothing1 in order to get key jump locations aligned on a suitable power-of-two boundary.
In GCC, you can use -falign-labels=n flag to specify a particular alignment policy, replacing -labels with -function, -loops, or -jumps if you want to be more selective. On -O2 and -O3 levels of optimization, it is enabled by default — without setting a particular alignment, in which case it uses a (usually reasonable) machine-dependent default value.
 #Instruction CacheThe instructions are stored and fetched using largely the same memory system as for the data, except maybe the lower layers of cache are replaced with a separate instruction cache (because you wouldn’t want a random data read to kick out the code that processes it).
The instruction cache is crucial in situations when you either:
 don’t know what instructions you are going to execute next, and need to fetch the next block with low latency, or are executing a long sequence of verbose-but-quick-to-process instructions, and need high bandwidth.  The memory system can therefore become the bottleneck for programs with large machine code. This consideration limits the applicability of the optimization techniques we’ve previously discussed:
 Inlining functions is not always optimal, because it reduces code sharing and increases the binary size, requiring more instruction cache. Unrolling loops is only beneficial up to some extent, even if the number of iterations is known during compile time: at some point, the CPU would have to fetch both instructions and data from the main memory, in which case it will likely be bottlenecked by the memory bandwidth. Huge code alignments increase the binary size, again requiring more instruction cache. Spending one more cycle on fetch is a minor penalty compared to missing the cache and waiting for the instructions to be fetched from the main memory.  Another aspect is that placing frequently used instruction sequences on the same cache lines and memory pages improves cache locality. To improve instruction cache utilization, you should group hot code with hot code and cold code with cold code, and remove dead (unused) code if possible. If you want to explore this idea further, check out Facebook’s Binary Optimization and Layout Tool, which was recently merged into LLVM.
 #Unequal BranchesSuppose that for some reason you need a helper function that calculates the length of an integer interval. It takes two arguments, $x$ and $y$, but for convenience, it may correspond to either $[x, y]$ or $[y, x]$, depending on which one is non-empty. In plain C, you would probably write something like this:
int length(int x, int y) { if (x > y) return x - y; else return y - x; } In x86 assembly, there is a lot more variability to how you can implement it, noticeably impacting performance. Let’s start with trying to map this code directly into assembly:
length: cmp edi, esi jle less ; x > y sub edi, esi mov eax, edi done: ret less: ; x <= y sub esi, edi mov eax, esi jmp done While the initial C code seems very symmetrical, the assembly version isn’t. This results in an interesting quirk that one branch can be executed slightly faster than the other: if x > y, then the CPU can just execute the 5 instructions between cmp and ret, which, if the function is aligned, are all going to be fetched in one go; while in case of x <= y, two more jumps are required.
It may be reasonable to assume that the x > y case is unlikely (why would anyone calculate the length of an inverted interval?), more like an exception that mostly never happens. We can detect this case, and simply swap x and y:
int length(int x, int y) { if (x > y) swap(x, y); return y - x; } The assembly would go like this, as it typically does for the if-without-else patterns:
length: cmp edi, esi jle normal ; if x <= y, no swap is needed, and we can skip the xchg xchg edi, esi normal: sub esi, edi mov eax, esi ret The total instruction length is 6 now, down from 8. But it is still not quite optimized for our assumed case: if we think that x > y never happens, then we are wasteful when loading the xchg edi, esi instruction that is never going to be executed. We can solve this by moving it outside the normal execution path:
length: cmp edi, esi jg swap normal: sub esi, edi mov eax, esi ret swap: xchg edi, esi jmp normal This technique is quite handy when handling exceptions cases in general, and in high-level code, you can give the compiler a hint that a certain branch is more likely than the other:
int length(int x, int y) { if (x > y) [[unlikely]] swap(x, y); return y - x; } This optimization is only beneficial when you know that a branch is very rarely taken. When this is not the case, there are other aspects more important than the code layout, that compel compilers to avoid any branching at all — in this case by replacing it with a special “conditional move” instruction, roughly corresponding to the ternary expression (x > y ? x - y : y - x) or, after handling overflow concerns, calling abs(x - y):
length: mov edx, edi mov eax, esi sub edx, esi sub eax, edi cmp edi, esi cmovg eax, edx ; "mov if edi > esi" ret Eliminating branches is an important topic, and we will spend much of the next chapter discussing it in more detail.
  Such instructions are called no-op, or NOP instructions. The one-byte x86 nop encoding, 0x90, historically aliases xchg eax, eax; assemblers also provide longer multi-byte NOP encodings for padding. They consume front-end space even when they require no back-end execution. ↩︎
title: Machine Code Layout

content:
When a compiler can prove that a value does not depend on runtime input, it may calculate the value during compilation and embed the result into the program. This optimization is called constant folding.
Constant folding is permitted by the C++ as-if rule, but it is not guaranteed merely because all arguments happen to be literals. A compiler may decide that a computation is too expensive to perform while compiling, or may simply miss the opportunity.
 #Constant ExpressionsThe constexpr specifier allows a function to participate in constant evaluation:
#include <cstdint> constexpr std::uint64_t fibonacci(unsigned n) { std::uint64_t a = 0, b = 1; for (unsigned i = 0; i < n; ++i) { std::uint64_t next = a + b; a = b; b = next; } return a; } static_assert(fibonacci(10) == 55); The static_assert requires a constant expression, so this particular call must be evaluated during translation. A constexpr function can also be called with runtime data, in which case it behaves like an ordinary function:
std::uint64_t runtime_fibonacci(unsigned n) { return fibonacci(n); // n is not generally known while compiling } If every potentially evaluated call must happen at compile time, C++20 provides consteval immediate functions:
consteval std::uint64_t compile_time_fibonacci(unsigned n) { return fibonacci(n); } constexpr auto f10 = compile_time_fibonacci(10); Calling compile_time_fibonacci with a runtime value is ill-formed instead of silently becoming a runtime computation.
Constant evaluation has evolved across C++ standards. Modern constexpr functions can contain loops and local state, and C++20 even permits dynamic allocation when the allocation is released within constant evaluation. They still cannot perform arbitrary runtime I/O or leave allocated storage behind. Compilers also limit evaluation depth or work so a mistaken exponential computation does not occupy the build machine indefinitely.
 #Lookup TablesCompile-time evaluation is useful for constructing static lookup tables while keeping their generation logic next to the data:
#include <array> constexpr int floor_sqrt(int x) { int r = 0; while ((r + 1) * (r + 1) <= x) ++r; return r; } consteval std::array<int, 1000> make_isqrt_table() { std::array<int, 1000> table{}; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) table[i] = floor_sqrt(i); return table; } inline constexpr auto isqrt = make_isqrt_table(); static_assert(isqrt[42] == 6); The table occupies space in the binary, and looking up a value is not automatically faster than computing it. Precomputation exchanges execution work for compilation time, binary size, memory traffic, and possibly cache capacity. It is most attractive when the table is small, reused often, and replaces a meaningfully expensive operation.
Even a fixed-trip-count runtime loop is not a constant-expression context:
std::uint64_t sum_first_100() { std::uint64_t sum = 0; for (unsigned i = 0; i < 100; ++i) sum += fibonacci(i); return sum; } An optimizer may unroll the loop and fold some or all calls, but the language does not require it. If compile-time evaluation is part of correctness or of the intended resource budget, express that requirement with static_assert, a constexpr variable, or a consteval function rather than hoping to observe it in optimized assembly.
title: Precomputation

content:
If a future address is known early, the memory system can start fetching its line before the program needs the value. This prefetching converts latency into an overlapped request and consumes some of the memory-level parallelism available in the machine.
Ordinary out-of-order execution already does this for independent loads in the instruction window. Two additional mechanisms reach farther:
 hardware prefetchers recognize address patterns in the stream of cache misses; software prefetch instructions give the processor a hint about a particular future address.  Both are speculative performance mechanisms. They can reduce latency, but they also consume request entries, cache capacity, translation resources, and bandwidth.
 #Hardware PrefetchingModify the random-cycle benchmark so that it visits cache lines in increasing order while visiting the fifteen remaining 32-bit words inside each line in a shuffled order. For $N$ divisible by 16, this constructs one cycle and closes it explicitly:
assert(N >= 16 && N % 16 == 0); std::vector<std::uint32_t> next(N); std::array<std::uint32_t, 15> offsets; std::iota(offsets.begin(), offsets.end(), 1); std::mt19937 rng(42); std::uint32_t tail = 0; for (std::uint32_t base = 0; base < N; base += 16) { std::shuffle(offsets.begin(), offsets.end(), rng); for (std::uint32_t offset : offsets) { next[tail] = base + offset; tail = base + offset; } if (base + 16 < N) { next[tail] = base + 16; tail = base + 16; } } next[tail] = 0; The core still cannot derive the next word from the instruction stream, but the requested line numbers form a simple sequence. On the historical Zen 2 test, the chain took about 3 ns per step over the measured range because the next lines usually arrived before use.
Prefetcher behavior is microarchitecture-specific. Many processors recognize one or more forward or backward streams and some fixed strides, but limits on stream count, stride, page crossing, and destination cache differ. Treat the flat result as a demonstration from one machine, not a promise that every linear-looking traversal is prefetched.
 #Software PrefetchingGCC and Clang expose a prefetch hint through __builtin_prefetch:
__builtin_prefetch(a.data() + index, 0, 1); The optional arguments describe a read (0) and low temporal locality (1). The GCC documentation is deliberately cautious: the compiler emits a target instruction if one exists, and the processor may treat it as a hint. The prefetch instruction itself is normally non-faulting on supported targets, but evaluating the address expression can still fault or invoke undefined behavior. Form an address inside a live allocation.
For an artificial pointer chain, we want a permutation that is irregular enough not to look like a normal stride but whose future state is cheap to compute. A full-period linear congruential map works if its parameters satisfy the right conditions. The claim that $2x+1$ modulo a prime always has period $n$ is false: its non-fixed orbits have a period dividing the multiplicative order of 2, hence dividing $n-1$.
Instead, choose a power-of-two size $n$ and
$$ f(x) = 5x + 1 \pmod n. $$
The increment is odd and $5-1$ is divisible by four, so the Hull–Dobell full-period conditions hold: every state belongs to one cycle of length $n$. This is useful for the experiment, not an endorsement of the generator’s statistical quality.
if (log_n == 0 || log_n >= 32) throw std::invalid_argument("log_n must be in [1, 31]"); const std::uint32_t n = 1u << log_n; const std::uint32_t mask = n - 1; auto step = [mask](std::uint32_t x) { return static_cast<std::uint32_t>((5ull * x + 1) & mask); }; std::vector<std::uint32_t> next(n); for (std::uint32_t x = 0; x < n; ++x) next[x] = step(x); Prefetching the immediate successor gives only one iteration of lead time:
std::uint32_t k = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < steps; ++i) { __builtin_prefetch(next.data() + step(k), 0, 1); k = next[k]; } On the original machine, this nearly doubled throughput once the working set was large enough:
 One-step software-prefetch experiment   #Jumping Ahead SafelyAffine maps compose. Rather than using 1 << D—which becomes undefined when the shift reaches the type width and overflows much earlier in intermediate arithmetic—we can exponentiate the affine transformation by squaring:
struct Affine { std::uint32_t mul; std::uint32_t add; }; Affine compose(Affine f, Affine g, std::uint32_t mask) { // f(g(x))  return { static_cast<std::uint32_t>((std::uint64_t{f.mul} * g.mul) & mask), static_cast<std::uint32_t>( (std::uint64_t{f.mul} * g.add + f.add) & mask) }; } Affine power(Affine f, std::size_t exponent, std::uint32_t mask) { Affine result{1, 0}; while (exponent != 0) { if (exponent & 1) result = compose(f, result, mask); f = compose(f, f, mask); exponent >>= 1; } return result; } std::uint32_t apply(Affine f, std::uint32_t x, std::uint32_t mask) { return static_cast<std::uint32_t>( (std::uint64_t{f.mul} * x + f.add) & mask ); } Compute Affine ahead = power({5, 1}, D, mask) once, then prefetch next.data() + apply(ahead, k, mask) on each iteration. After the initial warm-up, each hint is aimed $D$ dependent steps ahead.
Increasing $D$ does not multiply throughput by $D$. The speedup stops when the lead time covers the miss latency or when request queues, issue bandwidth, cache capacity, translations, or DRAM bandwidth saturate. Prefetching too far can evict the line before use; a wrong-path hint may waste all of its traffic.
 Several software-prefetch distances on the historical test  This is why software prefetching often fails in production. It is most attractive when the future address is reliable, there is useful computation between the hint and the load, and profiling shows latency rather than bandwidth is the bottleneck.
The x86 _mm_prefetch intrinsic also accepts hints such as _MM_HINT_T0, _MM_HINT_T1, _MM_HINT_T2, and _MM_HINT_NTA. These encodings express intended locality; they do not portably command an exact cache level, and a processor may ignore or reinterpret them. Hardware prefetchers are not harmless either: good designs throttle them under pressure, but an unnecessary stream can still evict useful lines and consume bandwidth.
title: Prefetching

content:
The minimum of an array is easy to compute and impossible to undo. That second property is what makes static range-minimum queries unusually fast.
Given an immutable array $a$, the range minimum query (RMQ) asks for
$$ \min{a_l,a_{l+1},\ldots,a_{r-1}} $$
on a half-open interval $[l,r)$. We will build the array once and answer many queries. Updates belong to a different problem; a segment tree trades constant query time for $O(\log n)$ queries and updates.
 #Overlapping Is HarmlessPrecompute the minimum of every interval whose length is a power of two:
$$ t[k][i] =\min{a_i,\ldots,a_{i+2^k-1}}. $$
The recurrence
$$ t[k][i] =\min(t[k-1][i],t[k-1][i+2^{k-1}]) $$
builds level $k$ from two adjacent intervals at level $k-1$.
For a query of length $L=r-l$, choose $k=\lfloor\log_2L\rfloor$. Two length-$2^k$ intervals, one starting at $l$ and one ending at $r$, cover the query:
$$ \operatorname{rmq}(l,r) =\min(t[k][l],t[k][r-2^k]). $$
They may overlap. This is correct because minimum is idempotent:
$$ \min(x,x)=x. $$
The same sparse-table query works for maximum, gcd, bitwise AND, and other idempotent associative operations. It does not work for sum: elements in the overlap would be counted twice.
 #A Level-Major Sparse TableStore each level contiguously. Construction then performs sequential reads from one level and sequential writes to the next:
#include <algorithm>#include <bit>#include <cassert>#include <cstddef>#include <utility>#include <vector> class SparseRMQ { std::vector<std::vector<int>> table; public: SparseRMQ() = default; explicit SparseRMQ(std::vector<int> values) { if (values.empty()) return; const std::size_t n = values.size(); const unsigned levels = unsigned(std::bit_width(n)); table.resize(levels); table[0] = std::move(values); for (unsigned k = 1; k < levels; ++k) { const std::size_t half = std::size_t(1) << (k - 1); const std::size_t length = half * 2; const std::size_t count = n - length + 1; table[k].resize(count); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) table[k][i] = std::min(table[k - 1][i], table[k - 1][i + half]); } } std::size_t size() const { return table.empty() ? 0 : table[0].size(); } int query(std::size_t l, std::size_t r) const { assert(l < r && r <= size()); const std::size_t length = r - l; const unsigned k = unsigned(std::bit_width(length) - 1); const std::size_t block = std::size_t(1) << k; return std::min(table[k][l], table[k][r - block]); } }; std::bit_width(length)-1 is a floor binary logarithm for positive length; rejecting empty intervals before the calculation avoids the zero case. Storing only valid starts makes higher levels progressively shorter, although the total is still $\Theta(n\log n)$ integers.
The query performs two data-dependent loads. They are independent, so an out-of-order core can issue them together, but a cache miss still dominates the handful of arithmetic instructions. Keeping every level in a separate contiguous allocation is simple; one flat allocation plus level offsets can reduce allocator metadata and improve control over alignment.
 #Paying Less MemoryFor $n=10^8$, even four bytes per element per level is too much. A practical compromise divides the input into blocks, stores one minimum per block, and builds a sparse table only over those minima.
A query scans at most two partial edge blocks and uses one constant-time query for all complete blocks in the middle:
#include <limits> class BlockedRMQ { static constexpr std::size_t B = 64; std::vector<int> values; SparseRMQ blocks; static std::vector<int> block_minima(const std::vector<int>& a) { std::vector<int> result; result.reserve((a.size() + B - 1) / B); for (std::size_t begin = 0; begin < a.size(); begin += B) { std::size_t end = std::min(begin + B, a.size()); auto first = a.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(begin); auto last = a.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(end); result.push_back(*std::min_element(first, last)); } return result; } public: explicit BlockedRMQ(std::vector<int> input) : values(std::move(input)), blocks(block_minima(values)) {} int query(std::size_t l, std::size_t r) const { assert(l < r && r <= values.size()); int result = std::numeric_limits<int>::max(); while (l < r && l % B != 0) result = std::min(result, values[l++]); const std::size_t full_end = r - r % B; if (l < full_end) { result = std::min(result, blocks.query(l / B, full_end / B)); l = full_end; } while (l < r) result = std::min(result, values[l++]); return result; } }; The auxiliary table contains $\lceil n/B\rceil$ values rather than $n$. A query performs $O(B)$ scalar work—at most $2B-2$ edge elements—plus two table loads. With a fixed $B$ this is constant in $n$, but the constant is real. Choose $B$ from the memory budget and query distribution, and vectorize the edge reductions if they become important.
For short ranges, the blocked version scans the entire query and may be faster than touching a distant upper table level. For long ranges, it saves enough memory that the top-level structure is more likely to remain cached. The smaller representation can win even while executing more comparisons.
 #Linear Space and Constant QueriesIt is possible to achieve all three desirable bounds for static RMQ:
 $O(n)$ preprocessing time; $O(n)$ space; $O(1)$ query time.  The route goes through Cartesian trees. The Cartesian tree of an array has the minimum at its root and recursively represents the left and right subarrays. An RMQ becomes a lowest-common-ancestor query between two tree positions.
Farach-Colton and Bender reduce LCA to RMQ on an Euler-tour depth sequence whose adjacent values differ by exactly one. Small blocks of such a $\pm1$ sequence have only a limited number of shapes, so all within-block answers can be tabulated by shape; a sparse structure over block minima handles the middle. Fischer–Heun generalizes the microblock idea directly to RMQ.
The asymptotics are optimal, but the implementation has more tables, encodings, and indirections than the blocked structure above. It pays off when memory is constrained and the query count is large. “Optimal” is a statement about a model; the crossover is an experimental fact.
 #Returning Positions and Handling TiesMany applications need the index of a minimum, not only its value. Store pairs (value,index) and define one total order, such as smaller value first and smaller index on ties. Every build and query operation must use the same order. If one layer chooses the leftmost minimum and another the rightmost, overlapping sparse-table queries can return inconsistent positions even though the minimum value is correct.
NaNs require a similar policy for floating-point arrays. std::min is not a mathematical total order over NaNs; decide whether a NaN propagates, is ignored, or is ordered explicitly, and test that contract.
 #Testing and WorkloadsFor small arrays, enumerate every nonempty interval and compare with a direct scan. Include equal values, monotone arrays, alternating extremes, lengths around powers of two, and arrays whose size is just below or above a block boundary. Randomized tests should vary both values and query lengths.
Performance depends heavily on the query distribution. Uniform random endpoints favor long ranges; many applications issue mostly short, nearby ranges. Report preprocessing time, bytes per element, and cold and warm query latency separately. If only a few queries are made, scanning can be faster than building any structure at all.
RMQ is a good example of optimization by algebra. Idempotence permits overlapping intervals; that removes a branchy decomposition from every query. Blocking then spends a bounded amount of arithmetic to buy locality and a much smaller index. The fastest structure follows from the operation’s laws and the machine’s memory hierarchy together.
 #Further Reading Bender and Farach-Colton, The LCA Problem Revisited, gives the $\pm1$ reduction behind linear-space constant-time RMQ. Fischer and Heun, Theoretical and Practical Improvements on the RMQ-Problem, develops succinct microblock structures. Alstrup et al., Nearest Common Ancestors: A Survey and a New Algorithm for a Distributed Environment, places the RMQ–LCA connection in context.
title: Range Minimum Query

content:
Optimizing for latency is usually quite different from optimizing for throughput:
 When optimizing data structure queries or small one-time or branchy algorithms, you need to look up the latencies of its instructions, mentally construct the execution graph of the computation, and then try to reorganize it so that the critical path is shorter. When optimizing hot loops and large-dataset algorithms, you need to look up the throughputs of their instructions, count how many times each one is used per iteration, determine which of them is the bottleneck, and then try to restructure the loop so that it is used less often.  The last advice only works for data-parallel loops, where each iteration is fully independent of the previous one. When there is some interdependency between consecutive iterations, there may potentially be a pipeline stall caused by a data hazard as the next iteration is waiting for the previous one to complete.
 #ExampleAs a simple example, consider how the sum of an array is computed:
int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i]; Let’s assume for a moment that the compiler doesn’t vectorize this loop, the memory bandwidth isn’t a concern, and that the loop is unrolled so that we don’t pay any additional cost associated with maintaining the loop variables. In this case, the computation becomes very simple:
int s = 0; s += a[0]; s += a[1]; s += a[2]; s += a[3]; // ... How fast can we compute this? At exactly one cycle per element — because we need one cycle each iteration to add another value to s. The latency of the memory read doesn’t matter because the CPU can start it ahead of time.
But we can go higher than that. The throughput of add1 is 2 on my CPU (Zen 2), meaning we could theoretically execute two of them every cycle. But right now this isn’t possible: while s is being used to accumulate $i$-th element, it can’t be used for $(i+1)$-th for at least one cycle.
The solution is to use two accumulators and just sum up odd and even elements separately:
int s0 = 0, s1 = 0; s0 += a[0]; s1 += a[1]; s0 += a[2]; s1 += a[3]; // ... int s = s0 + s1; Now our superscalar CPU can execute these two “threads” simultaneously, and our computation no longer has any critical paths that limit the throughput.
 #The General CaseIf an instruction has a latency of $x$ and a throughput of $y$, then you would need to use $x \cdot y$ accumulators to saturate it. This also implies that you need $x \cdot y$ logical registers to hold their values, which is an important consideration for CPU designs, limiting the maximum number of usable execution units for high-latency instructions.
This technique is mostly used with SIMD and not in scalar code. You can generalize the code above and compute sums and other reductions faster than the compiler.
In general, when optimizing loops, you usually have just one or a few execution ports that you want to utilize to their fullest, and you engineer the rest of the loop around them. As different instructions may use different sets of ports, it is not always clear which one is going to be overused. In situations like this, machine code analyzers can be very helpful for finding the bottlenecks of small assembly loops.
  The throughput of register-register add is 4, but since we are reading its second operand from memory, it is bottlenecked by the throughput of memory mov, which is 2 on Zen 2. ↩︎
title: Throughput Computing

content:
An object is aligned when its address is a multiple of the alignment required by its type. The C++ requirement is alignof(T), not sizeof(T): the two often happen to be equal for small scalar types, but they are different properties.
Alignment matters for correctness and performance. Some instructions require aligned operands. Even where unaligned loads are legal, an access that crosses a cache-line or page boundary may need two transfers and extra work to combine them.
 #Aligned AllocationEvery object and every array element is placed at an address satisfying alignof(T). A stricter alignment can be requested with alignas:
alignas(32) float values[N]; assert(reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(values) % 32 == 0); This is useful when an algorithm uses 32-byte AVX loads or stores. The instruction requires a 32-byte-aligned address; merely fitting inside a 64-byte cache line is not the same guarantee.
C++17 also provides std::aligned_alloc. Its size must be an integral multiple of the requested alignment, it returns null on failure, and its storage must be released with std::free:
constexpr std::size_t alignment = 32; const std::size_t bytes = N * sizeof(float); const std::size_t padded = (bytes + alignment - 1) / alignment * alignment; void *storage = std::aligned_alloc(alignment, padded); if (storage == nullptr) throw std::bad_alloc{}; auto *values = static_cast<float *>(storage); // use the storage for implicit-lifetime objects such as float std::free(storage); Supported extended alignments are implementation-defined, and Microsoft’s C runtime uses _aligned_malloc/_aligned_free rather than implementing std::aligned_alloc in the same way. For an over-aligned C++ object, aligned operator new and a matching aligned operator delete are another option.
An alignment can also be attached to a type:
struct alignas(64) CacheLineRecord { std::uint64_t value; }; static_assert(alignof(CacheLineRecord) == 64); static_assert(sizeof(CacheLineRecord) % 64 == 0); Every array element then starts on a 64-byte boundary. On a machine with 64-byte lines this isolates records, at the cost of rounding each record’s size up to a multiple of 64.
 #Structure LayoutFor an ordinary non-bit-field member, the implementation places the member at an offset satisfying alignof(member_type). It may insert padding before members and at the end of the structure so that every element of an array of the structure is properly aligned.
Consider this common ABI layout:
struct Data { char a; short b; int c; char d; }; On an ABI where short has alignment 2 and int has alignment 4, the layout is equivalent to:
struct DataLayoutExample { char a; // offset 0  char pad1[1]; short b; // offset 2  int c; // offset 4  char d; // offset 8; char itself never needs padding  char pad2[3]; }; static_assert(sizeof(DataLayoutExample) == 12); The exact size and offsets are ABI properties, not values guaranteed by the language. Check them with sizeof, alignof, and offsetof for the target that must interoperate with a file format or foreign interface.
 #Member OrderReordering members can reduce padding:
struct CompactData { int c; short b; char a; char d; }; On the same ABI this type occupies 8 bytes instead of 12. Sorting plain data members by decreasing alignment is a useful heuristic, but sorting by sizeof is not the rule and the heuristic is not a proof of optimality. Arrays, nested structures, base classes, ABI constraints, and intentionally separated hot fields can change the best layout.
Smaller is also not automatically faster. Put fields used together near one another, but separate independently written per-thread fields when false sharing is the larger cost.
 #Packed StructuresGCC and Clang provide a non-standard packed attribute:
struct __attribute__((packed)) PackedData { std::uint64_t value; bool flag; }; On those compilers the object typically occupies 9 bytes instead of the 16 used by the natural layout. A member may then be misaligned. The compiler can generate safe bytewise or unaligned accesses when accessing it directly, but taking its address and treating it as a normally aligned std::uint64_t * is not safe. Some ISAs handle unaligned loads efficiently, some impose a large penalty, and some fault for particular instructions.
Packing is most defensible for a specified external representation. Even then, byte order, object lifetime, and versioning need explicit handling; copying a native structure to disk is rarely a portable serialization format.
 #Bit-FieldsBit-fields assign a width in bits to a member:
struct Flags { std::uint32_t kind : 3; std::uint32_t index : 24; std::uint32_t valid : 1; }; Their allocation, alignment, direction, and straddling are implementation-defined. A bit-field cannot be addressed independently, and an array still advances by the whole-byte value sizeof(Flags): neighboring array elements are never merged across a fractional byte boundary by the C++ object model. Adding packed makes the layout a compiler/ABI contract, not a portable one.
For an exact 24-bit little-endian representation, explicit bytes are clearer and portable:
std::uint32_t load_u24_le(const std::byte *p) { return std::uint32_t(std::to_integer<std::uint8_t>(p[0])) | (std::uint32_t(std::to_integer<std::uint8_t>(p[1])) << 8) | (std::uint32_t(std::to_integer<std::uint8_t>(p[2])) << 16); } void store_u24_le(std::byte *p, std::uint32_t x) { p[0] = std::byte(x & 0xffu); p[1] = std::byte((x >> 8) & 0xffu); p[2] = std::byte((x >> 16) & 0xffu); } This avoids shifting negative char values, violating alignment or type-access rules, and reading a fourth byte outside the object. Compilers can combine the byte operations when the target has a profitable unaligned-load sequence. If a specialized loader deliberately reads four bytes, its API must require four accessible bytes and use memcpy or another alias-safe operation; masking the result does not legalize an out-of-bounds read.
title: Alignment and Packing

content:
Here is a function that divides an unsigned integer by ten:
#include <cstdint> std::uint32_t div10(std::uint32_t x) { return x / 10; } There is no reason for this tiny function to be interesting, except that its machine code normally contains no division. Optimizing compilers replace the constant divisor with a multiplication by a precomputed reciprocal followed by a shift. The derivation is subtle enough to occupy a good part of the integer division chapter, yet the optimization happens without being requested.
Compilers know a large collection of such arithmetic identities. More importantly, they know the conditions under which each identity is legal. This second part is why a handwritten “obvious optimization” is often either unnecessary or wrong.
 #Constant Folding and PropagationThe simplest arithmetic optimization is to do the work during compilation:
int f(int x) { constexpr int width = 7 * 9; return x * width + (3 - 3); } The expression becomes x * 63; the addition of zero disappears. If the caller supplies a constant x and the function is visible, the entire result can disappear too. This combination of constant folding, constant propagation, inlining, and dead-code elimination is the reason compile-time information is so valuable.
The constexpr keyword is not what performs the optimization. It makes an expression eligible for constant evaluation and, in some contexts, requires it. Ordinary code with known inputs can also be folded under the language’s as-if rule: the implementation may transform a program in any way that preserves its observable behavior.
Conversely, hiding a value behind a separately compiled function, a mutable global, or an unpredictable memory load may prevent propagation. Link-time optimization and header-defined templates help because they expose more of the program to the optimizer.
 #Strength ReductionStrength reduction replaces an expensive operation with a cheaper equivalent. The classic examples are multiplication or division by a power of two:
std::uint32_t mul8(std::uint32_t x) { return x * 8; } std::uint32_t div8(std::uint32_t x) { return x / 8; } std::uint32_t mod8(std::uint32_t x) { return x % 8; } For unsigned integers these become, respectively, a left shift, a right shift, and a bitwise and with seven. You should normally write the operation you mean. The compiler knows the target instruction costs, while x / 8 documents division and remains correct if the type or divisor changes.
Signed division is already less trivial. C++ division rounds toward zero, while an arithmetic right shift rounds negative odd values toward negative infinity. Replacing x / 8 with x >> 3 changes the result for values such as -9. The compiler either emits the required correction or uses the shift only when it can prove that x is nonnegative.
Strength reduction also happens inside loops. A source-level array access such as a[i * stride] does not necessarily multiply from scratch on every iteration. The optimizer can maintain a pointer and advance it by stride each time. This transformation is called induction-variable simplification, and it is one reason pointer arithmetic and indexing usually compile to the same code.
 #Hoisting InvariantsConsider applying an affine transformation to an array:
void normalize(float* a, int n, float lo, float hi) { for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = (a[i] - lo) / (hi - lo); } The denominator does not change between iterations. A compiler can move its computation out of the loop, calculate its reciprocal once, and multiply each element by it:
float scale = 1.0f / (hi - lo); for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = (a[i] - lo) * scale; Moving an unchanged expression out of a loop is loop-invariant code motion. For integer division, calculating one reciprocal can be a major saving. For floating point, replacing several divisions with multiplication changes rounding and exceptional behavior, so whether it happens depends on the requested floating-point model.
Loads can also be loop-invariant, but only if nothing in the loop may overwrite their memory. This is where aliasing contracts matter. If two pointers may refer to overlapping ranges, a store through one can invalidate a value loaded through the other, and the compiler must remain conservative.
 #Reassociation and ReductionsArithmetic expressions describe both a value and, sometimes accidentally, a dependency graph.
float sum(const float* a, int n) { float s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) s += a[i]; return s; } Each addition depends on the previous one. Splitting the sum into several accumulators exposes instruction-level parallelism, and packing those accumulators into vectors exposes SIMD parallelism. For integers whose overflow behavior permits it, compilers routinely perform this transformation.
For floating point, (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) because each addition rounds. Under strict IEEE semantics, arbitrary reassociation is therefore forbidden. Options such as GCC’s -fassociative-math relax specific rules; the broad -ffast-math group relaxes several more, including assumptions about signed zero, infinities, and NaNs. Clang documents its individual controls in its floating-point command-line reference.
This is not merely a choice between “accurate” and “a few bits less accurate.” Reassociation can improve a well-conditioned sum, destroy a carefully stabilized formula, or make behavior depend on the compiler and target. Enable relaxed arithmetic only when the numerical contract and tests permit each transformation. The rounding errors chapter develops these concerns in detail.
 #Fused OperationsMany processors have a fused multiply-add instruction that computes
$$ a \cdot b + c $$
with one final rounding. It is usually faster than a separate multiplication and addition, and often more accurate because the intermediate product is not rounded. Compilers can select it from a matching expression when the target supports FMA and the contraction rules allow it:
float polynomial(float x, float a, float b) { return a * x + b; } std::fma asks for fused semantics explicitly, even on a target where the implementation must emulate them. A compiler option may instead permit contraction of ordinary source expressions. These are different contracts, although they can lead to the same instruction.
Fused memory operands are another, unrelated x86 feature: an arithmetic instruction can read one operand directly from memory. That saves a separately encoded load instruction, but internally it may still decode into more than one micro-operation.
 #Narrower ArithmeticUsing a smaller type may reduce memory traffic and fit more elements in a SIMD register. It does not automatically make scalar arithmetic faster: general-purpose registers commonly operate at a fixed native width, and narrow values may require extension before use.
The profitable pattern is usually to store data narrowly and widen it for computation:
std::uint64_t sum_samples(const std::uint16_t* samples, std::size_t n) { std::uint64_t total = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) total += samples[i]; return total; } The accumulator must be wide enough for the largest possible sum. This is a proof obligation, not a compiler preference. Accidental signed overflow is undefined behavior in C++, while unsigned overflow wraps modulo a power of two. Choosing unsigned solely because it enables wraparound can make comparisons and loop termination harder to reason about; choose the type that matches the mathematical range.
 #What the Compiler Will Not InventLocal algebra is the compiler’s home ground. It will fold constants, eliminate identities, derive reciprocals, combine shifts, recognize rotations, simplify induction variables, and select target instructions. GCC lists the enabled transformations for each optimization level in its optimization options, although the result also depends on cost models and surrounding code.
It normally will not replace an unstable formula with a stable one, change a matrix representation, introduce a lookup table with a meaningful memory trade-off, or decide that approximate arithmetic is acceptable. Those transformations change an algorithm’s contract or resource usage.
A practical workflow is therefore:
 Write the clearest exact expression. Compile with the intended optimization level and target. Inspect the hot loop, not an isolated source line. If an operation remains expensive, identify which semantic condition blocks the rewrite. Express the missing precondition or perform a tested algorithmic transformation.  Memorizing bit tricks is less valuable than learning which facts make them true. The compiler has already memorized more of them than either of us.
title: Arithmetic Optimizations

content:
An integer is usually introduced as a number, but the processor also sees it as a small, fixed-size set. If bit $i$ is one, the set contains $i$; if it is zero, it does not. Addition moves carries through this set, multiplication combines shifted copies of it, and the bitwise instructions modify many membership flags at once.
This second interpretation is useful far beyond contest-style tricks. Memory allocators round sizes to powers of two, schedulers maintain masks of available CPUs, parsers classify bytes in parallel, and compressed data structures routinely store one Boolean value per bit. The important skill is not memorizing a page of incantations. It is recognizing when an integer is the right representation and then expressing the operation so that both the language and the hardware agree on its meaning.
 #Use Unsigned WordsFor a $w$-bit unsigned type, C++ arithmetic is performed modulo $2^w$. There is no exceptional overflow case:
$$ x + y \equiv (x+y) \pmod {2^w}. $$
This is exactly the algebra most bit-manipulation identities expect. Signed arithmetic is different: overflow is undefined behavior, while converting a large unsigned result to a signed type can produce a surprising negative value. A good default is therefore to do the bit work in a fixed-width unsigned type and convert only at a checked boundary.
Shifts have their own precondition. For x << k and x >> k, the shift count must be smaller than the width of x. Writing 1 << k is also a common bug because the literal 1 has type int; use uint64_t{1} << k when constructing a 64-bit mask.
#include <cstdint>#include <optional> std::optional<bool> test_bit(std::uint64_t x, unsigned k) { if (k >= 64) return std::nullopt; return ((x >> k) & 1u) != 0; } std::optional<std::uint64_t> set_bit(std::uint64_t x, unsigned k) { if (k >= 64) return std::nullopt; return x | (std::uint64_t{1} << k); } std::optional<std::uint64_t> clear_bit(std::uint64_t x, unsigned k) { if (k >= 64) return std::nullopt; return x & ~(std::uint64_t{1} << k); } The checks are part of the interface here: an invalid index produces std::nullopt rather than a false answer or a silent no-op. If the caller has already established k < 64, keeping that invariant outside the hot loop is normally better than checking it for every element.
 #Ask the Standard Library FirstSince C++20, the <bit> header provides portable names for most operations that used to require compiler-specific builtins:
   Operation Meaning     std::popcount(x) number of one-bits   std::countl_zero(x) zero-bits before the highest one-bit   std::countr_zero(x) zero-bits after the lowest one-bit   std::bit_width(x) number of bits needed to represent x   std::has_single_bit(x) whether x is a power of two   std::bit_floor(x), std::bit_ceil(x) neighboring powers of two   std::rotl(x, k), std::rotr(x, k) cyclic shifts    Unlike the older GCC __builtin_clz and __builtin_ctz, the standard counting functions have defined behavior for zero. GCC explicitly documents zero as undefined for those two builtins in its bit-operation reference, which is why wrapping them carelessly used to produce surprisingly creative bugs.
These functions describe intent and still compile to specialized instructions when the target has them. std::popcount, for example, may become popcnt; on another target it may become a short arithmetic sequence or a library call. The source code should normally specify the operation, while compiler flags specify the machine on which it is allowed to run.
#include <bit>#include <cstdint> struct bit_summary { int ones; int leading_zeroes; int trailing_zeroes; int width; }; bit_summary inspect(std::uint32_t x) { return { std::popcount(x), std::countl_zero(x), std::countr_zero(x), static_cast<int>(std::bit_width(x)) }; }  #Two’s-Complement IdentitiesUnsigned negation is defined as subtraction from $2^w$. Consequently, 0 - x has the same bit pattern commonly associated with two’s-complement -x, without involving signed overflow.
This gives two particularly useful identities:
#include <cstdint> std::uint64_t lowest_bit(std::uint64_t x) { return x & (0 - x); } std::uint64_t clear_lowest_bit(std::uint64_t x) { return x & (x - 1); } Why do they work? Subtracting one changes the lowest one-bit to zero and turns every lower zero-bit into one. AND-ing with the original word therefore removes exactly that bit. Negating a word performs the complementary transformation, leaving only the lowest one-bit common to both operands.
The zero case is worth stating rather than discovering later: both functions return zero for zero. The often-seen power-of-two test (x & (x - 1)) == 0 also accepts zero, so a complete version is x != 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0, or simply std::has_single_bit(x).
One practical application is checked power-of-two alignment:
#include <bit>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <optional> std::optional<std::uint64_t> align_up(std::uint64_t x, std::uint64_t alignment) { if (!std::has_single_bit(alignment)) return std::nullopt; const std::uint64_t mask = alignment - 1; if (x > std::numeric_limits<std::uint64_t>::max() - mask) return std::nullopt; return (x + mask) & ~mask; } The familiar one-line formula is still there, but its two real preconditions—power-of-two alignment and no addition overflow—are now visible.
 #Masks as Small SetsIf a problem has at most $w$ independent yes/no states, a $w$-bit word can represent the whole state. Union becomes OR, intersection becomes AND, symmetric difference becomes XOR, and complement becomes NOT followed by a mask that removes unused high bits.
This is especially convenient when enumerating subsets. The following loop visits every submask of mask, including zero, exactly once:
#include <cstdint>#include <utility> template<class F> void for_each_submask(std::uint32_t mask, F&& f) { std::uint32_t sub = mask; while (true) { f(sub); if (sub == 0) break; sub = (sub - 1) & mask; } } The subtraction finds the next smaller bit pattern, while the AND removes bits that are not members of the original set. If this is done for every $n$-bit mask, the total number of visits is $3^n$: each bit is either outside mask, inside mask but outside sub, or inside both.
Packed masks trade memory for extra work. They are excellent when bandwidth or cache capacity is the bottleneck, but less attractive when individual elements are updated concurrently: several logical values share one machine word, so an update may require a read-modify-write instruction and may create false sharing. Representation is part of the algorithm, not a free compression switch.
 #When One Instruction Is Not One Cyclex86 has increasingly specialized bit instructions: popcnt, count-leading/trailing-zero instructions, rotations, and BMI2 operations such as pext and pdep, which gather or scatter selected bits. The Intel Intrinsics Guide is useful for finding their interfaces, but an instruction’s existence does not make it universally fast. Latency and throughput differ substantially between microarchitectures, and some intrinsics expand into instruction sequences when the requested feature is unavailable.
The reverse is also important: handwritten tricks are often unnecessary. Compilers recognize x & (x - 1), rotations, byte swaps, power-of-two divisions, and many branchless selection idioms. A clever source expression can be slower than a comparison followed by cmov, or can prevent vectorization by obscuring what the loop computes.
The reliable workflow is the same as for any other low-level optimization:
 express the operation with unsigned arithmetic and explicit preconditions; prefer <bit> when it has the operation; compile for the real target and inspect the generated code; benchmark the entire loop, not an isolated instruction; keep the straightforward version unless the specialized one wins in the workload that matters.  Bit manipulation is powerful precisely because it crosses several levels at once: algebra modulo $2^w$, data representation, compiler pattern matching, and the instruction set. Most “bit hacks” go wrong when they account for only one of them.
title: Bit Manipulation

content:
A cache-aware algorithm chooses tiles, buffers, or fan-in using known $M$ and $B$. A cache-oblivious algorithm contains no parameters tuned to those values, yet its access order can still have an asymptotically good block-transfer count.
The usual analysis uses an ideal fully associative cache with $M$ words, blocks of $B$ consecutive words, and optimal replacement. Results often assume a tall cache, $M=\Omega(B^2)$. These are proof assumptions, not a description of every CPU. The value is that one recursive access order can be analyzed independently at L1, L2, the last-level cache, and another managed boundary.
Cache-oblivious does not mean automatically cache-efficient. A random permutation is oblivious to $M$ and $B$ too. The recursion and data layout must ensure that subproblems become contiguous and remain reusable once they fit.
Frigo, Leiserson, Prokop, and Ramachandran formalized the model and its matrix bounds in “Cache-Oblivious Algorithms”. The term is also unrelated to data-oblivious algorithms, which hide access patterns for security.
 #Rectangular Matrix TranspositionLet $A$ be a row-major $m\times n$ matrix and let $D$ be a separate row-major $n\times m$ destination. A simple loop can read rows of $A$ contiguously or write rows of $D$ contiguously, but not both. When the stride is large, the other side may use only one element from each transferred block.
Recursive transposition divides the longer dimension. Eventually a source tile and its destination tile are both small enough to remain cached, even though the program never tests $M$ or $B$.
The following implementation handles rectangular and odd dimensions. Source and destination must not overlap:
#include <cstddef>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> std::size_t checked_matrix_area(std::size_t rows, std::size_t columns) { if (rows != 0 && columns > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / rows) throw std::length_error("matrix size overflow"); return rows * columns; } void transpose_tile(std::span<const double> source, std::span<double> destination, std::size_t source_columns, std::size_t destination_columns, std::size_t row_begin, std::size_t row_end, std::size_t column_begin, std::size_t column_end) { const std::size_t rows = row_end - row_begin; const std::size_t columns = column_end - column_begin; if (rows == 0 || columns == 0) return; if (rows <= 16 && columns <= 16) { for (std::size_t row = row_begin; row < row_end; ++row) for (std::size_t column = column_begin; column < column_end; ++column) destination[column * destination_columns + row] = source[row * source_columns + column]; return; } if (rows >= columns) { const std::size_t middle = row_begin + rows / 2; transpose_tile(source, destination, source_columns, destination_columns, row_begin, middle, column_begin, column_end); transpose_tile(source, destination, source_columns, destination_columns, middle, row_end, column_begin, column_end); } else { const std::size_t middle = column_begin + columns / 2; transpose_tile(source, destination, source_columns, destination_columns, row_begin, row_end, column_begin, middle); transpose_tile(source, destination, source_columns, destination_columns, row_begin, row_end, middle, column_end); } } void transpose_out_of_place(std::span<const double> source, std::span<double> destination, std::size_t rows, std::size_t columns) { const std::size_t area = checked_matrix_area(rows, columns); if (source.size() != area || destination.size() != area) throw std::invalid_argument("matrix extent mismatch"); transpose_tile(source, destination, columns, rows, 0, rows, 0, columns); } The constant $16$ is only a recursion-overhead cutoff; it does not describe a cache. Recursing to individual elements gives the same asymptotic access order.
Under the ideal-cache and tall-cache assumptions, the transfer count is
$$ Q_{\mathrm{transpose}}(m,n) =\Theta\left(1+\frac{mn}{B}\right). $$
This is optimal up to constants because the algorithm must read and write $\Theta(mn)$ elements. In-place rectangular transposition is a different and substantially more complicated permutation problem; the code above makes no in-place claim.
 #Matrix Multiplication by Three-Way RecursionFor row-major matrices
$$ C_{ij}=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_{ik}B_{kj}, $$
where $A$ is $m\times p$, $B$ is $p\times n$, and $C$ is $m\times n$. A fixed triple-loop order makes at least one large matrix access unfriendly for some shapes. Cache-aware libraries solve this with tuned tiles.
A cache-oblivious version recursively splits the largest of the row, column, and reduction ranges. Splitting rows or columns creates independent output regions. Splitting the reduction range performs two contributions to the same output region, in order.
The code below initializes $C$ and supports arbitrary dimensions. The output span must not overlap either input span:
#include <algorithm>#include <cstddef>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> std::size_t checked_matrix_size(std::size_t rows, std::size_t columns) { if (rows != 0 && columns > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / rows) throw std::length_error("matrix size overflow"); return rows * columns; } void multiply_add_region(std::span<const double> left, std::span<const double> right, std::span<double> output, std::size_t inner, std::size_t columns, std::size_t row_begin, std::size_t row_end, std::size_t column_begin, std::size_t column_end, std::size_t inner_begin, std::size_t inner_end) { const std::size_t row_count = row_end - row_begin; const std::size_t column_count = column_end - column_begin; const std::size_t inner_count = inner_end - inner_begin; if (row_count == 0 || column_count == 0 || inner_count == 0) return; if (row_count <= 16 && column_count <= 16 && inner_count <= 16) { for (std::size_t row = row_begin; row < row_end; ++row) { for (std::size_t k = inner_begin; k < inner_end; ++k) { const double value = left[row * inner + k]; for (std::size_t column = column_begin; column < column_end; ++column) output[row * columns + column] += value * right[k * columns + column]; } } return; } if (row_count >= column_count && row_count >= inner_count && row_count > 1) { const std::size_t middle = row_begin + row_count / 2; multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, row_begin, middle, column_begin, column_end, inner_begin, inner_end); multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, middle, row_end, column_begin, column_end, inner_begin, inner_end); return; } if (column_count >= inner_count && column_count > 1) { const std::size_t middle = column_begin + column_count / 2; multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, row_begin, row_end, column_begin, middle, inner_begin, inner_end); multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, row_begin, row_end, middle, column_end, inner_begin, inner_end); return; } const std::size_t middle = inner_begin + inner_count / 2; multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, row_begin, row_end, column_begin, column_end, inner_begin, middle); multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, row_begin, row_end, column_begin, column_end, middle, inner_end);
