} void matrix_multiply(std::span<const double> left, std::span<const double> right, std::span<double> output, std::size_t rows, std::size_t inner, std::size_t columns) { if (left.size() != checked_matrix_size(rows, inner) || right.size() != checked_matrix_size(inner, columns) || output.size() != checked_matrix_size(rows, columns)) throw std::invalid_argument("matrix extent mismatch"); std::fill(output.begin(), output.end(), 0.0); multiply_add_region(left, right, output, inner, columns, 0, rows, 0, columns, 0, inner); } The routine performs $\Theta(mpn)$ arithmetic operations. Its advantage is the order of those operations, not a change in algebra.
For square $n\times n$ matrices, group the recursion into levels that halve all three index ranges. There are eight half-size multiplication subproblems. Once three participating submatrices fit in cache, a base subproblem moves $\Theta(M/B)$ blocks and performs $\Theta(M^{3/2})$ multiply-adds. The number of such base subproblems is
$$ \Theta\left(\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt M}\right)^3\right). $$
Multiplying gives the cache-miss bound
$$ Q_{\mathrm{multiply}}(n) =\Theta\left( \frac{n^2}{B} +\frac{n^3}{B\sqrt M} \right). $$
The scan term accounts for reading inputs and writing output. For rectangular matrices, the corresponding bound is
$$ \Theta\left( 1+\frac{mp+pn+mn}{B} +\frac{mpn}{B\sqrt M} \right). $$
The old-style recurrence $8Q(n/2)+O(n^2/B)$ is easy to misuse by charging whole-matrix traffic at every recursion node. The fitting-subproblem argument counts what must actually enter a cache after locality begins to pay off.
 #Theory and Production KernelsAn ideal-cache bound does not account for SIMD width, instruction scheduling, hardware prefetch, TLBs, associativity conflicts, NUMA placement, or parallel false sharing. Production matrix libraries use carefully packed and architecture-tuned kernels, often inside a hierarchy of tiles.
Cache-oblivious recursion remains useful as a portable outer decomposition and as a way to reason about every cache level at once. A practical hybrid can stop at a fixed small threshold and call a tuned kernel; the mathematical partition still does not encode cache capacity or line size.
Algebraic algorithms such as Strassen change the number of multiplications and introduce separate numerical and memory trade-offs. They are orthogonal to fixing the access order of classical multiplication and should be analyzed with their own recurrence rather than attached to the code above.
The core technique is simple but exacting: recurse on views, split dimensions without dropping odd rows or columns, and accumulate every reduction interval exactly once. Once those invariants hold, the cache analysis has something correct to describe.
title: Cache-Oblivious Algorithms

content:
Cryptography is often introduced as a collection of difficult arithmetic problems. That is a little like introducing aviation as a collection of strong metal alloys: the components matter, but the interesting question is how they are assembled into a system that remains safe when someone is actively trying to break it.
An adversary may read traffic, modify it, replay an old message, impersonate one endpoint, or measure how long a computation takes. Different tools address different parts of that list. Encryption alone does not prove who sent a message. A hash alone does not prevent an attacker from replacing both a file and its hash. A correct cipher inside an ambiguous protocol can still be completely insecure.
The first rule of practical cryptography is therefore simple: use a maintained, high-level protocol or library whose interface already encodes the required checks. The algorithms below are worth understanding, but implementing them is not a safe way to deploy them.
 #Primitives and Their JobsModern systems are built from several kinds of primitive:
   Primitive Has a secret key? Main purpose     cryptographic hash no compact, collision-resistant digest   message-authentication code (MAC) shared key integrity and authenticity between key holders   authenticated encryption (AEAD) shared key confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity   digital signature private/public key pair publicly verifiable origin and integrity   key derivation function (KDF) secret input derive separate keys with explicit context   key exchange or KEM private/public material establish a shared secret    These interfaces deliberately do less than a complete protocol. They do not decide who owns a public key, how keys are rotated, whether an old message may be replayed, or what bytes a structured message means. Those decisions need framing, versioning, identities, sequence numbers, and a precise threat model.
A useful distinction is between authentication and authorization. A valid MAC may prove that a holder of a shared key created a request; it does not prove that this holder is allowed to delete a database. Similarly, a digital signature proves a relationship between bytes and a private key, not that a human read or intended the document.
 #Symmetric Encryption Must AuthenticateAES is a standardized block cipher: for one key, it permutes 128-bit blocks. FIPS 197 specifies AES with 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys, but raw AES does not say how to encrypt a message longer than one block. That is the job of a mode of operation.
Applications should normally ask for authenticated encryption with associated data, or AEAD. Its abstract interface is
$$ (C,T)=\operatorname{Seal}_K(N,A,P), $$
where $P$ is plaintext, $K$ is a secret key, $N$ is a nonce, $A$ is associated data, and $(C,T)$ is ciphertext plus an authentication tag. Decryption returns either the complete plaintext or failure:
$$ \operatorname{Open}_K(N,A,C,T)\in{P,\operatorname{FAIL}}. $$
Associated data is authenticated but left visible. A network protocol can put its version, message type, sequence number, and routing fields there, preventing an attacker from changing how the ciphertext is interpreted. Variable-length fields must be encoded unambiguously.
RFC 5116 defines this interface and its nonce requirements. With common AEADs such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, a nonce must not repeat under the same key. Reuse can expose plaintext relationships and destroy authentication; a nonce is not merely an optional random decoration. Let a well-reviewed library manage it, or follow the protocol’s counter construction exactly.
Authenticated decryption is an all-or-nothing operation. Do not parse, display, decompress, or otherwise act on plaintext until the tag has been verified, and treat failure as ordinary hostile input. RFC 8439 specifies ChaCha20-Poly1305 and illustrates how a stream cipher and authenticator are composed into one AEAD construction. Designing a new composition from a cipher and a MAC is specialist work.
 #Hashes, MACs, and SignaturesA cryptographic hash function maps any byte string to a fixed-size digest. It is useful for content addressing, transcript construction, and checking a file against a digest obtained through a trusted channel. If an attacker controls both file and digest, the check proves nothing.
A MAC adds a shared secret. HMAC, standardized in RFC 2104, is a standard way to build a MAC from a suitable hash. Anyone who can verify an ordinary MAC also possesses the key needed to create another one, so a MAC does not provide public verifiability.
A digital signature separates those roles. The private key signs; the public key verifies. This is useful for software updates, certificates, and protocol handshakes, but only after the verifier has established whose public key it is. Signatures also need unambiguous serialization and domain separation: a signature intended for invoice:v1 should not silently validate the same bytes as a firmware authorization.
Use a complete signature scheme through a maintained library, not a raw group operation. For example, RFC 8032 specifies Ed25519 and Ed448, including encoding and verification rules that are just as important as the underlying curve arithmetic.
 #RSA as ArithmeticRSA is a useful example of a one-way public operation with a private inverse. Choose distinct primes $p$ and $q$, set
$$ n=pq,\qquad \varphi(n)=(p-1)(q-1), $$
and choose $e$ coprime to $\varphi(n)$. The private exponent $d$ satisfies
$$ ed\equiv 1\pmod{\varphi(n)}. $$
For a representative $0\le m<n$, the textbook operations are
$$ c=m^e\bmod n,\qquad m=c^d\bmod n. $$
The following tiny values make the identity testable without a big-integer library:
#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept> constexpr std::uint32_t mod_power(std::uint32_t base, std::uint32_t exponent, std::uint32_t modulus) { if (modulus == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("zero modulus"); std::uint64_t result = 1 % modulus; std::uint64_t x = base % modulus; while (exponent != 0) { if ((exponent & 1u) != 0) result = (result * x) % modulus; x = (x * x) % modulus; exponent >>= 1; } return static_cast<std::uint32_t>(result); } // p = 61, q = 53, n = 3233, e = 17, d = 2753. static_assert(mod_power(65, 17, 3233) == 2790); static_assert(mod_power(2790, 2753, 3233) == 65); This demonstrates only the number theory. Every parameter is intentionally tiny, the multiplication is not suitable for large moduli, and textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable. It is not an encryption or signature scheme.
Real RSA encryption uses an encoding such as RSAES-OAEP, and modern RSA signatures use a construction such as RSASSA-PSS. RFC 8017 specifies these schemes and their many validation requirements. Real implementations also need large keys, cryptographic randomness, constant-time arithmetic, blinding, and defenses against malformed-ciphertext oracles. Use a vetted implementation and keep encryption and signing keys separate.
Factoring $n$ reveals the private key, but that observation is not the whole security argument: the RSA problem, the encoding scheme, key generation, and implementation leakage all matter. Public-key cryptography is normally used to authenticate or establish a short shared secret; symmetric AEAD then protects the bulk data.
 #What HTTPS Actually DoesTLS 1.3 is a good example of primitives becoming a protocol. In a normal certificate-authenticated handshake:
 the client and server exchange supported parameters and ephemeral key shares; an ephemeral Diffie–Hellman computation establishes shared secret material; the server sends a certificate chain and signs the handshake transcript with the corresponding private key; both sides derive separate handshake and application keys with HKDF; Finished messages MAC the transcript, confirming that both sides derived the same keys; application records are protected with AEAD and sequence-derived nonces.  The exact state machine is specified in RFC 8446. A server may have an RSA certificate, but TLS 1.3 does not use RSA key transport: that RSA key signs the transcript. Resumption and pre-shared-key modes change parts of the handshake, and optional 0-RTT data is replayable, so applications must not put non-idempotent actions in early data.
Certificates solve the man-in-the-middle problem only if validation succeeds. The client must check the chain to an accepted trust anchor, the requested hostname, validity and usage constraints, and the transcript signature. Clicking through a certificate error discards the authentication property while leaving the connection looking encrypted.
Ephemeral key exchange provides forward secrecy: after ephemeral secrets have been erased, later theft of the certificate’s long-term signing key should not reveal previously recorded session keys. It does not protect an endpoint that was compromised during the session.
 #The Implementation Is Part of the ProtocolMathematical security assumes that secret-dependent behavior is not visible. Real machines expose timing, cache accesses, branch patterns, page faults, power use, and fault responses. A lookup table indexed by a secret or an early-exit tag comparison can turn a sound primitive into an oracle. Constant-time code is a whole-program property and should come from a cryptographic library designed and tested for the target platform.
Keys should come from an operating-system cryptographic random source, live in narrowly scoped storage, carry an identifier and algorithm version, and never enter logs or crash reports. Ciphertext formats should authenticate their version and metadata. Rotation needs a migration plan: deleting an old key before rewriting its data is data loss, while accepting an old algorithm forever defeats retirement.
Algorithm agility does not mean inventing combinations at runtime. It means following a versioned protocol with a reviewed upgrade path. NIST’s FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM for post-quantum key establishment, but combining classical and post-quantum mechanisms safely is itself a protocol decision. Adopt the construction supplied by an updated protocol and library.
Test implementations with published vectors, malformed inputs, and failure paths; fuzz the parser around the cryptographic core. Most importantly, make the secure operation the easy API: open should return either authenticated plaintext or an error, never “plaintext plus a Boolean that the caller might forget to inspect.”
Cryptography does not remove trust. It narrows trust to explicit keys, algorithms, implementations, and protocol state. Good engineering begins by writing those assumptions down—and by refusing to replace a reviewed construction with something that merely looks mathematically difficult.
title: Cryptography

content:
A hash table is often introduced as an array plus a clever formula that turns a key into an index. This description is mathematically sufficient and architecturally misleading.
The hash function only chooses where a search begins. Performance is mostly determined by what happens after two keys choose the same place: how entries are laid out, how many unrelated bytes are fetched, which condition terminates a failed lookup, and what deletion leaves behind. Two tables with the same expected $O(1)$ complexity can have very different memory traffic.
In this chapter, we will design a flat hash table in stages. We start with chaining, move the entries into one contiguous array, control long probe sequences with Robin Hood insertion, and finally separate one-byte metadata so that a SIMD comparison can reject many slots at once.
The result is not meant to replace a production container. A real generic map must deal with object lifetimes, exceptions, heterogeneous lookup, allocator rules, and iterator guarantees. Our goal is to understand the layout decisions underneath containers such as absl::flat_hash_map.
 #The Contract Comes FirstWe will discuss a map with these operations:
find(key) -> pointer to value, or not found insert(key, value) -> insert a new key, or replace its value erase(key) -> whether a key was removed reserve(n) -> prepare for at least n live entries Three counters will matter:
 capacity: the number of physical slots; size: the number of live entries; deleted: the number of tombstones.  The usual load factor is $\alpha=\text{size}/\text{capacity}$, but a table with tombstones is probed as if both live and deleted slots were occupied. Its operational load is
$$ \alpha_\text{occupied} = \frac{\text{size}+\text{deleted}}{\text{capacity}}. $$
Growth policy must use the second quantity. Otherwise a table can be only half full according to size() and still have almost no empty slots at which an unsuccessful search may stop.
We also assume that equal keys have equal hashes and that the hash distributes the workload well. The table can repair collisions; it cannot repair a function that sends every key to the same bucket. See Hashing for mixing and adversarial considerations.
 #Separate ChainingThe conventional implementation stores an array of bucket heads. Each head refers to a linked list, or sometimes a small dynamic array, of entries with the same bucket index:
buckets separately allocated nodes 0 ---------> [key,value,next] -> [key,value,next] 1 ---------> [key,value,next] 2 ---------> null 3 ---------> [key,value,next] -> [key,value,next] Chaining has pleasant semantics. Insertion does not need an empty slot in the primary array, erasing a node does not affect the search path of another key, and node addresses can remain stable across a rehash. It also has a hardware problem: a lookup may fetch a bucket pointer, follow one or more pointers to unrelated allocations, and compare only one key per cache miss.
This is a good trade when entries are large, stable addresses are part of the interface, or the table stores nodes for other reasons. For small keys and values, the pointers, allocator metadata, and poor spatial locality may cost more than the payload.
 #Open AddressingOpen addressing puts every entry directly in a fixed array. A collision means trying another slot according to a probe sequence. The simplest sequence is linear probing:
$$ i_j = (h(k) + j) \bmod C. $$
When the capacity $C$ is a power of two, the modulo becomes & (C - 1). This requires the low bits of the hash to be well distributed; using the key itself as the hash is not harmless merely because the code compiles.
Each slot has one of three states:
EMPTY the slot has never been occupied since the last rehash FULL the slot contains a live key and value DELETED the slot used to be full A lookup follows the probe sequence until it finds either the key or an EMPTY slot:
for (std::size_t i = hash(key) & mask; ; i = (i + 1) & mask) { if (state[i] == EMPTY) return not_found; if (state[i] == FULL && keys[i] == key) return &values[i]; // DELETED does not terminate the search. } The last comment is the core deletion invariant. Suppose keys A and B have the same home slot and B was placed after A. Clearing A to EMPTY would make a later lookup for B stop too early. A tombstone says, “nothing is stored here, but the probe history continues.”
 #Correct insertion with tombstonesInsertion remembers the first tombstone but keeps searching until it sees an empty slot or the key itself:
first_deleted = none for each slot in the probe sequence: if FULL and key matches: replace the value; size does not change; return if DELETED and first_deleted is none: first_deleted = this slot if EMPTY: target = first_deleted if one was seen, otherwise this slot construct the new entry at target size += 1 deleted -= 1 if target was a tombstone return Inserting immediately into the first tombstone is wrong: the same key may already exist later in the cluster. Incrementing size before determining whether the operation is a replacement is another common bug.
The table must also preserve at least one EMPTY slot. Otherwise a missing-key lookup has no terminating state and loops forever. In practice we rehash well before that point. A policy might rebuild when occupied slots exceed a chosen fraction of capacity, or rebuild at the same capacity when tombstones are the main problem. The best threshold depends on entry size, hash quality, probe scheme, and the ratio of successful to unsuccessful searches; 7/8 or 3/4 is a policy, not a theorem.
 #Rehashing is garbage collectionRehashing allocates a fresh array and inserts every live entry into it. This does three jobs at once:
 changes the capacity, clears all tombstones, recomputes probe sequences under the new mask.  Copying the old byte layout into a larger array would not work: home positions and stopping points have changed. For nontrivial C++ types, a generic implementation must construct entries in the new storage, destroy the old ones exactly once, and specify what happens if moving or hashing throws.
Most flat tables invalidate references and iterators during rehash. Node-based tables can offer stronger stability at the price of an extra indirection. This is an interface choice with a direct physical cost.
 #ClustersLinear probing has an excellent inner loop. Sequential metadata and entries are friendly to hardware prefetching, and one cache line supplies several candidates. Its weakness is primary clustering: an occupied run attracts insertions whose home position is anywhere inside or immediately before that run, so long runs tend to grow longer.
As $\alpha$ approaches one, the problem is not just that the average search grows. The tail becomes unpleasant: an occasional missing key scans a large fraction of the table. Lowering the maximum load factor buys empty stopping points, but also consumes memory and enlarges the working set.
Probe length should therefore be a first-class benchmark statistic. Average nanoseconds alone can hide whether a table is predictably fast or usually fast.
 #Robin Hood HashingRobin Hood hashing, introduced by Celis, Larson, and Munro, reduces the variance of probe lengths. Each resident entry has a displacement—the distance from its home slot. During insertion, the entry with the larger displacement keeps the current slot:
incoming displacement = 0 for each slot: if slot is empty: place incoming entry; stop resident displacement = distance(resident home, slot) if resident displacement < incoming displacement: swap resident and incoming entries incoming displacement = resident displacement advance; incoming displacement += 1 The metaphor is accurate: an unlucky key that has travelled far “steals” a position from a richer key that is still close to home. This does not abolish collisions or change the expected asymptotic bound. It makes displacement more even, which improves the tail and enables another lookup rule.
With ordinary Robin Hood insertion and no tombstones, a lookup can use the displacement invariant directly. If it has travelled distance $d$ and meets an entry whose displacement is less than $d$, the searched key cannot occur later: had it been present, Robin Hood insertion would not have allowed this less-displaced entry to precede it. The lookup can therefore terminate before reaching an empty slot.
Deletion must preserve that invariant. A standard solution is backward-shift deletion: after removing an entry, repeatedly move the following entry one slot backward until reaching an empty slot or an entry at its home position. Simply dropping a tombstone into the sequence and continuing to use early termination can produce false negatives unless the metadata and search rule are redesigned together.
Robin Hood insertion also moves existing objects. For large or nontrivially movable values, this may cost more than the saved probes. A common response is to keep small keys or indices in the flat table and store large payloads elsewhere.
 #One Byte of ControlSo far, testing a slot may require loading the entire key. A more cache-efficient design stores a small control byte separately for every slot:
control: [e][3a][d][17][e][e][62][...] entries: [ ][ K][ ][ K][ ][ ][ K][...] e = empty d = deleted xx = full, with a small hash fingerprint Split a wide hash into two parts:
 H1 chooses the initial group; H2, commonly seven bits, is stored in the control byte as a fingerprint.  To search a group, broadcast H2, compare it with 16 or 32 adjacent control bytes, and turn the result into a bit mask. Only matching bits require full key comparisons. A second mask reports empty bytes; if no candidate matches and the group contains an empty slot, an unsuccessful lookup can stop.
Conceptually, the hot loop becomes:
for (group g : probe_sequence(H1)) { unsigned candidates = match_fingerprint(g.control, H2); while (candidates) { unsigned lane = std::countr_zero(candidates); if (entries[g.start + lane].key == key) return &entries[g.start + lane].value; candidates &= candidates - 1; } if (match_empty(g.control) != 0) return not_found; } The exact SIMD operations, group width, sentinel bytes at the end of the allocation, and probe permutation are implementation details that must agree. Wrapping a vector load past the array end is not justified because the logical probe wraps; production tables either clone a control-byte suffix, pad the allocation, or handle the boundary explicitly.
This design is often called a Swiss table. The official Abseil Swiss Tables design notes describe the one-byte metadata, H1/H2 split, SIMD candidate mask, and the crucial distinction between an empty byte, which stops a search, and a deleted byte, which does not.
The fingerprint is only a filter. Seven equal hash bits do not prove key equality, and a poor hash that lacks entropy in H2 turns every group into many full key comparisons. Hash quality now affects both home positions and metadata selectivity.
 #Metadata updatesControl bytes make the state machine explicit, which is good, but they do not remove its obligations:
 publish an entry as FULL only after its key and value have been constructed; destroy the object before marking a full slot deleted; decrement deleted when a tombstone is reused; base growth on size + deleted; rebuild before there is no empty group; never treat the sentinel or cloned suffix as real capacity.  These orderings are still not enough for lock-free concurrency. A normal flat table permits no simultaneous mutation and lookup without external synchronization; data races remain undefined behavior even if a control byte happens to fit in one machine store.
 #Layout ChoicesFor a map, keys and values can be stored together:
struct entry { Key key; Value value; }; or in separate arrays. An array of structures needs one address computation and gives good locality when every successful lookup consumes the value. Separate arrays avoid fetching large values during unsuccessful searches and can make relocation of keys or indices cheaper. This is the same AoS versus SoA tradeoff seen elsewhere.
Alignment and padding matter. A nominal (uint32_t, uint64_t) entry may occupy 16 bytes, not 12, while a one-byte control array adds only one byte per slot. On the other hand, storing huge values inline makes rehashes and Robin Hood swaps expensive. There is no universally “flat” answer; sometimes the right table is flat metadata and keys pointing to stable payload nodes.
 #Hashing and the AdversaryPower-of-two tables expose weak low bits immediately. Before masking, mix integer keys with an avalanche-style function or use a library hash designed for the table. Strings need a real string hash, not a few selected characters. Hashing itself can dominate tiny lookups, so benchmark it separately.
Non-cryptographic mixing assumes benign input. If an attacker can choose keys and observe behavior, collision attacks can turn expected constant time into linear work. Use a keyed, denial-of-service-resistant hash or a container that provides one. Re-seeding on rehash can also make stored hash values and serialized layouts process-specific; that should be an explicit contract rather than an accident.
 #EvaluationHash table benchmarks are exceptionally sensitive to workload. At minimum, vary:
 table size across cache levels; load factor and tombstone ratio; successful versus unsuccessful lookup rate; insertion, replacement, and erasure mix; key and value sizes; hash cost and key distribution; reserved capacity versus repeated growth; warm and cold caches.  Report probe-count distributions alongside time. Include memory per live entry, because buying speed with a four-times-larger table may lose once the working set crosses a cache boundary. Keep the same hash function when comparing layouts, or report hashing as part of the difference.
The historical companion experiments for this chapter compare chaining, linear probing, Robin Hood insertion, and a 32-byte AVX2 control group on a Zen 2-era setup. They correctly reveal the progression from pointer chasing to contiguous probes to metadata filtering, but the sketches use a half- or three-quarter-full table, identity-like hashing, fixed integer sentinels, and synthetic random queries. Some also count replacements as new insertions and omit production deletion semantics. Their measurements are therefore evidence about that experiment, not a general speedup claim.
A stronger validation harness runs each operation against std::unordered_map or a simple sorted reference map, checking the entire contents after randomized sequences. It should force hash collisions, repeatedly erase and reinsert, replace existing keys, cross every growth threshold, use keys equal to any tempting sentinel value, and finish with missing-key lookups in a tombstone-heavy table.
 #Choosing a TableThe design space can be summarized without crowning one winner:
   Layout Main advantage Main cost     Separate chaining stable nodes, simple deletion pointers, allocation, poor locality   Linear probing compact and cache-friendly clustering and long negative probes   Robin Hood tighter probe-length distribution moved entries, deletion complexity   Control-byte groups many cheap rejections per load extra metadata and a more complex state machine    Use a mature implementation when the container is infrastructure. But when a hash table is the bottleneck, “expected $O(1)$” is only the beginning of the investigation. The useful questions are how many cache lines a miss touches, how the search knows it is over, and what yesterday’s deletions make today’s lookup do.
title: Hash Tables

content:
Our assembly programs have so far lived in an unusually peaceful universe. They read and write memory, perform arithmetic, and eventually return. Real programs also need to open files, allocate pages, receive network packets, and occasionally discover that the user has pressed a key.
The CPU cannot let an arbitrary program control these facilities directly. A process that could rewrite page tables or talk to a storage controller could inspect or destroy every other process on the machine. Instead, the operating-system kernel runs with privileges that applications do not have, and provides a narrow interface for requesting privileged work.
 #Protection Ringsx86 associates code with a privilege level. Operating systems conventionally run applications in ring 3 and the kernel in ring 0. Instructions that change address translation, interrupt handling, or other global machine state are privileged: executing them from user mode raises an exception rather than quietly handing the process the computer.
Memory is protected as well. Page-table entries specify whether a page is accessible from user mode, so a normal load from a kernel-only address faults before it can reveal anything. This division is the foundation of process isolation.
Applications still need kernel services, so the architecture provides controlled entry points. On 64-bit x86, the usual one is the syscall instruction. It does not mean “call whichever kernel address is in this register.” The kernel configures the entry address and processor state in advance. syscall transfers control there, changes privilege level, and saves enough user state for a later sysret or equivalent return path. Linux’s entry code then establishes a kernel stack and saves the remaining state before ordinary kernel code handles the request.
A system call is therefore a protected procedure call across an abstraction boundary.
 #The Linux System-Call ABISystem calls have their own calling convention. For the x86-64 Linux ABI:
   Value Register     system-call number rax   arguments 1–3 rdi, rsi, rdx   arguments 4–6 r10, r8, r9   return value rax    The fourth argument uses r10, not rcx, because the syscall instruction itself clobbers rcx; it also clobbers r11. The complete per-architecture table is maintained in the Linux syscall(2) documentation.
Here is a complete NASM program that writes a string and exits without using a C library:
global _start section .rodata msg: db "Hello, world!", 10 msglen: equ $ - msg section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; __NR_write mov edi, 1 ; STDOUT_FILENO lea rsi, [rel msg] ; buffer mov edx, msglen ; byte count syscall mov eax, 60 ; __NR_exit xor edi, edi ; status = 0 syscall ud2 ; exit does not return It can be assembled and linked with:
nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o ld -o hello hello.o This example intentionally ignores the return value of write. Production code must handle errors, interruptions, and partial writes. More importantly, it should normally call the standard library instead of embedding system-call numbers and ABI details. The GNU C Library explains why its system-call wrappers are more portable and may provide compatibility or thread-cancellation behavior in addition to the raw transition.
At the raw Linux interface, failures are returned as negative error numbers in rax. A libc wrapper normally converts this to -1 and stores the positive error number in errno. This is another small example of why “one C function call” and “one machine-level operation” are not interchangeable concepts.
 #What the Transition CostsCalling the kernel is more expensive than an ordinary function call. The processor crosses a protection boundary, application state must be preserved, arguments and pointers must be validated, and mitigations or tracing may add work. The requested service can then cost anything from a short table lookup to waiting for a disk.
A system call is a mode switch, but it is not necessarily a context switch. If the kernel can satisfy the request immediately, it returns to the same thread. A blocking read may instead put the thread to sleep and let the scheduler run another one. Conflating these two events makes system-call costs seem even more mysterious than they are.
The main optimization is usually to request useful work in larger units:
 buffered output combines many small writes; batched interfaces submit several operations together; memory allocators serve small requests from user-space arenas and ask the kernel for larger regions less often; asynchronous and non-blocking interfaces reduce the need to dedicate a blocked thread to each request.  Batching is not free. It may increase latency, retain more memory, or complicate error handling. As always, the right unit is determined by the workload rather than by a moral objection to system calls.
Some library operations avoid kernel entry entirely. Linux maps a small kernel-provided shared object, the vDSO, into each process. Functions such as clock queries can sometimes read kernel-maintained data and return in user mode; the library falls back to a real system call when necessary. The interface and its versioning rules are described in vdso(7). This is why tracing system calls is not always the same as tracing library calls.
 #Interrupts, Exceptions, and TrapsSeveral events can redirect the CPU to privileged code, but they have different causes:
 An interrupt is asynchronous with respect to the current instruction stream. A device or timer asks the CPU for attention. An exception is caused synchronously by an instruction, such as a page fault, division by zero, or invalid opcode. A system call is a deliberate synchronous transition requested by the program.  Architecture manuals sometimes use trap as a more specific exception category, while operating-system literature also uses it informally for controlled transitions in general. It is safer to describe the cause than to rely on the overloaded word.
Interrupt and exception handlers preserve an architectural state, identify the cause, and eventually either resume execution, deliver a signal, schedule another thread, or terminate the process. They are not categorically “off the normal path”: page faults, timer interrupts, and system calls are essential parts of normal operation. What matters for performance is their frequency, the work they trigger, and whether they disturb caches, translation state, or the currently running thread.
The same protected-transition idea appears one level lower when an entire operating system runs under another piece of privileged software. That is the subject of virtualization.
title: Interrupts and System Calls

content:
Number theory spent centuries as an unusually pure part of mathematics. Computers gave its abstractions a very practical cost model: a residue has to fit in words, multiplication has to avoid overflow, an inverse has to be constructed, and a large exponent has to become a short sequence of products.
This chapter starts with modular arithmetic and the algorithms behind inverses and exponentiation. Montgomery representation then shows how changing coordinates can remove division from a long modular computation. Finite fields extend the same ideas to error-correcting codes. The final sections separate three applications that are often conflated:
 cryptography needs precisely specified, side-channel-resistant primitives assembled into reviewed protocols; hashing maps data to compact values for tables, fingerprints, and integrity checks, with different adversarial requirements in each setting; pseudorandom generation expands a small state into reproducible samples, while operating-system entropy is needed for secrets.  The small C++ routines in this chapter are mathematical and performance examples. They make overflow bounds and algebraic preconditions visible; they are not substitutes for vetted cryptographic libraries.
title: Number Theory

content:
The fast Fourier transform computes convolution quickly by evaluating polynomials at complex roots of unity. Its arithmetic is approximate. If the coefficients are integers and an exact modular result is acceptable—or can later be reconstructed—the same butterfly can run in a finite field.
This is the number-theoretic transform (NTT). It replaces complex multiplication with modular multiplication, floating-point error with algebraic preconditions, and unrestricted power-of-two lengths with lengths supported by the chosen prime.
Those preconditions are the algorithm. A modulus being prime is not enough; the field must contain a root of the exact transform order. Padding beyond that order, using a nonprimitive root, or reconstructing coefficients larger than the modulus produces perfectly deterministic wrong answers.
 #Roots of Unity in a Finite FieldLet $q$ be prime. The nonzero residues modulo $q$ form a multiplicative group of order $q-1$. If $g$ is a primitive root and $n\mid(q-1)$, then
$$ \omega_n=g^{(q-1)/n}\pmod q $$
has order exactly $n$. We can define
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a_j\omega_n^{jk}\pmod q. $$
The inverse uses $\omega_n^{-1}$ and multiplies by $n^{-1}\bmod q$. Both inverses exist because the values are nonzero modulo a prime.
Pollard’s primary paper The Fast Fourier Transform in a Finite Field develops this construction and its use for integer-sequence convolution.
 #A Concrete FieldWe will use
$$ q=998244353=119\cdot2^{23}+1 $$
with primitive root $g=3$. This supports every power-of-two transform length through $2^{23}$. It does not support length $2^{24}$, and silently wrapping exponents does not manufacture the missing root.
All stored coefficients are canonical residues in $[0,q)$. Products fit in 64 bits:
$$ (q-1)^2<10^{18}<2^{64}. $$
The following C++20 transform is self-contained:
#include <algorithm>#include <bit>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> namespace ntt998 { using u32 = std::uint32_t; using u64 = std::uint64_t; constexpr u32 modulus = 998244353; constexpr u32 primitive_root = 3; constexpr std::size_t maximum_length = std::size_t(1) << 23; u32 power(u32 base, u64 exponent) { u32 result = 1; while (exponent != 0) { if (exponent & 1) result = u32(u64(result) * base % modulus); base = u32(u64(base) * base % modulus); exponent >>= 1; } return result; } void transform(std::span<u32> values, bool inverse = false) { std::size_t n = values.size(); if (!std::has_single_bit(n) || n > maximum_length) throw std::invalid_argument("unsupported NTT length"); for (u32 x : values) if (x >= modulus) throw std::invalid_argument("noncanonical NTT coefficient"); for (std::size_t i = 1, reversed = 0; i < n; ++i) { std::size_t bit = n >> 1; while ((reversed & bit) != 0) { reversed ^= bit; bit >>= 1; } reversed ^= bit; if (i < reversed) std::swap(values[i], values[reversed]); } if (n > 1) { for (std::size_t length = 2;; length *= 2) { u32 root = power(primitive_root, (modulus - 1) / u64(length)); if (inverse) root = power(root, modulus - 2); std::size_t half = length / 2; for (std::size_t first = 0; first != n; first += length) { u32 w = 1; for (std::size_t j = 0; j != half; ++j) { u32 even = values[first + j]; u32 odd = u32(u64(w) * values[first + j + half] % modulus); u64 sum = u64(even) + odd; values[first + j] = u32(sum >= modulus ? sum - modulus : sum); values[first + j + half] = even >= odd ? even - odd : even + modulus - odd; w = u32(u64(w) * root % modulus); } } if (length == n) break; } } if (inverse) { u32 inverse_n = power(u32(n), modulus - 2); for (u32 &x : values) x = u32(u64(x) * inverse_n % modulus); } } } // namespace ntt998 The loop structure matches the iterative radix-2 FFT: bit reversal, staged butterflies, reversed root for the inverse, and one final scaling. The differences are all in the arithmetic contract.
The exponent (modulus - 1) / length is integral because every accepted length divides $2^{23}$ and therefore divides $q-1$. Fermat’s theorem gives the inverse as $x^{q-2}$. A general NTT routine cannot hard-code these conclusions; it must verify or receive a proven modulus, root, and maximum order.
 #Modular ConvolutionPointwise multiplication of transformed coefficient arrays gives cyclic convolution modulo $q$. Zero-padding to at least a.size() + b.size() - 1 turns it into linear convolution modulo $q$:
#include <limits>#include <vector> std::vector<ntt998::u32> convolve_mod(std::span<const ntt998::u32> a, std::span<const ntt998::u32> b) { using namespace ntt998; if (a.empty() || b.empty()) return {}; constexpr std::size_t maximum = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max(); if (a.size() > maximum - b.size() + 1) throw std::length_error("convolution length overflow"); std::size_t needed = a.size() + b.size() - 1; std::size_t n = 1; while (n < needed) { if (n >= maximum_length) throw std::length_error("convolution exceeds NTT field order"); n *= 2; } std::vector<u32> fa(n, 0), fb(n, 0); std::copy(a.begin(), a.end(), fa.begin()); std::copy(b.begin(), b.end(), fb.begin()); transform(fa); transform(fb); for (std::size_t i = 0; i != n; ++i) fa[i] = u32(u64(fa[i]) * fb[i] % modulus); transform(fa, true); fa.resize(needed); return fa; } The input values must already lie in [0, modulus); transform checks them before mutation. Signed application coefficients can be mapped with a deliberate reduction such as
ntt998::u32 residue(std::int64_t x) { std::int64_t r = x % std::int64_t(ntt998::modulus); return ntt998::u32(r < 0 ? r + ntt998::modulus : r); } Reducing an out-of-range coefficient is an application decision. The low-level transform rejects it instead of guessing whether the caller intended a residue or made a range error.
 #Modular Is Not Automatically Exact Integer ConvolutionThe NTT returns each coefficient modulo $q$. To interpret that residue as an ordinary nonnegative integer, the true coefficient must be smaller than $q$.
If a and b are nonnegative, bounded by $A$ and $B$, then every convolution coefficient is at most
$$ \min(|a|,|b|)AB. $$
A single-modulus result is uniquely recoverable as a nonnegative integer only when this bound is strictly less than modulus. Check the bound with division rather than overflowing the calculation itself:
terms <= (modulus - 1) / A / B with zero handled separately.
For signed coefficients reconstructed into the centered interval $(-q/2,q/2]$, an absolute bound below $q/2$ is required. If the bound is larger, use several NTT-friendly primes and reconstruct with the Chinese remainder theorem. The product of the primes must exceed the nonnegative bound, or twice the signed absolute bound, and every chosen prime must support the padded transform length.
This is the exact-arithmetic counterpart of FFT error analysis. The NTT has no roundoff, but a violated coefficient bound aliases values by an exact multiple of $q$.
 #Why This Prime WorksThe factor $2^{23}$ in $q-1$ is what supports repeated radix-2 splitting. For a general desired length $n$, we need
 a modulus under which multiplication intermediates are safe or explicitly reduced; $n\mid(q-1)$; an element of order exactly $n$; a modular inverse of $n$; enough modulus product to reconstruct the intended coefficient range.  Testing only $\omega^n=1$ is insufficient: a root of smaller order also passes. If $n$ is a power of two, checking $\omega^{n/2}\ne1$ proves exact order once $\omega^n=1$. For arbitrary composite $n$, test against every prime divisor of $n$.
Primality and primitive-root claims should be established when defining a field, not rediscovered inside every transform. Fixed, reviewed parameter sets are easier to audit than user-supplied “prime and root” integers.
 #Mapping the Butterfly to HardwareThe NTT trades complex floating-point operations for integer multiplication and modular reduction. The memory access pattern is almost identical to the FFT, including the irregular bit-reversal permutation and contiguous blocks within each stage.
The reference code uses % modulus after 64-bit products. Because the modulus is compile-time constant, an optimizing compiler can replace general division with multiplication by a reciprocal and corrections. Hand-written Barrett or Montgomery reduction can make that choice explicit and can be useful in SIMD kernels, but it also expands the proof surface.
Butterfly additions need only one conditional correction because both inputs are canonical residues. Deferring reductions across several operations can expose more instruction-level parallelism, but the widened range must be proved against the integer type at every stage.
SIMD support varies by limb width and ISA. Vectorizing several butterflies is straightforward conceptually; 64-bit products and lane-wise modular reduction are the limiting operations on many targets. Multiple independent transforms or blocks can provide cleaner parallelism than forcing one butterfly into an inconvenient vector shape.
Twiddle powers are exact field elements, so there is no numerical drift. Precomputed tables still trade multiplication and exponentiation setup for cache traffic. Reusing a plan for many transforms can amortize bit-reversal indices and stage roots just as in an FFT library.
 #ValidationThe strongest basic property is exact round-trip equality:
inverse(transform(a)) == a for every supported length and canonical input. Also compare convolve_mod against the $O(nm)$ modular definition on randomized small arrays. Exercise lengths 1 and $2^{23}$, rejection of zero/non-power-of-two/too-large lengths, coefficients 0 and modulus - 1, empty convolution inputs, and padded lengths immediately on either side of a power of two.
Root tests should verify
$$ \omega^n=1,\qquad \omega^{n/2}\ne1 $$
for each supported radix-2 length above one. A convolution test alone may not reveal a scaling error if both reference and optimized paths accidentally use the same convention.
 #Reproducible EvaluationReport modulus, primitive root, maximum order, transform length distribution, forward/inverse mix, coefficient range, inclusion of allocation and root setup, reduction method, compiler flags, ISA target, CPU, and thread count. Distinguish transform throughput from end-to-end convolution and CRT reconstruction.
Compare with the FFT only under a shared application contract. A floating transform may support larger lengths and different coefficient ranges; an NTT may require several primes; their output guarantees are different. “Exact versus approximate” is not enough information to predict which complete pipeline is faster.
The NTT is elegant precisely because the butterfly survives unchanged. But complex roots existed for every length, while finite-field roots must be earned through factorization of $q-1$. Once the modulus, order, normalization, and coefficient bound are all explicit, the transform becomes a dependable exact convolution engine instead of a collection of competitive-programming constants.
title: Number-Theoretic Transform

content:
After optimizing a loop for long enough, every remaining instruction starts to look suspicious. This is a good time to stop asking “what else can I change?” and ask a sharper question: “what physical resource could make this version faster?”
A performance bound does not predict exactly how long a program will run. It proves that, under stated assumptions, it cannot run faster than some limit. Comparing several bounds often reveals which resource deserves attention and which proposed optimization cannot matter yet.
 #A Maximum of Lower BoundsSuppose one loop iteration needs:
 $U$ uops delivered by a front-end capable of $F$ uops per cycle; $N_r$ uses of each execution resource $r$, which accepts $C_r$ relevant uops per cycle; a loop-carried dependency with latency $D$ cycles; $Q_k$ bytes transferred through each memory boundary $k$, whose sustainable bandwidth is $B_k$ bytes per cycle.  Ignoring interactions for a moment, cycles per iteration are bounded below by
$$ T \ge \max\left( \frac{U}{F}, \max_r \frac{N_r}{C_r}, D, \max_k \frac{Q_k}{B_k} \right). $$
The maximum is important. Front-end work, arithmetic, and memory transfers can overlap, so adding all their isolated costs is usually too pessimistic. Yet none of the individual limits can be violated. If stores require at least one cycle per iteration, a hypothetical zero-cycle addition does not make the loop faster.
This model is still an approximation. A uop may be eligible for several ports, resources can be shared in complicated ways, and burst bandwidth differs from sustained bandwidth. Its purpose is to identify a candidate bottleneck that can be tested.
 #Front-End and Execution LimitsThe front-end has finite fetch, decode, and delivery bandwidth. Large instructions may cross fetch boundaries; branches can interrupt the stream; code that does not fit in the instruction cache or decoded-uop cache adds further delays. For a compact hot loop, the simplest bound is its delivered uop count divided by front-end width.
In the back-end, count resource demand rather than assembly lines. One x86 instruction may decompose into multiple uops, while fusion can let parts travel together through some stages. Each uop can use a particular set of execution resources. The tight resource bound is the best feasible assignment of these uops to their eligible resources, not merely the count of whichever mnemonic looks most exotic.
Instruction latency creates a different limit. In
s = ((s + x0) + x1) + x2; each addition needs the previous result. If the relevant addition latency is one cycle, this recurrence cannot advance more than once per cycle regardless of how many add units exist. Splitting a reduction across independent accumulators changes the dependency graph and can approach the throughput limit, as discussed in Throughput Computing.
Static tools can estimate these bounds. llvm-mca reports a block reciprocal throughput and resource pressure from LLVM’s scheduling model. It assumes an idealized surrounding loop and optimistic memory behavior, so it is a ceiling calculation, not a stopwatch.
 #Bandwidth: The Roofline BoundLet an implementation perform $W$ useful operations and transfer $Q$ bytes across a chosen memory boundary. If peak relevant compute throughput is $C$ operations per second and sustainable bandwidth is $B$ bytes per second, then
$$ T \ge \max\left(\frac{W}{C}, \frac{Q}{B}\right). $$
Define operational intensity $I = W/Q$ and performance $P = W/T$. Rearranging gives
$$ P \le \min(C, B \cdot I). $$
This is the basic Roofline model. At low intensity, the sloped bandwidth roof dominates. At high intensity, the flat compute roof dominates. Their intersection is the intensity required to make peak computation relevant.
For example, consider addition of two arrays of 32-bit values:
#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint> void add(const std::uint32_t* a, const std::uint32_t* b, std::uint32_t* c, std::size_t n) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) c[i] = a[i] + b[i]; } Each element performs one integer addition and logically transfers at least eight input bytes plus four output bytes. This is low operational intensity. SIMD reduces instruction overhead and raises the compute ceiling, but it does not reduce those twelve logical bytes. Once the relevant memory bandwidth is saturated, wider arithmetic alone has nowhere to obtain more data.
Actual traffic may be higher because of write allocation, imperfect locality, or unrelated users of the cache. It may be lower at a deeper memory boundary when data is reused in cache. Always state whether $Q$ describes source-level bytes, L1 traffic, last-level-cache traffic, or DRAM traffic.
 #Latency and Memory-Level ParallelismBandwidth says how many bytes can arrive over time; latency says how long one request takes. A sequential scan can keep many cache misses in flight, allowing their latencies to overlap. A linked-list traversal cannot request node $i+1$ until node $i$ reveals its address.
If a computation performs $N$ long-latency requests, each taking approximately $L$ cycles, and can sustain at most $K$ independent requests at once, then a rough lower bound is
$$ T \ge \frac{N \cdot L}{K}. $$
For a strict dependency chain, $K=1$. For several independent streams, $K$ may grow until load queues, miss-status buffers, translation resources, or bandwidth become limiting. Prefetching and restructuring pointer-based data do not make memory intrinsically faster; they try to increase $K$ or arrange for requests to begin earlier.
This explains why “the data fits in bandwidth” is not enough. A workload can consume little total bandwidth and still be completely latency-bound.
 #Branches and Other CeilingsUnpredictable control flow adds another workload-dependent limit. If a branch is mispredicted, younger wrong-path work is discarded and useful instruction delivery is interrupted. Unlike an execution-port count, this cost cannot be derived from the static instruction mix alone: it depends on data and branch history. Measure the misprediction rate on the intended workload, then compare a branchy implementation with the extra work and dependency cost of a branchless one.
Other ceilings include instruction-cache capacity, translation bandwidth, store-buffer capacity, and limits imposed by the algorithm itself. Comparison sorting, for example, has a comparison lower bound independent of how quickly the CPU can execute one comparison. A hardware limit and an algorithmic lower bound can both be true; the larger one controls the current implementation.
 #Peak Is Not Attainable PerformancePublished peak throughput assumes a favorable instruction mix, enough independent work, suitable vector width, and data already arriving at the required rate. Real code may use an instruction supported by only one unit, mix loads and stores that contend for address-generation resources, or fail to expose enough parallelism.
Frequency is not constant either. Vector width, power limits, temperature, active cores, and host policy can change it. Shared caches and memory channels introduce competition. For this reason, use measured sustainable bandwidth and the frequency observed during the benchmark when constructing a practical bound.
A disciplined analysis proceeds as follows:
 Pick the unit: one query, one element, one byte, or one loop iteration. Draw true dependencies and identify the longest recurrence. Count uops and demand on constrained execution resources. Count bytes at the memory boundary relevant to the working set. Compute several lower bounds and take their maximum. Measure hardware events to check whether the predicted resource is actually saturated.  If performance is far below every plausible bound, the model is missing something. If it is close to one bound, optimize that resource or change the algorithm so the bound itself moves. Once another bound becomes larger, stop polishing the old bottleneck. It has already done all the damage it can.
title: Theoretical Performance Limits

content:
Finding the minimum of an array is a reduction. Finding where that minimum occurs is a reduction carrying luggage: every candidate value brings an index with it.
That extra word changes the optimization problem. A vector minimum combines eight 32-bit values with one AVX2 instruction, but a vector argmin must also decide which indices survive, define what happens on ties, and reduce eight (value, index) pairs at the end. The fastest-looking loop is often the one that quietly gets one of those details wrong.
We will use a precise contract and then develop two implementations: a scalar oracle and a blocked SIMD algorithm that reads the array once plus one small block.
 #The ContractFor an array $a$ of length $n>0$, define
$$ \operatorname{argmin}(a)=\min{i\mid a_i=\min_j a_j}. $$
The outer min makes ties explicit: return the first occurrence. For an empty array there is no such index, so the interface returns std::nullopt.
#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <optional>#include <span> std::optional<std::size_t> argmin_scalar(std::span<const std::int32_t> values) { if (values.empty()) return std::nullopt; std::size_t best = 0; for (std::size_t i = 1; i < values.size(); ++i) if (values[i] < values[best]) best = i; return best; } The comparison is strict. Changing < to <= changes the result to the last minimum. Initializing the best value to INT_MAX without separately initializing an index also fails for an array consisting entirely of INT_MAX.
The standard-library equivalent is compact and has the same first-tie rule:
#include <algorithm> std::optional<std::size_t> argmin_standard(std::span<const std::int32_t> values) { if (values.empty()) return std::nullopt; auto it = std::min_element(values.begin(), values.end()); return static_cast<std::size_t>(it - values.begin()); } Whether either loop vectorizes is a compiler and target question. std::min_element is not inherently slow, and one old library/compiler result is not a reason to avoid it. Inspect the generated code and benchmark the exact toolchain.
 #Carrying Indices in VectorsThe direct SIMD translation keeps eight partial minima and eight corresponding indices. For a vector x and current minima m, form the signed comparison mask
$$ q=(x<m), $$
then update both registers under the same mask:
$$ m\leftarrow\operatorname{blend}(m,x,q),\qquad k\leftarrow\operatorname{blend}(k,i,q). $$
This is correct when the comparison is strict and the final horizontal reduction compares (value, index) pairs lexicographically. It also has some unglamorous engineering requirements:
 _mm256_load_si256 requires a 32-byte-aligned address; ordinary arrays do not promise that alignment, so a general routine needs loadu or a proven aligned fast path; a loop stepping by eight needs a scalar or masked tail; 32-bit vector indices wrap when the array has more than $2^{32}$ elements; the final reduction must prefer the lower index when two lanes contain the same value.  The value comparison, two blends, and index increment also create more work than a plain minimum. There is a simpler way to keep full-width std::size_t indices out of the vector loop altogether.
 #Find a Block, Then an IndexSplit the array into small blocks. Compute each block minimum with SIMD, keep the first block whose minimum strictly improves the global minimum, and finally scan only that block for the first matching value.
If the block size is $B$, the algorithm examines $n+B$ elements in the worst case. It has a useful invariant after processing blocks through $t$:
 best_value is the minimum of the processed prefix, and best_block is the first block containing that value.
 A strictly smaller block minimum replaces both. An equal one does not, so ties across blocks retain the earlier block. A forward scalar scan then resolves ties inside the chosen block.
Here is a complete AVX2 implementation for signed 32-bit integers. It accepts arbitrary lengths and unaligned data.
#include <algorithm>#include <array>#include <climits>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <immintrin.h>#include <optional>#include <span> std::int32_t block_min_avx2(const std::int32_t *data, std::size_t length) { // The public routine calls this only for nonempty blocks.  __m256i minimum = _mm256_set1_epi32(INT_MAX); std::size_t i = 0; for (; length - i >= 8; i += 8) { const __m256i x = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i *>(data + i)); minimum = _mm256_min_epi32(minimum, x); } alignas(32) std::array<std::int32_t, 8> lanes{}; _mm256_store_si256(reinterpret_cast<__m256i *>(lanes.data()), minimum); std::int32_t result = INT_MAX; for (std::int32_t x : lanes) result = std::min(result, x); for (; i < length; ++i) result = std::min(result, data[i]); return result; } std::optional<std::size_t> argmin_avx2(std::span<const std::int32_t> values) { if (values.empty()) return std::nullopt; constexpr std::size_t block_size = 256; std::int32_t best_value = INT_MAX; std::size_t best_block = 0; std::size_t best_length = std::min(block_size, values.size()); for (std::size_t base = 0; base < values.size(); base += block_size) { const std::size_t length = std::min(block_size, values.size() - base); const std::int32_t local = block_min_avx2(values.data() + base, length); if (local < best_value) { best_value = local; best_block = base; best_length = length; } } for (std::size_t i = 0; i < best_length; ++i) if (values[best_block + i] == best_value) return best_block + i; // Defensive fallback: the block minimum must occur in this block.  return std::nullopt; } _mm256_loadu_si256 removes the caller-facing alignment precondition. The loop condition i + 8 <= length prevents an out-of-bounds vector read, and the scalar loop handles every remaining element. Since the outer loop computes its length with values.size() - base, the final partial block is no different from any other.
The INT_MAX initialization is safe here. If the first block contains only INT_MAX, the strict comparison does not update best_block; it already names that first block, and the final scan finds index zero. A later all-INT_MAX block cannot steal the tie.
This code must be compiled for AVX2 and called only on a processor that supports it. A portable binary normally keeps argmin_scalar as a baseline and selects an AVX2 function through compile-time targets or runtime feature dispatch. The dispatch belongs outside the hot loop.
 #Why a Branch Can Be Fast—or TerribleThere is another attractive design. Compare each vector block with a broadcast global minimum, and enter a scalar slow path only if some lane may improve it. For independent values from a continuous distribution, the probability that element $i$ is a new record minimum is $1/(i+1)$, so the expected number of record updates is the harmonic number
$$ H_n=1+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1n=\log n+O(1). $$
On that distribution the slow branch is rare. On a decreasing array it is taken for every block. Duplicate-heavy, nearly sorted, adversarial, and correlated data fall somewhere else again. [[unlikely]] communicates a workload assumption to the compiler; it does not make the assumption true.
The blocked algorithm above avoids this distribution-dependent scalar slow path. It performs a horizontal reduction once per fixed block regardless of the order of the values. The block size still needs measurement: larger blocks reduce horizontal reductions but increase the final rescan and may interact differently with cache residency.
 #One Pass Versus TwoComputing the global minimum first and then using a vectorized equality search is especially simple:
auto minimum = vector_min(values); auto index = vector_find_first(values, minimum); It is robust, but it reads between one and two arrays’ worth of data: the second pass stops early only when the first minimum occurs early. For a cache-resident array this may be competitive. For a large array, a mandatory second memory pass can cost more than the index bookkeeping it saved.
Blocking is a compromise. It reads the entire array once and revisits at most $B$ values. The extra work is bounded rather than dependent on where the first minimum happens.
 #Historical ExperimentThe original 2022 experiment used $2^{13}$ integers, a 2 GHz Zen 2 core, GCC 9.3, and only two input families: pseudo-random values and a decreasing sequence. Its table called the unit “GFLOPS,” although no floating-point operation is involved; the numbers are more accurately billions of elements examined per second.
   implementation random decreasing     old std::min_element build 0.28 0.28   hand-written scalar 1.54 1.89   scalar with an unlikely hint 1.95 0.75   vector values and indices 8.17 8.12   branch on a candidate vector 8.51 1.65   two candidate vectors 10.22 1.74   32-element candidate block 22.44 2.70   minimum, then full search 18.21 12.92   minimum by block, then local search 22.23 19.29    These measurements preserve the useful shape of the experiment: a rare-path optimization can be spectacular on random data and collapse on decreasing data, while the blocked design is much steadier. They do not establish a universal 15-fold speedup. The compiler is old, the arrays fit in a small cache, the benchmark is noisy, and two distributions are not a workload study.
For new measurements, report elements per second and bytes per second, not FLOPS. Sweep length across cache boundaries; vary alignment and the position and multiplicity of the minimum; include increasing, decreasing, constant, random, and application traces; and retain the result so the optimizer cannot remove the scan.
 #Differential TestingThe scalar routine is a convenient oracle. Before timing the AVX2 version, compare it for:
 every length around vector and block boundaries: 0 through 17, 255 through 257, and 511 through 513; every byte offset compatible with int32_t in an oversized allocation; all-equal arrays and duplicate minima in different lanes and blocks; increasing and decreasing arrays; INT_MIN, INT_MAX, and mixtures of both; random arrays over both a wide domain and a tiny duplicate-heavy domain.  For every nonempty input, verify both the value and the first-tie property:
auto expected = argmin_scalar(values); auto actual = argmin_avx2(values); assert(actual == expected); assert(values[*actual] == *std::min_element(values.begin(), values.end())); Run the suite with address and undefined-behavior sanitizers. A vector loop that is correct only for the old aligned, power-of-two benchmark will usually fail on the first offset or tail case.
Argmin illustrates why SIMD programming is less about replacing scalar operators with vector operators than about choosing the right representation. Carrying eight indices is possible; arranging the computation so indices remain scalar is often better.
 #Further Reading The C++ working draft specifies the first-equivalent-element behavior of min_element. Intel’s Intrinsics Guide documents the AVX2 operations and their ISA requirements. The SIMD reduction and masking chapters develop the two primitives used by the blocked algorithm.
title: Argmin with SIMD

content:
Suppose we need to store a subset of the integers $0,1,\ldots,U-1$. A hash set stores the elements that are present. A bitmap stores one answer for every possible element:
$$ B_i = [i \in S]. $$
This sounds wasteful until the universe is reasonably dense. Then the representation uses exactly $U$ bits, has no hashes or pointers, and answers membership with one indexed load. More importantly, one machine instruction can combine 64 membership answers at once. Set intersection becomes bitwise AND; union becomes OR; difference becomes AND NOT.
Bitmaps are therefore both a data structure and a form of word-level parallelism. They are used for graph frontiers, allocation maps, database indexes, dynamic programming states, visited sets, and as the storage layer of probabilistic filters.
 #Packing the BitsUsing 64-bit words, bit $i$ lives in word $\lfloor i/64\rfloor$ at offset $i \bmod 64$:
#include <algorithm>#include <bit>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <vector> class bitmap { std::size_t bit_count_; std::vector<std::uint64_t> words_; void clear_unused_bits() { unsigned used = unsigned(bit_count_ & 63); if (used != 0) words_.back() &= (std::uint64_t(1) << used) - 1; } public: explicit bitmap(std::size_t n) : bit_count_(n), words_((n + 63) / 64, 0) {} std::size_t size() const { return bit_count_; } bool test(std::size_t i) const { return (words_[i >> 6] >> (i & 63)) & 1; } void set(std::size_t i) { words_[i >> 6] |= std::uint64_t(1) << (i & 63); } void reset(std::size_t i) { words_[i >> 6] &= ~(std::uint64_t(1) << (i & 63)); } void flip(std::size_t i) { words_[i >> 6] ^= std::uint64_t(1) << (i & 63); } void complement() { for (std::uint64_t &word : words_) word = ~word; if (!words_.empty()) clear_unused_bits(); } }; The cast before the shift is essential. 1 << 40 shifts a 32-bit int on common platforms and is not a way to construct bit 40. The index is assumed to be in range; a public container can add checked access separately rather than putting a branch in every internal operation.
The final word introduces another invariant. If $U$ is not divisible by 64, some physical bits do not belong to the logical universe. They must remain zero after operations such as complement. Otherwise cardinality and iteration may report elements greater than or equal to $U$.
For $U=0$, the word vector is empty, so even tail cleanup must avoid touching back(). Small boundary conditions have a way of becoming large memory errors in bit manipulation code.
 #Bulk Set OperationsIf two bitmaps describe the same universe, their set operations are simple loops:
for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words; ++i) result[i] = left[i] & right[i]; // intersection  for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words; ++i) result[i] = left[i] | right[i]; // union  for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words; ++i) result[i] = left[i] & ~right[i]; // difference  for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words; ++i) result[i] = left[i] ^ right[i]; // symmetric difference Each scalar iteration processes 64 elements. Compilers can also auto-vectorize these independent loops, processing several words per instruction. Once the arrays are large, however, there is little arithmetic left to optimize: reading two streams and writing one often makes the loop memory-bandwidth bound.
This changes how compound expressions should be evaluated. For
$$ R = (A \cap B) \cup (C \setminus D), $$
materializing both intermediate bitmaps performs unnecessary memory passes. Fuse the expression per word:
result[i] = (a[i] & b[i]) | (c[i] & ~d[i]); The CPU has no difficulty with the Boolean algebra; it is the extra traffic that hurts. Alignment can help vector loads and stores, but a correctly written unaligned loop is often already close to the bandwidth limit. Use profiling before building a library of architecture-specific versions.
 #CardinalityThe number of elements is the sum of population counts:
std::size_t cardinality(const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &words) { std::size_t result = 0; for (std::uint64_t word : words) result += std::popcount(word); return result; } std::popcount is C++20; on targets with a scalar population-count instruction it is normally compiled to that instruction. Wider ISAs may count several words at once, while older vector targets use lookup or arithmetic techniques. See SIMD reductions for the general pattern.
Maintaining cardinality eagerly makes count() constant time but adds work to updates. Setting a bit must first determine whether it was already set, and concurrent word updates need synchronization. A static query bitmap usually computes and caches counts; a write-heavy visited set often does not.
 #Iterating over Set BitsScanning all $U$ positions throws away most of the benefit when the set is sparse. Instead, skip zero words and repeatedly remove the least significant set bit:
template <class Function> void for_each_set_bit(const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &words, Function function) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words.size(); ++i) { std::uint64_t x = words[i]; while (x != 0) { unsigned bit = std::countr_zero(x); function(64 * i + bit); x &= x - 1; } } } The expression x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Calling countr_zero(0) would be invalid for several low-level intrinsics and gives the word width for the C++ function, so the nonzero loop condition is part of the algorithm, not decoration.
This traversal costs roughly one inner iteration per element plus one test per word. It is excellent for a sparse result and less attractive when nearly every bit is set; density can justify separate iteration paths.
The unused-tail-bits invariant now pays off again: the generic loop never needs to compare its generated index against the universe size.
 #Rank and SelectMembership is not the only useful bitmap query. Two operations form the indexing vocabulary of succinct data structures:
 $\operatorname{rank}_1(i)$ is the number of set bits in the prefix $[0,i)$; $\operatorname{select}_1(k)$ is the position of the zero-indexed $k$-th set bit.  A raw bitmap answers rank by counting all complete words before $i$ and the relevant prefix of one word. That is linear in the number of preceding words. For a static bitmap, store prefix cardinalities:
class rank_index { const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &words_; std::vector<std::uint64_t> prefix_; // prefix_[i] counts words [0, i)  public: explicit rank_index(const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &words) : words_(words), prefix_(words.size() + 1, 0) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i != words.size(); ++i) prefix_[i + 1] = prefix_[i] + std::popcount(words[i]); } std::uint64_t rank(std::size_t i) const { std::size_t word = i >> 6; unsigned offset = unsigned(i & 63); std::uint64_t result = prefix_[word]; if (offset != 0) { std::uint64_t mask = (std::uint64_t(1) << offset) - 1; result += std::popcount(words_[word] & mask); } return result; } }; The caller supplies $0 \le i \le U$. The definition uses a half-open prefix deliberately: rank(0) == 0, and rank(U) is the total cardinality.
One 64-bit prefix per 64-bit data word doubles the bitmap’s storage, which is often excessive. A practical compromise stores a wide cumulative counter once per large superblock and a small relative counter per smaller block. Rank then reads two counters and performs one popcount. By making the sampling hierarchy progressively sparser, the classic work beginning with Jacobson’s Succinct Static Data Structures supports constant-time rank and select with sublinear auxiliary space.
Select can use the same summaries in the opposite direction. First locate the block whose cumulative count straddles $k$, then locate the word, and finally select within that word. A simple static implementation binary-searches prefix_:
std::size_t select(const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &words, const std::vector<std::uint64_t> &prefix, std::uint64_t k) { // Precondition: k < prefix.back().  auto it = std::upper_bound(prefix.begin(), prefix.end(), k); std::size_t word = std::size_t(it - prefix.begin() - 1); unsigned within = unsigned(k - prefix[word]); std::uint64_t x = words[word]; while (within != 0) { x &= x - 1; --within; } return 64 * word + std::countr_zero(x); } This is $O(\log (U/64))$ for the binary search and at most 63 clear-lowest-bit steps. Faster word-select routines use broadword arithmetic or small tables. More important is choosing an index that matches the update model: every bit change invalidates a static prefix array, while a Fenwick tree or a hierarchy of mutable counters trades more update work and space for dynamic rank.
 #When a Plain Bitmap Is Too LargeA bitmap pays for the universe, not for the set. If identifiers range over $[0,2^{64})$ and only a million occur, allocating one bit per possible identifier is not an option. The alternatives exploit one of three kinds of structure.
 #Sparse positionsStore the set bits as a sorted array. Membership becomes binary search, iteration is trivial, and set intersection becomes a merge or a galloping search. Ignoring container overhead, $n$ values of $w$ bits use $nw$ bits instead of $U$. This wins when $n \ll U/w$; the exact crossover also includes cache behavior and the cost of the required operations.
An array is especially attractive when the set is static. Random insertion into its middle is expensive, while appending sorted values is cheap.
 #RunsStore intervals such as (start, length). A million consecutive set bits become one run; a million independently scattered bits become a million runs. Run-length formats are therefore excellent for sorted or clustered data and can expand on random data. Boolean operations must merge runs, so compressed size alone does not determine query speed.
 #Chunked hybrid layoutsA hybrid chooses a representation locally instead of once for the whole universe. Roaring bitmaps partition a 32-bit integer by its high 16 bits. For each present high half, the low 16-bit values are represented by a container:
high 16 bits low-half container 0x0001 -------> sorted uint16_t array 0x0002 -------> 65,536-bit bitmap 0x17af -------> runs A dense container occupies $2^{16}$ bits, or 8192 bytes. A sorted array of 4096 16-bit values also occupies 8192 bytes, which explains the natural transition near 4096 elements. Modern variants may use run containers when intervals are smaller still. The original and follow-up primary work reports the detailed array/bitmap/run algorithms and SIMD set operations; the important idea is that density is measured per chunk.
Operations then dispatch on a pair of container types:
 bitmap–bitmap uses word-wise Boolean operations; array–array uses merge, galloping, or vectorized intersection; array–bitmap probes or sets the listed positions; run combinations merge intervals or visit covered words.  The dispatch and top-level index add overhead, so a hybrid is not automatically better than a plain bitmap. It earns that complexity when the global universe is sparse but some local regions are dense, or when compressed size keeps more of the working set in cache.
 #Updates and ConcurrencySetting different bits in the same word is not independent at the machine level: both operations are read-modify-write updates of one 64-bit location. Without atomics or a lock, simultaneous updates are a data race and may lose a bit. With atomics, contention and false sharing can serialize otherwise unrelated work.
Useful parallel strategies include partitioning the universe by word ranges, giving each worker a private bitmap and reducing them with OR, or using atomic fetch_or when updates are sparse enough. The right choice depends on whether memory bandwidth, synchronization, or the final reduction is dominant.
Serialization also needs a contract: record the logical bit count, word byte order, and representation version. Dumping the in-memory uint64_t array bakes host endianness into the file and loses the number of valid bits in the tail.
 #Choosing the Representation   Representation Membership Bulk Boolean operations Space follows Best fit     Dense bitmap $O(1)$ one operation per word universe moderate or high density   Sorted positions $O(\log n)$ merge/gallop cardinality very sparse, mostly static sets   Run length search among runs merge runs number of runs long intervals   Chunked hybrid container lookup type-specific local density mixed sparse and dense regions    Do not choose from the table alone. Measure the operations your application performs, including the size of intermediate results. An intersection may turn two dense inputs into a sparse output; a query engine that keeps representing that result as a full bitmap can spend most of its time scanning zeros.
