That proviso will follow us throughout the chapter. “No false negatives” assumes correct hashing, successful construction, no unsupported deletion, no data races, and no update that reached the database but not the filter.
 #The Bloom FilterBurton Bloom’s original 1970 paper describes the classic construction. Allocate a bitmap of $m$ initially zero bits and choose $k$ hash-derived positions for each key.
Insertion sets all $k$ bits:
for i = 0 .. k-1: B[h_i(x)] = 1 A query returns “possibly present” only if all $k$ bits are set. Clearing one of them is not safe: the same bit may have been set by several keys.
The representation is exceptionally compact. It is also a useful example of a data structure whose performance and error probability are inseparable: more probes can reduce false positives but require more hashing and memory accesses.
 #Deriving the False-Positive RateAssume for the moment that all $kn$ bit choices made by $n$ inserted keys are independent and uniform. One particular bit remains zero with probability
$$ \left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)^{kn} \approx e^{-kn/m}. $$
It is therefore one with probability approximately $1-e^{-kn/m}$. An absent query is a false positive when all of its $k$ positions are one:
$$ p \approx \left(1-e^{-kn/m}\right)^k. $$
This is an approximation, not a per-instance guarantee. Bit states and probes are not perfectly independent, finite-size effects matter, and a real hash function is not a random oracle. It is nevertheless the standard and useful sizing model.
For fixed bits per key $b=m/n$, differentiating the expression gives the optimal real-valued number of probes:
$$ k^* = b \ln 2. $$
At that point about half of the bits are set, and
$$ p_{\min} \approx 2^{-k^*} = (0.6185\ldots)^b. $$
Solving for the required storage and then rounding to implementable values gives
$$ \frac{m}{n} = -\frac{\ln p}{(\ln 2)^2}, \qquad k \approx -\frac{\ln p}{\ln 2}. $$
For example, a target of one percent requires about $9.59$ bits per expected key and $k\approx6.64$, so seven probes is a reasonable starting point. Rounding the bitmap up and recomputing the expected rate with the actual $m$, $n$, and integer $k$ is better than quoting the continuous optimum.
Most importantly, $n$ is a capacity promise. If twice as many keys are inserted, the filter remains free of false negatives but its false-positive rate is no longer the advertised one. Filters should expose their design capacity, observed insertion count, and rebuild policy.
 #A Small ImplementationComputing $k$ unrelated hashes is usually unnecessary. Kirsch and Mitzenmacher’s primary work, Less Hashing, Same Performance, analyzes positions of the form
$$ g_i(x) = h_1(x) + i h_2(x). $$
The following implementation accepts two already mixed 64-bit hashes. It uses a power-of-two bitmap and makes the step odd, so the probe sequence can visit every bit instead of cycling through a smaller power-of-two subset:
#include <bit>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> class bloom_filter { std::vector<std::uint64_t> words_; std::uint64_t bit_mask_; unsigned probes_; public: bloom_filter(std::size_t bit_count, unsigned probes) : words_(bit_count / 64, 0), bit_mask_(bit_count - 1), probes_(probes) { if (bit_count < 64 || !std::has_single_bit(bit_count) || probes == 0 || probes > bit_count) throw std::invalid_argument("invalid Bloom filter shape"); } void add_hash(std::uint64_t h1, std::uint64_t h2) { h2 |= 1; // a full-period step modulo a power of two  for (unsigned i = 0; i != probes_; ++i) { std::uint64_t bit = h1 & bit_mask_; words_[bit >> 6] |= std::uint64_t(1) << (bit & 63); h1 += h2; // unsigned wraparound is defined  } } bool possibly_contains_hash(std::uint64_t h1, std::uint64_t h2) const { h2 |= 1; for (unsigned i = 0; i != probes_; ++i) { std::uint64_t bit = h1 & bit_mask_; if (((words_[bit >> 6] >> (bit & 63)) & 1) == 0) return false; h1 += h2; } return true; } }; Rounding the bit count up to a power of two may spend substantially more memory than the mathematical minimum. A general implementation can use fast range reduction for arbitrary $m$; the power-of-two version keeps the state transition visible.
The two input hashes must contain good entropy. They can come from independently seeded hashes or the halves of a suitable wide hash. Feeding the raw key into both arguments, or deriving both from the same weak low bits, does not satisfy the model. For attacker-controlled keys, use keyed hashing and treat the published false-positive probability as a benign-input estimate, not a security guarantee.
The class is deliberately single-threaded. Concurrent insertions need atomic word updates or external partitioning, and readers must be synchronized with writers according to the publication contract.
 #Why there is no eraseIf key a and key b set the same bit, clearing it while deleting a creates a false negative for b. A basic Bloom filter is insert-only.
A counting Bloom filter replaces bits with small counters, incrementing on insertion and decrementing on deletion. This costs more space and introduces saturation, underflow, and duplicate-insertion semantics. It is safe only when deleting an element known to have been inserted with a matching count. Asking the approximate filter whether an arbitrary key is present is not enough permission to decrement: a false positive could damage another key.
When a workload needs deletion, a counting Bloom filter is one option; a cuckoo filter is another. Neither makes update consistency with the authoritative set disappear.
 #The Memory-Access ProblemA classic Bloom query makes $k$ approximately random bit probes. If the filter fits in the last-level cache, this can be cheap. If it resides in RAM, the arithmetic may be dwarfed by several independent cache misses.
The misses do have memory-level parallelism, but a dependent hash pipeline, a small number of outstanding requests, or competition with the surrounding application can limit it. Increasing $k$ toward the mathematical optimum may therefore reduce the false-positive rate while making each query slower.
The real objective is system cost. If an absent key would trigger an operation costing $C$, the filter query costs $H$, and the false-positive probability is $p$, the expected cost for that absent key is
$$ H + pC. $$
The filter helps when $H < (1-p)C$. This is why an imperfect filter can be excellent in front of a disk and pointless in front of a tiny in-cache array.
 #Blocked Bloom FiltersA blocked Bloom filter uses part of the hash to choose one small block—often sized around a cache line—and places all remaining probes inside that block:
hash(key) -> block number | positions within the block The query then touches one local region instead of $k$ unrelated regions. The primary blocked-filter analysis by Putze, Sanders, and Singler explores this cache/hash/space tradeoff.
Locality is not free. Keys are distributed unevenly among blocks, so an unlucky block becomes fuller and has a higher false-positive rate. Positions inside a small block also have more correlation. A blocked filter generally needs different sizing from a classic Bloom filter to reach the same overall error target; substituting its block size into the classic formula is not a complete analysis.
Block size itself is hardware- and workload-dependent. One cache line avoids extra line fetches for an isolated query. Several smaller filters queried in a batch may benefit from different packing, and a concurrent writer may turn one popular line into a coherence hotspot.
 #Cuckoo FiltersA cuckoo filter stores short fingerprints in small buckets rather than setting bits. For key $x$, compute a fingerprint $f$ and two candidate buckets:
$$ i_1 = h(x), \qquad i_2 = i_1 \oplus h(f). $$
The XOR construction is reversible: knowing one bucket and the fingerprint identifies the other. A lookup reads the two buckets and searches for $f$.
If a bucket uses the all-zero fingerprint to mean “empty,” construction must remap a zero fingerprint to a nonzero value or store occupancy separately. Otherwise a real key can disappear into the representation’s sentinel.
Insertion places the fingerprint in either bucket. If both are full, it evicts a resident fingerprint, moves that fingerprint to its alternate bucket, and continues. This is the familiar cuckoo-hashing walk. It can exceed a relocation limit, at which point the implementation must grow, rebuild with a new seed, place the item in a stash, or report failure. Silently dropping the fingerprint would create a false negative.
Deletion is possible by removing a matching fingerprint from either candidate bucket, but its contract is narrower than it first appears:
 deleting a key that was not inserted can remove another key’s colliding fingerprint after a false-positive lookup; duplicate keys require reference counts or set semantics established outside the filter; concurrent relocation and lookup require a designed synchronization protocol.  Thus “supports deletion” means deletion of known inserted keys under the implementation’s duplicate policy.
Fingerprint width and bucket occupancy determine both space and false-positive probability. A rough intuition is that a query compares against up to twice the bucket size, each short fingerprint matching with probability around $2^{-f}$. The paper gives a fuller analysis; the simple product is not reliable near high occupancy or under correlated hashing.
Compared with a classic Bloom filter, the appeal is two localized bucket reads and dynamic deletion. The costs are a more complicated insertion path, possible construction failure, and sensitivity to high load.
 #Xor FiltersAn xor filter is built for a static set. It stores one $f$-bit value at each array position and maps a key to three positions. Construction chooses the stored values so that every member satisfies
$$ F[h_0(x)] \oplus F[h_1(x)] \oplus F[h_2(x)] = \operatorname{fingerprint}(x). $$
A query reads three values, XORs them, and compares the result with the key’s fingerprint. An absent key matches with probability close to $2^{-f}$ under the hashing model.
The interesting work happens during construction. The three positions define a random hypergraph. The builder repeatedly removes a key incident to a position of degree one, records that peeling order, and assigns fingerprints in reverse. Sometimes the graph cannot be fully peeled; construction then retries with a new seed or a larger array. Input keys should be deduplicated before building.
The primary xor-filter paper by Graf and Lemire evaluates this design against Bloom and cuckoo filters. Its attractive query path does not make it a general replacement: adding or deleting a key normally requires rebuilding the filter, and construction needs temporary storage for the key set and graph state.
Xor filters are therefore well matched to immutable database segments, index files, and periodically rebuilt snapshots. They are poorly matched to a stream that must become visible one insertion at a time.
 #Comparing the Designs   Filter Query locality Incremental insert Delete Construction caveat     Classic Bloom up to $k$ scattered bits yes no capacity determines error rate   Blocked Bloom one local block yes no block imbalance changes sizing   Cuckoo two small buckets yes known inserted keys relocation may fail and force rebuild   Xor three array positions no no static peeling can fail and retry    The table deliberately omits a universal “fastest” or “smallest” column. Results change with false-positive target, filter size relative to caches, hash cost, batch size, instruction set, load factor, and update mix. A structure that saves one bit per key may be slower if it adds a dependent cache miss; a filter with a higher false-positive rate may win if the protected operation is cheap.
There are many further designs—quotient filters, ribbon filters, binary fuse filters, and others—but they can be evaluated with the same questions:
 What exactly is the false-negative contract? What hash-independence model supports the advertised false-positive rate? How many independent memory regions does a query touch? Can insertion or construction fail, and how is failure surfaced? Which updates are supported without damaging other keys? What happens when actual cardinality exceeds planned capacity?   #Engineering the Whole System #Hash once when possibleIf the authoritative hash table already computes a high-quality wide hash, the filter may reuse carefully separated bits or derived values. This can save substantial work, but only when both structures document the coupling. Changing a seed, hash version, or serialization format must rebuild the filter.
Fingerprints are not cryptographic authenticators. They are deliberately short and collisions are expected.
 #Batch queriesSeveral independent filter queries expose memory-level parallelism. Software can compute their hashes, issue block or bucket loads, and finish earlier queries while later data arrives. This is often more portable than trying to vectorize a single query whose addresses are data-dependent.
 #Publish updates in the safe orderIf a filter fronts a database, inserting into the filter before committing the database can temporarily create a false positive, which is normally harmless. Committing the database first and delaying the filter can create a false negative, which violates the reason the filter exists. Deletion has the safe order reversed: remove the authoritative key first and clean up a deletion-capable filter afterward, leaving only a temporary false positive. Recovery and distributed replication make these orderings more complicated; they belong in the system contract.
For immutable segments, publish the data and its completely built filter as one versioned unit. For mutable structures, rebuilds commonly create a new filter beside the old one and switch readers only after it is complete.
 #Serialize the parametersA persisted filter needs its type, bit/fingerprint width, number of probes, capacity, hash algorithm and seed, byte order, and format version. Storing only the bitmap produces an object that may look valid and answer every query incorrectly after a software upgrade.
 #Validation and BenchmarkingFirst test the absolute property: every inserted key must query positive after every supported operation. Exercise zero keys, duplicate keys, rebuilds, full-capacity behavior, failed construction, and deletion according to the documented preconditions.
Then estimate false positives on keys independently drawn from the query distribution. Report the number of trials and uncertainty, not just a percentage. A filter tuned on random 64-bit integers may behave differently on structured strings if the hash or seeding is weak.
Finally measure the complete path:
 present and absent queries separately; filter sizes below and above each cache level; scalar and batched access; hash time included and excluded; the latency of the protected operation; insertion, rebuild, and peak construction memory; actual cardinality versus design capacity.  The false-positive formula predicts wasted authoritative lookups, while the benchmark measures how expensive the prediction machinery is. A good filter minimizes their sum. Its most valuable answer is still the cheap one: “do not look any further.”
title: Probabilistic Filters

content:
In the previous chapter, we studied memory from a theoretical standpoint, using the external-memory model to count transfers between a fast memory of size $M$ and an unbounded slow memory in blocks of $B$ words.
That model is intentionally sparse. It is often useful when an external transfer dwarfs the arithmetic performed on the transferred data, but it hides details that matter inside a computer: several cache levels, finite request queues, cache-line ownership, address translation, prefetching, associativity, and shared resources.
To optimize in-memory algorithms, we therefore need both models and measurements. Vendor manuals tell us what the machine is allowed to do; small experiments tell us what one particular machine actually did. Neither is sufficient on its own.
Experimental SetupMost graphs in this chapter are historical measurements from one laptop with an AMD Ryzen 7 4700U, a Zen 2 processor with:
 8 physical cores without simultaneous multithreading, configured near 2 GHz for the controlled runs; 32 KiB of 8-way L1 data cache per core; 512 KiB of 8-way L2 cache per core; 8 MiB of 16-way L3 cache, split into two 4 MiB regions shared by groups of four cores; 16 GiB of dual-channel DDR4-2666 memory, or 2666 MT/s rather than a 2666 MHz electrical clock.  These properties are specific to this processor and laptop configuration. Even processors sold under one family name can differ in cache topology, replacement policy, prefetchers, and memory configuration. AMD publishes the corresponding Family 17h Model 60h processor reference, while Linux exposes the topology through lscpu -C, lstopo, and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cache/.
Unless stated otherwise, the plots report useful work performed by the source program, not bytes observed on a physical bus. A cached store miss, for example, may transfer a whole line into the cache before eventually writing it back, while ten updates to a resident line may cause no lower-level transfer between them. Translating element updates per second into memory bandwidth therefore requires knowing the generated instructions, cache state, write policy, and number of passes.
The snippets are kept small for exposition. A real benchmark must also consume its result, control warm-up and placement, repeat the measurement, and inspect the generated machine code. The companion implementations live in the book’s code repository.
Reading the GraphsThe cliffs in these experiments are evidence, not labels printed by the hardware. To identify a cache or TLB boundary, vary one factor at a time, repeat around the suspected boundary, and corroborate the timing with hardware counters where possible. Alignment, physical page placement, frequency policy, another process, or a compiler update can otherwise move or erase the effect.
This chapter is inspired by Igor Ostrovsky’s “Gallery of Processor Cache Effects” and Ulrich Drepper’s “What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory”. They remain useful companions, but hardware and operating systems have evolved since they were written.
title: RAM & CPU Caches

content:
Ask a computer for a random bit twice with the same program state and it will normally return the same answer twice. This is not a defect. Most software does not generate new entropy; it expands a small seed into a long deterministic sequence that merely has the statistical shape required by the application.
Determinism is valuable for simulations, randomized algorithms, tests, and games. A failing run can be replayed from its seed, and generating each value costs only a few arithmetic instructions. It is disastrous when unpredictability is the requirement. Random number generation therefore begins by separating two jobs that unfortunately share one name.
 #Engines and DistributionsA pseudorandom number generator (PRNG), or engine, maintains a state and repeatedly produces fixed-width words. A distribution turns those words into the values the program actually requested: an integer in [0, n), a floating-point value in [0,1), a normal variate, or a shuffled permutation.
Keeping the layers separate prevents many subtle biases. The C++ random-number library follows exactly this design: its engine and distribution requirements specify uniform random bit generators separately from uniform_int_distribution and the other transformations.
The engine has several relevant properties:
 state size and period; statistical quality in the dimensions the application uses; cost and dependency latency per output; speed of seeding, copying, jumping, and creating independent streams; reproducibility across implementations; and, only for a cryptographic generator, resistance to predicting past or future output.  Passing a test suite checks some statistical consequences of these properties. It does not prove unpredictability, and a huge period does not by itself imply good output.
 #Linear Congruential GeneratorsThe classical linear congruential generator updates
$$ x_{i+1} = a x_i + c \pmod m. $$
With $m=2^w$, unsigned overflow performs the reduction for free. Suitable parameters can make the state visit all $2^w$ possible values, so the period looks ideal. The output is still highly structured: low bits can have short cycles, and tuples of consecutive values lie on a limited family of hyperplanes.
This distinction—good state traversal but visibly linear output—is useful. It explains why “the period is enormous” is not a sufficient generator review, and it motivates a modern pattern: use a cheap state transition, then apply a nonlinear-looking permutation before exposing the bits.
 #A Small General-Purpose GeneratorPCG is a family of permuted congruential generators. The underlying state follows an LCG, while an output permutation uses XOR, shifts, and rotation to mix the bits. Melissa O’Neill’s PCG paper describes the family, stream selection, and statistical evaluation.
Here is the 64-bit-state, 32-bit-output XSH-RR variant. It is compact enough to study and useful for ordinary randomized algorithms; it is not cryptographically secure.
#include <bit>#include <cstdint> class pcg32 { public: using result_type = std::uint32_t; pcg32(std::uint64_t seed, std::uint64_t sequence) : state_(0), increment_((sequence << 1u) | 1u) { operator()(); state_ += seed; operator()(); } result_type operator()() { const std::uint64_t old = state_; state_ = old * 6364136223846793005ULL + increment_; const auto xorshifted = static_cast<std::uint32_t>( ((old >> 18u) ^ old) >> 27u ); const auto rotation = static_cast<int>(old >> 59u); return std::rotr(xorshifted, rotation); } static constexpr result_type min() { return 0; } static constexpr result_type max() { return UINT32_MAX; } private: std::uint64_t state_; std::uint64_t increment_; // odd; low 63 bits of sequence select a stream }; The two warm-up calls are part of seeding: they mix both the initial state and stream parameter into the recurrence. Two objects with identical parameters produce identical sequences, which is exactly what reproducible experiments need.
Do not use this listing as a reason to invent a generator by changing constants. Generator parameters, seeding, and output permutations are one design. Use a maintained implementation when compatibility or long-term statistical behavior matters.
 #Mapping to a Range Without BiasThe tempting expression generator() % bound is biased unless the engine’s range size is divisible by bound. If an engine had 256 possible byte outputs and bound were 6, residues 0 through 3 would each have 43 preimages, while 4 and 5 would have only 42.
Rejection sampling removes the excess part of the source range. Daniel Lemire’s multiply-and-reject method maps a 32-bit word through the high half of a multiplication and normally avoids division in the loop:
#include <cstdint>#include <stdexcept> std::uint32_t bounded(pcg32& generator, std::uint32_t bound) { if (bound == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("bound must be positive"); std::uint64_t product = std::uint64_t{generator()} * bound; std::uint32_t low = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(product); if (low < bound) { const std::uint32_t threshold = (std::uint32_t{0} - bound) % bound; while (low < threshold) { product = std::uint64_t{generator()} * bound; low = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(product); } } return static_cast<std::uint32_t>(product >> 32); } For ordinary application code, std::uniform_int_distribution is clearer and delegates this problem to the library. The explicit version matters when a range conversion is proven to be a bottleneck or when a serialized algorithm requires fully specified behavior.
Floating-point conversion has similar edges. Dividing an integer by the engine’s maximum can produce exactly 1, which violates the common half-open [0,1) contract. Use a distribution or std::generate_canonical instead of reconstructing its scaling rules casually.
 #Seeds, Streams, and Parallel ProgramsA seed is an input, not a quality certificate. Seeding every worker with the current second can give many workers the same state; seeding with consecutive integers may create related streams in generators whose initialization was not designed for it.
Choose a policy based on the application:
 Tests should print or store the exact seed and generator version. Scientific results should record enough state to reproduce the run, including stream assignment and distribution parameters. Independent workers should use a documented stream-selection, jump-ahead, or counter-based construction—not merely seed + thread_id unless the generator specifies that use. Work stealing and nondeterministic scheduling require extra design if results must be bit-for-bit reproducible.  Counter-based generators are attractive for parallel work because output is a function of a key and counter rather than a mutable predecessor. A worker can own a counter range, and the program can regenerate any value without replaying the stream. The Random123 paper, “Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1, 2, 3”, develops this model for CPUs and accelerators.
 #Randomness for SecurityPCG, Mersenne Twister, xorshift-family generators, and ordinary LCGs are not appropriate for keys, nonces that require unpredictability, password-reset tokens, or session identifiers. Statistical quality is not enough: after observing outputs, an attacker must still be unable to recover state or predict another output.
For these tasks, obtain bytes from the operating system or a vetted cryptographic library. On Linux, getrandom draws from the kernel cryptographic random source and handles early-boot initialization semantics better than opening a device path by hand. Other operating systems provide corresponding APIs. A protocol may then expand or structure that randomness with a specified cryptographic construction such as ChaCha20; the IETF construction is documented in RFC 8439.
std::random_device is not a portable synonym for an operating-system CSPRNG. The C++ interface permits implementation-defined behavior, so security-sensitive software must verify what its platform and library actually provide.
Never seed a security generator from a timestamp, process ID, address, or general-purpose PRNG. Such values may be different without containing meaningful entropy.
 #Testing and PerformanceThe first validation layer consists of exact properties: known-answer tests, full-period proofs where applicable, serialization round trips, range bounds, and deterministic replay. Statistical batteries then search for patterns. TestU01 provides families of empirical tests and illustrates an important limitation: passing the tested sample sizes is evidence against specific defects, not proof that no defect or predictor exists.
Benchmark the operation the application uses. A raw engine may be fast while bounded sampling rejects often; a generator with excellent throughput may have a long dependency latency in a single stream; a large state may hurt when thousands of workers each own one; and a vector generator helps only when consumers can use a batch of values.
Random generation is therefore another case of separating model from mechanism. Decide whether the goal is reproducibility, statistical simulation, parallel stream management, or adversarial unpredictability. Then choose an engine, distribution, and seeding interface whose guarantees match that goal—rather than asking one mysterious rand() function to do all four.
title: Random Number Generation

content:
Return once more to the strided increment, but keep the number of useful updates fixed at $N=2^{13}$ while growing the allocation with the stride $D$:
constexpr std::size_t N = 1u << 13; std::vector<std::uint32_t> a(D * N, 0); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); i += D) ++a[i]; The production benchmark checks that D * N does not overflow, allocates on the heap, and consumes a checksum. For $D \ge 16$, successive accesses are at least one 64-byte line apart, so there are $N$ useful accesses and approximately $N$ touched data lines. Yet the historical curve stops being flat as $D$ grows:
 Historical stride experiment over a wider range  The additional bottleneck is address translation. Programs issue virtual addresses, while caches and memory ultimately need physical locations and access permissions. A translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent virtual-page to physical-frame translations so that most loads do not require a page-table walk.
The Zen 2 test core was documented with two relevant levels for ordinary 4 KiB pages:
 64 L1 data-TLB entries, covering at most $64 \times 4\ \text{KiB}=256\ \text{KiB}$ of distinct pages; 2048 L2 TLB entries, covering at most $2048 \times 4\ \text{KiB}=8\ \text{MiB}$.  “Coverage” is only a capacity upper bound. TLBs are set-associative, page sizes may share structures, and the access pattern can conflict before every entry is useful.
At $D=256$, the allocation spans
$$ 8192 \times 256 \times 4\ \text{bytes}=8\ \text{MiB}. $$
The stride is 1024 bytes, so four accesses land in each 4 KiB page and exactly 2048 pages are touched. Beyond this point, the working translations no longer fit in the nominal L2 TLB. A miss triggers a hardware page walk; its page-table entries may themselves hit in paging-structure caches or ordinary data caches, so “going to the main page table” is not one fixed-latency operation.
 #Larger PagesIncreasing the page size lets each TLB entry translate more data. Common x86-64 sizes are 4 KiB, 2 MiB, and, where supported and configured, 1 GiB. Other architectures and operating systems expose different sets.
Linux offers two distinct mechanisms:
 hugetlbfs and MAP_HUGETLB use explicitly reserved huge pages; Transparent Huge Pages (THP) can promote eligible ordinary mappings and fall back to base pages.  The global THP policy is visible in sysfs:
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled # typical output: always [madvise] never Changing it is a privileged, system-wide operation, for example:
echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled Under madvise, a program can mark an eligible range as a THP candidate:
const std::size_t bytes = round_up_to_base_page(array_bytes); void *ptr = mmap(nullptr, bytes, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0); if (ptr == MAP_FAILED) throw std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category()); if (madvise(ptr, bytes, MADV_HUGEPAGE) != 0) { const int error = errno; munmap(ptr, bytes); throw std::system_error(error, std::generic_category()); } // Fault and initialize the mapping after giving the advice. // ...  munmap(ptr, bytes); round_up_to_base_page is an application helper using the page size returned by sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE). mmap supplies base-page alignment, which is enough for madvise; direct allocation of a naturally aligned 2 MiB THP has stronger alignment conditions, and only aligned subranges can be promoted.
Most importantly, MADV_HUGEPAGE is advice, not an allocation guarantee. The kernel may allocate a huge page on a later fault, collapse base pages asynchronously, split it later, or keep base pages because of fragmentation or policy. The Linux THP documentation describes this best-effort behavior. Verify an experiment through /proc/<pid>/smaps fields such as AnonHugePages, together with the kernel’s THP counters, rather than assuming the call succeeded semantically because it returned zero.
Windows large pages are explicit rather than transparent. A process must obtain SeLockMemoryPrivilege, query GetLargePageMinimum, round the size accordingly, and then request MEM_LARGE_PAGES with VirtualAlloc. Microsoft’s large-page documentation also requires checking allocation failure; the privilege is intentionally not granted to ordinary processes by default.
 #Performance and CostsThe huge-page variants flattened the stride curve on the historical test system:
 Stride experiment with huge pages  They also reduced dependent-load latency by roughly 10–15% for some large working sets:
 Pointer-chasing experiment with huge pages  Those are plausible TLB benefits, not universal speedups. Huge pages can also:
 waste physical memory when only a small part of a promoted region is used; add page-fault, zeroing, reclamation, or compaction latency; interact differently with cache indexing and DRAM address mapping; be unavailable inside a container, virtual machine, fragmented host, or restricted account.  Use them for large, densely used mappings after measuring both steady-state throughput and allocation/tail latency. For sparse data structures, improving spatial locality often reduces data-cache misses and TLB pressure simultaneously, without relying on a particular huge-page policy.
title: Memory Paging

content:
Reading an integer is easy when it happens once. Reading a few gigabytes of them is a small systems problem disguised as elementary arithmetic.
There are really three different jobs involved:
 obtaining bytes from a file or a socket, finding the boundaries of the next token, converting the digits inside that token to an integer.  Formatted input functions do all three, together with locale handling and a fairly generous grammar. This is exactly what we want for a configuration file and often much more than we want for a machine-generated stream of decimal integers. In this chapter, we will separate these jobs, define a deliberately narrow grammar, and then optimize the hot part without quietly changing what the parser accepts.
The distinction is important. Replacing scanf with mmap does not make digit conversion free, and replacing a scalar digit loop with SIMD does not make one system call per byte acceptable. Optimizing the wrong layer is a surprisingly effective way to produce a very sophisticated slow program.
 #The ContractWe will parse a signed 64-bit integer from a half-open byte range [first, last). The token has the following grammar:
integer := [ '+' | '-' ] digit+ digit := '0' ... '9' There is no leading whitespace in this low-level function: tokenization is the caller’s job. On success, the parser returns a pointer to the first non-digit. On failure, it distinguishes an invalid token from a value outside the range $[-2^{63}, 2^{63}-1]$, and it leaves the output unchanged.
This is close to std::from_chars, with one intentional difference: the standard function does not accept a leading + for integers. If its exact grammar is suitable, use it first. It is non-allocating, locale-independent, and already has the right range-based interface.
Here is a complete scalar implementation of our slightly different contract:
#include <charconv>#include <cstdint>#include <limits> struct parse_result { const char *next; std::errc error; }; parse_result parse_i64(const char *first, const char *last, std::int64_t &output) { const char *p = first; bool negative = false; if (p != last && (*p == '+' || *p == '-')) { negative = (*p == '-'); ++p; } if (p == last || *p < '0' || *p > '9') return {first, std::errc::invalid_argument}; const std::uint64_t positive_limit = std::uint64_t(std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max()); const std::uint64_t limit = positive_limit + std::uint64_t(negative); std::uint64_t magnitude = 0; bool overflow = false; do { unsigned digit = unsigned(*p - '0'); if (!overflow) { if (magnitude > (limit - digit) / 10) overflow = true; else magnitude = magnitude * 10 + digit; } ++p; } while (p != last && *p >= '0' && *p <= '9'); if (overflow) return {p, std::errc::result_out_of_range}; std::int64_t value; if (!negative) { value = std::int64_t(magnitude); } else if (magnitude == positive_limit + 1) { value = std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min(); } else { value = -std::int64_t(magnitude); } output = value; return {p, {}}; } The apparently fussy limit calculation is what makes -9223372036854775808 work. Its magnitude does not fit in an int64_t, so negating a signed intermediate would overflow. We accumulate into an unsigned type and handle that one endpoint explicitly.
The check is written as
$$ x \le \left\lfloor\frac{L-d}{10}\right\rfloor $$
before evaluating $10x+d$. Therefore the multiplication itself never overflows. The parser also continues to the end of an oversized digit sequence after detecting overflow. This makes next useful for recovery and prevents malformed input from being reinterpreted as a second number.
 #Getting the BytesThe slowest imaginable input loop calls a library function for every character. The next-slowest merely hides that call behind a nicer interface. The first important optimization is to operate on blocks.
fread, a buffered stream, and a hand-written read loop can all provide blocks. The exact choice is usually less important than obeying two rules:
 process only the number of bytes that were actually returned; preserve the unfinished token at the end of a block and prepend it to the next one.  The second rule is easy to miss because benchmark generators often end every line with a newline and happen to align favorably. Real files are under no obligation to cooperate.
A block reader can be organized like this:
#include <array>#include <cstdio>#include <string> std::string carry; std::array<char, 64 * 1024> buffer; while (std::size_t n = std::fread(buffer.data(), 1, buffer.size(), stdin)) { // Append bytes until the last complete token, parse complete tokens,  // and keep the unfinished suffix in `carry` for the next iteration. } // At EOF, parse `carry` as a final token even if there is no delimiter. Production code normally avoids appending every block to a std::string: it parses the complete prefix in place and copies only the short suffix. The logical structure stays the same. If a token can be arbitrarily long, the carry buffer must be growable or the parser must impose and report a maximum token length.
Memory mapping can remove an extra copy for regular files, but it is not a drop-in replacement for input. Pipes are not seekable, empty files need special handling, mapping can fail, and the mapped region still has an exact end that vector loads may not cross. See system calls and memory mapping for the underlying mechanisms.
 #Formatted input and synchronizationThe usual progression in a C++ benchmark is:
 std::cin with its default configuration; std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false) and an untied input stream; scanf or another formatted C interface; block input plus a specialized converter.  Disabling synchronization can remove coordination with C streams, but it does not turn operator>> into a narrow decimal parser. Formatted input still has a wider contract and more state. Conversely, a custom converter fed one byte at a time is still dominated by input overhead. Benchmarking the layers separately tells us which change helped.
 #The Scalar LoopFor a positive token, conversion is Horner’s rule:
$$ x = (((d_0) \cdot 10 + d_1) \cdot 10 + d_2) \cdots 10 + d_{k-1}. $$
It performs one dependent multiply-add per digit. On modern out-of-order processors, different tokens can overlap, but the digits of one token form a dependency chain. This is the first real computational bottleneck after buffering.
There is also a branch deciding whether the current byte is a digit. It is predictable for a regular file such as one positive integer per line, and much less predictable for mixed token lengths and separators. A branchless rewrite is not automatically better: it often adds instructions to every digit merely to avoid one correctly predicted branch. This is a case for measurement, not aesthetic preference.
Before reaching for intrinsics, try std::from_chars and inspect the generated code. Library implementations are allowed to specialize common bases and widths, and unlike a benchmark sketch they already specify invalid input and overflow behavior.
 #Eight Digits at OnceWhen there are at least eight known digits available, we can shorten the dependency chain with SWAR—SIMD within a register. Load eight bytes, turn them into numerical digits, and combine neighboring fields in a tree:
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 \_/ \_/ \_/ \_/ 12, 34, 56, 78 \___/ \___/ 1234, 5678 \_______/ 12345678 The following x86-oriented routine is safe for unaligned input because memcpy is used for the load. It succeeds only when all eight bytes are decimal digits:
#include <cstdint>#include <cstring> bool parse_8_digits(const char *p, std::uint32_t &output) { std::uint64_t x; std::memcpy(&x, p, sizeof x); // exactly eight accessible bytes  // This test works byte-wise on little-endian machines. For a decimal  // byte, both expressions leave the high bit clear; an out-of-range byte  // sets at least one high bit.  constexpr std::uint64_t high_bits = 0x8080808080808080ULL; if (((x + 0x4646464646464646ULL) | (x - 0x3030303030303030ULL)) & high_bits) return false; x -= 0x3030303030303030ULL; x = (x * 10 + (x >> 8)) & 0x00ff00ff00ff00ffULL; x = (x * 100 + (x >> 16)) & 0x0000ffff0000ffffULL; x = (x * 10000 + (x >> 32)) & 0x00000000ffffffffULL; output = std::uint32_t(x); return true; } This is not a replacement for the scalar parser. It is a fast path. The caller must first know that eight bytes are accessible, incorporate the chunk into the current magnitude with the same overflow check, and fall back for the remaining zero to seven digits. The constants also assume little-endian byte order; portable code needs an endian-specific load or a byte swap.
The tree has logarithmic depth instead of eight serial multiply-adds, which is the useful part. The arithmetic itself is cheap enough that validation, token boundaries, and the cost of moving data can easily become dominant.
 #SIMD Is Usually a Tokenizer FirstVariable-length integers are an inconvenient SIMD workload. A 256-bit register may contain three complete tokens, half of a fourth, and several delimiters. The lanes do not know where one integer ends and the next begins.
SIMD is still excellent at classifying bytes. For ASCII input, compare a vector against '0' and '9', combine the results, and extract a bit mask. The set bits identify digits—or, after inversion, token boundaries. We can then:
 skip long spans without examining every byte individually; locate delimiters with ctz on the mask; dispatch fixed-size digit runs to routines such as parse_8_digits; process the final partial vector with a scalar tail.  Two safety details matter more than the particular intrinsic:
 A full-width load is allowed only when that many bytes remain. For the tail, copy the remaining bytes into a padded local array or use a masked load whose architectural contract permits it. Classification is not validation of the whole token. Signs, empty fields, overflow, and unexpected punctuation still need defined behavior.  An alternative is to transpose several independent byte streams and update several integer accumulators in parallel. This exposes instruction-level parallelism, and it was the most interesting idea in the historical companion experiments for this chapter. It also creates partition-boundary repair work and assumes a very regular format. For a fixed-width data feed that may be a fine trade; for a general integer parser it is usually too much machinery.
The broader lesson is that SIMD need not perform the entire algorithm to be useful. Separating structural scanning from semantic conversion is also the central idea behind high-throughput parsers such as the primary research on SIMD JSON parsing.
 #Benchmarking the ParserInteger parsing results are unusually easy to overstate. A useful benchmark records at least:
 the distribution of token lengths and signs; the delimiter grammar; whether the input is already resident in memory; whether validation and overflow detection are enabled; whether the checksum or consumer work prevents dead-code elimination; whether bytes, integers, or both are used as the denominator; compiler, flags, ISA target, CPU, and frequency policy.  A parser specialized for eight unsigned digits followed by a newline solves a different problem from scanf("%lld"). Comparing them can illuminate the price of the wider contract, but it does not make them interchangeable.
The repository’s original experiments were run around 2022 on a Zen 2 processor with Clang 13 and included buffered, memory-mapped, branchless, SIMD, and transposed variants. They are useful experimental archaeology, not portable performance promises: several variants assume newline-delimited non-negative integers, complete buffers, or convenient padding. This chapter therefore keeps the optimization ideas while giving the boundary conditions first-class status.
 #ChecklistFor a high-throughput integer reader, the winning order is usually:
 freeze the accepted grammar and error semantics; read blocks and handle short reads and final tokens correctly; use from_chars or a checked scalar loop as the reference implementation; profile tokenization and digit conversion separately; add fixed-width SWAR fast paths for common lengths; use SIMD to classify bytes when structural scanning is still expensive; differential-test every optimized path against the reference on boundaries and random input.  The last point is essential. Test 0, -0, both signed endpoints, one-past-each-endpoint, every token length around the fast-path width, all split positions at a buffer boundary, invalid signs, empty tokens, embedded punctuation, and an EOF immediately after the last digit. Fast input code tends to be correct on ten million random numbers and wrong on the eleventh byte of a carefully chosen file.
Next, we will perform the inverse operation in Writing Decimal Integers. It has the same separation between conversion and I/O, but a rather different dependency structure.
title: Reading Decimal Integers

content:
Consider a loop that adds the elements of an array:
std::uint32_t sum(const std::uint32_t *data, std::size_t n) { std::uint32_t result = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) result += data[i]; return result; } The additions are independent except for the accumulator. A compiler can split that dependency into several partial sums and process multiple elements with one instruction. This is single instruction, multiple data (SIMD): one vector instruction interprets a wide register as several fixed-size lanes and performs the same operation in every lane.
 One scalar operation compared with one SIMD operation  On x86-64, SSE instructions commonly operate on 128-bit vectors, AVX and AVX2 extend many operations to 256 bits, and AVX-512 adds 512-bit operations plus mask registers and many new forms. A 256-bit register holds eight 32-bit integers, but that does not make every loop eight times faster. Dependencies, instruction throughput, remainder handling, memory bandwidth, and frequency or power limits can all reduce the gain.
The original benchmark for this chapter ran almost twice as fast after enabling AVX2: roughly 2.43 seconds became 1.24 seconds on its particular compiler and Zen 2 laptop. That measurement demonstrates wider auto-vectorization on one setup; it is not a portable ratio.
Enabling an ISA is also a correctness decision. Compiling an entire binary with -mavx2, -march=native, or a global target pragma permits AVX2 instructions anywhere in that scope. Running the result on a processor or operating system that cannot execute them may raise an illegal-instruction exception. Portable binaries keep a baseline implementation and dispatch to separately compiled SIMD implementations only after a runtime feature check.
Extensions, Not Generationsx86 extensions accumulated over time, but they are not one simple sequence in which every new label contains every previous instruction. AVX-512 in particular is a family: AVX512F is the foundation, while features such as AVX512BW, AVX512DQ, AVX512VL, VNNI, and VPOPCNTDQ have separate feature bits and appear in different combinations. Test every subset an implementation actually uses.
This does not mean AVX-512 abandoned backward-compatible register design. In 64-bit mode, the first sixteen 128-bit XMM and 256-bit YMM registers are the low parts of ZMM0–ZMM15, and AVX-512 expands the architectural vector file to 32 ZMM registers. Intel explicitly describes this compatibility in its AVX-512 overview. What is not backward compatible is the binary: an older CPU cannot decode instructions from a newer extension.
 A historical overview of selected Intel SIMD extensions  Compilers often vectorize regular loops automatically. This auto-vectorization is usually the best starting point because the source remains readable and the compiler can select an ISA and handle tails. It is not omniscient, however. Aliasing, alignment, control flow, reductions, and irregular data movement can block or weaken the transformation.
The rest of this chapter works primarily with AVX2 intrinsics to expose those constraints. Each kernel will state its ISA, alignment, and padding requirements explicitly; production code must provide a baseline or runtime-dispatched alternative.
title: SIMD Parallelism

content:
To compute the exact sum of an arbitrary array, we must inspect every element: an unread value could change the answer. The same obstacle applies to an exact maximum, an exact number of distinct keys, or a complete list of frequent items. If even one block may contain decisive information, no clever layout makes an exact algorithm sublinear.
Approximation changes the question. Instead of “return the answer,” we ask for an estimator whose error is at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, or for a deterministic summary with a stated additive error. The improvement comes from weakening the output contract, not from making the unread data disappear.
Two models are often grouped under the word sublinear:
 A sublinear-time algorithm has random access to a dataset and probes only a sample of it. A streaming algorithm reads every update once but uses memory much smaller than the stream.  A one-pass sketch is linear-time, not sublinear-time. It is useful because its memory, communication, and later query cost are sublinear. Keeping these resources separate prevents many misleading complexity claims.
 #Sampling a Bounded MeanSuppose a fixed dataset contains $N$ values $x_i\in[0,1]$ with mean
$$ \mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i. $$
Draw $k$ indices independently and uniformly, with replacement, and let $\hat\mu$ be the sample mean. Hoeffding’s inequality gives
$$ \Pr\left[|\hat\mu-\mu|\ge\varepsilon\right] \le 2e^{-2k\varepsilon^2}. $$
Thus it is sufficient to choose
$$ k\ge\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}. $$
The sample count does not depend on $N$. It depends on the value range, independence, desired absolute error, and failure probability. If values lie in $[a,b]$, rescale them and pay a factor of $(b-a)^2$. If the quantity of interest is a rare event, a small additive error may be useless as a relative guarantee; stratified or importance sampling may be needed.
Uniform sampling also assumes we can reach a random record without scanning the blocks before it. On an unindexed compressed stream, “choose a random index” may itself require linear work.
 #Sampling an Unknown-Length StreamWhen the stream length is not known in advance, reservoir sampling maintains a uniform sample in one pass. Store the first $k$ items. When item $i$ arrives, choose a uniform integer in $[0,i)$ and keep the item exactly when that integer is below $k$, replacing the selected reservoir entry.
#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <iterator>#include <limits>#include <random>#include <stdexcept>#include <vector> template<class InputIt, class Generator> auto reservoir_sample(InputIt first, InputIt last, std::size_t sample_size, Generator& generator) -> std::vector<typename std::iterator_traits<InputIt>::value_type> { using value_type = typename std::iterator_traits<InputIt>::value_type; std::vector<value_type> sample; if (sample_size == 0) return sample; sample.reserve(sample_size); std::uint64_t seen = 0; for (; first != last; ++first) { if (seen == std::numeric_limits<std::uint64_t>::max()) throw std::length_error("stream index does not fit"); ++seen; if (sample.size() < sample_size) { sample.push_back(*first); continue; } std::uniform_int_distribution<std::uint64_t> pick(0, seen - 1); const std::uint64_t index = pick(generator); if (index < sample_size) sample[static_cast<std::size_t>(index)] = *first; } return sample; } After processing $n\ge k$ items, every item is present with probability $k/n$. The proof is inductive: an old reservoir item survives step $n$ with probability $1-1/n$, while the new item enters with probability $k/n$. Jeffrey Vitter’s reservoir-sampling paper develops faster skipping variants for streams where generating one decision per item is expensive.
Reservoir sampling uses $O(k)$ memory, but it still reads $n$ items. It is the canonical example of a streaming-space improvement rather than a sublinear-time one.
 #Deterministic Heavy HittersSampling can miss an item near the frequency threshold. The Misra–Gries algorithm gives a deterministic alternative.
Fix $k\ge2$ and maintain at most $k-1$ item counters. An arriving item increments its counter if present, occupies an empty counter if available, and otherwise decrements every counter, removing zeroes. Here is the direct version for 64-bit item identifiers:
#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <limits>#include <stdexcept>#include <unordered_map> class misra_gries { public: explicit misra_gries(std::size_t k) : k_(k) { if (k < 2) throw std::invalid_argument("k must be at least two"); counters_.reserve(k - 1); } void add(std::uint64_t item) { if (auto it = counters_.find(item); it != counters_.end()) { if (it->second == std::numeric_limits<std::uint64_t>::max()) throw std::overflow_error("counter overflow"); ++it->second; return; } if (counters_.size() < k_ - 1) { counters_.emplace(item, 1); return; } for (auto it = counters_.begin(); it != counters_.end(); ) { if (--it->second == 0) it = counters_.erase(it); else ++it; } } const std::unordered_map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t>& candidates() const noexcept { return counters_; } private: std::size_t k_; std::unordered_map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t> counters_; }; Let $f_x$ be the true frequency of item $x$ in a stream of length $n$, and let $c_x$ be its stored counter, taking $c_x=0$ when absent. Then
$$ f_x-\frac{n}{k}\le c_x\le f_x. $$
In particular, every item with $f_x>n/k$ must remain as a candidate. The stored counter is a lower bound, not the exact frequency. If the input can be read again, a second pass counts only the candidates and removes false positives.
Why does the bound hold? Each decrement step accounts for $k$ distinct stream occurrences: the untracked arriving item and one occurrence represented by each of the $k-1$ counters. There can be at most $n/k$ such steps, and each step can reduce the remembered contribution of any one item by at most one.
The original Misra–Gries paper develops the comparison-based algorithm and its bounds. The straightforward hash-table implementation has an $O(k)$ worst-case update when all counters are decremented, although those full decrements are limited by the accounting argument. More elaborate representations can make latency smoother.
 #Count–Min SketchMisra–Gries keeps candidates but does not directly estimate every item’s frequency. A Count–Min sketch stores a rectangular array of counters. Each of $d$ rows has a hash function chosen independently from a pairwise-independent family mapping keys into $w$ columns. Updating item $x$ increments counter $(j,h_j(x))$ in every row; querying takes the minimum of those $d$ counters.
For an insertion-only stream, let $f_x$ be an item’s frequency and let
$$ m=\sum_x f_x $$
be the total count. Choose
$$ w=\left\lceil\frac{e}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil, \qquad d=\left\lceil\ln\frac{1}{\delta}\right\rceil. $$
For any fixed queried item $x$, the estimate $\hat f_x$ satisfies
$$ f_x\le\hat f_x\le f_x+\varepsilon m $$
with probability at least $1-\delta$. Collisions can only increase a counter, which gives the lower inequality; Markov’s inequality bounds the collision mass in one row, and taking the minimum makes all rows fail only with probability $\delta$.
The qualifier “fixed” matters. If a program chooses among millions of queries after seeing their estimates, the one-query guarantee is not automatically simultaneous. A union bound or a stronger analysis must account for the number and adaptivity of queries.
The original Count–Min paper describes point, range, and inner-product queries. Its basic array uses $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta))$ counters, independent of the number of distinct keys. Negative updates require the turnstile-model analysis; the simple insertion-only overestimate guarantee above no longer follows.
 #Distinct ValuesCounting distinct keys exactly requires remembering a set in the worst case. HyperLogLog instead hashes each key, uses some hash bits to choose a register, and records the longest observed zero prefix in the remaining bits. Long zero prefixes are rare, so their maxima reveal the scale of the unseen set.
With $r$ registers and ideal hash behavior, the original HyperLogLog analysis gives an asymptotic relative standard error of approximately
$$ \frac{1.04}{\sqrt r}. $$
This is a standard deviation under the model, not a deterministic error bound or a universal high-probability interval. Practical implementations also need the paper’s bias and range corrections, a sufficiently wide hash, and a defined treatment of duplicate serialized values.
 #Merging and Adversarial InputsMany sketches are valuable because summaries can be combined without replaying raw data:
 Count–Min arrays with identical dimensions and hash functions merge by counter-wise addition. HyperLogLog registers with identical parameters and hash function merge by component-wise maximum. Misra–Gries summaries can be combined by adding candidate weights and reducing back to the counter budget. Reservoirs require a weighted merge that accounts for the number of source items; concatenating two reservoirs is biased when their source streams have different lengths.  The parameter and hash identity are part of the serialized sketch format. Merging summaries with different seeds may produce a plausible-looking but meaningless answer.
Random hashing also defines the adversary model. A proof may assume the stream is fixed independently of secret random choices. If clients can learn a fixed non-cryptographic hash and then choose keys, they may manufacture collisions. Use an appropriate randomized or keyed hash construction, rotate secrets according to the surrounding protocol, and do not present an average-case sketch guarantee as an adversarial security boundary.
Finally, count the whole resource budget. A sketch with few counters may still perform several random cache accesses per update; wide counters may dominate its memory; and a tiny summary does not make the initial stream free to read. Benchmark update throughput and merge cost, but choose parameters from the mathematical error contract first.
Sublinear algorithms are useful because they say exactly what was traded away. The result is not “probably close” in the abstract: it is close under stated bounds, randomness, query patterns, and failure probability. Those qualifiers are the algorithm.
title: Sublinear Algorithms

content:
Minimal loops are useful for isolating one hardware effect, but performance engineering becomes interesting when the effects interact. A faster arithmetic kernel may expose memory bandwidth; a compact representation may enable SIMD; a branchless transformation may add enough work to lose on short inputs.
The case studies in this chapter begin with a correct reference implementation, identify the active constraint, and change one layer of the algorithm at a time. Historical measurements are labeled with their machine and workload. Treat them as evidence for the explanation, then reproduce the experiment on the system that matters.
Each optimized implementation keeps its domain attached: alignment, padding, integer ranges, instruction-set support, numerical error, preprocessing cost, and input distribution are part of the algorithm. The aim is not to collect record claims. It is to practice moving from an abstract operation count to a tested program whose dataflow matches the hardware.
title: Algorithms Case Studies

content:
Data used together should usually be stored together. This improves spatial locality: one fetched line supplies several useful fields, adjacent lines are friendly to prefetchers, and translations cover more work.
The familiar choice is between:
 an array of structures (AoS), where all fields of one record are consecutive; a structure of arrays (SoA), where each field forms its own consecutive stream.  Neither layout is universally better. AoS favors operations that consume most fields of one record. SoA favors operations that consume one or a few fields from many records and often makes SIMD access simpler.
 #A Dependent-Load ExperimentTo isolate this trade-off, modify the random-cycle benchmark so that each successor is encoded as the XOR of $D$ fields. Let $N$ be the total number of 32-bit fields and $M=N/D$ the number of nodes.
For AoS, node i occupies the consecutive range data[i * D ... (i + 1) * D):
const std::size_t M = N / D; std::vector<std::uint32_t> order(M), data(M * D); std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0); std::mt19937 rng(42); std::shuffle(order.begin(), order.end(), rng); auto field = [&](std::size_t node, std::size_t j) -> std::uint32_t & { return data[node * D + j]; }; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < M; ++i) { const std::uint32_t node = order[i]; const std::uint32_t successor = order[(i + 1) % M]; std::uint32_t encoded = successor; for (std::size_t j = 1; j < D; ++j) { field(node, j) = rng(); encoded ^= field(node, j); } field(node, 0) = encoded; } std::uint32_t k = order[0]; for (std::size_t step = 0; step < steps; ++step) { std::uint32_t successor = 0; for (std::size_t j = 0; j < D; ++j) successor ^= field(k, j); k = successor; } The original article accidentally interleaved the cycle-construction and filler loops and indexed the wrong dimension. In the corrected construction above, XORing all $D$ initialized fields recovers exactly the intended successor.
For SoA, only the storage and accessor change:
std::vector<std::uint32_t> data(D * M); auto field = [&](std::size_t node, std::size_t j) -> std::uint32_t & { return data[j * M + node]; }; The same initialization and traversal then access $D$ separate streams. The benchmark checksum must consume k, and separate AoS and SoA functions should be compiled so the optimizer can specialize their address calculations.
 Historical AoS and SoA dependent-load measurements  With 32-bit fields and a 64-byte line, up to sixteen fields of one AoS node fit in a line. SoA may need one line per field when its column spacing is large. The maximum line-count ratio is therefore about sixteen for this layout, although alignment, $D$, prefetching, and reuse change the exact number. Contiguous AoS fields also admit a straightforward SIMD XOR reduction.
SoA remains the right choice when an operation needs only field j: it reads one dense array instead of dragging the other $D-1$ fields through cache. Layout follows the access pattern, not the name of the data structure.
 #Address-Mapping SpikesThe historical SoA curve has sharp spikes when $M=N/D$ is a large power of two. Column j begins 4M bytes after column j-1, so a power-of-two $M$ preserves many address bits across all $D$ simultaneous streams. They can collide in cache sets, TLB sets, DRAM banks, or a combination of these resources.
The timing alone does not prove which one. The fields are consumed once at each traversal step, so saying they “must be stored temporarily in cache and re-fetched” is not a sufficient explanation: a line evicted after its last use costs nothing by itself. A defensible diagnosis varies the base offsets and page size, inspects generated code, and records cache, TLB, and memory-controller events available on that processor.
Huge pages made most points modestly faster but made the $D=64$ point almost ten times slower in this particular run:
 Historical SoA results with transparent huge pages; logarithmic scale  One plausible contributor is physical address layout. With 4 KiB pages, only the low 12 virtual-address bits are necessarily preserved in the physical address; distinct physical page frames can disturb a large virtual stride. A 2 MiB mapping preserves 21 low bits and makes more of that stride visible to physical cache and DRAM indexing. But LLC hashes, page placement, channels, banks, and row selection are platform-specific, so this is an inference from the experiment rather than a complete explanation.
This is also a counterexample to “huge pages can never hurt.” They change more than TLB capacity, and an address pattern can become worse even when translations improve.
 #Consecutive versus Dispersed LinesTo separate line count from placement, replace each field with one line-sized value while retaining AoS order:
struct alignas(64) PaddedValue { std::uint32_t value; std::array<std::byte, 60> padding{}; }; static_assert(sizeof(PaddedValue) == 64); const std::size_t M = N / (16 * D); std::vector<PaddedValue> data(M * D); auto field = [&](std::size_t node, std::size_t j) -> std::uint32_t & { return data[node * D + j].value; }; The factor of sixteen keeps the total byte footprint comparable to the original 32-bit-field experiment. Both padded AoS and dispersed SoA now fetch roughly $D$ lines per node, but the padded AoS lines are consecutive:
 Consecutive and dispersed cache-line layouts  For $D=63$, the consecutive layout was roughly one third faster once the allocation exceeded the last-level cache. At smaller sizes it could be slightly slower:
 Fixed-D comparison across working-set sizes  Equal line counts do not imply equal cost. Consecutive lines are easier to prefetch, use fewer translations, form full DRAM bursts, and are more likely to share an open DRAM row. Dispersed lines may provide more bank-level parallelism, so even the direction depends on the controller and access order.
 #DRAM Rows and BanksDRAM is divided into channels, ranks, bank groups, banks, rows, and columns. To access a closed row, the controller issues an activate operation that raises the row into a bank’s sense amplifiers—the row buffer. Column read or write commands then transfer part of that open row. Accessing a different row in the same bank generally requires a precharge followed by another activate.
 Simplified DRAM row-buffer organization  A row hit avoids the precharge/activate sequence and is therefore cheaper than a row conflict. But activate, column, precharge, read/write turnaround, and data-transfer timings are not equal, so a row hit is not universally “three times faster.” Requests to different banks can also overlap, and the memory controller reorders them.
Row size and the mapping from physical address bits to channels, banks, and rows depend on the DIMMs and controller and are often undocumented. The historical one-third difference is consistent with better spatial service—row hits, bursts, and prefetching—but the graph by itself cannot assign the whole gain to one row-buffer mechanism.
The practical lesson is broader and more reliable: choose AoS or SoA from the fields each hot operation consumes, avoid identical power-of-two spacing across many streams, and benchmark the final layout at the working-set sizes and thread placement that matter.
title: AoS and SoA

content:
new looks like a primitive operation, but it crosses several layers. C++ establishes an object’s lifetime, a user-space allocator finds suitably aligned storage, and the operating system eventually maps virtual pages to physical memory. Most calls stop at the allocator’s fast path; some refill a shared pool; a much smaller number request pages from the kernel.
This separation explains two common surprises. Allocation can be expensive without making a system call, because it may contend on shared metadata or miss in caches. Conversely, reserving a large virtual range can be cheap until the program first touches its pages. “How much memory did we allocate?” has several answers: requested payload, allocator-reserved bytes, committed pages, resident pages, and bytes currently reachable by the program.
 #Storage Is Not an ObjectC and C++ expose related but different interfaces. The POSIX allocation functions return raw storage; C++ new expressions allocate storage and then construct objects in it. A delete expression destroys an object before deallocating its storage.
Mixing these layers causes bugs:
 malloc must be paired with free, and new[] with delete[]; raw bytes do not automatically run constructors or destructors; a pointer becomes invalid when its object’s lifetime ends, even if the same address is reused immediately; an over-aligned type requires storage satisfying that stronger alignment; realloc may move the allocation, invalidating the old pointer when it succeeds.  RAII containers and smart pointers encode these rules in types and should be the default. A custom allocator changes where storage comes from; it does not suspend the language’s lifetime rules.
 #What a General-Purpose Allocator DoesCalling into the kernel for every 24-byte object would waste both time and pages. General-purpose allocators acquire memory in larger runs and subdivide it.
A typical small-object path looks like this:
 round the request to a size class; pop a free object from a local list for that class; if the list is empty, refill it with a batch from a central structure; if no suitable run exists centrally, split a run of pages obtained from the back end.  Deallocation follows the reverse path. Large requests often bypass small-object bins and consume whole page runs, which can later be coalesced with adjacent free runs.
Google’s current TCMalloc design, for example, describes a per-CPU or per-thread front end, per-size-class transfer and central free lists, and a page-heap back end. This is one implementation, not a language guarantee, but the hierarchy illustrates a general principle: batch expensive coordination and keep the common operation local.
Metadata must answer two questions quickly: which size class owns this address, and when has an entire run become free? Allocators may keep headers next to objects, use bitmaps, or maintain a separate page map. Corrupting that metadata with an out-of-bounds write can make a later, unrelated free fail; the allocation call shown in a crash is not necessarily the source of the bug.
 #Two Kinds of FragmentationInternal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated slot. If a 33-byte request is served from a 40-byte size class, seven bytes are unavailable to anyone else. Alignment and per-object metadata add similar overhead.
External fragmentation is free space split into the wrong shapes. An allocator may own plenty of free bytes but no sufficiently large contiguous run. At the page level, one live object can prevent the allocator from returning an otherwise empty span to the operating system.
This creates resident amplification:
$$ \text{amplification} =\frac{\text{resident bytes retained for the heap}} {\text{live application payload}}. $$
The ratio depends on allocation sizes and, crucially, lifetimes. Interleaving one long-lived object with many short-lived objects can strand every span. Grouping objects by lifetime often helps more than changing the free-list search policy.
Returning memory to an allocator also does not promise an immediate drop in resident set size. The block may stay in a thread cache, an arena, or a partially occupied span for reuse. Allocators such as jemalloc expose decay and purge policies precisely because reuse latency and resident footprint are competing objectives.
 #Concurrency Trades Locks for MemoryA single locked free list serializes an allocation-heavy parallel program. Thread-local or per-CPU caches let most operations proceed without a central lock, then transfer objects in batches. The cost is extra cached memory for every active thread or CPU and more work when one worker frees objects allocated by another.
Multiple arenas similarly reduce contention by partitioning the heap, but a free run in one arena may not satisfy demand in another. More concurrency can therefore increase fragmentation. On NUMA machines, the thread that first writes a page often influences its physical placement, so allocating on one socket and using the data on another may add remote-memory traffic.
Allocator locality is not object locality. Two small objects returned consecutively may share a cache line and suffer false sharing when different cores update them. Conversely, a linked structure built from individually allocated nodes can scatter across many pages even if allocation itself is fast. Layout and ownership still need to be designed at the data-structure level.
 #Match the Allocator to the LifetimeThe best deallocation operation is sometimes none at all. A compiler pass, request handler, or parser may create many objects that all die together. A monotonic arena advances through large buffers and releases them as a group.
C++17 provides this policy through std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource. The following function copies temporary strings into a local arena, consumes them, and lets the whole arena disappear on return:
#include <array>#include <cstddef>#include <memory_resource>#include <span>#include <string>#include <string_view>#include <vector> std::size_t copied_bytes(std::span<const std::string_view> input) { std::array<std::byte, 4096> local_buffer{}; std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena( local_buffer.data(), local_buffer.size() ); std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> copies{&arena}; copies.reserve(input.size()); for (std::string_view value : input) copies.emplace_back(value); std::size_t total = 0; for (const auto& value : copies) total += value.size(); return total; } The resource is declared before the container, so the container and its strings are destroyed first. Their individual deallocations do nothing; the arena releases its upstream buffers at destruction. The local array is only an initial buffer—larger inputs automatically request more memory from the upstream resource.
No pointer into copies may escape the function. Calling arena.release() while live objects still refer to its storage would invalidate them, and the resource does not call object destructors on the application’s behalf. The current C++ specification states these semantics explicitly in monotonic_buffer_resource.
When objects have independent lifetimes but mostly repeat a few sizes, a pool resource can reuse fixed-size blocks instead. std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource avoids internal synchronization and therefore belongs to one synchronization domain; its synchronized counterpart pays for sharing.
 #Remove Allocations Before Optimizing ThemChanging the global allocator is not the first optimization. Start with the ownership graph:
 use values or contiguous containers instead of separately allocated nodes when stable addresses are unnecessary; call reserve when a defensible upper bound is known; reuse buffers across iterations; store variable-sized payloads in one backing region plus offsets; batch objects with the same lifetime; avoid hidden allocation in formatting, callbacks, and temporary strings.  These changes reduce allocator work and improve cache and TLB locality. Replacing one general-purpose allocator with another may help a particular workload, but there is no universal winner: request-size distribution, thread handoff, lifetime mixing, and acceptable resident memory all affect the result.
Measure allocation count, requested and retained bytes, size distribution, lifetime, and the threads that allocate and free. Then measure the surrounding operation. A pool that makes allocate faster can still lose overall by increasing cache misses or keeping too many pages resident.
 #Safety Is Part of PerformanceAllocator mistakes frequently survive a benchmark and fail under a different schedule or input. A safe implementation needs explicit answers to several questions:
 Is count * element_size checked for integer overflow before requesting storage? Who owns each object, and can every error path release it exactly once? Are size, alignment, and allocation/deallocation APIs matched? Are destructors run before an arena is reset? Can another thread still read an object when its storage is recycled? Does an out-of-memory result propagate without using a null or half-constructed object?  Concurrent memory reclamation is a separate problem from concurrent allocation. Removing a node from a concurrent structure can be lock-free, but recycling its storage while another reader still holds its address is a use-after-free. Hazard pointers, epochs, reference counting, or a lock are possible reclamation protocols; a faster free call is not one.
Use sanitizers in tests. Clang’s AddressSanitizer documentation covers heap use-after-free, buffer bounds, and allocation/deallocation mismatches. Fuzz allocation failure and unusually large sizes as well as the normal path. Custom allocator code sits underneath much of the program, so one unchecked offset can turn into corruption far from its origin.
 #Pages Are the Final UnitAt the bottom of the stack, an allocator obtains and releases virtual address ranges in pages. Physical memory is commonly committed lazily when those pages are first written, as described in the virtual memory section. This is why virtual size can greatly exceed resident size without being a leak.
It is also why page-level behavior belongs in allocator benchmarks. Touching one byte in every page incurs page faults and translation entries; walking compactly through the same number of bytes may not. Huge pages can reduce TLB pressure but increase the amount of memory stranded by partial use. Purging pages lowers resident memory but may trade future reuse for new faults.
Memory management is therefore a layout problem, a lifetime problem, and a concurrency problem before it is an API problem. General-purpose allocators are sophisticated compromises. Use them by default, remove avoidable allocation at the caller, and specialize only when a measured lifetime pattern gives the specialized allocator a simpler contract.
title: Memory Management

content:
Converting an integer to decimal looks like parsing played backwards. At the level of arithmetic it almost is; at the level of performance it is not.
While parsing, the next digit arrives in the order in which Horner’s rule needs it. While formatting, the easiest operation gives us the digits in reverse order:
$$ d = x \bmod 10, \qquad x \leftarrow \left\lfloor x / 10 \right\rfloor. $$
The last decimal digit appears first, so we either write backwards into a temporary buffer or discover the digit count in advance. Division is also more expensive than multiplication. Finally, once conversion becomes fast, emitting many tiny strings can cost more than producing them.
As in Reading Decimal Integers, we will keep two layers separate:
 conversion turns one integer into a byte range; buffering combines many ranges into large writes.  This separation gives us a useful reference implementation and prevents a faster output buffer from being mistaken for a faster conversion algorithm.
 #Start with to_charsFor ordinary C++ code, the first choice should be std::to_chars:
