#include <charconv> char buffer[21]; auto [end, error] = std::to_chars(buffer, buffer + sizeof buffer, value); The integer overload is locale-independent, performs no allocation, writes no terminating zero, and reports a buffer that is too small. A signed 64-bit decimal representation needs at most 21 bytes: 20 digits and a minus sign.
These details are more than interface niceties. Locale-aware functions may need grouping and formatting state, returning a std::string allocates for sufficiently large output, and a terminating zero is wasted work when the result is immediately appended to another buffer. A range-returning primitive composes naturally with all of these uses.
We will nevertheless implement the conversion, both to understand it and to establish a reference for more specialized paths.
 #Writing BackwardsThe simplest formatter repeatedly divides by ten and writes the remainders from right to left:
#include <algorithm>#include <cstdint> // The caller provides space for at least 21 bytes. // The returned pointer is one past the last written byte. char *write_i64(char *output, std::int64_t value) { char temporary[21]; char *end = temporary + sizeof temporary; char *p = end; bool negative = value < 0; std::uint64_t x = std::uint64_t(value); if (negative) x = std::uint64_t(0) - x; do { std::uint64_t quotient = x / 10; unsigned remainder = unsigned(x - quotient * 10); *--p = char('0' + remainder); x = quotient; } while (x != 0); if (negative) *--p = '-'; return std::copy(p, end, output); } The unsigned subtraction used for negative values deserves attention. Converting a negative signed integer to uint64_t is well-defined modulo $2^{64}$; subtracting that result from zero produces its magnitude. This works for INT64_MIN, while -value in the signed type would overflow.
Zero is handled by the do loop. The function writes no terminator because the returned range already describes the result. If the caller cannot guarantee 21 writable bytes, the function needs last as another argument and must report insufficient space before writing anything.
On an optimizing compiler, division by the constant 10 is normally not an integer div instruction. It is transformed into multiplication by a precomputed reciprocal followed by shifts and corrections. The general method is developed in Granlund and Montgomery’s primary paper, Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication. Writing the division as / 10 gives the optimizer more freedom than copying one machine-specific magic constant from an assembly listing.
The loop still has a dependency chain: the next quotient needs the previous quotient. We can reduce its length by producing more than one digit per iteration.
 #Two Digits per DivisionThere are only one hundred two-digit strings. A 200-byte table is small enough to stay hot, and dividing by 100 halves the number of loop iterations:
#include <algorithm>#include <cstdint>#include <cstring> constexpr char digit_pairs[] = "00010203040506070809" "10111213141516171819" "20212223242526272829" "30313233343536373839" "40414243444546474849" "50515253545556575859" "60616263646566676869" "70717273747576777879" "80818283848586878889" "90919293949596979899"; char *write_i64_pairs(char *output, std::int64_t value) { char temporary[21]; char *end = temporary + sizeof temporary; char *p = end; bool negative = value < 0; std::uint64_t x = std::uint64_t(value); if (negative) x = std::uint64_t(0) - x; while (x >= 100) { std::uint64_t quotient = x / 100; unsigned remainder = unsigned(x - quotient * 100); p -= 2; std::memcpy(p, digit_pairs + 2 * remainder, 2); x = quotient; } if (x < 10) { *--p = char('0' + x); } else { p -= 2; std::memcpy(p, digit_pairs + 2 * unsigned(x), 2); } if (negative) *--p = '-'; return std::copy(p, end, output); } The final branch is what suppresses a leading zero for one-digit values. All earlier groups must contain exactly two digits, including groups such as 03, so table lookup is convenient.
This routine is small, portable, and usually a strong baseline. It also illustrates an important property of lookup tables: their cost is not just the number of loads. A table may remove arithmetic but introduce an extra dependency and consume cache capacity. Two hundred bytes is benign; tables indexed by large chunks of the input may not be.
 #Larger chunksWe can split a number in base $10^4$ or $10^8$, format the most significant chunk without padding, and write every later chunk at a fixed width. This decreases the number of dependent divisions further and exposes independent work inside a chunk.
For example, after
$$ x = q \cdot 10^8 + r, $$
the lower eight digits can be produced as four table lookups. Leading zeroes are required in that lower chunk, which removes length-dependent branches. The upper chunk is handled in the same fashion until the first nonzero group.
Constant divisors again become reciprocal multiplications, but the details vary with integer width and target ISA. The useful abstraction is not the magic multiplier; it is the decomposition into a short serial chain of large quotients followed by independent fixed-width conversion.
 #Counting Digits without Floating PointAnother family of formatters writes forward. It first computes the number of decimal digits, reserves that range, and fills it from the end. The tempting implementation is floor(log10(x)) + 1, but floating-point rounding near powers of ten makes it a poor correctness primitive.
A robust method uses the binary length as an estimate and corrects it with a table of powers of ten. For 64-bit values there are only twenty thresholds:
constexpr std::uint64_t powers_of_10[] = { 1ULL, 10ULL, 100ULL, 1000ULL, 10000ULL, 100000ULL, 1000000ULL, 10000000ULL, 100000000ULL, 1000000000ULL, 10000000000ULL, 100000000000ULL, 1000000000000ULL, 10000000000000ULL, 100000000000000ULL, 1000000000000000ULL, 10000000000000000ULL, 100000000000000000ULL, 1000000000000000000ULL, 10000000000000000000ULL }; A branch tree, lower_bound, or a bit-length-to-estimate table plus one comparison can select the digit count. Which version wins depends on the input distribution. Uniform 64-bit values are mostly 19 or 20 digits; counters and database identifiers often occupy a much narrower range. Benchmark the distribution you have.
 #Buffering the OutputAfter conversion, writing each number separately can dominate the whole program. A system call has a fixed cost, and even a buffered library stream pays locking and bookkeeping for each invocation.
The standard pattern is a staging buffer:
#include <array>#include <cstdio>#include <stdexcept> class integer_writer { std::array<char, 64 * 1024> storage{}; char *cursor = storage.data(); public: integer_writer() = default; integer_writer(const integer_writer &) = delete; integer_writer &operator=(const integer_writer &) = delete; void flush() { std::size_t n = std::size_t(cursor - storage.data()); if (n != 0 && std::fwrite(storage.data(), 1, n, stdout) != n) throw std::runtime_error("output error"); cursor = storage.data(); } void write(std::int64_t value) { // 21 bytes for the integer and one for the newline.  if (storage.data() + storage.size() - cursor < 22) flush(); cursor = write_i64_pairs(cursor, value); *cursor++ = '\n'; } ~integer_writer() { // Real code should call flush explicitly so that errors can be handled;  // destructors must not let an exception escape.  if (cursor != storage.data()) std::fwrite(storage.data(), 1, std::size_t(cursor - storage.data()), stdout); } }; This example uses fwrite, which may itself be buffered. That is harmless, although writing directly to a file descriptor and handling partial write calls is another reasonable design. For a socket, backpressure and interruption are part of the contract; a short write is not success.
The staging buffer also gives conversion routines a useful guarantee: enough contiguous space is available for their worst-case output. That removes a capacity branch from the middle of the digit loop.
 #Why SIMD Is Harder HereSIMD arithmetic can convert several integers in parallel, but their decimal strings have different lengths. Even after the digits have been computed, they must be packed into a contiguous byte stream. This variable-position store is often the awkward part.
There are three favorable cases:
 fixed-width fields: timestamps, zero-padded identifiers, and protocol fields have predetermined destinations; batched homogeneous values: if most numbers have the same digit count, vectors can share a formatting path and their outputs can be compacted predictably; large chunks: within an eight-digit chunk, multiply-add and shuffle instructions can combine or expand fixed groups in parallel.  For mixed 64-bit values, a scalar two-digit table can remain competitive because it does little setup and stores exactly the required bytes. Recent primary work on SIMD integer-to-decimal conversion uses parallel multiply-add operations and variants adapted to homogeneous and heterogeneous digit lengths; it is a useful demonstration that the arithmetic can be vectorized, not a reason to assume every output pipeline benefits equally.
AVX-512 compress stores and wider shuffles change the packing tradeoff, while ARM and older x86 targets offer different building blocks. A production implementation should therefore dispatch by ISA or rely on a well-tested conversion library, rather than exposing a single intrinsic sequence as a portable algorithm.
 #Measuring Integer OutputA conversion benchmark should write into memory and consume the resulting length and bytes. An output benchmark should include the final sink. These are different measurements.
Record at least:
 signedness and the distribution of decimal lengths; whether delimiters and signs are included in the byte count; whether output stays in cache, goes to /dev/null, or reaches storage/network; buffer size and flush policy; compiler, flags, standard library, CPU, and ISA target; both integers per second and bytes per second.  Avoid a checksum that can be computed directly from the input without materializing the formatted bytes: an optimizer may notice more than expected. A robust test compares the produced range byte-for-byte with std::to_chars across boundary values and randomized inputs.
The historical companion directory for this chapter explored quotient decomposition, precomputed tables, and AVX2 gathers on Zen 2. Those programs compute a synthetic checksum instead of emitting decimal strings and assume mapped, aligned binary input. They are useful sketches for studying dependencies, but they do not by themselves establish a formatter’s end-to-end throughput.
 #ChecklistFor most programs, the practical route is short:
 use std::to_chars into caller-owned storage; batch many results before calling the operating system; if conversion is still hot, try a two-digit table or a proven library implementation; specialize fixed-width chunks before attempting general variable-width SIMD; test zero, INT64_MIN, INT64_MAX, every power-of-ten boundary, and insufficient output space; measure conversion and I/O independently, then measure them together.  Integer formatting rewards simple machinery. Once division by a constant has become multiplication, the remaining bottleneck is often not arithmetic at all—it is deciding where the bytes go.
title: Writing Decimal Integers

content:
Data structures expose more performance dimensions than a single batch algorithm. A layout can improve lookup throughput while increasing update latency, memory use, preprocessing time, or contention. Even the same operation changes character when queries are independent, dependency-chained, skewed toward hot keys, or mixed with updates.
The case studies in this chapter keep those trade-offs explicit:
 Binary Search establishes half-open search contracts and compares sorted and Eytzinger layouts. Static B-Trees widen search nodes and separate record storage from navigation. Search Trees add ownership, occupancy, duplicates, and insertion to a B+ layout. Segment Trees compare binary, Fenwick, and wide layouts for dynamic range sums.  Correctness comes first: empty structures, past-the-end answers, duplicate keys, partial levels, legal extreme values, and arithmetic bounds are part of each interface. Performance comparisons then report the workload, query mix, memory footprint, target ISA, and whether the measurement is latency or reciprocal throughput.
A review of the CPU cache system, branching, and benchmark noise is useful before reading the implementation sections.
title: Data Structures Case Studies

content:
Integer conversion is mostly arithmetic in base ten. Floating-point conversion is arithmetic plus a proof.
Consider the text 0.1. Its value is exactly $1/10$, but no finite binary fraction equals $1/10$. A parser must choose the nearest representable binary value. A formatter then faces the reverse problem: it should print enough decimal digits to identify that value, but usually no more than necessary. Both directions must make the same choice at boundaries where two floating-point numbers are almost equally close.
This chapter is about optimizing the conversion pipeline without weakening that contract.
 #What Does “Correct” Mean?A floating-point input grammar may contain a sign, integer and fractional digits, a decimal exponent, and special values such as infinity and NaN. The numerical part can be written as
$$ (-1)^s M\cdot10^e, $$
where $M$ is an integer assembled from the digits and $e$ accounts for both the decimal point and the explicit exponent.
Parsing normally promises correct rounding: return the representable value nearest to the exact real number under the specified rounding rule. This includes subnormal values, overflow, underflow, and decimals lying extremely close to a midpoint.
For output, three contracts are common:
 fixed precision: print a requested number of digits after the decimal point; significant digits: print a requested number of meaningful digits; shortest round trip: print the shortest decimal that parses back to the original binary value.  These are different problems. Six digits after the point is not sufficient for every float, and seventeen significant digits are sufficient to round-trip every double but are often not shortest.
The constants in std::numeric_limits describe the distinction:
#include <limits> static_assert(std::numeric_limits<float>::max_digits10 == 9); static_assert(std::numeric_limits<double>::max_digits10 == 17); max_digits10 is a sufficient number of significant decimal digits for binary-to-decimal-to-binary round trips. It is not a buffer size and not a claim that every shortest representation has that many digits.
 #Why the Naive Parser FailsA tempting parser accumulates a double, divides by a power of ten for the fractional part, and calls pow(10, exponent). It has three problems.
First, it rounds after nearly every digit, so the final error is not necessarily the correctly rounded value of the original decimal. Second, pow is a general transcendental routine doing far more work than a bounded integer exponent requires. Third, long inputs overflow the accumulator or discard digits without tracking whether the discarded suffix changes the rounding direction.
A sound design separates syntax from conversion:
 scan characters and record sign, significant digits, and decimal exponent; keep as many leading digits as fit in a machine integer and remember whether discarded digits were nonzero; convert the integer significand times a power of ten to binary; detect ambiguous cases and use an exact fallback.  Most real-world inputs contain at most 19 significant digits and moderate exponents. Fast parsers exploit this common case with precomputed powers of five and wide integer multiplication. Since
$$ 10^e=2^e5^e, $$
the power of two mainly adjusts the binary exponent, while multiplication or division by a cached power of five determines the significand bits. A high-half product provides the leading bits without constructing an arbitrary-precision integer.
The difficult part is not producing a nearby answer; it is proving when those leading bits determine the unique correctly rounded answer. Eisel–Lemire-style algorithms make this fast path explicit and fall back for truncated, extreme, or midpoint-adjacent inputs. The fallback is rare, but deleting it changes the function’s contract.
 #Use the Narrowest Standard InterfaceFor locale-independent conversion in modern C++, std::from_chars avoids allocation and null-terminated strings. It returns both an error code and the first unconsumed character:
#include <charconv>#include <optional>#include <string_view>#include <system_error> std::optional<double> parse_double(std::string_view text) { double value; const char* first = text.data(); const char* last = first + text.size(); auto [end, error] = std::from_chars( first, last, value, std::chars_format::general ); if (error != std::errc{} || end != last) return std::nullopt; return value; } Checking end is essential. Without it, "1.25ms" is accepted as the valid prefix 1.25. Whether whitespace, a leading plus sign, hexadecimal notation, or NaN belongs to the language is a protocol decision; the from_chars grammar is intentionally narrower than some C library functions.
std::to_chars provides the matching allocation-free output path. With no precision argument, the general format chooses a shortest representation that round-trips through the corresponding parser:
#include <array>#include <charconv>#include <stdexcept>#include <string> std::string format_double(double value) { std::array<char, 64> buffer; auto [end, error] = std::to_chars( buffer.data(), buffer.data() + buffer.size(), value, std::chars_format::general ); if (error != std::errc{}) throw std::runtime_error("floating-point buffer too small"); return std::string(buffer.data(), end); } The 64-byte buffer is an interface bound chosen for the supported format, not max_digits10. Production code should make that bound a documented invariant or retry with a larger buffer.
from_chars and to_chars remove locale state, allocation, and formatted-stream machinery. They do not guarantee that every standard-library implementation uses the same internal algorithm or has the same throughput. Check the library version along with the compiler when benchmarking.
 #Finding the Shortest DecimalEvery finite binary value owns an interval of real numbers that round to it. For a normal value $v$, the interval boundaries lie near the midpoints between $v$ and its predecessor and successor. A shortest formatter seeks the decimal with the fewest significant digits that lies inside this interval and resolves inclusivity according to the rounding rule.
Older algorithms generated digits while repeatedly testing these boundaries, sometimes using multiprecision arithmetic. Ryu and Dragonbox changed the cost model by reducing the problem to fixed-width integer arithmetic and tables of powers. They compute scaled interval bounds, generate decimal digits, and stop as soon as one candidate uniquely identifies the original binary value.
This is why “printing the stored mantissa” is the wrong mental model. The stored significand is binary. Decimal output is a search for a short name whose rounding interval contains that binary number.
For a requested fixed precision, the objective changes. The formatter must round to a decimal place even when that representation does not round-trip. Financial code should also ask whether binary floating point is the correct representation at all; a scaled integer or decimal type may express the contract more directly.
 #The Batch Is Larger Than the NumberOnce the conversion kernel is fast, surrounding work becomes visible:
 locating token boundaries; validating separators and protocol grammar; copying substrings into temporary buffers; allocating one string per output value; issuing small reads or writes; reporting the position of malformed input.  Keep input in a contiguous buffer and pass pointer ranges or string_views into the converter. Append output into a reusable buffer and flush it in large blocks. Do not copy a token merely to add a terminating zero for an API that accepts a range.
SIMD can help find structural characters and classify bytes across several candidate numbers at once. The numeric conversion itself is harder to vectorize because token lengths, exponents, and fallback conditions diverge. Parsers such as simdjson use SIMD heavily for document structure while retaining carefully designed scalar number conversion. Parallelism should follow the shape of the work rather than the label “parser.”
 #Testing the CornersRandom human-readable decimals exercise the common path but barely touch the rounding boundaries. A useful differential suite includes:
 zero and negative zero; the smallest subnormal, largest subnormal, smallest normal, and largest finite value; neighboring values around powers of two and ten; decimals exactly at and immediately around rounding midpoints; very long digit strings with sticky nonzero suffixes; exponent overflow and underflow; malformed signs, decimal points, exponents, and trailing characters; every special value the chosen grammar claims to support.  For formatting, generate floating-point values by randomizing their bit patterns, format them, parse the result, and compare bits for every finite value. Also compare against a trusted implementation, because a formatter and parser sharing the same bug can round-trip each other’s mistakes.
Benchmark several corpora separately: short telemetry values, fixed-precision financial-like records, uniformly distributed bit patterns, and known hard cases. Average token length and fallback rate belong next to throughput results.
 #Choosing an ImplementationUse the standard charconv interface when its performance and platform support meet the requirement. It gives the optimizer a small, locale-independent boundary and keeps application code independent of the conversion algorithm.
When conversion dominates a measured workload, use a reviewed implementation with an explicit correctness claim. Fast_float implements Eisel–Lemire parsing with fallbacks; Ryu and Dragonbox implement shortest formatting. Integrating one of them is safer than reproducing its tables and boundary proof inside an application.
The deeper optimization lesson is the same as in integer conversion: separate the common representable case from the rare case that needs more machinery, but never confuse “rare” with “impossible.” The slow path is part of the proof.
 #Further Reading Ulf Adams, Ryu: Fast Float-to-String Conversion, derives a fixed-width shortest formatter. Daniel Lemire, Number Parsing at a Gigabyte per Second, develops the Eisel–Lemire fast path and its ambiguity checks. The WG21 charconv proposal specifies the allocation-free C++ interface and its round-trip goals. William Clinger, How to Read Floating Point Numbers Accurately, explains why exact fallback cases exist.
title: Reading and Writing Floating-Point Numbers

content:
Finding a byte in memory is a reduction: compare many positions and return the first match. Finding a string is a filtering problem: reject almost every position cheaply, then verify the survivors.
That distinction matters more than the catalog of classical algorithms. On ordinary text, a two-byte filter may eliminate hundreds of candidates with a few vector instructions. On repetitive input, the same filter may accept every position, and only a worst-case linear algorithm prevents quadratic behavior.
 #The ContractLet the haystack contain $n$ bytes and the needle contain $m$ bytes. We return the smallest $i$ such that
$$ \mathtt{haystack}[i..i+m)=\mathtt{needle}[0..m), $$
or report no match. By the convention used by std::string_view::find, the empty needle matches at position zero.
This chapter searches bytes. UTF-8 code points, canonical equivalence, case folding, and locale-aware matching are different contracts. A byte search can locate an ASCII delimiter in UTF-8 safely, but it does not implement a general Unicode search.
The reference implementation is deliberately boring:
#include <cstring>#include <string_view> std::size_t find_naive(std::string_view text, std::string_view pattern) { if (pattern.empty()) return 0; if (pattern.size() > text.size()) return std::string_view::npos; const std::size_t candidates = text.size() - pattern.size() + 1; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < candidates; ++i) if (std::memcmp(text.data() + i, pattern.data(), pattern.size()) == 0) return i; return std::string_view::npos; } Its worst case is $O(nm)$: searching for aaaaab in a long run of a rechecks nearly the entire prefix at each position. For many real inputs, however, memcmp rejects on the first byte and the constant is small. A better implementation should preserve that common-case economy without inheriting the worst case.
 #What the Classical Algorithms BuyKnuth–Morris–Pratt preprocesses the needle’s borders and never moves backward in the text, guaranteeing $O(n+m)$ comparisons. Its inner loop follows failure links, which can be branchy and dependent.
Boyer–Moore compares from the end and uses mismatches to skip candidate positions. Horspool’s simplified bad-character table is often effective for medium or long needles over a large alphabet. Its best cases inspect much less than $n$ text, but the skip behavior depends on the input and variant.
The Two-Way algorithm factors the needle around a critical position and combines forward comparisons with periodicity information. It uses constant auxiliary space and guarantees linear time. Variants of it are used in production C libraries because they handle both random and periodic strings without a large preprocessing table.
No asymptotic theorem selects one winner for every $m$. Implementations normally dispatch: an empty or one-byte needle has a specialized path, short needles use compact filters, and longer or adversarial searches use a linear-time core.
 #Filtering Candidate Starts with AVX2For a match of length $m\ge2$, both the first and last bytes must agree:
$$ T[i]=P[0] \quad\text{and}\quad T[i+m-1]=P[m-1]. $$
AVX2 can test 32 starting positions at once. The following function never loads beyond the haystack: the vector loop runs only when all 32 candidate starts—and therefore both 32-byte loads—are valid.
#include <bit>#include <cstdint>#include <cstring>#include <immintrin.h>#include <string_view> std::size_t find_avx2(std::string_view text, std::string_view pattern) { const std::size_t n = text.size(); const std::size_t m = pattern.size(); if (m == 0) return 0; if (m > n) return std::string_view::npos; if (m == 1) { const void* p = std::memchr(text.data(), static_cast<unsigned char>(pattern[0]), n); return p ? std::size_t(static_cast<const char*>(p) - text.data()) : std::string_view::npos; } const std::size_t candidates = n - m + 1; const __m256i first = _mm256_set1_epi8(pattern.front()); const __m256i last = _mm256_set1_epi8(pattern.back()); std::size_t i = 0; for (; i + 32 <= candidates; i += 32) { const __m256i a = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i*>(text.data() + i)); const __m256i b = _mm256_loadu_si256( reinterpret_cast<const __m256i*>(text.data() + i + m - 1)); uint32_t mask = uint32_t(_mm256_movemask_epi8( _mm256_and_si256(_mm256_cmpeq_epi8(a, first), _mm256_cmpeq_epi8(b, last)))); while (mask != 0) { unsigned bit = unsigned(std::countr_zero(mask)); std::size_t candidate = i + bit; if (std::memcmp(text.data() + candidate, pattern.data(), m) == 0) return candidate; mask &= mask - 1; } } for (; i < candidates; ++i) if (text[i] == pattern.front() && text[i + m - 1] == pattern.back() && std::memcmp(text.data() + i, pattern.data(), m) == 0) return i; return std::string_view::npos; } Compile this function only for an AVX2 target and dispatch to a scalar implementation on unsupported CPUs. Loading through an intrinsic pointer is the interface expected by x86 compilers, but it does not make overreading an allocation legal; the loop bound is what provides safety.
For independent uniformly distributed bytes, a first-byte filter accepts about $1/256$ of positions and two independent byte tests about $1/65536$. Natural language is neither uniform nor independent, but the reduction is often still dramatic. When the needle begins and ends with common bytes, selecting two rare internal bytes can improve the filter. Their offsets must then be included in the second load and in the bounds proof.
Repetitive data is the failure mode. Searching for aaaaaaaaab in aaaa... makes the first-byte test useless and the last-byte test decisive; searching for an all-a pattern makes both useless and calls memcmp at every position. A production search can count failed verifications and switch to Two-Way after the filter stops being selective.
 #Why memchr Deserves Its Own PathThe one-byte case has no verification step and no preprocessing. Standard C libraries provide highly tuned memchr implementations with architecture dispatch, vector loops, safe page-boundary handling, and small-input paths. Replacing them with a hand-written AVX2 loop is unlikely to improve a whole program and may lose portability.
The same idea extends to two- and three-byte needles: compact specialized loops can avoid a general algorithm’s setup. Dispatch itself has a cost, so the length thresholds should be measured on the target library and workload.
 #Hashes and Multiple PatternsRabin–Karp computes a rolling fingerprint for each $m$-byte window and verifies positions whose fingerprint matches the needle. It is useful when many windows share work or when several needles use the same hash machinery. A hash match is not normally proof of equality; verification preserves exact semantics. Adversarial inputs also require a keyed or otherwise robust strategy if collision-driven worst cases are a security concern.
Searching for hundreds of patterns independently wastes text bandwidth. Aho–Corasick builds an automaton that advances all prefix states in one pass and reports every matched pattern. High-performance regular-expression engines go further, combining literal filters, finite automata, and SIMD. The optimization unit is the entire pattern set, not one call to find.
 #Benchmarking SearchSearch time depends on more than $(n,m)$. Record at least:
 whether a match exists and where the first match occurs; needle length and periodicity; alphabet size and byte distribution; the number of false candidates reaching verification; whether preprocessing is amortized over one or many haystacks; cache state and total bytes read.  A benchmark containing only absent random needles measures the filter’s happiest path. Add matches at the beginning and end, one-byte needles, long common prefixes, low-alphabet data, and periodic adversarial cases.
Differential testing is straightforward: compare every result with std::string_view::find over randomized byte strings, then enumerate all short strings over a two- or three-symbol alphabet. Small exhaustive tests are particularly good at finding tail errors and empty-pattern disagreements. Run AddressSanitizer as well; a vector search can return correct answers for years while still reading one byte beyond an allocation.
 #A Practical DispatchA robust exact search commonly looks like this:
 handle empty, oversized, and one-byte needles; use a compact SIMD or word-at-a-time filter for short and medium needles; verify candidate positions with a tuned equality routine; fall back to a worst-case linear algorithm when periodicity or excessive candidates make filtering ineffective; use a multi-pattern algorithm when the query set, rather than one needle, is reused.  The fastest comparison is the one not performed. SIMD wins here by rejecting candidate positions, while linear-time string algorithms win by proving which positions can be skipped. Good library implementations use both arguments.
 #Further Reading Boyer and Moore’s original string-search paper develops right-to-left matching and skip tables. Crochemore and Perrin, Two-Way String-Matching, gives the constant-space linear algorithm. The GNU C Library strstr source shows a production dispatch with short-needle and linear-time paths. The Hyperscan paper describes SIMD-aware matching for large pattern sets.
title: String Searching

content:
“How fast can we sort?” is not one question. It is a suitcase full of them.
Are the keys arbitrary objects or fixed-width integers? Are comparisons cheap? Must equal keys retain their input order? May the algorithm allocate another array? Is the input random, nearly sorted, reverse sorted, or mostly duplicates? A sorting benchmark that omits these details measures a workload no one can reproduce.
This case study develops two deliberately different algorithms:
 an unstable comparison sort with $O(n\log n)$ worst-case complexity; a stable four-pass radix sort specialized for 32-bit unsigned keys.  The point is not to replace a mature standard library with two pages of code. It is to expose the choices a production implementation has to make—and to build references sturdy enough for honest experiments.
 #The Ordering ContractA comparison function used for sorting must define a strict weak ordering. Informally:
 nothing is less than itself; if $a<b$ and $b<c$, then $a<c$; if neither of two values is less than the other, they are equivalent, and this equivalence behaves transitively.  a <= b is not a valid comparator. Neither is an ordinary floating-point < over a domain containing NaNs: the induced “equivalence” is not transitive. A broken comparator does not merely choose a strange order; it violates the sorting algorithm’s precondition.
Two equivalent elements need not be equal. Records can compare only by surname, timestamp, or bucket number while carrying different payloads. This is where stability matters:
input: (key 2, Alice), (key 1, Bob), (key 2, Carol) stable: (key 1, Bob), (key 2, Alice), (key 2, Carol) An unstable sort may exchange Alice and Carol. std::sort is unstable; std::stable_sort preserves their relative order. Stability is a semantic requirement, not a performance adjective.
 #Comparison Sorting Has a FloorA comparison gives at most two outcomes. Distinguishing all $n!$ possible input permutations therefore requires a decision tree of height at least
$$ \lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil=n\log_2n-O(n) $$
in the worst case. Clever instructions can reduce time per comparison, but no comparison sort escapes the $\Omega(n\log n)$ bound on arbitrary distinct keys.
Quicksort is attractive because partitioning is sequential and cache-friendly. Its unprotected worst case is quadratic. Heapsort guarantees $O(n\log n)$ and uses constant auxiliary storage, but its access pattern and comparison count are often less friendly. Insertion sort is quadratic, yet excellent on tiny ranges because its loop is small and nearby elements are already hot.
Introsort combines all three: partition like quicksort, switch to heapsort if partitioning becomes suspiciously deep, and finish small ranges with insertion sort.
 #An Executable IntrosortThe implementation below is intentionally conventional rather than record-seeking. It accepts random-access iterators, a strict weak comparator, and copy-constructible values. The copy requirement keeps the pivot independent while elements are exchanged; industrial implementations do more work to support move-only types efficiently.
#include <algorithm>#include <concepts>#include <cstddef>#include <functional>#include <iterator>#include <utility> template<std::random_access_iterator Iterator, class Compare> void insertion_sort(Iterator first, Iterator last, Compare &compare) { for (Iterator current = first; current != last; ++current) { std::iter_value_t<Iterator> value(std::move(*current)); Iterator hole = current; while (hole != first && compare(value, *(hole - 1))) { *hole = std::move(*(hole - 1)); --hole; } *hole = std::move(value); } } template<std::random_access_iterator Iterator, class Compare> std::pair<Iterator, Iterator> partition_three_way(Iterator first, Iterator last, Compare &compare) { using value_type = std::iter_value_t<Iterator>; const value_type pivot = *(first + (last - first) / 2); Iterator lower = first; Iterator current = first; Iterator upper = last; while (current != upper) { if (compare(*current, pivot)) { std::iter_swap(lower, current); ++lower; ++current; } else if (compare(pivot, *current)) { --upper; std::iter_swap(current, upper); } else { ++current; } } return {lower, upper}; // [lower, upper) is equivalent to pivot } template<std::random_access_iterator Iterator, class Compare> void introsort_loop(Iterator first, Iterator last, unsigned depth, Compare &compare) { constexpr std::iter_difference_t<Iterator> insertion_cutoff = 24; while (last - first > insertion_cutoff) { if (depth == 0) { std::make_heap(first, last, compare); std::sort_heap(first, last, compare); return; } --depth; auto [lower, upper] = partition_three_way(first, last, compare); // Recurse into the smaller side and loop over the larger one.  // This bounds stack depth independently of pivot quality.  if (lower - first < last - upper) { introsort_loop(first, lower, depth, compare); first = upper; } else { introsort_loop(upper, last, depth, compare); last = lower; } } insertion_sort(first, last, compare); } template<std::random_access_iterator Iterator, class Compare = std::less<>> requires std::sortable<Iterator, Compare> && std::copy_constructible<std::iter_value_t<Iterator>> void introsort(Iterator first, Iterator last, Compare compare = {}) { const std::size_t length = static_cast<std::size_t>(last - first); if (length < 2) return; unsigned floor_log2 = 0; for (std::size_t x = length; x > 1; x >>= 1) ++floor_log2; introsort_loop(first, last, 2 * floor_log2, compare); } The three-way partition establishes
[ first, lower ) < pivot [ lower, upper ) == pivot under the comparator [ upper, last ) > pivot and is especially important for duplicate-heavy input. A two-way partition can repeatedly recurse over values equal to the pivot; this one removes the entire equal region at once.
After twice the floor of $\log_2 n$ partition levels, the routine stops trusting its pivots and heap-sorts the remaining range. That gives the $O(n\log n)$ worst-case bound. Recursing only into the smaller outer partition keeps stack usage $O(\log n)$; the larger partition is processed by the surrounding loop.
This sort is not stable. The partition swaps equivalent records without preserving their order. Making the insertion-sort base case stable does not repair the swaps that happened above it.
 #What this implementation does not claimThe middle element is a simple pivot, not necessarily the best pivot. Production sorts use sampling, pattern detection, carefully tuned partition loops, and type-specific optimizations. The cutoff 24 is a parameter, not a constant of nature. std::sort should remain the first baseline, and the C++ standard specifies its complexity and result—not one mandatory internal algorithm.
 #Branches, Moves, and RepresentationsPartitioning has at least three potential costs:
 comparisons, which may be a single integer instruction or an expensive function; unpredictable branches, especially on mixed random keys; moving records, which may copy four bytes or relocate a large object.  Optimizing one can worsen another. A branchless partition often writes every element to temporary buffers; that is attractive for small keys and less attractive for large records. Sorting pointers or compact indices reduces movement, but the later indirection can destroy locality. Caching an expensive derived key may save comparisons while increasing memory traffic.
This is why “comparisons per second” and “elements per second” are both incomplete metrics. Record the number and size of moves, key extraction cost, allocated bytes, and where the sorted representation will be consumed next.
 #Escaping the Comparison BoundFixed-width integer keys reveal more information than one comparison bit. A radix sort can inspect one digit of every key, group equal digits, and repeat. For 32-bit keys and 8-bit digits, there are exactly four passes and 256 counters per pass.
The following least-significant-digit (LSD) sort is stable and accepts every span length. It uses one auxiliary array of $n$ words.
#include <algorithm>#include <array>#include <cstddef>#include <cstdint>#include <span>#include <utility>#include <vector> void radix_sort_u32(std::span<std::uint32_t> values) { if (values.size() < 2) return; std::vector<std::uint32_t> scratch(values.size()); std::uint32_t *source = values.data(); std::uint32_t *destination = scratch.data(); for (unsigned shift = 0; shift < 32; shift += 8) { std::array<std::size_t, 256> count{}; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < values.size(); ++i) ++count[(source[i] >> shift) & 0xffu]; std::array<std::size_t, 256> position{}; std::size_t total = 0; for (std::size_t digit = 0; digit < count.size(); ++digit) { position[digit] = total; total += count[digit]; } // Forward traversal plus monotonically increasing positions makes  // this distribution stable.  for (std::size_t i = 0; i < values.size(); ++i) { const unsigned digit = (source[i] >> shift) & 0xffu; destination[position[digit]++] = source[i]; } std::swap(source, destination); } // Four passes are even, so source normally points back to values.  // Keep the copy for robustness if the digit schedule is later changed.  if (source != values.data()) std::copy_n(source, values.size(), values.data()); } Why must every pass be stable? After the first pass, values are ordered by bits 0–7. The second pass groups by bits 8–15 while retaining the earlier order inside each group, so they are ordered by bits 0–15. Induction extends this argument through all 32 bits. An unstable counting pass would discard the work of the lower digits.
For signed two’s-complement int32_t, use the transformed key
$$ k(x)=\operatorname{bits}(x)\mathbin{\mathtt{xor}}\mathtt{0x80000000}. $$
Flipping the sign bit maps INT_MIN to zero and preserves signed order over the remaining bit patterns. Apply this transformation only when selecting digits; keep the original record as the payload.
For records, distribute the entire record—or an index into a record array—according to its 32-bit key. The forward traversal preserves the input order of equal keys, so the same code structure gives a genuinely observable stable sort. Moving large records four times may dominate the key work, which is another reason to consider sorting indices.
 #The Radix Cost ModelThe four-pass routine performs $O(4n+4\cdot256)$ work, but asymptotic notation hides its main cost. Each pass reads and writes the entire array, for about 32 bytes of traffic per 32-bit value over four passes, before cache effects and write allocation. It also allocates another $4n$ bytes.
Comparison sorting is often better for tiny arrays, expensive-to-move records, generic comparators, or when allocation is forbidden. Radix sorting becomes attractive when keys are cheap fixed-width integers, arrays are large enough to amortize the histograms, and bandwidth can sustain the passes. Wider digits reduce passes but enlarge histograms; narrower digits do the opposite.
Signed integers are easy. Floating-point keys require a more careful monotone bit transform, including a policy for negative zero and NaNs. Strings need variable-length digit handling and have a cost proportional to inspected characters, not merely record count. “Radix sort” names a family, not one drop-in replacement for std::sort.
 #Stable Comparison SortingWhen keys are generic and equal records must retain order, use a stable comparison algorithm. Merge sort is the usual starting point: merge adjacent sorted runs into an auxiliary buffer, alternating source and destination until one run remains. It has predictable $O(n\log n)$ comparisons and sequential memory access, at the price of auxiliary storage and repeated record movement.
Adaptive stable sorts can exploit runs already present in the input. A production decision should compare against std::stable_sort on actual record types; reusing the unstable introsort above with a tie-breaking original index changes the key and movement cost, and is not equivalent to obtaining stability for free.
 #There Is No Historical Sorting Record HereThe original book contained only an empty sorting page. Its companion repository has an unfinished partition experiment: the scalar partition exists, while the advertised AVX path is a placeholder, and no complete sorting benchmark or validation harness is present. There is therefore no defensible “faster than std::sort” number to preserve.
This absence is useful. A partition microbenchmark does not measure pivot selection, recursion, equal-key handling, small-range cleanup, fallback behavior, or end-to-end movement. Publishing its best number as a sorting result would compare a part with a whole.
 #Benchmarking a SortGenerate input outside the timed region and restore it before every repetition. Sorting the same buffer repeatedly mostly measures the already-sorted case. Retain a checksum or consume the result so the optimizer cannot discard the call.
At minimum, test:
 uniform random keys over a wide domain; already sorted and reverse-sorted inputs; constant, binary, and few-unique keys; organ-pipe, sawtooth, and long-run patterns; nearly sorted data with controlled local disturbances; real key and record distributions from the application.  Sweep sizes across cache and memory boundaries. Report the compiler, flags, library, processor, record layout, key extractor, stability requirement, allocation policy, and whether input copying is included. Use time per element as the primary result, but also inspect comparisons, branches, cache misses, and bytes moved to explain it.
 #Correctness Before TimingFor scalar keys, differential testing is straightforward:
auto expected = input; auto actual = input; std::sort(expected.begin(), expected.end()); introsort(actual.begin(), actual.end()); assert(actual == expected); assert(std::is_sorted(actual.begin(), actual.end())); Run the same oracle for radix_sort_u32, including empty arrays, lengths around small-sort and radix boundaries, all bit patterns at the signed edges, duplicate-heavy inputs, and random full-width values. For custom comparators, verify permutation preservation separately because equivalent records may appear in different valid orders.
To test stability, attach each record’s original position, sort by key alone, and assert that positions increase within every equal-key group. To test generic introsort, include move-counting values, stateful comparators, and types whose values are much larger than their keys. Address and undefined-behavior sanitizers should be part of the differential suite.
Sorting rewards specialized engineering, but it punishes vague specifications. Decide what “ordered” and “equal” mean, decide whether equal records may move, and decide which key representation the algorithm is allowed to inspect. Only then does it make sense to count cycles.
 #Further Reading David Musser introduced the depth-limited hybrid in Introspective Sorting and Selection Algorithms. McIlroy, Bostic, and McIlroy discuss practical bytewise designs in Engineering Radix Sort. The C++ working draft specifies the contracts and complexity guarantees of sort and stable_sort.
title: Sorting

content:
Matrix multiplication is where several modest optimizations learn to cooperate. Change the loop order and memory becomes sequential. Block the loops and cache lines are reused. Keep a tile of the result in registers and loads are reused. Apply SIMD and one instruction updates eight cells. None of these ideas is sufficient alone; together they separate a textbook triple loop from a BLAS kernel.
They also create plenty of places to cheat accidentally. Square-only code hides dimension errors. A microkernel that assumes multiples of 16 has no tail. Aligned loads turn an allocation choice into an undocumented precondition. Counting one fused multiply-add as one FLOP understates both measured throughput and machine peak by a factor of two.
We will begin with a complete rectangular contract, build a reference implementation, and then optimize it without losing the awkward cases.
 #Dimensions and StorageLet $A$ be $M\times K$ and $B$ be $K\times N$. Their product $C=AB$ is $M\times N$:
$$ C_{ij}=\sum_{p=0}^{K-1}A_{ip}B_{pj}. $$
All matrices below are row-major. Their leading dimensions lda, ldb, and ldc are row strides measured in elements, not bytes:
A(i,p) = a[i * lda + p] B(p,j) = b[p * ldb + j] C(i,j) = c[i * ldc + j] A stride may exceed the logical width because rows are padded or are views into larger matrices. The operation overwrites the logical $M\times N$ region of C; it leaves row padding untouched. The spans for A, B, and C must not overlap. If aliasing is required, copy the overlapping input before calling the kernel.
Empty dimensions are well-defined. If $M=0$ or $N=0$, nothing is written. If $K=0$, every logical element of C is set to zero.
 #Validate the ViewPointer arithmetic is part of correctness. Before entering a hot loop, verify both the stride and the last address a logical matrix may use.
#include <cstddef>#include <limits>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> std::size_t matrix_extent(std::size_t rows, std::size_t columns, std::size_t stride) { if (rows == 0 || columns == 0) return 0; if (stride < columns) throw std::invalid_argument("matrix stride is smaller than width"); const std::size_t limit = std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max(); if (rows - 1 > (limit - columns) / stride) throw std::length_error("matrix extent overflows size_t"); return (rows - 1) * stride + columns; } void require_matrix(std::size_t available, std::size_t rows, std::size_t columns, std::size_t stride) { if (matrix_extent(rows, columns, stride) > available) throw std::out_of_range("matrix span is too short"); } The last logical row starts at (rows - 1) * stride; adding columns gives the one-past extent. Checking the multiplication before performing it prevents validation itself from overflowing.
 #A Numerical ReferenceThe reference accumulates each dot product in double and rounds once when storing a float. Products of two binary32 values are exactly representable in binary64, and the wider accumulator is much more accurate than the optimized binary32 kernel. It is deliberately a correctness oracle, not a performance baseline.
#include <cmath>#include <cstddef>#include <span> void matmul_reference(std::span<const float> a, std::span<const float> b, std::span<float> c, std::size_t m, std::size_t k, std::size_t n, std::size_t lda, std::size_t ldb, std::size_t ldc) { require_matrix(a.size(), m, k, lda); require_matrix(b.size(), k, n, ldb); require_matrix(c.size(), m, n, ldc); for (std::size_t i = 0; i < m; ++i) { for (std::size_t j = 0; j < n; ++j) { double sum = 0; for (std::size_t p = 0; p < k; ++p) { sum = std::fma(static_cast<double>(a[i * lda + p]), static_cast<double>(b[p * ldb + j]), sum); } c[i * ldc + j] = static_cast<float>(sum); } } } This also fixes a common initialization bug. A routine implementing C = A*B must overwrite or clear C; a loop containing only c[...] += ... instead implements C += A*B and depends on the caller’s previous contents.
 #Counting Work CorrectlyFor $K>0$, each output dot product performs $K$ multiplications and $K-1$ additions. The exact count is
$$ MN(2K-1). $$
Performance reports conventionally use $2MNK$, counting one multiply and one add per inner update. A fused multiply-add performs both operations with one instruction and is therefore counted as two FLOPs per lane. For a runtime $t$ seconds,
$$ \text{GFLOP/s}=\frac{2MNK}{10^9t}. $$
This convention slightly overcounts the first addition into zero but makes implementations and hardware peaks comparable. It must be stated; “operations” is otherwise ambiguous.
 #Change the Loop OrderThe literal i-j-p loop reads a row of A sequentially but walks down a column of row-major B with stride ldb. Transposing B makes both dot-product operands sequential, at the cost of allocation, copying, and a horizontal SIMD reduction.
There is another option. Exchange the inner loops:
zero C for i in [0, M) for p in [0, K) alpha = A[i,p] for j in [0, N) C[i,j] += alpha * B[p,j] Now the inner loop streams through rows of B and C. It is a scaled row addition: broadcast one value from A, multiply a vector from B, and accumulate it into C. There is no horizontal reduction, and the compiler sees a straightforward vector loop when the non-aliasing contract is available.
This order reuses one A element across an entire row, but it repeatedly visits C and rereads B for every row of A. Cache blocking will address both problems.
 #A Real AVX2/FMA Row KernelFirst isolate the vectorizable inner operation. This implementation uses unaligned loads and stores and has a scalar tail, so neither addresses nor lengths need special treatment.
#include <cmath>#include <cstddef>#include <immintrin.h> void add_scaled_row_avx2(float *output, const float *input, float alpha, std::size_t length) { const __m256 scale = _mm256_set1_ps(alpha); std::size_t j = 0; for (; length - j >= 8; j += 8) { const __m256 x = _mm256_loadu_ps(input + j); const __m256 y = _mm256_loadu_ps(output + j); const __m256 result = _mm256_fmadd_ps(scale, x, y); _mm256_storeu_ps(output + j, result); } for (; j < length; ++j) output[j] = std::fma(alpha, input[j], output[j]); } Compile this function for AVX2 and FMA—for example with a dedicated target attribute or a translation unit built with -mavx2 -mfma—and dispatch to it only after checking processor support. AVX2 does not itself imply FMA in a runtime feature test.
An aligned packed path may replace loadu with load, but only when every row start and panel offset satisfies the instruction’s alignment. Padding the total allocation is not enough if the row stride destroys alignment on the next row.
 #Cache Blocking with Complete TailsPartition the output into row and column panels and the reduction dimension into depth panels. The logical computation becomes
$$ C_{I,J}\mathrel{+}=A_{I,P}B_{P,J} $$
for every triple of panels. If the active pieces of A, B, and C fit appropriate cache levels, values loaded for one update can serve many nearby updates before eviction.
The following macro-kernel calls the real AVX2 row kernel. The block sizes are parameters rather than alleged universal constants, and min-style tails are written without overflowing base + block.
#include <algorithm>#include <cstddef>#include <span>#include <stdexcept> void matmul_blocked_avx2(std::span<const float> a, std::span<const float> b, std::span<float> c, std::size_t m, std::size_t k, std::size_t n, std::size_t lda, std::size_t ldb, std::size_t ldc, std::size_t row_block = 48, std::size_t depth_block = 128, std::size_t column_block = 128) { require_matrix(a.size(), m, k, lda); require_matrix(b.size(), k, n, ldb); require_matrix(c.size(), m, n, ldc); if (row_block == 0 || depth_block == 0 || column_block == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("matrix block size must be positive"); if (m == 0 || n == 0) return; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < m; ++i) std::fill_n(c.data() + i * ldc, n, 0.0f); for (std::size_t ii = 0; ii < m;) { const std::size_t i_end = ii + std::min(row_block, m - ii); for (std::size_t jj = 0; jj < n;) { const std::size_t j_end = jj + std::min(column_block, n - jj); for (std::size_t pp = 0; pp < k;) { const std::size_t p_end = pp + std::min(depth_block, k - pp); for (std::size_t i = ii; i < i_end; ++i) { for (std::size_t p = pp; p < p_end; ++p) { add_scaled_row_avx2( c.data() + i * ldc + jj, b.data() + p * ldb + jj, a[i * lda + p], j_end - jj); } } pp = p_end; } jj = j_end; } ii = i_end; } } Every logical index remains within the extents validated at entry. j_end - jj may be any positive length, so the last column panel and its final SIMD vector are both safe. The block loops advance to their computed ends, which avoids unsigned overflow from blindly adding a fixed step near SIZE_MAX.
This is a robust teaching kernel, not yet a BLAS microkernel. It broadcasts one A value and updates one row at a time, leaving register reuse across output rows to the cache rather than exploiting it explicitly.
 #Register BlockingTo reuse B in registers, compute several rows of C at once. A $6\times16$ AVX2 microkernel keeps twelve 8-float accumulators:
initialize c00 ... c51 to zero for p in the packed depth panel b0 = load 8 values of B[p, j:j+8] b1 = load 8 values of B[p, j+8:j+16] for each of 6 output rows r ar = broadcast A[i+r, p] cr0 = fma(ar, b0, cr0) cr1 = fma(ar, b1, cr1) store the twelve accumulators One pair of B loads feeds twelve vector FMAs, and the independent accumulators hide FMA latency. The tile size is architecture-specific: vector width, register count, FMA latency and throughput, load ports, and address-generation capacity all influence it. A 6-by-16 choice suitable for one AVX2 core is not a law for AVX-512, Arm SVE, or even another AVX2 microarchitecture.
Full tiles take the hot path. Bottom and right edges need separate smaller kernels, masked operations where available, or zero-padded packed panels. Calling the full kernel on a partial tile and “copying only the valid answer” is still an out-of-bounds read unless the inputs were genuinely padded.
 #Packing PanelsBlocking promises reuse only if cache layout cooperates. BLAS-style implementations usually pack panels into contiguous temporary buffers:
 padding makes microkernel dimensions exact and gives tails defined zero values; fixed strides remove address arithmetic from the hot loop; controlled alignment enables aligned vector accesses; compact panels avoid conflict patterns caused by unfortunate original strides; the same packed B panel is reused by many A row panels.  Packing has a cost, so its loop order matters. Pack a panel once, use it many times, and amortize the copy. Tiny matrices may finish faster with the direct kernel because there is not enough reuse to repay packing.
Use RAII-owned buffers and check allocation failure. If using std::aligned_alloc, remember that the requested byte count must be a multiple of the alignment; rounding the row width does not necessarily round the whole allocation. Initialize padded elements before a microkernel reads them.
Kazushige Goto and Robert van de Geijn’s anatomy of high-performance matrix multiplication develops this packed macro-kernel/microkernel organization in detail.
 #FMA and Numerical Results_mm256_fmadd_ps(a, b, c) computes $ab+c$ with one rounding instead of rounding the product and sum separately. That is usually more accurate, but it can differ in the last bits from scalar multiply followed by add. Blocking and register tiling may also change the order in which partial sums are combined.
Floating-point addition is not associative:
$$ (x+y)+z\ne x+(y+z) $$
in general. Consequently, two correct matrix kernels need not be bitwise identical. Compare the optimized binary32 result with the wider reference using a documented absolute and relative tolerance, preferably also a normwise error. Include cancellation-heavy matrices, very small and very large magnitudes, zeros, and the application’s policy for infinities and NaNs.
The flag -ffast-math does much more than permit FMA: it allows reassociation and weakens behavior around NaNs, infinities, signed zero, and the floating-point environment. Use it only if those semantic changes are part of the contract. Explicit FMA intrinsics do not require granting all of them.
 #Historical Benchmark, RecountedThe original experiment recorded an $N=1920$ square multiplication compiled with GCC 13 on a 2 GHz Zen 2 system. Its embedded log survives, although the harness does not preserve enough information about thread pinning, BLAS configuration, repetitions, or uncertainty for a modern comparison.
The old plots counted one multiply-add as one “useful operation.” The table below keeps the recorded times but recomputes throughput with the conventional $2N^3/t$ definition:
   archived variant time (s) conventional GFLOP/s     baseline triple loop 13.586 1.042   huge-page experiment 16.750 0.845   transposed B 12.377 1.144   auto-vectorized 3.117 4.541   explicit vectors 3.076 4.602   6-by-16 kernel 2.243 6.312   cache blocked 0.461 30.675   allocation removed 0.408 34.693   copying/padding removed 0.304 46.592   archived BLAS run 0.275 51.495    Under the page’s stated assumption of two 256-bit FMA instructions per cycle, a 2 GHz core has a conventional binary32 peak of
$$ 8\ \text{lanes}\times2\ \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{FMA lane}} \times2\ \frac{\text{instructions}}{\text{cycle}} \times2\cdot10^9\ \frac{\text{cycles}}{\text{s}} =64\ \text{GFLOP/s}. $$
The original 32-GFLOP/s figure used the same one-operation-per-FMA convention as its plots. Correcting the arithmetic preserves the ratios: the last custom experiment was about 90% of the archived BLAS result and about 73% of the assumed peak. It does not turn the old, multiples-of-48-only kernel into a portable BLAS replacement, nor establish a record across processors or libraries.
AMD’s Software Optimization Guide for Family 17h Processors is the primary architecture reference for validating assumptions on that processor family; measured clocks and instruction throughput still belong in the benchmark record.
 #Benchmarking and ValidationValidate before timing. For many small rectangular shapes, compare the blocked kernel against the wider reference using random strides and padding. Include:
 every dimension from zero through the SIMD width; dimensions just below and above each block size; tall, wide, and thin matrices—not just squares; unaligned span offsets and padded leading dimensions; $K=0$, identity matrices, zero matrices, and one-hot rows; small integral floats, for which exact expected answers are easy; random and cancellation-heavy floating-point inputs.  Fill padding with sentinels and verify it remains unchanged. Run with address and undefined-behavior sanitizers. Compare all $M\times N$ logical outputs, not a checksum alone; retain a checksum only in the timed harness to prevent dead-code elimination.
For performance, report $M$, $K$, $N$, all three strides, transpose flags, scalar type, thread count, affinity, compiler flags, library build, warm-up policy, and whether packing or allocation is timed. Sweep shapes and sizes. A square $1920\times1920$ benchmark says little about a neural-network layer shaped $1\times4096$ by $4096\times11008$.
Use a tuned BLAS library as the end-to-end baseline. Its sgemm interface also supports scaling and accumulation,
$$ C\leftarrow\alpha AB+\beta C, $$
plus transposed operands. The simpler overwrite-only function in this chapter corresponds to $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0$.
Matrix multiplication is a model case because the final inner loop is almost comically small. The hard work is arranging that loop’s operands: dimensions make them meaningful, strides make them reachable, packing makes them regular, blocking makes them resident, and register tiling makes them reusable. SIMD is the last multiplication sign, not the first idea.
 #Further Reading Goto and van de Geijn, Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication. The reference BLAS defines the conventional matrix interfaces used for comparison. AMD’s Family 17h Software Optimization Guide documents the relevant cache and execution architecture. The floating-point error and cache blocking chapters cover the numerical and memory models used here.
title: Matrix Multiplication

content:
Optimization is the process of discovering which constraint is active and changing the program so that a different constraint becomes active. That is why isolated tricks age badly and models age well.
A loop can be slow because it performs unnecessary work, waits on one dependency chain, misses in cache, exceeds memory bandwidth, feeds an unpredictable branch, saturates an execution port, or simply never appears in the program’s profile. Each cause suggests a different transformation. Applying all transformations indiscriminately produces complicated code that is still limited by the original bottleneck.
This chapter condenses Part I into a repeatable investigation.
 #1. Define the Program You Are OptimizingWrite down the workload before timing it:
 What inputs occur in production, including empty, tiny, adversarial, and malformed cases? Which output differences are acceptable: none, a floating-point tolerance, or a probabilistic error rate? Is the objective throughput, median latency, tail latency, startup time, memory use, energy, or cost? Which processors, operating systems, and compiler targets must the binary support?  These choices are algorithmic constraints. -ffast-math is not an optimization for a program that requires IEEE exception behavior; reading past the end of an array is not an optimization for an interface that does not provide padding; -march=native is not a deployment strategy for a binary distributed to unknown machines.
Keep a simple reference implementation. Test the optimized version against it on boundary cases and randomized inputs. The faster the code becomes, the more valuable an independent definition of “correct” becomes.
 #2. Establish a Reproducible BaselineBuild an optimized binary with debug information and the actual deployment configuration. Record the compiler version, flags, processor, input generator, and benchmark command.
Measure enough work that timer overhead is negligible, but preserve the workload’s intended state. A warmed cache measures steady state; a cold cache measures something else. Neither is inherently more honest.
Inspect variation before comparing means. Randomize or interleave competing implementations, collect independent batches where possible, and report the statistic that matches the objective. The probability and measurement appendix develops the underlying assumptions.
 #3. Find the Expensive RegionUse instrumentation and sampling to identify where time is spent. Start at the program level: eliminating a function that consumes 20% of the run is more promising than halving an instruction that consumes 0.2%.
Then narrow the question. Hardware counters, annotated assembly, and machine-code analyzers can distinguish several broad limits:
 front-end stalls or excessive instruction count; a long dependency chain; execution-port pressure; branch mispredictions; cache or TLB misses; exhausted memory bandwidth; system calls, allocation, synchronization, or I/O outside the kernel.  Counters are evidence, not diagnoses. A cache-miss count matters only after relating misses to bytes, latency, overlap, and elapsed time. A model should predict the direction and rough size of the change you are about to make.
 #4. Remove Work Before Accelerating ItThe largest speedups usually come from changing what is computed.
Use an appropriate algorithm and data structure for the actual input range. Precompute values that are reused. Hoist loop-invariant work. Replace repeated parsing, allocation, hashing, or virtual dispatch with a representation that performs it once. Batch transitions across expensive boundaries such as system calls and storage requests.
Asymptotic complexity still belongs at the top of the checklist. Performance engineering extends algorithm analysis; it does not excuse skipping it.
 #5. Choose a Hardware-Friendly RepresentationRepresentation determines which operations become cheap.
 Fixed-point reciprocals turn division by reused constants into multiplication. Montgomery space turns modular reduction by an odd modulus into low-word cancellation and a shift. Bitmaps replace pointer-heavy sets over dense universes with word operations. Structure-of-arrays layouts let scans load only the fields they use; array-of-structures layouts keep fields of one object together. Flat and blocked trees exchange pointer chasing for predictable cache-line access.  This is often the bridge between an algorithmic idea and an instruction-level speedup. SIMD works well after data has been arranged into homogeneous lanes, not before.
 #6. Make Memory Access DeliberateCount bytes as well as operations. When a kernel is bandwidth-bound, deleting arithmetic may have no measurable effect.
Prefer sequential traversal and compact data. Block computations so reused working sets fit a useful cache level. Separate hot fields from cold fields. Avoid storing materialized intermediates when producing and consuming them in one pass is possible.
For latency-bound pointer chains, seek independent requests that create memory-level parallelism, or replace pointers with indices and packed layouts. Software prefetching is a last-mile technique for a stable access pattern the hardware cannot learn; it spends instructions and bandwidth and must be scheduled far enough ahead without reading invalid addresses.
External-memory algorithms apply the same principle at a larger block size: sort and scan runs, batch random requests, and use branching factors matched to transfer blocks.
 #7. Expose Independent WorkAn out-of-order core overlaps instructions only when dependencies allow it. If every iteration waits for the preceding result, the reciprocal throughput of an instruction is irrelevant; latency sets the pace.
Break artificial dependencies, use multiple accumulators for associative reductions, and unroll enough to expose independent operations. Stop when code size, register pressure, or memory traffic becomes the new limit. Consult instruction tables and inspect the emitted machine code rather than counting source operators.
Branches are dependencies on control. Keep predictable branches: they are cheap and often clearer. For genuinely unpredictable conditions, consider conditional moves, masks, lookup tables, or partitioning the data—but compare the extra work against the cost of a misprediction. Branchless code is not automatically faster and may perform operations that the branch would have skipped.
 #8. Vectorize the Right LoopSIMD requires the same operation across independent lanes. Before reaching for intrinsics:
 make the loop bounds and aliasing contract visible to the compiler; use a contiguous layout and remove loop-carried dependencies; check the vectorization report and generated assembly; handle tails and alignment explicitly; write intrinsics only when the compiler still lacks information or the algorithm itself must change.  Vector width does not guarantee proportional speedup. Loads, stores, shuffles, conversions, frequency behavior, and horizontal reductions remain. Multi-version a binary or choose a conservative target when the deployment population is heterogeneous.
 #9. Transform Arithmetic with Contracts AttachedStrength reduction is powerful precisely because arithmetic operations have unequal costs. It is also a common source of silent errors.
State ranges before changing integer arithmetic. Prove that intermediate values do not overflow—or use unsigned wraparound when modulo-$2^w$ arithmetic is intentionally required. Handle zero before calling count-trailing-zero intrinsics. Remember that signed division rounds toward zero and signed overflow is undefined in C++.
For floating point, decide which identities the application permits. Reassociation changes rounding; reciprocal approximations change error; flushing subnormals changes tiny values; fused multiply-add rounds once rather than twice. Measure numerical error alongside running time.
 #10. Re-measure and SimplifyAfter each material change:
 rerun correctness tests and sanitizers where applicable; inspect the new profile to confirm the intended bottleneck moved; benchmark on representative machines and input distributions; remove changes that do not earn their complexity; document preconditions and the evidence that justified the remaining ones.  Optimization ends when the objective is met, not when every loop contains an intrinsic. The best final implementation often has a portable baseline, one or two carefully chosen specialized kernels, and a dispatch boundary that keeps the rest of the system ordinary.
 #The Short VersionIf only one page survives, keep this sequence:
 Specify correctness, workload, machine population, and metric. Preserve a reference implementation and representative tests. Build and measure the real program. Profile to locate the limiting region and resource. Remove unnecessary work and choose a better representation. Improve locality and expose independent operations. Vectorize or specialize only where the model predicts a gain. Re-test, re-measure, and write down the assumptions.  The craft is not knowing a long list of tricks. It is being able to explain, before and after a change, where each cycle and byte had to go.
title: A Performance Engineering Checklist

content:
Performance measurements vary. Interrupts arrive, addresses change, predictors learn, caches retain history, and the processor changes frequency. Probability is what lets us separate a repeatable effect from this background variation—and what lets randomized algorithms make useful promises without predicting every run.
This appendix develops the small part of probability and statistics used throughout the book. It is not a substitute for experimental design, but it should make the assumptions behind an average, an error bar, or a “with high probability” claim visible.
 #Probability Spaces and Random VariablesA random experiment has a sample space $\Omega$ of possible outcomes. An event is a subset of $\Omega$, and a probability measure $P$ assigns events numbers between zero and one, with $P(\Omega)=1$ and additive probabilities for disjoint events.
A random variable is a function from outcomes to values. A die roll, for example, may have $\Omega={1,2,3,4,5,6}$ and $X(\omega)=\omega$. For a fair die,
$$ P(X=k)=\frac16. $$
An indicator $I_A$ for an event $A$ is a random variable equal to one when $A$ occurs and zero otherwise. Indicators are a simple bridge between logic and arithmetic.
For a discrete random variable, its probability mass function lists $P(X=x)$. A continuous variable instead has a density $f$ whose integral gives interval probabilities:
$$ P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x),dx. $$
The probability of any exact real value can be zero even though some value must be observed. Densities are not probabilities at a point; they are probabilities per unit of the horizontal axis.
 #Conditional ProbabilityWhen $P(B)>0$, the probability of $A$ after learning that $B$ occurred is
$$ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}. $$
Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, equivalently when learning one does not change the probability of the other.
When $P(A)>0$ as well, writing the same intersection in the other order gives Bayes’ rule:
$$ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}. $$
The factor $P(A)$ is the prior. Ignoring it causes the base-rate fallacy. If a rare hardware fault triggers a detector, the probability that the fault actually occurred depends not only on the detector’s accuracy but also on how rare the fault was before the alert.
 #ExpectationThe expected value of a discrete random variable is its probability-weighted average:
$$ \operatorname E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x). $$
For a fair six-sided die it is $3.5$. No roll produces 3.5; expectation describes the long-run average, not a required outcome.
Expectation is linear:
$$ \operatorname E[aX+bY]=a\operatorname E[X]+b\operatorname E[Y]. $$
This identity does not require independence. That makes indicator variables unusually effective: if
$$ X=\sum_i I_i, $$
then
$$ \operatorname E[X]=\sum_i P(I_i=1), $$
even when the events strongly affect one another.
 #Fixed Points of a PermutationChoose a permutation of $n$ elements uniformly and let $I_i$ indicate that position $i$ contains element $i$. Each element is equally likely to occupy each position, so $P(I_i=1)=1/n$. The number of fixed points is $X=\sum_i I_i$, and
$$ \operatorname E[X] =\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname E[I_i] =n\cdot\frac1n =1. $$
The indicators are not independent, but linearity makes that irrelevant.
 #Expected Comparisons in QuicksortAssume all keys are distinct and the pivot is chosen uniformly in every recursive subarray. Index the keys by sorted order. Keys $i<j$ are compared exactly when the first pivot selected from
$$ i,i+1,\ldots,j $$
is one of the two endpoints. Therefore,
$$ P(i\text{ is compared with }j)=\frac{2}{j-i+1}. $$
Summing the indicators for all pairs gives
$$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname E[C] &=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\frac{2}{j-i+1}\ &=2(n+1)H_n-4n\ &=\Theta(n\log n), \end{aligned} $$
where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number. This is a complete expected-time argument; saying that the pivot is “in the middle on average” is not, because unbalanced recursive costs are nonlinear.
 #Variance and CovarianceExpectation locates a distribution. Variance measures its squared spread:
$$ \operatorname{Var}(X) =\operatorname E[(X-\operatorname E[X])^2] =\operatorname E[X^2]-\operatorname E[X]^2. $$
Its square root, the standard deviation $\sigma$, has the same units as $X$. For a constant $a$,
$$ \operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X). $$
The covariance
$$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) =\operatorname E[(X-\operatorname E[X])(Y-\operatorname E[Y])] $$
controls the variance of a sum:
$$ \operatorname{Var}(X+Y) =\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y) +2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). $$
Independent variables have zero covariance, although the converse is not generally true.
For $n$ independent, identically distributed observations with variance $\sigma^2$, the sample mean
$$ \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i $$
has variance
$$ \operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}. $$
Its standard deviation—the standard error of the mean—shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. Getting one extra decimal digit from repetition alone is expensive: it requires roughly one hundred times as many independent samples.
 #Computing Variance StablyThe formula $E[X^2]-E[X]^2$ can lose most of its precision when the mean is large and the variation is small. Welford’s recurrence updates centered sums without subtracting two nearly equal large numbers:
#include <cstddef> struct RunningStats { std::size_t n = 0; long double mean = 0; long double m2 = 0; void add(long double x) { ++n; long double delta = x - mean; mean += delta / n; m2 += delta * (x - mean); } long double sample_variance() const { // Precondition: n >= 2.  return m2 / (n - 1); } }; The denominator $n-1$ estimates the population variance from a sample. If the collected values are the entire population of interest rather than a sample, divide by $n$ instead.
 #Concentration BoundsAn expectation does not say how often a variable is close to it. Concentration inequalities turn moments or range bounds into probability statements.
 #Markov and ChebyshevFor a nonnegative random variable $X$ and $a>0$, Markov’s inequality states
$$ P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname E[X]}a. $$
It follows from $aI_{X\ge a}\le X$ by taking expectations.
Applying Markov to $(X-\mu)^2$ gives Chebyshev’s inequality:
$$ P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le\frac1{k^2}. $$
These bounds need very few assumptions and are correspondingly loose. They are useful for proofs that must hold for arbitrary distributions, not usually for tight benchmark error bars.
 #Hoeffding’s InequalityIf $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and each lies in $[0,1]$, then
$$ P(|\bar X-\operatorname E[\bar X]|\ge\varepsilon) \le2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}. $$
To make this probability at most $\delta$, it is enough to take
$$ n\ge\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}. $$
The assumptions matter. Reusing correlated pseudo-samples or stopping an experiment as soon as the desired result appears invalidates the calculation.
