 #The Birthday ThresholdHashing repeatedly asks how many random values fit into $m$ buckets before a collision becomes likely. For $n\le m$ independent uniform choices, the probability of no collision is
$$ P(\text{no collision}) =\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{m}\right). $$
When $n$ is small relative to $m$, using $\ln(1-x)\approx-x$ gives
$$ P(\text{no collision}) \approx \exp\left(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}\right). $$
The transition therefore occurs around $n=\Theta(\sqrt m)$, not around $m$. With a 64-bit uniformly random hash, roughly $2^{32}$ values already put collisions on a constant-probability scale.
Linearity of expectation gives the expected number of colliding pairs,
$$ \operatorname E[C]=\binom n2\frac1m, $$
and Markov proves that the collision probability tends to zero when $n^2/m\to0$. Proving that it tends to one in the opposite regime needs the exact product, a second-moment argument, or another lower bound; expectation alone cannot provide both directions.
 #Monte Carlo and Las Vegas AlgorithmsSuppose a shape covers an unknown fraction $p$ of a unit square. Sample points uniformly and let $I_i$ indicate whether point $i$ is covered. The estimator
$$ \hat p=\frac1n\sum_i I_i $$
is unbiased: $E[\hat p]=p$. A Bernoulli variable has variance
$$ p(1-p)\le\frac14, $$
so the estimator’s standard deviation is at most $1/(2\sqrt n)$. Hoeffding gives a distribution-free finite-sample guarantee: $n\ge\ln(2/\delta)/(2\varepsilon^2)$ ensures absolute error below $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
An algorithm that has a bounded running time but may return an approximate or occasionally wrong answer is usually called Monte Carlo. An algorithm that always returns a correct answer but has random running time is Las Vegas. Random-pivot quicksort is Las Vegas: pivot choices change the work, not the sorted result.
 #From Samples to Error BarsLet $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be independent observations from a stable distribution with mean $\mu$ and finite variance. For sufficiently regular data, the central limit theorem makes the standardized sample mean approximately normal as $n$ grows. When the variance is estimated from the same sample, a common interval is
$$ \bar x;\pm;t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}, $$
where $s$ is the sample standard deviation and $t$ is a Student-$t$ quantile. Under the model assumptions, repeating the complete experiment many times would make a fraction $1-\alpha$ of such intervals cover $\mu$.
This is a confidence interval, not a probability distribution over the already-fixed parameter. It also says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter.
Latency distributions are often skewed or heavy-tailed. In that case, report the quantity the user experiences:
 a mean for total throughput or expected cost; a median for a typical request; high quantiles for tail-latency objectives; a full histogram or empirical distribution when one number conceals important modes.  Bootstrap intervals can estimate uncertainty for medians and other statistics, but resampling individual observations still assumes those observations are exchangeable. It cannot repair a confounded experiment.
 #Designing Performance ExperimentsThe largest benchmark errors are usually systematic, not statistical. A million repetitions do not fix measuring the wrong workload. A defensible comparison should address the following points.
Choose an experimental unit. Timing every iteration inside one process does not necessarily produce independent samples; those iterations share frequency, cache, predictor, and allocator state. Often the independent unit is a complete randomized batch or a fresh process.
Pair competing implementations. Run A and B under nearby conditions with the same generated input, randomize or alternate their order, and analyze paired differences or log-ratios. Independent “all A, then all B” runs can mistake thermal drift for a speedup.
Separate warm-up from the workload. Warm-up may be appropriate for steady-state service code and wrong for startup latency. State which regime is being measured instead of automatically discarding inconvenient samples.
Predeclare the statistic and stopping rule. Repeatedly checking significance and stopping at the first favorable result inflates false-positive rates. Looking at twenty variants and reporting only the best does the same unless the comparison accounts for selection.
Report effect size and uncertainty. “Statistically significant” can describe a useless 0.1% change after enough repetitions. A speedup with an interval, workload, and machine description is more informative than a bare $p$-value.
Keep correctness in the experiment. Compare outputs against a reference over the benchmark’s actual input distribution. An implementation that silently assumes alignment, nonempty input, or absent overflow is a different program unless those conditions are part of the contract.
Good statistics cannot manufacture reproducibility, but they make uncertainty explicit. The practical rule is simple: randomize what you cannot control, pair what you can compare, preserve raw observations, and make every probability statement name its assumptions.
 #Further Reading The NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods is a practical reference for estimation and experimental design. Peter McCullagh’s What Is a Statistical Model? is a useful reminder that an error bar belongs to a model, not to a dataset by itself. Georges et al., Statistically Rigorous Java Performance Evaluation, discusses many benchmarking pitfalls that apply beyond managed runtimes.
title: Probability and Measurement

content:
An algorithm does not run on the RAM model. It runs through a compiler, an instruction set, a speculative out-of-order core, several caches, a virtual-memory system, and whatever operating system happened to schedule it. Asymptotic analysis deliberately hides these details; performance engineering begins when the hidden constants become the problem.
This book studies the boundary between algorithms and modern hardware. The first part is about one CPU thread: how to measure it, reason about it, and reshape an algorithm so that the core can execute more useful work in parallel. The recurring subjects are instruction-level parallelism, arithmetic, memory locality, and SIMD. The final chapters put these ideas back together in complete algorithms and data structures.
The goal is not to replace asymptotic complexity. A linear algorithm still loses to a logarithmic one eventually, and no arrangement of intrinsics rescues a fundamentally unsuitable data structure. The goal is to add the missing levels of the model: the input sizes we actually process, the work each operation expands into, and the paths that data follows through the machine.
 #PrerequisitesThe intended reader is comfortable with elementary algorithms and data structures and can read C or C++. Familiarity with calculus, probability, and modular arithmetic is helpful in a few chapters; the required ideas are introduced where they are used.
No prior assembly or computer-architecture course is required. The architecture chapters build a working model from the instruction-set boundary upward. It is intentionally a programmer’s model: detailed enough to predict many performance effects, but not a substitute for a processor-design text or a vendor manual.
Most examples use C++ on x86-64 with GCC or Clang. These choices make the generated machine code easy to inspect and give us mature SIMD intrinsics and profiling tools. The principles transfer to other compiled languages and architectures, but instruction availability, ABI rules, cache geometry, and compiler behavior do not. Platform-specific examples say which assumptions they need.
 #How to Read This PartThe chapters form three broad layers.
Foundations, Chapters 1–5. Complexity models explain why elapsed time cannot be inferred from operation counts alone. Computer architecture follows a program from source-level control flow to instructions and operating-system interaction. Instruction-level parallelism develops the core model of latency, throughput, dependencies, and speculation. Compilation and profiling show how to inspect what actually happened.
Mechanisms, Chapters 6–10. Arithmetic and number theory derive transformations that replace expensive operations or change their representation. External memory and CPU caches study locality at two scales. SIMD turns data-parallel work into explicit vector operations.
Case studies, Chapters 11–12. The algorithm and data-structure chapters start from correct baselines and optimize complete workloads. They are not a bag of independent tricks. Each one combines several earlier ideas and makes their interactions visible.
Reading in order gives the cleanest dependency graph, but it is not mandatory. A reader who already knows assembly can start with instruction-level parallelism. Someone with a concrete vectorization problem can read the SIMD chapter first and follow its links backward. The case studies are most useful after the relevant mechanism chapters, because copying optimized code without its preconditions is an efficient way to copy bugs.
 #The Experimental ContractPerformance is an empirical property of a complete program on a particular system. A benchmark result should therefore be read together with:
 the processor and its enabled instruction-set extensions; the compiler, version, flags, and relevant source code; the input distribution and size; the statistic being reported and the number of repetitions; the state that may affect the result, such as cache warmth, frequency scaling, allocation, and thread placement.  Historical measurements in the case studies are evidence for a mechanism on the named machine, not universal constants. The point of a “five times faster” result is the explanation that survives after the number does not. Re-run the benchmark on the target system before adopting an optimization.
Correctness comes first. Examples avoid undefined behavior where practical, document ranges that prevent overflow or overread, and separate exact transformations from approximations. Short fragments may omit application-level error handling, but omitted handling is not permission to omit it in production. Cryptographic examples in particular are educational mathematics, never a recommendation to implement security protocols from scratch.
 #A Useful Optimization LoopMost successful investigations follow the same cycle:
 Define the workload and verify a simple implementation. Measure enough of the whole program to locate the limiting resource. Form a hardware-level hypothesis: a dependency chain, branch misses, memory traffic, front-end pressure, or insufficient parallel work. Change one important thing and preserve a reference implementation for differential testing. Measure again, inspect the generated code when necessary, and keep the change only if the explanation and evidence agree.  Starting with source-level cleverness reverses this order. It often optimizes cold code, moves cost elsewhere, or exchanges a visible instruction for less visible memory traffic. A profiler is not an oracle, but it is a better opening move than guessing.
 #ScopePart I focuses on single-threaded CPU performance. Operating-system effects, shared caches, and storage appear where they affect one thread, but synchronization, multicore algorithms, GPUs, and distributed systems belong to later parts.
The book emphasizes transferable models rather than a catalog of current processors. Hardware and compilers evolve. Latencies, cache sizes, and favored instruction sequences will change; conservation laws are more durable. Work must enter through a finite front end, dependencies limit overlap, bytes must cross finite-bandwidth links, and representations determine which operations are cheap.
 #Code and ContributionsThe book source is hosted in the Algorithmica repository, and companion experiments live in the code repository. Examples in the text are kept small enough to explain; the companion programs provide benchmark scaffolding and historical context.
Corrections are welcome, especially when they include a minimal counterexample, a primary reference, or a reproducible measurement. Performance literature improves the same way performance code does: keep a trustworthy baseline, make a falsifiable claim, and test it where the claim is supposed to hold.
